en: Preface to the *Abstract of Eminent Monks*:

I have already published the *Guides to the Buddhas and Patriarchs* and the *Awakening the World from the Garden of Dharma*. These works contain detailed accounts of the direct transmission of the single mind, the spiritual responses between the realms of the living and the dead, and so forth.
However, the biographies of eminent monks are like the nature of space: while it is devoid of all manifold characteristics, it does not reject them.
The various characteristics of those [works] are fully manifested. The *Nai* (Nanhai) tradition includes both the *Zheng* (Original) and the *Xu* (Continuation).

Whether from the Liang or the Ming dynasties, they comprise four fascicles in total, all classified according to ten categories. I remarked in surprise: "To have both primary and secondary sources—how can you say it is peerless?
To be constrained by format and precedent—how can you claim it is solitary? I considered that, apart from not re-recording what has already been carved in previous volumes, I shall now stop here.
It is divided into four fascicles and titled *The Abstract*. First, regarding the excellence of taking the Way: Majestic and imposing, he sits and cuts off the myriad divergent paths;

standing out with clarity, he is utterly free from coming and going. Second, regarding the excellence of taking the Dharma: Though it is said to be dense and impenetrable to the wind, from antiquity to the present there has been no gap between them.
Third, regarding the excellence of his character: In every turn, he stands solitary and precarious amidst the ten thousand things.

Matters come to rest; having attained the ultimate meaning through following conditions, what more is there to seek? The myriad beings and the process of creation ride upon this power; a single segment of numinous light pervades every place it touches. These four principles take up the loftiness of its transformation:

where the sun and moon shine does not reach, and where heaven and earth cover and support do not adhere. When the kalpa-fire destroys all, it remains eternally at peace; when the ten thousand phenomena vanish, its entire body is revealed. Although it is thus, [The text continues: ...it is like a great ocean that can hold the heavens and earth, yet it does not leak a drop when poured into a hair’s breadth.

It is like a great mountain that can contain the sun and moon, yet it does not lose a grain of dust when struck by a speck of dust. It is like a great furnace that can melt the mountains and rivers, yet it does not suffer a single crack when struck by a hammer. It is like a great mirror that can reflect the heavens and earth, yet it does not lose a single reflection when struck by a blade of grass. Although it is thus, [the text continues].
Blue does not blue itself; yellow does not yellow itself; red does not red itself; white does not white itself.

Only when one realizes that the clouds have gathered and the moon is bright can one know that these things are both vertical and horizontal. If one asks whether there is sameness or difference within this, I would respond:

"When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it enters the water. For to read the scriptures, one must first possess the eyes for reading the scriptures; to see the ground, one must open the vision.

On the day of ascending the heights during the ninth month of the Jiawu year, the monk Xu Changzhi, a man of no reliance, respectfully inscribed this preface for his father Zhou. Upon the ground, how many people would conceive the notion of a rope upon seeing hemp? How much more so, then, to mistake a rope for a snake?
This is the narrative. [Seal] Respectfully inscribed by the monk Xu Changzhi on the day of ascending the heights in the ninth month of the Jiawu year. For his father, Zhou. Preface.
There is no biography for this eminent monk. To compose a biography of such an eminent monk is like attempting to paint empty space;

empty space is inherently devoid of all characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those very characteristics. This is how the layman Jinweng described his own origins. There are many editions of this collection:
the "Sengbao" (Treasures of the Sangha) of Shimen, the "Shenseng" (Divine Monks) of the Tripitaka, and the "Wu... of Jichuan.
Regarding the *Deng* (Lamp) and *Lei'an zhi pudeng* (Universal Lamp of Thunder Hermitage), each adheres to its own particular view to establish the doctrine of its own school.

Those who read these works have no means by which to determine their right or wrong. This is because the former masters’ selection of analogies was refined and detailed, while their formulation of principles was singular and correct.
Only through such refinement and singularity is the way of composing a book fully realized. [Thus it was with] Qin’gong for a long time...

Traversing the realms of the Dharma, his patriarchal eye was luminously clear, penetratingly seeing that the ancients' "reaching down of the hand" resides within a single transmission which is categorized into four:
namely, the Way (Dao), the Dharma, the Categories (Pin), and Transformation (Hua). These are distinct without being confused and specialized without being intermingled;

yet some attempt to measure them with their own private conceptions, which is utterly contrary to the Venerable One’s intent in making such distinctions and establishing these gradations. I— (Note: The final character "予" (I) indicates the author's signature or conclusion.)

This refers to those who compile the history of the Sangha. It is like a *maṇi* jewel that has been transformed; one cannot seek it by means of blue, yellow, red, or white, nor can one seek it externally through blue, yellow, or white.
When Confucius edited the *Shi* and established the *Li*, he compiled them each into separate books to facilitate later students;
scholars followed these works as their models, and they became sacred classics for all eternity. Only Master Jin was able to embody this intention.
He has freely wielded his pen to bestow his compassion; his merit is no less than that of Mount Ni.

Those who peer upon this venerable elder with the narrow vision of a tube not only fail to recognize the venerable elder, but they likewise fail to recognize a high monk. Among them, some may offer these words:
"From antiquity to the present, such a long duration has passed. Such profound spiritual transformations and mystical awakenings have been so numerous. The ocean of Dharma and its waves of meaning—"
This profound expanse—yet those who have composed treatises to record its events are as numerous as these.
To wish, in the end, to encompass all its subtle mysteries within a mere few hundred sheets—is this not to show people a narrow and limited perspective? Jingweng said:
"I merely select and extract its essential points."
Compiled by the Monk Jian at the Zhaochen Hall in Guli. The Way of the Venerable Ones is lofty;
their majestic appearance illuminates the myriad phenomena, worthy of contemplation and emulation.

Serving as mirrors and tortoises for the world, their illustrious names remain undiminished through a thousand and ten hundred generations. Thus, the One Way shares a common wind. Shi Shemoteng was originally a native of Central India. He was well-versed in the sutras of both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions and made it his constant practice to travel for the purpose of conversion.
Previously, while traveling through a small tributary state of India, he preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. At that time, a hostile nation invaded the borders.
Shemoteng remarked alone, "The sutra says that those who can expound this Dharma are protected by earth deities, which causes their dwelling place to be peaceful and happy. Now, [the enemy]..."

When the arrow-tip first struck, was it not for the sake of benefit? He then vowed to forget his own life and went in person to mediate and persuade them, ultimately bringing the two nations into harmony and joy;
thus he gained a distinguished reputation. Reaching the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, Emperor Ming dreamed one night of a golden man flying through the air and arriving.
He then assembled his ministers in great numbers to interpret the dream. The learned official Chen Fan Yi offered this reply: "Your servant has heard that in the West..."
The realm has a deity whose name is Buddha. That which Your Majesty dreamed must surely be this.

The Emperor agreed with this and immediately dispatched Cai Yin, a Court Physician, along with Qin Jing, a student of the Imperial Academy, and others as envoys to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma.
Kāṅ and his companions encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga there and invited him to return to the land of Han.

Mātanga vowed to propagate the teachings and, undaunted by weariness or hardship, braved the shifting sands to reach Luoyang. Emperor Ming received him with great honor and provided a vihāra outside the West Gate of the city for him to reside in;
this was the beginning of the presence of śramaṇas in the land of Han.
Shi Daochong’s surname was Zhang, and his secular name was Bin. During the transition between the Northern Qi and the Northern Wei, he was a great Confucian scholar at the National Academy.
Among those such as Yuan Xiansheng, who were esteemed throughout the realm, there were Li Fan, Zhang Bin, Qi Qiao, and An Xi;

wherever their talents were directed, all turned to him as their master. Later, they all relied upon An [Fashou] as their disciples. When Daochong reached maturity, he led over a thousand followers to Zhao.
In Yuanshi County of the prefecture, by the side of Yijiao Temple, he asked for water from the temple. A novice monk brought it to him;

when [the guest] asked how many particles of dust there were before it could be drunk, the novice—who had never previously engaged in such internal matters—was at a loss and could not answer. He then splashed the water on his own face, whereupon the guest was deeply ashamed.
He said to his followers, "It is not that I am disgraced by this water; rather, it is to manifest that the Buddha-dharma is inconceivable.

I shall now entrust my heart to this Way; you should each disperse. He then left home at the monastery. Being intelligent and broad-minded, he was fully ordained. He subsequently entered the Western Mountains to extensively seek out the various scriptural collections (*piṭakas*).
His spiritual faculties were profound and outstanding, and he sighed with regret that he had come to know [the truth] so late. Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei dynasty held the Buddha in high esteem.

Regarding the *Dharmapada*: when the Indian Brahman monk Bodhiruci first translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* at Ziji Dian and Ratnamati at Taiji Dian, each was provided with a guard detail, and communication between them was prohibited.
This was done to ensure that their respective exegeses were not subject to exaggeration or error.
The work began in the first year of the Yongping era and was only completed in the fourth year. Upon cross-referencing and collating the texts, it was found that they were indeed identical.

Regarding the two [versions], they were not identical. Nà (Narendrayaśas) said, "They are certainly not the same; there is a difference in a single character. Everyone was collectively amazed and praised this. Tǒng visited Narendrayaśas to inquire about the ultimate depths [of the doctrine].

Thereupon, [the Master] bestowed upon him the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and instructed him privately for three winters. Following what he had heard, Tǒng produced a commentary (*shù*), which immediately began to circulate and was studied widely.
His reputation soared with great breadth, and his excellence was highly esteemed throughout Yè. At that time, the civil officials and literary masters of the court were Wèi Shòu and Xíng Zǐcái.

Yang Xiuzhi and others once graced the imperial banquet and achieved success through their official studies. Since they had cast off the net of worldly affairs, neither form nor name remained for them to rely upon.
When they came together to listen [to the Dharma], the Emperor recognized their devotion in silence. Thereupon, they collectively cultivated the Three Great Vows and exhausted their single mind.

As sorrow and joy followed one another, the matter was subsequently reported to the throne. Because their virtue overflowed the times and their mission was destined, and because the principle lay in honoring excellence, the Emperor daily bestowed three *jin* of gold.
The two craftsmen became scholars and transmitted the Way to over a thousand people. Among them, the most eminent were Sengxiu, Faji, Dantali, Hanyi, and Ruguo.

Shi Baochang’s surname was Cen. He was a native of Wu Commandery. From his youth, he possessed a broad and quick intellect; though his primary occupation was farming, he supplemented his livelihood by seeking work as a copyist.
Even with a cursory glance at texts, he was able to memorize them with ease. At the age of eighteen, he entered the service of Vinaya Master Sengyou.

He then entered the monastic order. Regarding the study of the Sūtras and Vinaya, he was renowned for his lineage of disciples. Residing at Zhuangyan Temple, he extensively gathered the words of various masters and distilled their essential principles.

Furthermore, considering that the primary means to enlighten both the clergy and the laity is to prioritize universal utility and accessibility, he followed the retired scholar Gu Daokuang, Lü Sengzhi, and others to study and listen to the Classics, Histories, *Zhuangzi*, and the *Book of Changes*. This occurred during the final years of the Qi dynasty, when they were beset by turmoil.

He traveled eastward as far as Min and Yue to investigate his former studies. In the fourth year of the Tianjian era, he returned to the capital. Thereupon, the Emperor appointed him as the abbot of Xin’an Temple.

At that time, the heavens and earth were like gathering clouds and thunder, yet all was peaceful from near and far; the winds and rains were harmonious, and the hundred grains reached a bountiful harvest.

This was to provide superior support for the Triple Gem so that blessings might extend to the common people. The Emperor then issued an edict ordering [Huijiao] to chant and to compile and collect the records in their entirety.

These works were compiled according to the needs of the times: some for establishing merit and averting calamities, some for performing repentance rites to eliminate obstacles, some for making offerings to and receiving deities and spirits, and some for sacrificing to the Dragon Kings.

Categorized by their respective classes, they nearly comprise one hundred fascicles. The names of the deities of the Eight Divisions are contained in three fascicles, encompassing profound mysteries and detailing ancient and modern accounts with varying degrees of brevity and detail.
Consequently, all petitions and requests were personally reviewed by the Emperor. This was in the seventh year of the Tianjian era.

The Emperor, considering that the ocean of the Dharma is vast and profound and difficult for those of shallow understanding to explore, issued an edict to the monk Zengmin of Dinglin Upper Monastery to compile an essential digest of the various sutras in eighty-eight fascicles.
He further issued an edict to Zhizang of Kaishan Monastery to compile the *Liyi* (Exegesis of Principles) of the various sutras.

It was titled *Yilin* (Forest of Meanings) and consisted of eighty fascicles. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Senglang of the Jianyuan era annotated the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in seventy-two fascicles;
Baochang both recited and praised their merits, synthesizing them from beginning to end to complete the volumes.

When Emperor Jianwen was in the Chunfang (Palace of the Heir Apparent), he was particularly devoted to the Inner Teachings and compiled the *Fobao Lianbi* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure) in over two hundred fascicles, ordering Baochang to...

He compiled and categorized its various types, ranging from the detailed to the concise. Because the Buddha-dharma is profound and abstruse, making it difficult for those of limited understanding to penetrate, the Emperor further decreed that he should expound and systematically explain the principles and grand meanings of Buddhism;
this work was titled the *Xùfǎlún Lùn* (Treatise on the Continued Turning of the Dharma Wheel) and comprised over seventy fascicles in total.

Furthermore, he compiled the *Zhuanfaji* (Collection of Dharma Assemblies) in one hundred and thirty fascicles. Once the Emperor had personally inspected it, it was circulated both within and outside the palace.

In the fourteenth year [of the reign], an imperial decree was issued for the monk Sengshao of Anle Temple to compile a catalog of the scriptures in the Hualin Buddha Hall; however, this did not satisfy the Emperor’s wishes.

Consequently, an order was given to revise it once more, and Sengshao was subsequently appointed to oversee the Baoyun Scripture Repository in the Hualin Garden to search for lost and neglected texts, ultimately producing three volumes.

These were used for offerings to the Emperor. Furthermore, by imperial decree, he compiled the *Jīnglù yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) in fifty-five fascicles and the *Fàn shèngsēng fǎ* (Ritual for Feeding the Holy Sangha) in five fascicles.
The Emperor also annotated the *Dàpǐn jīng* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in fifty fascicles. At that time, the Buddhist teachings flourished to such an extent that they could not be fully described.
Since Emperor Wu responded to the destiny of his time at the age of thirty-seven, he has occupied the throne for forty-nine years.

Because his late Empress passed away early, he has constantly harbored a sense of sorrow and lamented, saying: "Though I possess the dignity of the Four Seas, there is no way to fully express my boundless grief.
Therefore, he has devoted himself to the Buddhist scriptures, taking the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* as the fertile field of his heart—the source from which all Buddhas arise.

Furthermore, he eliminated calamities and cleansed his karmic burdens, collecting and gathering various sutras, personally composing commentaries and annotations, and presiding over the Dharma seat to lecture, recite, and propagate the teachings.
By means of these roots of goodness, he elevated his spiritual consciousness; during two successive reigns, he sacrificed himself to serve as an attendant to the monks.
At every instance of almsgiving, the earth shook in response. He maintained a continuous succession of vegetarian feasts and lectures, never ceasing the turning of the Dharma wheel.

For Emperor Wen of the Taizu era, he established the Great Aijing Monastery at the Bamboo Ravine on Mount Zhongshan. Its construction was magnificent and ornate, appearing as if it were a celestial palace.

Enclosed by a surrounding wall, it housed more than a thousand monks who were provided with the four requisites. In the central courtyard’s main hall stood a sandalwood image, [standing] several... [feet tall].

It was eighteen *zhang* in height. Furthermore, within the temple, in the Longyuan (Dragon Abyss) Hall, he commissioned a gilded bronze statue eighteen *zhang* high, to which he personally offered worship.
Whenever he entered to prostrate himself, he would sob and choke with emotion, unable to restrain himself; among his attendants, there were none who did not shed tears.
Moreover, for the sake of Empress Dowager Xian, he constructed [a monastery] on the western bank of the Qingxi River, east of the road leading to Yangcheng Gate.

The Dazhidu Monastery is located in the Jiali district of the capital. Its site is high and clear, commanding a broad view; it lies at the midpoint of the imperial circuit and is a prominent strategic point for both river and land routes.

The halls and pavilions are vast and spacious, and there is a seven-story jeweled pagoda. In the main hall, a gold statue eighteen *zhang* in height was also fashioned to extend merit for the deceased.
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs recite and lecture upon the scriptures during the four seasons. On the day the monastery was completed, the Emperor turned to his ministers and said:
He constructed these two temples to offer blessings to the two Emperors, thereby manifesting his boundless affection and conveying his thoughts for those long departed.

Yet, he could not dispel the grief of the "Liao-e" (The Caltrops) poem; thus, he returned to the Inner Palace to erect the Zhijing Hall and the Jingyang Terrace, establish the chambers of the Seven Temples, and set up the thrones of the two Emperors.
All rites were fully prepared, and as he looked upon the ceremonial caps, hairpins, and jewelry boxes, his longing was stirred at the mere sight of them at dawn.
He remained in a state of profound grief. His clothing was light and warm, changing according to the seasons; his food was exquisite and fragrant, offered at the appropriate times.
Yet, because of state affairs, the Emperor was unable to attend to the meals morning and evening, attending only on the first and fifteenth days of the month to personally present the offerings.
Finding no one to look up to, his inner heart collapsed, as if burning and searing. He further composed fifty "Linked Pearl" verses (*liánzhū*) to clarify [his feelings].
Filial Piety. Furthermore, he composed the "Fu on Filial Thought" (*Xiósī fù*) to extensively encompass the root of filiality.

As for its ability to bring peace to the sovereign and order to the people, transforming customs and changing social mores, it surpasses all ages and is beyond praise. Thus, Emperor Yuan said: "I humbly examine how our Sovereign practices filial piety:
as the four seasons shift and change, he is not swayed by prosperity or decay; as the five virtues alternate, he does not alter his conduct based on status or rank."

When his heart faced the court, he was solemn and silent; his thoughts for those lost like a glimpse through a crack in a door grew ever more profound. As he sat with folded arms upon the palace veranda, his grief for his parents—like trees felled by the wind—became even more acute.

He purified himself in the ancestral temple and reverently performed sacrifices at the suburban altars; before he had even spoken, tears fell, and though his countenance did not change, his sorrow was intense.
This is what is meant by "grief that lasts a lifetime. Indeed, it was thus for Emperor Shun of Yu, Yu of Xia, King Wen of Zhou, and Emperor Wu of Liang. Ten thousand...

In discussing those who have carried forward the teachings of filial piety, there are but four such individuals. Furthermore, because the national schools were restricted by the barriers of social rank between the noble and the humble, he subsequently established five colleges to recruit men of talent from all backgrounds, regardless of status.
Consequently, the two traditions of Confucianism and Buddhism flourished side by side in glory.
Leading his contemporaries, he repeatedly received imperial edicts and participated in the work of translation.
Shi Fajian was a native of Lu County in Guanghan. His surname was Zhu. He could recite one thousand scrolls of sutras.

Although he often had much leisure time and would wander about mingling with the common people, he would suddenly close his door and not emerge for several days, abstaining from food entirely; one could hear only the sound of him reciting the sutras.
However, he chanted with a low voice, the sound not reaching beyond his immediate vicinity.

A man leaning against the wall overheard him as he approached, hearing only a continuous, flowing murmur like the surging waves of an underground stream. When Prince Wuling was descending to the east, he appointed his younger brother Gui to govern Yizhou.
The Wei dynasty dispatched General Wei Chi-hui to replace [the governor] in Shu. Once Gui had surrendered, the many renowned monks within the city were all placed under detention.
At night, a brilliant light suddenly appeared. Wei Chi-hui sent men to investigate the light and found that while all the other monks were asleep, only Fa Jian sat upright reciting a sutra;
the light issued from his mouth. Upon hearing this, Wei Chi-hui went to Fa Jian’s location in person and prostrated himself before him in worship.
He sat and listened until dawn, when he finally ceased. Huijing asked, "What sutra is the Dharma Master reciting from last night?
He replied, "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the lower fascicle, ten scrolls. Huijing said, "Why do you not recite it from the beginning? He replied, "I have reached this point in my recitation.
Huijing asked, "How much of it has the Dharma Master recited? He replied, "I resolved my mind with the intention to..."
He had recited one *piṭaka*, and had now finally completed a thousand fascicles. [The Master] wished to test him, saying, "I shall ask you to recite them all in their entirety;
will it not cause you some fatigue? Fajian replied, "The reading and recitation of the scriptures is the constant duty of a śramaṇa; how could I dread such toil?

Thereupon, a high seat was prepared, and he ordered the assembly of monks to hold their own copies and listen. Fajian ascended the seat and began his recitation, which was as rapid as a swift torrent.

It poured down like a torrent into a steep ravine. As for its intonation of phrases and syllables, and its inhalation and exhalation of breath, it was sometimes like a clear breeze entering a tall pine tree.
Those with keen intelligence heard but a lingering resonance; those whose feelings were detached and whose minds were wandering merely gazed at the dust of its tracks.

For seven days and seven nights, the count reached a full thousand times, yet it still did not cease. Xu Jingqi rose up from afar and said, "Your disciple’s military affairs will not allow me to remain long."

"Stop. Please take your leave from here. Thereupon, the monks all dispersed. After Huijing had gone out, he sighed and said, "Since the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, Ānanda has been called 'Total Retention' (Dhāraṇī).
How could anyone surpass this? Yet, in Shu, there is such a person as this!"
Thus, he was always secure in peace and happiness. How marvelous, how marvelous! He passed away at the age of eighty.

As for Shi Hui-gong, he was a native of Chengdu in Yizhou and surnamed Zhou. Before the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddha-dharma, he formed a bond with Hui-yuan of the same monastery to pursue their studies with diligence.
While Yuan traveled directly to Chang’an to seek out and gather teachings, Gong went far away to Jingzhou and Yangzhou.

He traveled to the capital to seek the Way, where he heard the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Upon returning to Yizhou, he lectured and taught them; both monastics and laypeople revered him, and offerings of alms accumulated in great abundance.
Later, when Saṅghabhadra returned from Jiangzuo, the two met; they joyfully recounted their experiences, for they had been separated for over thirty years.
They stayed together for several nights, engaging in conversation; Huiyuan’s speech flowed forth like a spring, while Daocong remained entirely without words.
Huiyuan asked Daocong, "We have been separated for a long time, and now that we have met, I rejoice in this joyful reunion.

What is there to discuss? Yet I perceive that you, Venerable Sir, have nothing to say. Is it perhaps that you have attained nothing? Daocong replied, "By nature I am dull and inferior; I understand nothing at all."
Huiyuan said, "I do not understand much at all. Could you not recite a single scripture? Senggong replied, "I can only recite one scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
Huiyuan’s expression grew stern as he said, "The Avalokiteśvara Sūtra—children as young as toddlers can recite it.
Why trouble someone of your great standing? Moreover, when you were a youth, you left the household life and made a vow with me."

"To realize the fruit of the Way, how could it take more than thirty years? To do nothing but recite a single scroll of scripture no larger than a finger—this is not the act of one who is dull-witted or indolent.
I request that we sever our ties; I pray that you, Dharma Master, will depart soon, so as not to increase the afflictions of those far away.
Gong replied, "Though the scripture is small, it was spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth. Those who revere and honor it shall obtain immeasurable merit; those who treat it with contempt..."

"One who harbors pride incurs immeasurable sin. I pray that you will temporarily set aside your anger. I shall recite this scripture once for the sake of the Dharma Master, after which we shall part forever.
Yuan laughed loudly and said, "The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*—the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—I have already lectured upon it more than a hundred times.
Why do you now wish to disturb my ears? Gong replied, "The Book of Documents says: 'If a person can...'"
"The Way propagates people; it is not that people propagate the Way. One should simply listen to the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart. How could one discard the Dharma because of a person?
Yet [Daoxuan] proceeded to construct an altar in the courtyard, placed a high seat within the altar, circumambulated the altar several times, and prostrated himself. He then ascended the high seat.
Only when he had no choice did [Hui]gong sit upon a large couch beneath the eaves to listen. When Gong first raised his voice to chant the title of the sutra, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth."
A fragrant incense smoke filled the hall and its chambers. When [the Master] entered the Tuṣita Heaven, celestial music was played and four kinds of flowers rained down.

When the recitation ended and he descended from his seat, the music and flowers finally ceased. Huiyuan prostrated himself at his feet in worship; tears flowed profusely as he expressed his gratitude, saying, "I, Huiyuan, am a foul-smelling corpse.
How could I dare to walk beneath the light of heaven? I beg you to stay for a moment and grant me your instruction. Daogong replied, "This is not something I can do."
"It is possible; it is simply through the power of the Buddhas. That very day, he brushed off his robes, offered a long bow, and followed the current away, with no one knowing where he had gone.
Shi Tanlun, whose secular surname was Sun, was a native of Juyi in Beizhou. He left home at the age of thirteen and resided at Xiufu Temple under the guidance of Chan Master Duan.
Duan instructed Lun, saying, "Bind your mind to the tip of your nose; you shall thereby attain stillness. Lun replied, "If I perceive [anything]..."
[The Master said: "Focus the mind on the tip of the nose. [The student replied,] "Originally I could not perceive the characteristics of the mind; I do not know what it is that can be focused upon.

Everyone marveled at these words and sighed, saying, "How is it that one who studies so recently has attained such profound realization? Therefore, he remains at the end of the assembly. At the time of performing prostrations and repentance, [the student] immediately entered meditative absorption.

When the great assembly snapped their fingers [to rouse him], his mind remained constantly respectful. Later, while carrying his alms bowl to the hall, before he had even reached mid-path, he stood upright and firm.

He entered meditative absorption, holding his alms bowl without it tilting even slightly. The Master greatly admired this and, on another occasion, told him: "I shall have you practice seated meditation first to purify the turbid mind.
It is like peeling an onion; one must peel away layer by layer until it is finally pure. Dalu said, "If there were an onion to be seen, there could be peeling.
Since from the very beginning there is no onion, what is there to peel? The Master said, "This is a great root, a great..."

The stalks were beyond my reach; I did not dare to employ them for labor. After the offerings were presented, he neither recited scriptures nor prostrated before the Buddha, doing none of these things at all.
He simply remained shut in his room and would not come out. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he focused solely on the mind free from discursive thought, thus fulfilling his vow.

Next, the person in charge of the monastery’s annual affairs was informed to guard the monastic property and strictly command the household members, saying: "Dogs have their own separate food; do not give them the monks' gruel. The family...

People regarded this as an ordinary matter and did not heed his words. However, the dog then vomited out the monks' gruel right before them; both the clergy and the laity were humbled by his reverent caution.
Furthermore, when scholars of the Abhidharma came to debate and question him, he would dispel their arguments with a single word, remaining entirely unimpeded.
In the second year of the Renshou era, Empress Xian passed away. A meditation hall was being constructed, and she summoned him to reside there; yet upon his return, she immediately closed it.

Guān continued his habitual practices as before; people of the time called him "Lún the Recliner. There was a Dharma Master named Xiàncàn of Xingshān Monastery, a preeminent figure among the "Three Kingdoms Debaters" whose learning was unsurpassed.
Finding it strange that Lún remained reclining in meditation, Xiàncàn remarked, "His speech is pure and profound," and so he entered the room to converse with him, investigating right and wrong.
Lún smiled and said, "Examine me as you please. Thus, for three days and three nights, they took delight in the Dharma.
Sengmen expounded the boundless Prajñāpāramitā, [comparing it to] empty flowers and water from a mirage; being without clothing or master, he established neither right nor wrong.

His fundamental nature was pure. Sengcan then prostrated himself on the ground in reverence. While Sengmen was in the capital, his skillful means attracted the Vinaya Master Xuánwǎn and the Dharma Master Jìnglín, who led their disciples, including Sēngjiè and Jìng, to come and go to receive the Dharma. This was at the end of the Wǔdé era.
His illness became severe. At the side of Zhuangyan Temple, he sat in profound stillness.

When someone asked where he would be reborn, he replied, "The world of inexhaustibility," and then fell silent once more. The monks sought the location of his cold touch with their hands and privately informed others, saying, "The cold has reached his knees.
As the four elements separated, there must have been suffering; Tanlun said, "This suffering, too, is empty. Someone asked, "When you relinquish this life..."
"What is it? he asked. He replied, "After death, wrap me in straw mats and discard me; do not perform any other rites.

He spoke again, asking, "Has the fifth watch bell been struck yet? He replied, "Not yet. A short while later, when the *vina* struck the bell, he was found to have already passed away. He was over eighty years old.
Following his instructions, the disciples and others carried him to the South Mountain, where they laid his body bare and scattered it in the middle of the wilds.

Shi Zhichao’s secular surname was Tian. He was a native of Fengyi in Tongzhou. From his early childhood, his wisdom and capacity surpassed those of others. Disgusted with the world, he sought the Way;
however, his parents relied upon him and hoped he would carry on their lineage, so he followed the Confucian stream and extensively studied the various classics and compendiums.
When he approached middle age, he privately arranged a marriage for himself. Upon hearing of this, Zhichao sought to avoid such worldly defilement and fled into the forests and wilds. His parents...

Zhoumi sought a marriage alliance, but [Chao] suppressed it on account of their marital bond. At first, they shared a single mat as their dwelling; in the end, they likewise concealed themselves together in a private room. There was only one bed placed there.

Chao then removed his felt mat and spread it upon the floor, ordering his wife to sit upon it while he himself occupied the bed. Maintaining a solemn meditative posture, he diligently preached the Dharma for her.
His words were exceedingly clear and authoritative, whereupon the wife shed tears, prostrated herself in gratitude, and took leave, saying she would trouble him again and again.

Through the nights and days, his devotion was like that toward a golden image; though he was repeatedly enticed and exhorted, his sincerity surpassed the quality of jade. Since his resolve was firm and difficult to uproot, his parents finally relinquished him to his own will.
At the age of twenty-seven, he went to Chan Master Huizàn of Kaishua Temple in Bingzhou, where he left the household life and received full ordination.
Having personally advanced in the stages of the precepts, he specialized in the practice of ritual observances and immediately traveled to Dingzhou to seek out and study the Vinaya.

He compiled the essential points and excised the redundancies. When his five summer retreats were not yet complete and his mastery of the three teachings was only roughly perfected, he returned to his native land.

He entered Qian Shan to the northwest of Taiyuan, where he gathered and attracted outstanding talents to establish a Chan monastery. Morning and night he practiced diligently, awakening both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
In the first year of the Daye era, when the administrative regulations were strict and clear, he was surrounded at the temple gate and forbidden from [entering].

He departed. When Chao heard of this, he was filled with lamentation and submitted a remonstrance. Donning his robes and raising his mendicant’s staff, he set out for the provincial capital and eventually reached Jiangdu.

He reported the matter to the authorities; however, the Interior Minister deemed it a non-urgent issue and did not facilitate his audience. This continued until the many troubles at the end of the Sui dynasty.

Bandits and rebels were rampant, and the people flowed like water into ditches and ravines; those who died accounted for the greater half. Yet Sengchao gathered his followers in joyful assembly, with surplus grain never failing.

They only feared that as robbers and thieves oppressed one another, they would be driven to flee and disperse. He then exhorted them with the precepts of the Dharma, saying: "Do not let your resolve waver.

When the mirror of karma confronts you, where can you escape its resonance? The assembly was moved by these words, and their initial intentions were transformed. According to the regulations, he entered meditative cultivation.

Regarding ritual practice, he never ceased his daily recitations. Once, while sitting in meditation at night, a band of thieves suddenly burst through the door, brandishing torches and brandishing white blades as they descended upon him.
Yet, the entire assembly remained upright and composed, their countenances identical in expression. The thieves then threw themselves prostrate on the ground, bowing in submission and seeking refuge.

Hui-chao accordingly guided them with appropriate means and bestowed the Dharma according to their capacities. Moved by this, they gave rise to a heart of reverence and, with palms joined, [proceeded].

[He] retired. When the High Ancestor established his cause at Taiyuan, people from all directions gathered there. Sengchao, considering that the Way resides in all living beings and that righteousness dwells within the merit of those who ride upon it, immediately led his companions to Jinyang to reside at Ningding Temple.
There were several hundred practitioners of Chan study; their conduct was pure and solemn, establishing a model for others.

Both monastics and laypeople revered him, and those of high and low status alike looked up to him with respect. When the Imperial Banner pointed southward and the Three Prefectures were cleared of dust, in the second year of Yining, Sengchao—
Leading more than twenty disciples and sons, he proceeded to the capital to offer his congratulations. Emperor Wu, having long held him in high esteem, treated him as if he were an immortal;

he invited him to ascend the Taiji Hall and accorded him exceptional honors. In the private quarters of the residence of Pei Ji, Duke of Wei and Minister of the Left, a dwelling was established for the monks.
He invited the assembly to reside there, and through many cycles of winter and summer, their practice became ever more rigorous. At that time, in Lantian...

At Huagan Temple on Mount Shan, the śramaṇas Lingrun, Zhixin, Zhiguang, and others—whose profound understanding of the Dharma grasped its subtle mysteries and who held the study of the mind in high esteem—sought one another out as kindred spirits and invited [the Master] to reside upon that mountain.
As they gathered there based on their shared affinity, followers arrived like clouds.

In the fifth year of the Wude era, he entered Guanjishan, where he established a community of meditation companions; those who came to observe him were transformed, their worldly minds refined. Furthermore, at Fenyin...

In the administrative seat of Jiexiu County in the prefecture, he established Guangyan Monastery, which was magnificent and imposing, resembling a divine palace. The master and his disciples were solemn and harmonious.
Suddenly, having contracted an illness, he passed away at the city monastery on the fifteenth day of the third month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
He was seventy-one years old at his passing.
Shi Daojie’s secular surname was Yang; his ancestors were descendants of Yang Zhen, the Han Dynasty Grand Marshal (Taishou) of Hongnong. He resided in Mingtiao, An-yi, Hedong.
By nature, his intelligence was exceptionally sharp and his mind vast, transcending the mundane world. Having planted the roots of virtue in past lives, his heart grew weary of worldly conventions.
Chen. In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, when he was nearly twenty years of age, he went to the Dharma Master Zhenying.

Zhenying, discerning his lofty and outstanding character, immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, instructing him to study the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures. By nature pure and refined, he was clear and bright in his cultivation;

his power of hearing and retention was as lucid as a mirror. Later, he went to Mount Xiántóu to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*. After one month, he had mastered it. He reflected deeply within himself, saying: "The Sūtra says: 'I would rather wish for a little...'"
He heard that one who wishes to understand the profound meanings and attain mastery must rely on extensive travel.

In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he went to the master He Ji in Qingzhou to study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. Master Ji looked at him and said, "Your appearance is noble and imposing, and you possess a refined manner of discourse.
Your learning may be shallow, but your insight is far-reaching; my school of thought will surely flourish through you. Not long after, Master Ji passed away. Thereupon...
As he traveled throughout the territory of Qi, there were at that time Zang Ji and An Yi, both renowned as sages; he followed them to receive the Way.
He also went to the two masters of the *Abhidharma* treatises, Cang and Ji of Wei, where he listened to the *Abhidharma* (*Pitan lun*).

Furthermore, under Qinghe Dao Shang and Hong Kai of Ji Jun, he listened to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* from beginning to end for four years, exhausting its five sections (*pañcaskandha*) by searching through it from top to bottom.
He consulted the Master of Dharma, who repeatedly caused Mr. Gai to stretch his neck and heave long sighs of relief. He once established Gai’s interpretation, saying:

"The *Śāstra* states that there is only the single sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), yet it possesses three distinctions. This passage does not mean that the single nature of 'suffering-as-suffering' (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is designated as the sensation of suffering, and that the three sensations are spoken of merely according to worldly convention.
Rather, it is precisely within the single sensation of suffering that the three sensations are spoken of according to convention. This is the meaning of the Sūtra."
The Master of the School (Buddhadeva) maintains this view, and Guṇavarman describes it as his own tenet; can it not be so? Guāi said, "Indeed. Jié said:

"If a fruit arises to repay a cause, then one might as well say that a painful sensation is a pleasant sensation; likewise, a cause could be said to produce a fruit, and one might say that an evil karma is a wholesome karma.
If you say that a wholesome karma produces a pleasant fruit because a wholesome karma is not an evil karma, then one might as well say that a pleasant sensation repays [a wholesome cause]."
There is a virtuous cause, and there is pleasant sensation rather than painful sensation.

If you say that pleasant sensation is the retribution for a virtuous cause, yet its essence is actually painful sensation, then it would also follow that a virtuous karma produces a pleasant fruit, yet its essence is actually an unwholesome karma.

If you say that it is in fact only a single painful sensation, which is called "false pleasure" according to worldly sentiment, then it would also follow that it is in fact only a single unwholesome karma, which is called "false virtue" according to worldly sentiment. At this point, one is left utterly bewildered.
Later, he remarked, "This disciple possesses an intelligence that transcends the common crowd; it is difficult to find anyone with whom he can engage in discourse.
I am old; shall the great promotion of the Way rest upon you? Thereupon, his disciples all bowed in submission. In the nineteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he traveled from Wei to Ye.

He listened to Master Lin’s lectures on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. Furthermore, at the residence of Vinaya Master Hong, he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Traveling eastward, he was summoned by Prince Han of the Sui dynasty.
There, he encountered Zhi-nian of Cangzhou and Fa-leng of Hejian, both of whom widely propagated the teachings of the Northern Dynasties.

Seizing this opportunity, he immediately went to follow them, listening to and admiring the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* while reading the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. For a full three years from beginning to end, he thoroughly mastered the depths of the texts; he once raised difficult questions regarding...
The Master Nian said: "If contact is empty and is not the sense-base of contact, then consciousness should likewise be empty and not the abode of consciousness.

If it is the case that consciousness is not a constituent part [of itself] yet is the abode of consciousness, then contact should likewise not be a constituent part [of itself] yet be the sense-base of contact.
At that time, Master Nian merely smiled and gazed directly at him. In the second year of the Renshou era, he again followed Dharma Master Leng to hear the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
In the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, it is said that at that time, the gates of the Dharma were wide open and masters gathered like clouds.
The great scholar Jizang, who had mastered both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, as well as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the Vinaya-piṭaka of Śunakṣatra, assembled all the teachings of his era.

During the Jin Restoration, he traveled extensively among lecture halls for six years, observing the similarities and differences between various schools and posing difficult challenges to them all. Thus, the saying went in Bingzhou: "The Great Head."
Jie was killed by an assassin. When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty passed away and the rebellion at Jinyang broke out, he returned to his hometown.

There, he lectured on the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, each five or six times. He reflected to himself: "I have merely occupied myself with verbal explanations, while the path of my mind remains vast and desolate.

As for the arising of wisdom, it will not manifest without meditative concentration. He consequently ceased his lectures and went to Magu to rely upon Chan Master Zhenhui, where he studied seated meditation.

Deliberating with mindfulness and wisdom, he delved deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). His wisdom marveled, saying: "I have always thought that those such as the Dharma Master, having followed the teachings from the very beginning, would find it difficult to subdue the turbulent stream of afflictions.
How is it that, having only recently begun his practice, he is already able to dwell in meditative visualization? Is this not surely the result of cultivation in previous lives?

Later, relying on the *Anapanasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) of the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*, he focused his contemplation for two nights. His insight and understanding became brilliantly clear, and he remarked: "This is indeed the Dharma of Shenxu."

The Master said: "Yesterday, I attempted to practice the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* according to the treatises. While the meditative object was extremely clear, my breath became so constricted that it pressed upon my heart, making me sit uncomfortably on my mat.
To eliminate this affliction, I must ultimately seek instruction on how to dispel it; I request you to compose a work comparing the various sūtras on *ānāpāna*."
He arranged them in sequential order to eliminate stagnation.

Previously, he had studied the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, as well as the various schools of Nāgārjuna and Āraṇyaka, which clarify the sixteen special excellences (*viśeṣa*) and the characteristics of the six types of *ānāpāna*. He demonstrated these to [Mazu], who then practiced accordingly until his realization became even more luminous and pure.
Later, he went to Magu to present what he had realized. Huì remarked, "Excellent! You possess great faculties; you have shed [all attachments]."
The various scholars at Quanzhong had not yet reached this point [in their studies]. In the first year of the Wude era, they requested that he propagate the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Sengjie laughed and said, "To halt one's carriage to practice dhyāna is merely a method for self-benefit; to expound and spread the Dharma is truly for the benefit of others.

As for attaining both benefits, one must speak by day and remain silent at night, so that the small and great vehicles may both be thoroughly understood. Thereupon, he propagated and disseminated the *Triṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The rest were all [monks]. He constantly followed the Master’s teachings, with more than one hundred disciples. Those capable of external propagation numbered over two thousand.
He was selective in his friendships and moved among scholars; he was frugal with wealth and meager in food. He spoke neither of suffering nor joy, and his mind was unshaken by pleasure or anger.

When the community residing on the crags appointed him as their monastic leader, he passed away from illness on the mountain on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Zhenguan era.
The monk Xuanzang’s original name was Wei; his surname was Chen. He was a descendant of Chen Zhonggong of Taichou during the Han dynasty.

Xuanzang intended to propagate the fundamental teachings of the Buddha, and thus traveled to the kingdom of Kāmarūpa within the borders of East India. Because of the local customs there, the people all followed heterodox paths;
their followers numbered in the tens of thousands. Although the Buddha-dharma was widespread elsewhere, it had not yet reached that land; therefore, he went there.
Upon his arrival at the royal court, he was praised for his superior mastery and his profound, far-reaching spiritual insight.

The King said, "This is unprecedented! He received it upon his head in reverence and took refuge [in the Triple Gem].
To the east of this kingdom, it borders the Western Man tribes of Shu; the road there should take two months to reach. At that time, King Śīlāditya and his ministers said: "To the east..."
The Prince of the Tufan [Tibetan] Kingdom heard that there was a Mahāyāna master from China whose virtue and morality were widely renowned and whom the King held in high esteem.

The King dispatched an envoy to say to King Kumāra: "Please send the Chinese Dharma Master to join us at the kingdom of Cīnabhukti. Thus spoke the Prince of the Tufan Kingdom.
He ordered ten thousand elephant troops and thirty thousand square boats to accompany Xuanzang up the Gaṅgā River to join King Śīlāditya.

Upon first seeing him, he prostrated himself and touched his feet in full reverence. He scattered flowers and offered verses;

Xuanzang replied, "He is the current Son of Heaven who governs the realm. He is a Great Sage who has dispelled disorder and restored the Right Way, and whose grace extends to the six [directions]."
Thus, this verse was composed. The King then invited him into his temporary palace and presented various offerings.

"For what reason have you descended here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. Is there perhaps another place for rest and relaxation?

The Master pointed to the rear and said, "There is a separate small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the site of the hermitage; surrounding the hut were only tigers, wolves, and other such beasts.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of fear. The Master said, "There is still this [fear] remaining. The Patriarch then sat in meditative repose.

On a stone, he had written the single character for "Buddha. Upon seeing it, the Master was struck with awe. The Patriarch said, "There is still this remaining. The Master bowed his head and requested an explanation of the essential truth.

The Patriarch said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind. The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all centered in the source of the heart.
All gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom, as well as spiritual powers and transformations, are entirely and inherently complete within it."
They do not depart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, from the very beginning, empty and quiescent. All causes and effects are like dreams and illusions.
There is no triple world to escape, and there is no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature and characteristics.
The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; there is nothing further lacking.
How is it any different from that of the Buddha? You need only allow your mind to be free and at ease. Do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to clarify the mind.
Do not give rise to greed or anger, nor harbor sorrow or anxiety. Be expansive and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions. Do not perform various good deeds, nor...
"Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, whatever one encounters through the eyes or meets with conditions—all is the wondrous function of the Buddha.

The Master asked, "Since you do not permit the practice of contemplation, when objects arise, how does the mind counteract them? The Patriarch said, "Objects and conditions have neither good nor evil."

Beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not insist on naming them, from where could deluded sentiments arise? Once deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind functions freely through its various cognitions.
You need only follow the mind with ease and spontaneity; without further applying antidotes, this is called the eternally abiding Dharma-body.
Shi Yuangui’s secular surname was Li. He was a native of Yiguan. Endowed with a spirit of extraordinary brilliance, he was broad-minded, generous, and refined.
He vowed to leave the household life and, in the second year of the Yongchun era, completed his ordination. He then registered his name at Xianju Monastery to study the Vinaya.

He adhered strictly to the Vinaya alone. Later, he realized the Chan school at Shaolin Temple and attained great penetration into the essentials of the mind. He subsequently chose a site to build a hermitage in Pangwu within the mountains.

At that time, there was a man wearing a high cap and trousers with pleated skirts, leading a large retinue; he walked with light steps and a relaxed gait, announcing his arrival to pay his respects to the Great Master.
Huiguang, observing that the man’s appearance was imposing and his spirit extraordinary, said to him: "Welcome, O benevolent one! For what purpose have you come?"
He arrived and said, "Do you recognize me, Master? Guī replied, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all as one. How could I distinguish or recognize you?
The spirit replied, "I am the deity of this mountain. I can bring benefit or harm, life or death, to people."
The Master said, "How could I allow you to see me with one eye? Guì replied, "You can bring life and death to others, but I am fundamentally unborn;
how then can you kill me? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you. Can you destroy space and yourself?
If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished. You, however, are not even capable of that."
"It is so. Furthermore, how could you possibly cause my birth and death? The Spirit of Mount Yue bowed his head and prostrated twice, saying, 'I pray that you will grant me the Right Precepts.
Guì said, 'Since you, O Spirit, have requested the precepts, you are already possessed of them. Why is this? Because there is no precept apart from the precept; what further precept could there be? "
The deity said, "This is the principle. I have heard of it, but it is obscure and dim; I seek only the precepts from you, Master. I shall become your disciple.

though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become old; though undergoing transformation all day long, one does not become agitated; and ultimately, one reaches the state of total stillness."
Yet they do not constitute rest or awakening. This means that although one marries, it is not a wife; although one feasts, it is not taking; although one holds the handle, it is not power;
