He replied, "Venerable Sir, you may go ahead; I shall follow like a shadow. After traveling five *li*, the neighbor had already arrived. When he was ordained at Luoshi Temple, eleven years passed.
Suddenly, he thought of his two parents and took leave to return home for a visit. His father had lost his sight, and his mother had passed away.

Three years had already passed. He went to the temple of Mount Tai to seek his deceased mother’s hidden whereabouts. He immediately spread out his sitting mat and recited the Lotus Sūtra, vowing that he would see King Tianqi as his goal.
That night, the deity of Mount Tai indeed summoned his neighbor and asked why he was so earnestly suffering.
The neighbor replied, "My mother, Lady Wang, has already completed the mourning period since her passing. I venture to ask the Great King, where is my mother now?"
"Where is she? The king looked at his clerks, who replied, "The Lady Wang is currently imprisoned and undergoing suffering. The neighbor said, "What crime has my mother committed?
The king said, "When she gave birth to the Monk, she ate chicken eggs and took a head-pustule from the White Master; it is for these reasons."

It was due to your official duties that your neighbors wailed in grief and were utterly exhausted; they sought the King’s favor to grant you exemption, saying, "While there is a fixed destiny for your bonds, there is no way to release you.
Nevertheless, they said, "For the sake of the Dharma Master, we request that you go to Mount Mao to pay homage at the Stūpa of King Aśoka; perhaps then you may be pardoned.

Your neighbor set out on the road the following morning and arrived at the Mountain Temple in Guzhang. There he prostrated himself, lamenting with sorrow, as his five limbs touched the ground in worship.
When he finished, he cast his tally-sticks and found they numbered forty thousand. Suddenly, he heard the voice of someone calling for a neighbor;
looking toward the clouds, he saw his mother, who said to him, "By your power, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. I have come to inform you. In an instant, she vanished.
Shi Shenhui’s secular surname was Gao; he was a native of Xiangyang. While still young, his nature was upright and intelligent.

He followed a teacher to receive the transmission of the Five Classics, through which he mastered their profound and subtle mysteries. Subsequently, he studied the works of Zhuangzi and Laozi, until his inner mind became vast and clear. Upon reading the *Book of the Later Han*, he came to understand the teachings of the Buddha (Buddhism).
Thereupon, he devoted himself to the Buddhist doctrine and had no intention of pursuing an official career. He took leave of his parents and went to the local government office.
Dharma Master Haoyuan of Guochang Temple left the household life and recited various scriptures; he mastered them as easily as turning over his hand.

He maintained the great Vinaya precepts in their entirety and did not crave the mere act of lecturing. Hearing that Chan Master Huineng of Caoxi in Lingbiao was vigorously propagating the Way of the Dharma, he traveled there on foot to meet him.
Huineng asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from nowhere. Huineng said, "Then you do not return?"
He departed. [Nanquan] replied, "There is nowhere to which one can return. Nanquan said, "You are far too lost in the vastness. He replied, "My physical conditions are currently on the road.
Nanquan said, "Because you yourself have not yet arrived. He replied, "I have now already arrived; furthermore, there is no lingering or staying. He resided at Caoxi for several years.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively to seek out famous sites and traces. In the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, he resided at Longxing Temple in Nanyang.
He subsequently propagated the Chan teachings widely in Luoyang, where his reputation and brilliance were fully manifested. Previously, throughout the two capitals, everyone had followed Shenxiu;

however, upon seeing Huineng’s realization of the mind and the style of the Sixth Patriarch, the path of gradual cultivation was swept away, and the Southern and Northern schools were for the first time distinguished as separate lineages.
In the fourteenth year, An Lushan of Fanyang raised troops and turned them toward the center; the two capitals were laid waste, and the imperial court took refuge in Ba and Shu.

The Vice Commander-in-Chief Guo Ziyi led his forces to suppress and annihilate the rebels. However, as provisions for transport and supply were utterly exhausted, he employed the expedient strategy of the Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, Pei Mian:
each great prefecture was established with a *kaitan* (ordination platform) to ordain monks, thereby collecting "incense-water funds" to assist the military requirements.

Initially, when the capital city fell first, Amoghavajra happened to be among the wild grasses. At that time, Lu Yi had been slain by the rebels, so the assembly requested that Amoghavajra preside over the altar rites for the ordination of monks.
At that moment, the temples and palaces had been completely reduced to ashes; thus, he temporarily established a single courtyard, providing everything from his own meager resources.
Within it, he constructed a square altar, and all the wealth and silk obtained were immediately used to support military expenses. (Emperor Daizong)
Guo Ziyi recovered the two capitals, and Huiji’s practical contributions were of considerable benefit.
Emperor Suzong issued an edict for him to enter the palace for service and commanded the Master Carpenter to construct a dwelling for the Chan Master within Heze Temple.
Shi Chuntuo was originally a man from the Western Regions who traveled to the capital, where he was held in high esteem by all.
During the Shangyuan era, he announced his intention to travel eastward. Those who saw him noted that his countenance was like that of a youth, yet he was already six hundred years old.

His speech was vigorous and his movements remained undiminished by age. When Emperor Daizong heard of this, he issued an edict for him to enter the court, treating him with the utmost honor and providing him with abundant provisions.
[The Emperor] sought the way to preserve his years. Tuo said: "The spirit and mind delight in stillness. Now they are turbidized by the realm of sensory dust; how can you attain profound tranquility?
If you seek to preserve your years apart from simplicity and stillness, it would be like climbing a tree to pluck lotuses—how could that be possible?
If Your Majesty wishes for longevity, you must attain peace of mind through simplicity and purity. When the spirit is at peace, life is long; when desires are few, the body [is preserved]."
"Peaceful. As for the arts [of the future] beyond this point, they are unknown to this poor monk. Because of this, the Emperor came to hold him in profound esteem.
In the third year of the Yongtai era, he foreknew that his end was near and sent his disciple to present his robes and bowl to the Emperor. The Emperor bestowed purple robes upon the disciple.
Tuo finally passed away at Zhenguosi Temple.
During the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, he asked Chan Master Huizhong, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? The Master then rose to his feet and said:
"Do you understand? [The Emperor] said, "I do not. The Master said, "Hand the pure pitcher over to me, old monk. The Emperor asked again, "What is the Samādhi of Non-contention?
The Master said, "Donor, you are walking upon the crown of Vairocana’s head. The Emperor asked, "What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Do not mistake it for your own pure Dharma-body. The Emperor asked again; the Master did not look at him and said:
"I am the Son of Heaven of the Great Tang. Why do you, Master, not deign to look at me? The Master said, "Do you see empty space? The Emperor said, "I see it.
The Master said, "Does it blink its eyes and look back at Your Majesty? Later, when the time for his *nirvāṇa* arrived, he took his leave of Emperor Daizong.
Daizong asked, "After the Master’s passing, what will you leave behind as a record? The Master said, "Construct one seamless [monument]."

[The Emperor requested] a pagoda. The Emperor said, "Go to the Master and obtain a model for the pagoda. The Master replied, "After this poor monk has passed away, there is an attendant named Yingzhen who will know of this matter;

I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict to question him. After the Master had passed away, the Emperor issued an edict to question Yingzhen. Yingzhen recited a verse, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
South of Xiang and north of Tan, there is a land filled with gold. Beneath the Shadowless Tree, all board the same boat;
atop the Lapis Lazuli Palace, there is no one who knows. After becoming an Arhat, he resided at Mount Danyuan.
Shi Wuye’s secular surname was Du; he was a native of Shangluo in Shangzhou. His mother, Lady Li, heard a voice from the air saying, "May I dwell here?
and she subsequently conceived. On the evening of his birth, an extraordinary light filled the room. By the time he reached childhood, he took no pleasure in play.

When walking, he always kept his gaze straight ahead; when sitting, he sat in the full lotus position (*paryaṅka*). When he reached the age of nine, he informed his parents that he wished to take refuge with Master Zhiben of Kaiyuan Temple in his native commandery.
Thereupon, the master bestowed upon him the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the *Viśeṣacintibrahmaparipṛcchā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other sūtras.

He could read five lines simultaneously, and after a single recitation, there was nothing he did not remember. At the age of twelve, he received the tonsure and entered the monastic order. Whenever he attended lectures...

He studied with such ease that he understood immediately upon hearing it. Whenever his fellow students had points they did not comprehend, he would analyze them for them accordingly, and all reached the profound mysteries.

By the age of twenty, he received full ordination from Master You of Xiangzhou. Within a single summer retreat, he was able to master the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifenlü shu*) and could expound upon it;
furthermore, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the monastic community, keeping his dharma assembly open throughout both winter and summer.
Without weariness, he later heard that Da Ji of Hongzhou was the preeminent leader of the Chan school. He went specifically to pay his respects.
Upon seeing him, Da Ji regarded him with wonder. Zhiye knelt and said, "Regarding the literature of the Three Vehicles, I have roughly exhausted its essential meanings.

However, I have often heard it said in the Chan school that 'the very mind is Buddha,' yet I truly have not been able to understand this. Da Ji said, "It is precisely this very mind that you have not understood which is [Buddha]."
It is not a separate entity; there is nothing further that is not understood. When one does not understand, this is delusion (*moha*); when one understands, this is awakening (*bodhi*).
Delusion is the sentient being; awakening is the Buddha. The Way is not separate from sentient beings—how could there be a Buddha existing elsewhere? It is just like a hand forming a fist.
Quan was a complete master of the hand. Upon hearing these words, he attained sudden enlightenment. Weeping and sobbing with grief, he said to Daji:

"I previously believed that the Buddha-way is long and distant, and that only after diligent suffering through vast eons could it finally be accomplished. Today I have finally realized that the true reality (*dharmakāya*) is inherently complete from the beginning.
All phenomena arise from the mind; they possess only names and lack any substantial reality."
Daji replied, "So it is, so it is. The nature of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing;
all phenomena are from the very beginning empty and quiescent. As the Sūtra says: 'All dharmas, from their origin, are eternally of the mark of quiescence.

It also says: 'The ultimate end is the house of emptiness and quiescence,' and: 'The emptiness of all dharmas is the seat. This is where the Buddhas and Tathāgatas dwell, having nothing upon which to rely."

Regarding the dwelling place: if one understands it thus, one dwells in the abode of emptiness and silence, sits upon the throne of the empty Dharma, and whether lifting or lowering the feet, never departs from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Understanding is attained in a single word, with no further gradual stages; this is what is meant by "ascending the mountain of *nirvāṇa* without moving the feet.
Having already received the transmission of the Mind-Seal, he proceeded to Caoxi to pay homage at the Patriarch’s stupa, and then traveled on to Mount Lu and Mount Tianmu.
He traveled to the Imperial Altar and various famous mountains, searching everywhere for sacred traces. From Luoyang to Fengyi, he stayed at Ximing Monastery;

the monastic community all wished to nominate him as a Great Virtue (*bhadanta*) for the two streets of Chang’an. Fayue sighed silently and said, "To draw near to kings and high ministers is not my aspiration.
Thereupon, he went to Shangdang, where the Regional Commander and Minister of State Li Baozhen, along with Ma Su, repeatedly...

He had distinguished himself in battle. Furthermore, he inspired Wang Wujun to join him in defeating Zhu Tao; his merits were many and his power was great. Yet, he delighted in hearing of the virtuous and good;

even if they were a thousand li away, he would certainly present ceremonial gifts to attract them. He held profound respect for those with established reputations and conduct, attending to them with offerings morning and evening.
As he moved back and forth with his banners and standards, he often showed signs of weariness. He said to his disciples, "I originally fled the bustle and the fame-and-profit of the Central Kingdom;
now, to again be burdened by receiving lords here—how could this delight the mind? Having spoken, he wandered through Mianshang Baofu Mountain and then proceeded to Mount Qingliang.
At Jinguesi Temple, he read the Tripitaka for as many days as there are stars in the heavens, fulfilling this vow.
When he had finished his work there, he once again struck his mendicant’s staff and traveled south. Upon reaching the West River, he initially stayed at the Zhongxiang Monastery.
There, the Prefectural Governor Dong Shuchan invited him to reside at the Kaiyuan Vihāra. Fayue said to his disciples, "Since arriving here, I no longer have any intention of traveling further.
Could it be that my karmic conditions lie here? Thereupon, he struck the bell to announce to the assembly and let out a lion’s roar.
He rained down the great rain of the Dharma for nearly twenty years, and the people of Bing and Fen were all converted to his teachings.

Emperor Xuanzong, having reigned for fourteen years, had long admired his virtuous reputation; he subsequently issued an imperial decree inviting him to enter the palace, but [the Master] declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.

The following year, another imperial edict was issued, yet he continued to feign illness as before. In the year Emperor Muzong ascended the throne, his sacred heart was filled with devotion and he longed to pay homage;
he therefore commanded Lingxi Gong, the Monastic Registrar of the Two Streets, to travel afar with the imperial decree to invite him.
Master Ye said, "I shall go, provided the journey is appropriate. Thereupon, he shaved his head and bathed, and upon reaching the central [temple],...
At night, he addressed his disciples, Huìqín and others, saying: "The nature of your seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing is coeval with the great void;
it is neither born nor extinguished. All objective realms are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning; not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus confused by objects. Once confused by objects, they transmigrate without end. You must always know the nature of the mind."
It has existed inherently from the beginning; it is not produced through causal conditioning. Like a vajra, it is indestructible. All phenomena are like shadows and echoes;
they possess no substantial reality. Therefore, a sutra says: "Only one thing is real; the other two are not true.
Constantly realizing that all is empty, there is not a single thing that accords with the mind. This is the point of mental focus shared by all Buddhas. You [should understand this].
"Practice this with diligence. Having finished speaking, he sat in the full lotus posture and suddenly passed into stillness.

During the Dazhong era of the Shizong reign, Zongmi was summoned to the inner court and granted purple robes. The Emperor repeatedly questioned him on the essentials of the Dharma, and court officials looked up to him with devotion.

Prime Minister Pei entered deeply into the inner sanctum of his teachings and received instruction as an external protector. The Master [observed that] Chan practitioners and scholars of the doctrinal schools...

They slandered one another, whereupon [Zongmi] composed the *Chan Yuan Zhi Quan Yi Zang* (A Single Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan). Its preface states briefly: "Chan is a term from India;
'source' refers to the fundamental, awakened true nature of all sentient beings. It is also called Buddha-nature, and it is also called the mind-ground.

Awakening to it is termed wisdom (*prajñā*); cultivating it is termed meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When concentration and wisdom are taken together, they are collectively termed Chan. This nature is the fundamental source of Chan."
Therefore, it is called the "Source of Dhyāna" (Chanyuan). To forget the emotions and accord with this is the practice of dhyāna (chanxing).

If one discusses the principles of dhyāna without speaking of its practice, one fails to distinguish between the linguistic traditions of China and India. Moreover, this true nature is not only the source of the gate of dhyāna, but also the source of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called "Dharmatā" (Faxing). It is also the source from which sentient beings experience delusion and awakening; therefore, it is called "Tathatā" (Rushi).
The ālayavijñāna is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "Buddha-nature. It is also the source of the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas;
therefore, it is called the "Mind-ground. These myriad practices do not exceed the six pāramitās, and dhyāna is merely one among them, specifically the fifth.
How could the true nature be designated solely as the practice of a single dhyāna? [This applies to] the Three Vehicles.
If a person seeks the Noble Path, they must necessarily cultivate dhyāna; apart from this, there is no other door.

One must simply realize that one's own mind is originally pure and fundamentally free from afflictions. The nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete within it. This mind is itself the Buddha; ultimately, there is no difference between them.
To practice in reliance upon this is the Dhyāna of the Supreme Vehicle, also called the Pure Dhyāna of the Tathāgata. Furthermore—
It is called the Samādhi of One Practice, and it is also called the Samādhi of Suchness. This is the root of all samādhis.
Shi Xuanjian was the son of Zhou of Jianzhou; he left home at an early age, received full ordination according to his seniority, and thoroughly investigated the Vinaya Piṭaka.

He thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sutras on nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*). Once, while lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he was commonly known as "Zhou the Vajra.
He often said to his fellow students: "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss; a tiny speck is cast upon a sharp blade, yet the blade remains unmoved.
Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this. Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the south were flourishing, the Master’s spirit...
Feeling dissatisfied, he set off carrying the *Qinglong Shuchao* (The Qinglong Commentary). While on the road to Liyang, he saw an old woman selling cakes.
Stopping to rest his shoulder, he bought some cakes for refreshment. The woman pointed to his pack and asked, "What writing is this?

The Master replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao*. The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? The Master replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question for you. The Master—
"If you say you have it, I will give you a snack; if you say you do not have it, go elsewhere for now. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I wonder, Elder, which mind will you light?
The Master remained silent. He then went to Longtan. One night, while standing in attendance, Longtan said: "Furthermore—"
“Why do you not go down? The Master said, “I take my leave,” and he went out. He returned and said, “It is dark outside. Guishan lit a paper candle and passed it to the Master.
As the Master reached out to receive it, Guishan blew it out. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Guishan said:
"What did you see? The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of all the old monks under heaven.
On the following day, Longtan ascended the seat and said to the assembly, "Among you there is a man whose teeth are like a forest of swords and whose mouth is like a basin of blood;
he cannot be turned back by a single blow of the staff. In the future, he will stand atop a solitary peak and uphold my [Dharma]."
The Master was about to depart. He gathered the commentaries and sub-commentaries and piled them before the Dharma Hall. Holding up a torch, he said:
"To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void; to exhaust all worldly pivot-points is like casting a single grain into a vast abyss.
Thereupon, he burned them and took his leave with prostrations.
Shi Congshen went to visit Nanquan. Finding Nanquan reclining at rest, he asked, "Where have you recently come from?
The Master replied, "Ruixiang. Nanquan asked, "Did you see the Ruixiang? The Master said, "I did not see the Ruixiang; I only saw the Reclining Tathāgata.
Nanquan then sat up immediately and held him in high esteem, granting him permission to enter his room. On another day, Congshen asked Nanquan, "What is the Way? Nanquan—
[Zhao] said, "The ordinary mind is it. The Master asked, "Can one still direct oneself toward it? Zhao said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate.
The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing. If one truly reaches the Way of non-doubt, it is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive.
At these words, the Master awakened to the principle and then said, "The golden Buddha is not passed through the furnace; the wooden Buddha is not passed through the axe."
Fire. A clay Buddha does not cross water. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Among thousands and tens of thousands of people, all are men seeking the Buddha; among them, can you find a single true man of the Way?

If you are a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the sickness of the mind be the most difficult to cure. Before the world existed, this nature already existed; when the world perishes, this nature—
"Do not harbor [doubts]. It is simply this very host. Why seek it elsewhere? A certain old woman requested that he recite the *Tripitaka*.

The Master, however, stepped down from his seat, circumambulated once, and said, "The recitation of the *Tripitaka* is finished. The woman said, "I have come specifically to request you to recite it."
The entire Tripitaka. Why then do you only turn the Half-piṭaka? One day the Master asked a newly arrived monk, "Have you ever been here before?
The monk replied, "I have. The Master said, "Go and drink tea. He then asked another monk, who replied, "I have not been here before. The Master said, "Go and drink tea.
The head of the monastery asked, "Why is it that for having been here, he is told to 'go and drink tea,' and for not having been here, he is also told..."
“Go drink tea,” [the Master] said. He summoned the head of the monastery; when the attendant responded, the Master said, “Go drink tea.
Again, a monk asked, “The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master said, “When I was in Qingzhou, I made a cotton robe that weighed seven *jin*.
A monk asked, “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? The Master said, “No. The monk continued, “Even up to the Buddhas...”
"Down to the ants, all possess Buddha-nature. Why is it that the dog does not? The Master said, "Because it still possesses the consciousness of karmic activity.
The Master said, "The great assembly is driven by the twelve hours; I, the old monk, am driven by the twelve hours."
Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo of Ezhou was the son of the He family in Quanzhou. In his youth, he paid respects to Qingyuan Yi, under whom he received the tonsure.
He then went to Baoshou Temple in Chang’an to receive full ordination and studied various sections of the Sūtras and Vinaya. He moved freely within the Zen gardens and befriended Xuefeng and Qinshan.
Departing from Daci Mountain in Hangzhou, he traveled by stages to Linji; it happened that at this time, Linji had returned [to his home region].
Ji then visited Yangshan. Later, he went to study under Deshan. Taking up his sitting cloth, he ascended the Dharma hall and looked around.
Deshan asked, "What is this? The Master gave a shout. Deshan said, "Where does the old monk’s fault lie? The Master replied, "A double case. He then descended and entered the hall.
Deshan remarked, "This master is somewhat like a true traveler on the pilgrimage. On the following day, [Deshan] questioned him.
Xuanzhen asked, "Venerable, were you the one who arrived yesterday? He replied, "I was. Xuanzhen said, "Where did you learn this pretense?
The Master said, "Quanhuo never deceives himself. Xuanzhen said, "In the future, do not let me down.
Once, while Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Deshan’s monastery, the meal was late. Deshan took up his bowl and went down to the refectory.
While Yangshan was drying his rice-cloth on the mountain peak, he saw Deshan and said, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded; where are you going with your alms bowl?
Deshan then returned directly to his quarters. Yangshan reported this to the Master (Linji), who said, "How great indeed is Deshan!"
“[The Patriarch] has not yet realized the final phrase. Upon hearing this, Mount [Dongshan] ordered his attendant to summon the Master and ask him:

“Do you refuse to acknowledge me, old monk? The Master secretly revealed his intention, whereupon Mount ceased [his questioning]. The following day, when he ascended the hall, it was indeed different from his usual manner.

When the Master reached the front of the Sangha Hall, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying: “I am glad that the old fellow at the head of the hall has finally realized the final phrase! He—[the Patriarch]—...
Later, no one in the world could do anything with him. Nevertheless, he lived for only three years (after three years, he indeed manifested his passing).
One day, while conversing with Xuefeng and Qinshan, Xuefeng suddenly pointed to a bowl of water. Qinshan said, "The water is clear; the moon appears.
Xuefeng said, "The water is clear; the moon does not appear. The Master kicked away the water bowl and departed. The Master resided at Yanguan in Ezhou.

Daoyou encountered a period of suppression [of the monastic community] and became a ferryman by a lake. He hung a board on each bank; whenever someone came to cross the ferry, he would strike the board once.
The Master would say, "Who is it? If someone replied, "I wish to go to the other side," the Master would then dance with his oars to welcome them.
One day, an old woman came carrying a baby in her arms and said, "I do not ask about 'presenting the oar and dancing with the oars'—[but what about this?]"
"Tell me, from where did the child in the old woman’s hand come? The Master struck her. The old woman said, "I have given birth to seven sons;
six did not meet with a true知音 (zhīyīn—'one who knows the sound'), and this one alone was not worth keeping, so I threw him into the water.

Later, the Master dwelt in a hermitage on Mount Wòlóng (Wòlóngshān) at Dōngtíng (Dòngtíng). Disciples gathered there in great numbers. He said, "I once studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for seven or eight [days]."
In his later years, he saw two or three passages of meaning that seemed like the talk of a patch-robed monk (śramaṇa). He said, "Rest, rest.
At that time, a monk came forward, bowed, and requested the Master to give an exposition. The Master said, "The intent of my teaching is like the three dots of the letter *A* (𑖀).
The first dot is placed toward the east; it opens the eyes of all bodhisattvas. The second dot is placed toward the west; it [opens] the [eyes] of all bodhisattvas..."
The life-force of the *sattva*. Third, one places a dot above and below, dotting the crowns of all Bodhisattvas;
this is the meaning of the first section. Furthermore, it is said: "The intent of my teaching is like Maheśvara, who splits open his face and raises a single eye";
this is the meaning of the second section. Furthermore, it is said: "The intent of my teaching is like a drum smeared with poison; when struck once,"
All who heard of it, whether far or near, were struck with grief. This is the third section of meaning. A monk from under Jia Shan went to Shi Sang;
as soon as he stepped across the threshold, he said, "I hope you are well. Shi Sang said, "There is no need for that, Reverend. The monk said, "In that case, take care."
He went back to the Master’s quarters and asked as before whether he had been practicing. The Master sighed once. The monk said, "In that case, I shall take my leave.
As he was about to turn back, the Master said, "Though you are but a junior, you are indeed capable of maintaining your practice. The monk returned and reported this to Jia Shan.
Shangshang Tang said, "The other day, a monk from the lineage of Yantou and Shishuang came out and related the previous story exactly as it happened.
When the monk had finished speaking, Shangshang asked, 'Does the assembly understand? The assembly was silent.
Shangshang said, 'If no one can say anything, I shall speak without sparing even my two eyebrows. He then said, 'Although Shishuang has [this]...'"
"There is the sword that kills, yet there is no sword that gives life. Yantou also possessed the sword that kills and the sword that gives life.

Once, while you and Luoshan were surveying the site for a pagoda, as you were resting, Luoshan bowed and asked, "Master, is it not true that thirty years ago, when you were at Dongshan, you did not approve of Dongshan? You replied, "It is so. He asked again, "Master, is it not also true..."
“This is Shide Mountain,” he said. “And yet you do not approve of Shide Mountain. The Master said, “I do. Shide said, “I do not approve. De Shan did not ask further;
rather, he asked, “As for Dongshan, what deficiency does he have? The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, “Dongshan is a fine Buddha, but he simply lacks radiance.
Shide bowed. The Master once told the assembly, “When this old man departs, I shall let out one great roar and then go. Tang.
After the Guangqi era, bandits rose up in the Central Plains and everyone fled their lands; yet the Master remained seated in tranquility as if nothing were amiss.
One day, when the rebels arrived in great numbers and demanded provisions that he could not provide, they stabbed him with blades. The Master’s countenance remained composed;
he let out one great cry and passed away, the sound heard for many tens of li. His disciples later cremated his remains and obtained forty-nine *śarīra* relics.
The assembly erected a stupa for him.
Chan Master Wenyuan of Guangfeng Monastery on Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyang Prefecture was a native of Jiaxing. His surname was Zhang.

In his youth, he relied upon Vinaya Master Zhicheng of Kongwang Temple to leave the household life and shave his head. He received full ordination at the platform in Pilu (Vilinyā) and attended upon Master Cheng.

For several years, he thoroughly investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka. Because his own fundamental matter remained unclarified, he went to visit Muzhou. As soon as Muzhou saw him approaching, he closed the door.
The Master knocked on the door. Muzhou asked, “Who is it? The Master said, “It is I. Muzhou asked, “What are you doing?

The Master said, “My own fundamental matter remains unclarified; I beg the Master for instruction. Muzhou opened the door, and upon seeing him, immediately closed it again. The Master did this repeatedly.
He knocked on the gate for three consecutive days. On the third day, the Governor opened the gate; the Master entered, whereupon the Governor seized him and said, "Speak! Speak!
The Master hesitated, and the Governor immediately pushed him out, saying, "A wheel-rim from the time of Qin! He then shut the gate, injuring the Master's foot.
From this, the Master attained awakening. The Governor pointed him toward Xuefeng. When the Master arrived at Xuefeng’s manor, he saw a...

The Master asked the monk, "Elder, are you going up the mountain today? The monk replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Entrust a kōan (a causal phrase) to the Abbot for me; however, you must not say it was the words of another person. The monk replied, "I understand. The Master said: [The Master then sent him off. The monk went up the mountain and delivered the message to the Abbot. The Abbot asked, "Where did you get this? The monk replied, "From the Master at the West Hall. The Abbot said, "Bring it here. The monk brought it back. The Abbot read it and said, "This is truly the words of a true man of the Way. He then gave the monk a robe and a bowl as a reward. When the monk returned to the Master, the Master asked, "How did the Abbot respond? The monk related the events in detail. The Master said, "He is indeed a man of great capacity. The Master then gave the monk a robe and a bowl as well. Later, the Master asked the monk, "Did you tell the Abbot that it was my words? The monk replied, "No, I did not. The Master said, "If you had told him so, he would have struck you dead on the spot. The monk asked, "Why did you not tell him yourself? The Master replied, "If I had told him myself, he would have struck me dead on the spot. The monk then asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "An ancient mirror reflects the face; A single hair pierces the eye. If you can see through this, Then you will know the source of the spring. The monk bowed deeply and departed. The Master sighed and said, "This fellow has truly attained the marrow. The next day, the Master summoned the monk and asked, "Have you forgotten the previous matter? The monk replied, "I have not forgotten. The Master said, "Bring it here. The monk brought it back. The Master said, "This is truly the words of a true man of the Way. He then gave the monk a robe and a bowl as a reward. When the monk returned to the Master, the Master asked, "How did the Abbot respond? The monk related the events in detail. The Master said, "He is indeed a man of great capacity. The Master then gave the monk a robe and a bowl as well. Later, the Master asked the monk, "Did you tell the Abbot that it was my words? The monk replied, "No, I did not. The Master said, "If you had told him so, he would have struck you dead on the spot. The monk asked, "Why did you not tell him yourself? The Senior Monk went into the mountains and saw the Master ascending the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the monk stepped forward, clasped his wrists, and stood on the ground, saying, "This old fellow wears an iron cangue around his neck; why does he not cast it off?

Feng said, "That was not your words. The monk said, "It was my words. Feng said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff!

Feng said, "Let the assembly go to the estate to welcome the 'Five Hundred-fold Man of Knowledge' (a term for a great teacher) who has arrived. The next day, the Master [arrived].
He ascended Xuefeng Peak. As soon as the Master saw him, he asked, "For what reason have you reached such a state? The Master then bowed his head. From that time on, they were in accord.

Having studied together for many years, Xuefeng secretly transmitted the seal of the school to him. The Master left the mountain range and traveled extensively to visit various masters, investigating their diverse methods until he had exhausted them all.
His sharp eloquence was formidable and peerless, becoming widely renowned throughout the world. Later, he arrived at Lingshu Temple, where he attained a profound resonance with the teachings of Zhi.
Regarding the statement that Master Sheng received the position of Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera):

when it was first known that Master Sheng had resided at Lingshu for twenty years without appointing a Head Seat, he would often say, "My Head Seat has been born," "My Head Seat is tending the ox," and "My Head Seat is traveling on pilgrimage."

One day, he ordered the bell to be struck. The assembly went out from the outer gates of the three entrances to welcome the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera). When the Master arrived, they directly invited him into the Head Seat’s quarters to unpack his belongings.

Later, the Abbot of Guangzhu commanded the Master to take charge of the Lingshu Monastery. On the day of the opening of the hall, the Abbot came in person and said, "I, your disciple, request your instruction.
The Master replied, "Before one's eyes, there is no other path. Thereupon, he asked the assembly, "From the time of the ancient masters onwards..."
What is lacking in this great matter? To tell you that there is "nothing" is already to bury you.
Nevertheless, you must reach this state before it can be attained. Do not ask haphazardly just to satisfy your immediate curiosity;
your own mind is pitch black. Great matters lie ahead tomorrow and the day after. To conceive of a thought is already an error, let alone to speak words.
There is a phrase. Is it that not directing the mind toward it? Do not misunderstand this. What else is there?
You people, when you hear someone speak of the meaning of the Patriarchs, you immediately ask for talk that transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs.
But what do you call a Buddha? What do you call a Patriarch? First, explain the principle of that which transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs. Ask about the "going forth."
"The three realms! You take these three realms and look at them: what sights, sounds, sensations, or cognitions are there that obstruct you?
What sounds, objects, or phenomena are there that you can perceive? What is it that you perceive? The ancient sages were at their wits' end."
Transversely manifesting the body for the sake of beings—this is called "the entire body is the absolute truth. To perceive every single thing as its very essence is impossible.
When I say to you, "Right now, what matter is there? it already constitutes a mutual obscuration. There are two kinds of illness when light does not penetrate through:
first, being unenlightened in all places such that there is something before one's face; second, having penetrated through to the emptiness of all phenomena.
It is as if there is something vaguely present; this too is because the light has not been fully penetrated. Furthermore, there are two kinds of illnesses regarding the Dharmakāya.
First, having attained the Dharmakāya, one fails to forget the attachment to dharmas, and because one's own views still persist, one remains seated within the realm of the Dharmakāya.
Second, even if you manage to penetrate through the Dharmakāya, you must not let it pass unexamined; you must scrutinize it with great care.
"Come! What manner of breath is there? This too is illness. The Master taught the Way at Lingshu Yunmen for thirty years.

In the seventh year of the Qiandao era, on the tenth day of the fourth month of the Jisi year (1009 CE), he passed away peacefully. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the abbot’s quarters.

Shi Yuan’an was a native of Linyou in Fengxiang. He left home as a youth and received full ordination; he mastered the sutras and śāstras and sought the Way from Linji.
Linji would often praise him before the assembly, saying, "A single arrow from the gate of Linji—dare anyone face its point?
Having received this seal of approval, the Master considered himself sufficient. One day, he took his leave of Linji, who asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "To the South."
"Go! Linji said, striking the ground with his staff once and adding, "If you can pass through this, then go.
The Master (Huangbo) then gave a shout; Linji struck him, whereupon the Master bowed and departed. The following day, Linji ascended the hall and said:
"Under Linji’s gate there is a crimson-tailed carp that has shaken its head and wagged its tail as it headed south. I know not in whose pickle jar it will be drowned."

After the Master had finished his travels, he went directly to Jia Shan and set up a hermitage there. For a year, he did not visit Jia Shan. Jia Shan composed a letter and ordered a monk to deliver it.

Upon receiving it, the Master sat down immediately; yet he reached out his hand again for the letter. The monk was at a loss for words. The Master struck him and said, "Go back and report this to the Abbot.
When the monk returned and reported it, Jia Shan said, "If this monk had opened the letter, within three days [the Master] would certainly have arrived."
"Come. If you do not open this letter, this man cannot be saved. The Master indeed arrived three days later;
seeing Jia Shan, he did not prostrate, but instead stood facing him with his hands joined at his chest. Jia Shan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix's nest—it is no match for its kind."
[The Master] went out. The Master said, "I have come from afar to seek your presence; I request that you grant me an interview. Yunmen said, "Before my eyes there is no *sāriputra* (disciple);

As it is said, when Dongshan was struck three times with the staff, did he have the 'lot' to receive the blows, or did he not?
Nan replied, "He had the lot to receive the blows. Ming assumed a stern expression and said, "If that is so, then from morning until evening..."
"When magpies screech and crows caw, there is likewise a share of receiving the staff. Ming then sat upright, received three incense offerings from Nan, and paid his respects.
Ming asked again, "Zhaozhou said of the old woman of Mount Tai, 'I have thoroughly investigated and exposed her. Tell me, where exactly was it that he exposed the old woman?
Nan broke into a cold sweat and could not provide an answer. For several days, Ming entered the room to request a resolution.
Zhaozhou Ming only used insults and abuse. One day, Nan said, "Is abuse not the compassionate Dharma-gift?
Ming asked, "Do you take my words as being about abuse? At this, Nan attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "Standing out from the forest is Zhaozhou."
The old wife has seen through him; there is no ground for it. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror. Travelers, do not treat the road as an enemy.
He presented this to Ciming, who gave his approval.
Shi Zonggao’s sobriquet was Dahui; because he resided at Miaoxi Hermitage, he was also called Miaoxi.

He was born into the Xi family of Xuancheng and was the reincarnation of Yunfeng Yue. Possessing spiritual roots from a long time past, his wisdom-nature was innate. When he was only twelve years old...
He immediately sought out Master Huiyun Qi. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk. Initially, he studied under the gate of the Dong lineage.

Because of the sharpness of the master’s verbal prowess, an elder of the Dong lineage lit incense on his arm and transmitted the mind-seal to him. The master, however, did not accept this himself and departed.
Having relied on Zantang Zhun for a long time without attaining resonance, Zantang fell ill and sent him to see Yuanwu.

Yuanwu was residing at Zhaojue in Sichuan, so the Master hesitated and did not proceed. One day, he heard that an imperial decree had been issued to transfer Yuanwu’s residence to Tianning Temple in Bianjing.
He said with joy, "Heaven has granted this old man to me. He then traveled ahead to Tianning to welcome Yuanwu, calculating to himself: "This shall be my end."
The Ninth Summer. If those in other quarters were to falsely claim that I am right, I would depart wearing my "Treatise on the Absence of Chan.

Upon meeting Wuzhuo, who was opening the hall for teachings, he cited a monk’s question to Yunmen: “What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen replied, “Walking upon the water east of the mountain.
Wuzhuo said, “Tianning does not say it that way; I simply tell him: ‘A fragrant breeze comes from the south,’ and then [he points to] the hall.”

A slight coolness arose within the Master’s chamber. Upon hearing this, the Master’s past and future suddenly severed; he attained enlightenment and said: "It was not easy for you to reach such a state.
However, it is a pity that you have died and cannot yet live again. To have no doubt regarding words and phrases is a great illness.
Have you not heard it said: 'Letting go at the precipice, one spontaneously accepts it; after death, one revives once more—this cannot deceive the Buddha. You must believe this."
There being these reasons, he was appointed to reside at Jue-mu Hall as an attendant not engaged in administrative affairs.

Later, hearing that Master Wuzhuo had been asked about the saying, "A phrase exists or does not exist; it is like a vine leaning against a tree," the Master then asked him, "I heard that when you were with the Fifth Patriarch, you once asked him about this same story.
I do not know what the Fifth Patriarch said. Wuzhuo laughed and...
He did not answer. The Master said, "Since you questioned the Abbot before the assembly at that time, why should it trouble you to speak now?

Being at his wit's end, Wuzhuo said, "I asked the Fifth Patriarch, 'What is the meaning of the phrase: "The phrase exists, yet the phrase does not exist; like a vine leaning against a tree"? The Patriarch replied, "'It cannot be described, nor can it be painted.

He asked again, "'When the tree falls and the vine withers, what then? The Patriarch replied, "'The mutual dependence.'"* *Note: The term "xiang" (相) here refers to the state of mutual interdependence or the condition of being mutually defined.*
He came accordingly. Master [Wu] immediately released him, whereupon he attained great enlightenment and said, "I understand! Wuzhuo cited several preceding causal episodes to interrogate him;
in every instance, his responses were unhindered. Delighted, Wuzhuo said to him, "Now I know that I did not deceive you."
He then composed the *Record of the True Lineage of Linji* and entrusted it to him, charging him with the duties of the secretarial office.

Not long after, Yuanwu returned to Shu, whereupon the Master withdrew into obscurity and lived in a thatched hut. Later, he spent the summer retreat at Huqiu, where he was reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the passage concerning the Bodhisattva of the Seventh Ground attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he suddenly attained a profound and clear realization of what Tanzhang had previously shown him regarding the story of Aṅgulimāla carrying his alms bowl.

The Circumstances of Saving a Childbearing Woman. In the seventh year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, an imperial decree ordered the Master to reside at Shuangjing. One day, news arrived that Yuanwu had passed away;
the Master composed a written memorial for the funeral service himself. That same evening, he gave a small-scale sermon (xiaocan), citing a monk’s question to Changsha regarding Nanquan’s passing.
"Where have you gone? The Sandalwood Monk said, "I am a donkey in the eastern village and a horse in the western village.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Sandalwood Monk said, "If you want to ride me, you ride; if you want to dismount, you dismount. If it were Jingshan, it would not be so.
If a monk were to ask my late teacher Yuanwu where he has gone after his passing, I would tell him: 'He has fallen into the Avīci Hell.'"
"What is the meaning? [The Master] said, "When hungry, one eats molten copper; when thirsty, one drinks iron dregs. "Is there anyone who can save such a person?
He replied, "No one can save them. "Why cannot they be saved? He replied, "Because this is the ordinary meal of this old man.

In the fifth month of the eleventh year, Qin Hui accused the Master of being a partisan of Zhang Jiu-cheng. Consequently, his monastic robes and certificate were revoked, and he was exiled to Hengzhou.
In the tenth month of the thirty-sixth year, an imperial edict was issued to transfer him to Meiyan. Not long after, he was restored to his secular appearance and released to return home.

By imperial decree, he was to reside at Ayuwang Monastery; subsequently, an edict was issued ordering the Master to take up residence at Mount Jing, where he extensively propagated the school of Yuanwu. In the spring of the Xinsi year.
He retired to Myeongwol Hall. One night, the assembly saw a star fall to the west of the temple, its trailing light blazing brilliantly.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested a slight illness. On the ninth day of the eighth month, he said to the assembly, "I shall depart tomorrow.

That evening at the fifth watch, he wrote a final testament by hand and entrusted his posthumous affairs to the community. A monk named Ryoeon requested a verse, and the Master wrote it out in large characters: "Born..."

Just so. Even in death, it is just so. Whether there is a verse or not, what does it matter? He passed away peacefully at the age of seventy-five, having spent fifty-eight summer retreats in the monastic community.
His posthumous title was Pujue (Universally Awakened), and his stupa was named Baoguang (Jewel Light).
Shi Shouchun, whose style name was Fodeng, was the son of the Shi family of that commandery. Initially, he visited Master Guangjian Ying, but did not find resonance.
He then went to see Fojian, following the assembly to seek instruction; however, he made no progress at all. Thereupon, he sealed his bedding and declared:
"If I do not attain thorough penetration in this life, I swear never to unfold this again. From then on, he sat by day and stood by night as if mourning a parent, for more than...
After seven weeks, Fojian suddenly ascended the hall and said, "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma.
Upon hearing this, Xun attained sudden enlightenment. Fojian remarked, "What a pity! A bright pearl has been picked up by this madman.
He then questioned him, saying, "Lingyun said: 'Since the first time I saw the peach blossoms, until now I have never again doubted.'"
"What is it that he does not doubt? Xun said, "Do not say that Lingyun has no doubts; even now, if one seeks a point of doubt, it is utterly unattainable.
Jian said, "Xuan Sha said, 'It is perfectly accurate, most perfectly accurate. I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate.
Wherein lies his failure to reach the ultimate? Xun said, "I deeply understand that the Master’s heart is filled with such compassionate concern. Jian nodded in agreement.
Xun bowed, rose, and presented this verse: "All day long I gazed at the sky without lifting my head; only when the peach blossoms were in full bloom did I raise my eyes.
Even if you possessed a net that could cover the heavens, once you have penetrated the secure barrier, you may simply rest. Master Jian instructed him to protect and uphold [the Dharma].
That evening, as he was spreading out his bedding, he spoke in a stern voice, saying, "This time, Upādhya Yaoshun, you may sleep soundly.

When Yuanwu heard this, he privately doubted that it would be so and said, "I must test him before I can accept it. He then sent someone to summon him; they subsequently went out for a walk in the mountains together.
They happened upon a pond. Yuanwu pushed Xun into the water and immediately asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch?
Xun replied, "The pond is deep, so the fish gather. Yuanwu asked, "What was it like after he saw him? Xun replied, "The tree is tall, so it beckons the wind."
[The Master] asked, "What is it like when seeing and when not yet seeing? Xun replied, "Stretching out one's legs is within drawing them back in.
Yuanwu greatly approved of this. Later, he entered the world; he first presided over Heishan, then Tianxing, followed by Heshan and Tianning.
In the Jia-yin year of the Shaoxing era, he said to the layman Zheng Ji: "The eighth day of the tenth month is the anniversary of the passing of our late master Fojian. At that time, I—"
It was perfect. When he eventually returned to the south of Zhang, on the fourth day of the tenth month, Tanji sent his younger brother, Sengdaoru, to inquire after him.
Huijun said, "Your coming is exactly at the right time. Although I and Fojian were born from the same branch, we shall ultimately not die from the same branch."
"Tomorrow morning, you may find a small boat for me. Daoru said, "I require one that is long and high.
Xun replied, "About five feet high. Three days later, at the crowing of the cock, he sat upright as usual. His attendant requested a verse, and Xun said, "I have not composed one.
Having spoken thus, he passed away. At his cremation, his tongue remained unburnt.
Shi Huiyuan was the son of the Peng family of Meishan. At the age of thirteen, he received the tonsure under Zongbian of Yaoshi Monastery.
He first attended the lecture hall of Daci and subsequently studied under Chan Master Lingyan Hui. He attained some degree of insight.

Coinciding with this, Yuanwu led his realization and resided at Zhaojue; Huiyuan went to join him. He happened upon Yuanwu’s general discourse, in which Yuanwu raised the case of Layman Pang asking Mazu, "Do not give..."

Yuan was the companion-in-dharma of Wanfa. One day, while at a distance, Yuan suddenly attained sudden enlightenment and collapsed among the assembly. The assembly helped him up, whereupon Yuan said, "I have awakened from my dream.
Later that night, during the small *sīmān* (private instruction), Yuan came forward and asked, "Pure and naked, empty with not a single thing;
bare-boned and poor, with not a single coin. My door is broken and my house is ruined; I beg the Master for relief. Wuzhuo replied, "The seven treasures and eight jewels."
Once, Nanquan seized [Wuzu] by the collar. Yuan said, "Calamity does not enter the door of a prudent household. Wuzu said, "The pivot does not leave its station;
you have fallen into a sea of poison. Yuan then gave a shout. Wuzu struck the meditation seat with his staff and asked, "Have you taken this blow yet?
Yuan shouted again. Wuzu shouted twice in succession. Yuan then bowed. From that time on, his spiritual edge became sharp and piercing, meeting no resistance whatsoever.

He entered the world [of public ministry]. Initially, he resided at Gaotingshan to manifest filial piety. On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Qiandao era of the Song dynasty, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Lingyin Monastery.
Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "What is it like when 'this very mind is Buddha'? He replied: "The crown of the head is divided into points. The monk asked:
"What is it like when 'neither this mind nor that Buddha'? He replied: "Earrings of golden rings. The monk asked: "Neither this mind nor..."
“The Buddha is not a thing. [The Emperor asked,] “Then how is it? Yuan said, “A bald-headed asura dances the *zhazhi*.
On the fifteenth day of the second month of the seventh year, [Yuan] was summoned to Xuande Hall and granted a seat. Emperor Xiaozong asked, “How can one escape birth and death?
Yuan replied, “If one does not awaken to the Great Way, one will ultimately never be able to escape. The Emperor asked, “How does one attain awakening? Yuan replied, “It is originally present.”
The nature of this—when investigated thoroughly—there is none who does not awaken to it. The Emperor asked, "What is it like after awakening?
Yuan said, "Only after awakening does one know that the naked body is manifest before one, with not even a hair’s breadth of any perceivable form. The Emperor nodded in agreement.
The Emperor asked again, "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' what is that? Yuan said, "There is no dharma before one's eyes; Your Majesty, what do you call 'mind'? The Emperor said:
"What is the mind? Huairang stood with his body upright and hands at his sides, saying, "It is just this. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

On the seventh day of the eighth month in the autumn of the eighth year, he summoned Huairang to the Eastern Pavilion and offered him a seat. The Emperor said, "The other day, while in a dream, I suddenly heard the sound of a bell and then woke up.
I do not know how this dreaming and waking are related. Huairang replied, "Does Your Majesty ask about the dream, or do you ask about the waking?"
If one asks about awakening, it is precisely the language of sleep; if one asks about dreaming, there is no difference between dreaming and awakening. Who could be taught to make such distinctions?
A dream is itself an illusion. To know illusion is to be detached from it; the awakened mind is unmoving. Therefore it is said: "If one can transform things..."

[Zhao]zhou said, "It is identical to the Tathāgata. The Emperor asked, "If dreams and illusions are non-existent, from where does the sound of the bell arise? [Zhao]zhou said, "It arises from the place of questioning.
The Emperor asked again, "The other day, while sitting here in this pavilion, I suddenly thought of the saying, 'Not being a companion to the myriad dharmas.
I have a certain point of view on this. [Zhao]zhou said, "I wish to hear it. The Emperor said, "'The four seas are not too many. [Zhao]zhou said, "A single mouth..."
"What if one were to completely suck up the waters of the West River? The Emperor said, "There has never been any deficiency.

Yuan said, "As soon as one engages in thought, it becomes an extraneous dharma. Even if it were like cutting a spinning wheel or a flash of lightning, there would be no connection whatsoever. Why is this so?"
Because the Dharma is non-dual, he saw no dualistic views; because the mind is without a separate mind, it was like the sky having no second sun.
The Emperor was delighted and bestowed upon him the title "Great Master Hai" (Ocean). In the first month of the third year of the Chunxi era, he suddenly felt a slight ailment.

On the day of Shangyuan, he spoke this verse: "Bend and break the scale-weight; overturn the official proclamation. Suddenly emerging before the trigger-mechanism, the wild bird flies beyond the pass. He sat peacefully.
He passed away and remained for seven days; his countenance did not change, and he was interred whole within a stupa.
Shi Anmin, whose courtesy name was Miyin, was the son of the Zhu family of Jiading. He initially gained renown by lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in Chengdu.

At that time, Yuanwu resided at Zhaojue Temple, so Anmin went to visit him. He happened upon Yuanwu’s informal discourse (*xiaocan*), during which Yuanwu raised the story of the National Teacher calling out to his attendant three times.

Regarding this causal condition, Zhaozhou took it up and said: "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters themselves do not take shape, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest.
"Where is it that the traces are already manifest? When Min heard this, he was filled with doubt. He went to the incense burner and entered the room [to seek instruction].

Wuzhuo asked the Master of Lectures, "Which sutra are you expounding? He replied, "The Śūraṅgama Sūtra. Wuzhuo said, "In the Śūraṅgama, there are seven places where the mind is sought, and there is the 'entry and return'..."
Wuben was discerning his views. "Ultimately, where does the mind reside? Many disciples presented their interpretations of the meaning, but Wuben did not approve of any of them.
The disciples requested further instruction again. Wuben told them, "The literary patterns have already been revealed. At that time, a monk happened to request instruction on the *Ten Mysteries*.

When Wuben raised the question, "What is the appearance of the Mind-Seal you hold? Wuben spoke in a stern voice, "The literary patterns have already been revealed. Upon hearing this, the disciple was delighted. However...
He considered himself to have reached the ultimate. When he was shown the "tongs and hammer" (the methods of Zen instruction), he was at a loss for what to do.

One day, he said to Wuzhuo, "I request that you do not raise the topic of a koan; wait until I speak it myself. Wuzhuo replied, "Agreed. Min said, "When one habitually brandishes the mallet or raises the whisk, is this not what is taught in the scriptures:
'All phenomena in all worlds, every mark that exists, are all the wondrously luminous true mind of Bodhi'? Wuzhuo laughed and said, "You originally..."

He came here to make his living. The layman said, "When you shout 'Down! and strike the meditation bench, is this not 'turning the hearing back to hear the nature,' whereby the nature achieves the Unsurpassed Way?
Yuanwu said, "Have you not seen it stated in the sutras that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and forms?
At these words, the layman was liberated. Thereupon, he ceased his lectures and attended upon Yuanwu, due to that realization.

He left Sichuan and resided at Jia Shan. The local people followed him, and Wuzhu gave a small-scale discourse (xiaocan) for the assembly. He cited the kōan regarding the "ancient sail not yet hoisted.

When the man heard this, he did not yet understand it and requested a definitive resolution. Wuzhu said, "Ask me. The man repeated the previous story, and Wuzhu said, "The cypress tree in front of the courtyard.
At that moment, the man attained clear penetration and said to Wuzhu, "The ancients said, 'It is like a single drop falling into a vast abyss'—how different [this is from that]!"
Not knowing that the great ocean had been cast into a single drop, Wuxue laughed and said, "What can be done with this fellow? He spoke a verse, saying:
"Do not boast of having mastered the *Lengyan* in four sections; Lower your mental state and investigate thoroughly from the very depths. Do not emulate Master Liang who went personally to Mazu."
He was like Deqiao visiting Longtan; for seven years he traveled back and forth to Zhaojue, and for three years he soared above the Azure Cliffs.
Today, I trouble you to serve as the First Seat, appearing like an udumbara flower amidst a thicket of blossoms.

Before long, he opened a Dharma center at Baoning and later moved to Huazang, where he widely propagated the Way of Yuanwu. Afterwards, he manifested illness at his native mountain; upon cremation, śarīra relics were discovered.
There was a considerable surplus; people even found it by digging the earth for a foot or so, and it was especially radiant, lustrous, and pure.
His heart and tongue remained undecayed, and a stupa was erected for them.
Shi Baoyin, styled Biefeng, was the son of the Li family from Jiazhou. In his youth he mastered the Six Classics, and as an adult he thoroughly investigated the Seven Histories.

Suddenly weary of the mundane world, he set his mind upon the ancient scriptures of India. He then received the full precepts from Qingsu of Dingshan and went to listen to lectures on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*, fully grasping their essential meanings.
Realizing that laboriously counting grains of sand was ultimately not liberation, he subsequently relied upon Chan Master Min Yimian of Mount Zhongfeng.
Yimian cited the question: "When arising and ceasing do not cease, what is it like? Yimian rebuked him, saying: "It is this!"
"Who is it that arises and ceases? Upon hearing this, the Master attained great enlightenment. When Yuanwu returned to Zhaojue, he sent the Master to visit him.
Following the assembly into the inner room, Yuanwu asked, "How do the sages of the past receive people? The Master held up his fist. Yuanwu said, "This is what I, an old monk, use.
What is it that the sages of the past use? The Master struck him with his fist. Yuanwu also raised [his own fist].
They crossed their fists and stopped with a great laugh. Later, he visited Da-hui at Mount Jing. Da-hui asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From West Sichuan.
Da-hui said, "Before you even left Jianmen Pass, I would have given you thirty blows of the staff. He replied, "It was not fitting for me to trouble the Master. Da-hui was pleased.
Subsequently, he went forth and, by imperial decree, resided at Xuedou. In the autumn of the seventh year of the Chunxi era, the Emperor summoned the Master.
He asked about the Way. [Zongmi] was granted a shoulder sedan and entered Xuande Hall. The Emperor said, "Do the sages of the Three Teachings not fundamentally share this same principle?
He replied, "It is like empty space; whether east, west, south, or north, it is originally no different. The Emperor said, "However, the gateways established by the sages are indeed different.
For instance, Confucius established his teaching through the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean). Zongmi said, "It is not merely the 'Mean'."

How, then, is the world established? Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Worldly speech, the occupations for sustaining life, and so forth, are all not in contradiction with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Without destroying worldly appearances, one accomplishes the supramundane Dharma."
The Emperor said: "In this age, many of the scholar-officials who study Confucius are merely skilled in words and language;

they do not perceive the Way of the Master, nor do they understand the mind of the Master. Only the Chan school of the Buddhists does not teach by means of written texts, but points directly to the source of the mind, enabling sudden awakening and entry [into enlightenment].
Thus, they remain undisturbed at the moment of birth and death; this is truly superior."
Yin said: "It is not only that later generations have failed to see the heart of the Master.

Even when we look back at Yanzi of the Confucian school, who was hailed as one who embodied the Master's form, he exerted all his life's strength yet could only say, 'Looking for him, he is before me;
suddenly, he is behind me,' never managing to grasp him. Yet the Master clearly opened the eight characters wide and spoke to his disciples: 'Two or three...'"
"Do you think I am hiding anything from you? I have nothing hidden from you. There is no action of mine that I do not share with you, my disciples;
this is simply Qiu. Judging by this, the Master never once avoided his disciples, yet the disciples themselves failed to understand him.
As Zhang Shangying once said: "Only after studying Buddhism was I able to truly understand Confucianism. This—
"His words are indeed [profound]. The Emperor said, "My own thought is also that this is so. The Emperor asked again, "What kind of person was Zhuangzi?
Yinyuan replied, "He was merely a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) within the Buddha-dharma, a person at the level of a Śrāvaka or below.

This is because those of the Lesser Vehicle loathe the body as if it were shackles and discard wisdom as if it were mixed poison; they seek to incinerate the body with fire and enter the realm of non-action. This is precisely like Zhuangzi."
What you have called "the body being made like withered wood and the mind being made like dead ashes" does not apply to those of the Mahāyāna.
They do not realize Bodhi until all sentient beings have been saved. This is just as Yi Yin said:
"I am one of the people of Heaven who has first awakened; I shall use this Way to awaken these people. If there were even a single person who did not receive its...
"To me, it is as if I were pushing them and casting them into a ditch. The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict for him to reside at Mount Jing. He ascended the hall and said:

"The Buddhas of the three periods of time expound hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of phrases from a single phrase; they gather those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of phrases back into that single phrase."
It rests entirely upon a single phrase. In the gate of the Patriarchs, there is not even half a phrase. If you simply act like this, how many painful blows of the staff do you deserve?
You all, tell me: are the Buddhas right, or are the Patriarchs right?

If you say the Buddhas are right and the Patriarchs are not, or that the Patriarchs are right and the Buddhas are not, you have not yet abandoned grasping and rejecting. If you say that Buddhas and Patriarchs are both right at once, or both not right at once—[what then?]
This is indeed so; it is not a matter of mere superficiality. For now, let us cut through this tangle of vines: how would you say it? After a long silence, he said:

"A tiger wearing a paper hat—amusing, yet startling. In the second month of the tenth year [of the Shaoxing era], the Emperor annotated the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Yuanjue jing*) and bestowed an imperial decree upon the Master to compose a preface for its circulation.
In the eleventh month of the first year of the Shaoxi era, he went to visit Chan Master Zhice to bid him farewell.

When the date for his passing was set, the Master said, "The channel will be completed when the water arrives. He then took paper and wrote these nine characters: "On the seventh night of the twelfth month, at the hour of cockcrow.

Indeed, he passed away on that very day. His body remained for seven days with a radiant complexion; his hair grew longer and the crown of his head remained warm. He was buried in full body on West Ridge.
The memorial stele was titled *Cibian* (Compassionate Eloquence), and the stupa was named *Zhiguang* (Wisdom Light).

Shi Miguang, styled Huian, was the son of the Li family in Min. From birth, he spoke little and seldom smiled; however, whenever he heard monks chanting the *Banzhou Sanmei Jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra), he would rejoice.
At the age of fifteen, he followed Chan Master Wenhui and shaved his head. He delighted in investigating a multitude of books. One day, he reflected:
Having shaved his head and donned the dyed robes, he intended to attain thorough enlightenment; yet, did he instead become intoxicated by worldly classics?
He first visited Yuanwu, then studied under Huangbo Xiang and Gao'an Wu; their dialogues and words were all in accord. Because bandits had risen in Huai and Chu, he returned to visit Foxin.
It happened that Daohui was staying at Guangyin, so [Feng] went to him. Daohui said, "Try to cite one or two instances of what you have attained while in the Buddha-mind.
Guang said, "When the Buddha-mind ascended the hall, he took up the public case of Puhua and said: 'The Buddha-mind is not like this.'"
"When one does not come in this way at all, what then? [Zhaozhou] struck him across the spine. "Let him manifest his body throughout the entire world," said [Zhaozhou].
Huì asked, "What is your intention? [Guǎng] replied, "I do not approve of that final footnote he added. Huì said, "This is precisely using a disease to remove a disease.
Guǎng remained resolute and could not find it convincing. Huì said, "You must simply contemplate and examine it for yourself. Guǎng did so, and eventually—
He thought this was not so. After ten days had passed, he recalled how Master Haiyin Xin had once remarked: "The thunder is vast and loud, yet there are no raindrops at all.

At that moment, Guang’s mind became unobstructed, and he hurried to inform Dahuì. Dahuì questioned him regarding the words of Daozhe Jue who saw Langya, as well as the statement that Xuansha had not yet reached full penetration.
After Guang had answered, Dahuì laughed and said: "Although you have taken a step forward, you have merely failed to settle in a specific place. It was like...
When a person cuts down a tree, a single stroke at the root severs its life-force. If you were to cut at the branches, could you possibly sever that life-force?
Nowadays, people everywhere are speaking of Chan in great abundance, yet their perspectives are all like this; what benefit does it have for the actual matter?
As for the authentic lineage of Yangqi, there are only three or four people remaining. Guangwen departed in indignation. The next day, Huai asked him, "Have you returned?"
"Is there any doubt? he asked. [Wuzu] replied, "There is nothing to doubt. Huì said, "As for the ancients meeting one another, they knew whether a person was genuine or not before a word was spoken;

or upon hearing their speech, they immediately recognized the depth or shallowness of their realization. How is this principle to be understood? Guāng stood trembling with sweat pouring down his body.
He did not know where to go. Huì instructed him to investigate the words "with phrase" and "without phrase. As Huì passed by Yunmen’s hermitage, Guāng also accompanied him as an attendant.
One day he asked, "I have reached this point but cannot attain thorough penetration. Where does my illness lie? Huì said, "Your illness is most chronic.
Why do the physicians of the world fold their hands in helplessness? Others die and cannot live; you, however, are now alive."

Shi Shanji, whose style name was Juezong, was the son of Lou of Yue. His mother, Lady Wang, dreamed that a divine monk bestowed upon her a white lotus, whereupon she became pregnant.

At the end of the Yuan dynasty, one day he suddenly informed the assembly, sat upright, and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age and had sixty-three years of monastic seniority.

He did not speak or laugh frivolously, and each day he recited several thousand words from the classics and histories, never forgetting a single character throughout his life.

Subsequently, the Master returned once more to Gupingtian Temple on Mount Tiantai, where Wang Sikou Jingsuo of Linhai entered [the path]."

He traveled to the mountains to seek the Way, establishing friendships beyond formal boundaries. He subsequently moved to Mount Huading and Mount Tianzhu, where he practiced the Great and Small Amitābha Repentances for six years.

Dispelling delusion: when the gloom has spread for ten thousand *li*, sitting peacefully at the edge [of existence], one intends to open the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
