Shi Yuanwu, whose style name was Miphan, was surnamed Jiang and was a native of Yixing. From birth, he was dignified and solemn; during his youth, reflecting on the impermanence of the world, he diligently recited the Buddha’s name.
Upon accidentally encountering the *Platform Sutra*, he realized that there was a point of entry into the supreme path of the Chan school.

Whenever he traveled through the mountains or passed through cities and markets, he engaged in investigation and inquiry in all circumstances. One day, while carrying firewood across a mountain, he was struck by a pile of wood and attained awakening.
Upon hearing that the Dharma was being transmitted at Yumen and performed at Longchi, he went there to serve [the Master] and receive the tonsure.

After three years had passed, he frequently examined his own mind and state, and whenever he encountered the teaching that "heaven and earth share a single root" and "all things are of one body," he would request further instruction; however, he was often rebuffed.

He rebuked him. [Zhaozhou] harbored resentment and fell ill; consequently, he closed the mountain gate. When Guishan passed by the gate, they discussed the principles of having a mind and being without a mind.
The Master presented a verse, saying: "Mind and mind are one's own mind; Existence and non-existence are both one's own mind. Existence and non-existence are both one's own mind;

Without mind, there is no 'one's own mind. Guishan did not grant him permission. After another three years, he was appointed to oversee the affairs of the monastery. He exerted himself with vigorous diligence, and suddenly—
On the summit of Mount Tongguan, he realized that the sentient and the insentient were radiantly manifested as equal.

He then went to visit the Dragon Pond at the capital, where the Master of the Pond tested him; subsequently, he entrusted him with the Dharma of Non-abiding and sent him south to travel. From Shuangjing, he proceeded to Liangmu.
Tiantai [Zhili] had his long-standing doubts resolved by various eminent masters, yet none failed to be struck with wonder and exclaim that they had never before experienced such things.
When Zhili returned to [Fengxue] Chanshi, he sought the Master’s counsel on how to support the Buddha-dharma. The Master presented him with the verse on "Praise and Punishment:

Thirty Strokes of the Staff," to which Zhili joyfully handed over his fly-whisk. Not long after, Zhili passed away. The Master, moved by the profound kindness of this "Dharma-milk," observed a period of mourning for three years, remaining solitary and forlorn.

Suffering from lingering illness, he kept his mind fixed upon every object before him. In the *dingyi* year of the Great Ming Wanli era, he traveled far to Mount Kuangheng; returning, he rested at Tongxuan Temple on Mount Tiantai.
There, the wind of his school spread widely. The following year, responding to the invitation of Jinsu, he dwelt among the thorns and brambles, subsisting on wild chrysanthemums and morning glory.
Dragon-elephants vied with one another to seek refuge under him. Before long, magnificent halls rose up, fully conforming to the regulations of a monastic forest (*saṃghārāma*).

He supported ten thousand monks in his meals. Wherever the Master traveled, those who came to gaze upon and pay homage—both monastics and laypeople—were so numerous and crowded that they blocked the roads, making it impossible to proceed.
Even from places separated by mountains and rivers at a distance of several thousand *li*, people would labor over every inch of the journey to request his presence. For them, the Master...

In dispelling ignorance and guiding those with stagnant understanding, it was as if he were personally receiving the hot iron rod [of discipline]. Thus, his teachings and influence spread to the four quarters.

In the winter of the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era, he returned from Huangbo to Jinsu; those who sought refuge from all directions increased even more. Changzhi entered the inner chamber and was granted the dharma name Tongchang.
Huang Yuangong, the Magistrate of Li, invited him to reside at Tiantong. Formerly, Mount Tiantong stood preeminent among the Five Mountains.

Upon his arrival, he found that the site had been submerged by a great flood; amidst the red cliffs and verdant walls, only desolate ruins remained. He consequently undertook the task of reconstruction.
After ten years, the pavilions and halls were lofty and grand, the chambers and rooms were layered and interconnected; from afar, it appeared like rising clouds and gathering mists.

The assembly of those carrying calabash staffs and straw hats was thrice as numerous as the grains of gold at Sūvarṇadvīpa. Once the Master had completed the restoration of the ancestral pagodas, he immediately intended to withdraw into seclusion.

His vow was to provide instruction throughout his entire life. He took up the seventeen hundred koans of the past and, with his fly-whisk, severed all entanglements and cleared away the clouds and mist.

As for those he guided—ranging from princes, dukes, and elders down to slaves and the lowliest of the low, from the five bhikṣus and ten disciples to even those of the icchantika class—he universally gathered them in with his compassionate light. Just as...
A verse composed spontaneously says: "Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one sleeps at will; Who cares for the heavens of east, west, south, or north?
Only I am uniquely honored, my entire body manifest; When someone comes to question me, I simply offer a coarse fist. The author of this work is Fachengbian.

Like the sound of a bell or the reflection in a mirror, he does not fall into the obstacles of language and writing. Wherever the Dharma banner raised by the restorer is honored, it becomes a jeweled monastery (*ratnagṛha*).
Yet, with but a single staff and a single fly-whisk, he wanders freely beyond all things, never creating a single mark of dwelling.

In the Xinsi year of the Chongzhen era, Grand Preceptor Tian, acting on the command of the Imperial Noble Consort Tian, personally carried purple robes into the mountains to request that the Master perform a dharma ritual.
He then invited the Master to reside at the Great Baoen Temple in the Southern Capital; however, the Master declined the offer on account of his advanced age and physical frailty.
On the seventh day of the seventh month of that year, he manifested illness and passed away while seated in the full lotus posture. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on South Hill at Tiantong.
The monk Tongrong, whose style name was Feiyin, was surnamed He and was a native of Fucheng. At the age of fourteen, he took refuge under Master Zhudong at Huishan.
Fahai first visited Shouchang and Boshan, and later heard of Mipan at Yunmen. Subsequently, hearing that Mipan was staying at Houshan, he went there to pay his respects.
He was struck [by the master], whereupon all his former cleverness and intellectual views were completely dissolved like ice. Yun then asked him: "The fragrant breeze blows from the south."
"A subtle coolness arises in the halls and pavilions. How do you understand this? The Master said, "The water flows cold from the edge of the rocks;
the wind comes fragrant from within the flowers. Yun then withdrew. Subsequently, Yun became the abbot of Jinsu and was appointed to the position of West Hall.
The following year, he accompanied [the Master] to Huangbo, where the lineage robe and whisk were conferred upon him.
In the *bǐzǐ* year of the Chongzhen era of the Great Ming, the Master moved from Huangbo to Jinsu; in the *bǐxū* year, he moved to Tiantong; he then moved to Chaoguo, and subsequently to Foyan.
In the *Gengyin* year of the Great Qing Shunzhi era, the Master accepted an invitation from the local military commander, the district magistrate, and various local gentry to ascend Mount Jing.

There he forged and refined his disciples, never flagging through cold or heat. An imperial gift of a staff and a verse was bestowed upon him, which read: "The manifestation before one's eyes cannot be depicted;
its wondrous operation transcends the mundane, leaving no trace of delusion. Pointing out the human realm, it clears and opens the orthodox lineage—just like [the teaching of] Tiantong."
The Master said: "Tell me, where do the patriarchs of successive generations establish their dwelling and sustain their lives?
Is it in heaven or among men? Be glad to know there is no connection. Is it in the palaces of Māras or the realms of Buddhas? Be glad to know there is no connection.
Is it that they cannot abide where there is a Buddha, and must hurry past where there is no Buddha? Be glad to know there is no [connection]."
Regarding this negotiation: if you can here discern the matter with absolute clarity and certainty, it is clearly like an iron bun—let it be bitten crosswise or chewed vertically as you wish;
there is no hindrance, and everyone has their share. Furthermore, Chaoguo showed [his students] by saying: "Exhaustively investigate and examine: what is the meaning?

I say: The Great Way is thus vast and expansive; the ten directions have no boundaries, and all eight sides are free from obstruction.

Wherever the eyes look and wherever the hand points, high and low are universally responded to, and left and right one encounters the source. To take from it is inexhaustible; to use it is never-ending.
Every matter returns to the ultimate source; every instance accords with the pivot. When the Great Function manifests, it does not abide by fixed rules. How could this be...?
It is not for those who seek the most perfect and sudden Dharma-gate. Furthermore, a spontaneous verse by Jing-shan says: Five peaks unfold like five lotus flowers;
The secluded abode of the Brahma palace is truly praiseworthy. Successors of the Dragon and Elephant lineage are beyond counting;
The ancestral lamp continues its flame without bound. Azure pines flank the path as they soar into the void; Verdant bamboos hide the heavens as the sun slants down. I have ascended this Dharma seat.

He spoke of the profound; surrounded by ten thousand mountains, he sat cross-legged with a smile. With a single heart of compassionate concern, he was diligent and tireless, unaware that old age was approaching.

Shi Haoming, whose style name was Poshan, was the son of the Jian family from Shu. Having received the full precepts in his early twenties, he followed the Dharma Master Hui to lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
When his doubts remained unresolved despite his inquiries, he left Shu and resided at Mount Poutou.
After three years of strenuous exertion, while walking in meditation, he suddenly beheld a level world and inadvertently fell down the cliff, injuring his foot. This occurred at midnight.
He turned over; in his intense pain, he attained realization and cried out, "Injustice! Injustice! A layman asked, "Is your foot hurting, Master?
The Master struck him across the face with a single palm and said, "This is not your realm. He subsequently studied under Boshan, then under Yunmen, and later under Tiantong.
The boy asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "Yunmen. The boy asked, "When did you set out? The Master said, "The sun rises red over the Eastern Mountain.
The boy said, "What does the sun rising red over the Eastern Mountain have to do with you? The Master said, "Old as you are, old as you are!"
There was still this lingering talk. The monk said, "Since I am thus, from where do all these complications of yours come?

The Master roared a shout with great majesty and immediately entered the room. Later, the monk asked, "When there is no letting out from within and no letting in from without—at such a time, what serves as the boundary?

A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas arise from the mind; the myriad dharmas cease within the mind. If they neither arise nor cease, where does the mind reside? The Master said, "Xie San-niang does not recognize four characters.

turning pale with alarm, he said, "The earth is tilting as the army marches—how can Bo possibly be captured? He then sent Huian to inquire of Fotudeng.

Shi Le followed this advice and ultimately made use of his services. Later, Shi Le usurped the title of Heavenly King of Zhao and acted as Emperor;

Thereafter, his devotion to Daocheng became even more earnest. Shi Hu had a son named Bin, who was later adopted as a son by Shi Le.

Shi Le loved him exceedingly; however, he suddenly fell ill with a violent disease and died. Two days had already passed when Shi Le said, "I have heard that when the Prince of Guo died, Bian Que was able to restore him to life.

He enchanted some willow twigs with incantations, and in a short while [the boy] was able to rise; after a moment, he had recovered. From then on, he raised most of his young sons within Buddhist temples.
Whenever the eighth day of the fourth month arrived, Fu Le would personally go to the temple to perform the ritual ablution for the Buddha and make vows on behalf of his children.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of the Jianping era, the sky was calm and windless, yet a single bell atop the stupa rang out by itself.
Fo Tucheng said to the assembly, "The sound of the bell says that there will be a great national mourning before the end of this year. In the seventh month of that year, Shi Le died;
his son Shi Hong succeeded him to the throne. After a short time, Shi Hu deposed Hong and established himself as ruler, moving the capital to Ye and adopting the era name Jianwu.
Shi Hu devoted himself wholeheartedly to Tucheng, treating him with even greater reverence than he had shown to Shi Le. He then issued an edict stating: "The Monk is a great [asset] of the state."

As for the title of "Treasure" (Bǎo), he did not accept the conferred rank; as for high emolument, he would not receive it. Since honor and emolument were not his concern, by what means could his virtue be signaled?
From this point forward, it was appropriate that he be clothed in brocade and silk, and ride in an ornately carved carriage.

On days of court assembly, when the Upādhyāya ascended the hall, all officials from the rank of *Chángshì* downward assisted in lifting the sedan chair, while the Crown Prince and the various dukes supported him from the sides as he ascended. At that time, Crown Prince Shísuì plotted...
[The Prince] acted perversely. He said to his inner attendant: "The Upādhyāya possesses supernatural powers; should he discover my plot, he will come tomorrow. You must eliminate him first.
On the fifteenth day of the month, Fotudeng was about to enter the palace for an audience with Shi Hu. He said to his disciple Senghui: "Last night, a celestial deity called out to me, saying:
'If you enter tomorrow, do not pass by anyone. Should I happen to pass by someone, you must stop me. Fotudeng—

Fashi Sui was constantly entering [the meditation chamber] to check on Daosheng. Sui knew that Fotudeng was inside. He waited for a long time, enduring great hardship. When Fotudeng was about to ascend the Southern Terrace, the monk Huì pulled at his robe.
Fotudeng said, "The matter cannot be stopped. Before he had even settled into his seat, he rose. Sui insisted on keeping him, but could not stop him. His plan was consequently thwarted.
Returning to the temple, he sighed and said, "The Prince’s rebellion is about to succeed. I wish to speak, yet it is difficult to speak; I wish to endure it, yet I cannot."

It was difficult to bear. Consequently, he calmly offered a reprimand to Hu regarding the matter, but in the end it could not be resolved. Suddenly, the incident broke out, and only then did [Hu] realize the truth of Fotudeng’s words.
Later, when Guo Heilüe led troops to campaign against the Qiang tribes in the northern mountains of Chang’an, he fell into an ambush set by the Qiang.
At that time, Fotudeng was seated in his hall with the disciple Fachang by his side; Fotudeng’s expression turned somber, and he said, “Master Guo is now in peril. He began to chant—
The assembly of monks offered prayers for his well-being, and Fotucheng himself also offered prayers. After a short while, he said again, "If he emerges from the southeast, he will survive;
if he heads in any other direction, he will fall ill. He prayed once more. A moment later, he said, "He has escaped. More than a month later, Helü returned.

He himself stated that he had fallen into a Qiang encirclement and escaped to safety by fleeing toward the southeast. Upon calculating the date and time, it was precisely the moment when Fotudeng had offered his incantations and vows.
Shi Hu’s son, the nominal Grand Marshal and Duke of Yan, Shi Bin, was stationed as the Governor of Youzhou.

A multitude of wicked men gathered together and used this as a pretext to commit violence. Fo Tucheng cautioned Shih Hu, saying, "Last night, a celestial deity told me to quickly collect the horses and return them;
by autumn, you shall suffer from festering sores. Shih Hu did not understand these words, yet he immediately issued orders to all locations to collect the horses and send them back.
That autumn, someone slandered Fu Bin to Shi Hu. Hu summoned Bin and whipped him three hundred times; he then executed Bin’s biological mother, Lady Qi.
Hu drew his bow and notched an arrow, personally supervising the execution of Bin’s punishment. Finding the punishment too light, Hu then slew five hundred people with his own hands.

Tong Cheng remonstrated, saying, "The mind must not be indulged; death cannot be brought back to life. According to ritual, one does not personally slaughter animals, for it would wound the bonds of affection.

How could there be a Son of Heaven who personally carries out punishments? Thus, Shi Hu desisted. Later, when the Jin army emerged from the Huai and Si rivers, all the cities north of the Long Mountains were besieged.
As the three frontiers sent urgent pleas for help and public sentiment became distressed and turbulent, Shi Hu said with indignation, "My devotion to the Buddha..."
"He provided offerings to the Sangha, yet foreign invaders were subsequently brought about; thus, the Buddha has no divine power. On the following morning, Fotucheng entered early.
The tiger questioned Cheng regarding this matter, and Cheng therefore admonished him, saying: "In a past life, Your Majesty was once a great merchant leader.

When you reached a monastery in Kaśmīra, you once made offerings during a great assembly that included sixty arhats; my humble self was also present at that assembly at that time, having attained the Way."
A person said to me, "This master’s life is at its end; he is destined to receive the body of a chicken.
Later, when you rule the land of Jin, this man will become your king. Is this not indeed a blessing? Border skirmishes and military incursions are but the normal affairs of a state;

why do you harbor resentment and slander the Triple Gem, giving rise to such poisonous thoughts in the night? Thereupon, the tiger attained faith and enlightenment, knelt down, and apologized. The tiger once asked Fo Tucheng, "The Buddha-dharma prohibits killing."
"I am the sovereign of the world; were it not for punishments and executions, there would be no way to bring stern clarity to the realm.

Since I have violated the precept against killing living beings, even though I serve the Buddha, how could I possibly obtain blessings? Seng-cheng replied, "When an emperor serves the Buddha, he should embody reverence and accord his heart with the Way."
To manifest and clarify the Three Jewels: one must not be tyrannical or cruel, nor harm the innocent.

As for those who are wicked, foolish, and reckless—those whom transformation cannot move—one should simply execute those who deserve execution and punish those who deserve punishment. However, if one is tyrannical and acts according to one's own whims, killing and harming those who are not guilty, [this is a transgression].

Although Shi Hu disregarded wealth and served the Buddha, he lacked understanding regarding calamities. While Hu was unable to follow all [of Daorong’s] advice, the benefit he derived from it was nonetheless not small.
At that time, there was a prolonged drought from the first month until the sixth month. Shi Hu dispatched his crown prince to Fankou, west of Linzhang, to pray for rain.
After a long time had passed without any response, Hu ordered Fotudeng to go himself. Immediately, two white dragons descended into the shrine.
On that day, there was heavy rain over an area of several thousand *li*, and that year’s harvest was bountiful. Fo Tucheng frequently sent his disciples to the Western Regions to purchase incense.

the bandits were startled for no apparent reason and cried out, "Reinforcements have arrived! They abandoned their prey and fled. Later, Hu repaired an old stupa in Linzhang.

Beneath the ground lies a dew-receptacle pedestal and a Buddhist image, over which the forest vegetation has grown thick. You may excavate and retrieve them. He then drew a map and gave it to the messenger.

[The Emperor] asked for someone of superior strength; as soon as such a person was found, he was sent to propagate the teachings, and Xu Xing granted his permission.

At that time, the monastic community in Guanzhong looked upon one another with a sense of deficiency, none daring to step forward. Kumārajīva said to Sengrong: "This non-Buddhist is exceptionally intelligent compared to others; if we debate him, he will surely prevail.

If you were so inclined, the axle of the Wheel of Dharma would be shattered—how could such a thing be allowed? What I have observed rests upon you alone.

They all assembled before the imperial palace. The monastic community from the Guanzhong region gathered from all directions. Daorong engaged with the Brahmin in debate, their sharp arguments soaring into the profound mysteries;

"Can you protect it? How could it possibly be obtained? Huiliang said, "If this is truly due to merit, let it be shared with you, my benefactor.

The temple possessed so much bronze that even after taking but one-tenth of it, the boat was already full.
On the head of the divine bed, there was only a spittoon, inside of which was a lizard about two feet long, darting in and out. Sengliang did not take it and departed;

yet he did not waver in his resolve. The Emperor was greatly incensed and ordered him to renounce the Way and serve as General Guangwu, stationed at the Hall of Splendor (Huadong Dian).

Although Huiyuan’s conduct became like that of a layman, his mind remained settled in meditation and the precepts, never failing in his integrity. After a short while, the Emperor passed away, and Empress Dowager Zhao issued an order:
He was granted leave to return and resided at Zhengsheng Temple. Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty personally served the young sovereign and was constantly anxious about the unpredictable future;

When Emperor Gao ascended the throne, he treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher. When Emperor Wu succeeded him, he likewise showed him the utmost respect as a teacher. Crown Prince Wenhui once went to the temple.
He went to inquire after his health. Since Huiyuan did not command him to sit, Wenhui performed a prostration and remained standing.

He then asked Huiyuan, "If one offers worship by playing the *baochui* and the *qingnao* drums, what kind of merit does this produce? Huiyuan replied, "In the past, when the Bodhisattva offered eighty thousand musical performances to the Buddha, it was still not equal to a sincere heart.
Now, you blow through bamboo tubes and beat dead ox-hide drums; how is this even worth mentioning?"
The king, his nobles, and their consorts, as well as the officials and commoners from the four quarters, all received the precepts from him and followed the etiquette due to a teacher.

Yuan was also skilled at chanting and exhortation, and he expounded the Dharma in accordance with the sutras. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill; at that time, a fire broke out near the temple, and the temple lay downwind.
As the flames were about to reach him, the disciple wished to carry Huiyuan out of the monastery. Huiyuan said, "If the Buddha is being burned, what use is there for me to live?
He then focused his mind with single-minded devotion to the Three Jewels. Thereupon, all three sides were consumed by fire, yet only the monastery remained unscorched.
In the second year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of eighty-seven, he passed away.

Shi Tanwu-zui, surnamed Dong, was a native of Wuan. From his youth, he received the transformation of the Way; his reputation spread throughout both the court and the common world. He recited the sutras and śāstras and strictly upheld the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He was particularly fond of *dhyāna*, and his mind was empty, tranquil, and serene. At times, he would lead others by example, and all held him in high esteem and veneration.

Furthermore, he was extensively versed in both the profound mysteries and Confucianism, and he was especially clear in expounding the Way. Most weary of worldly entanglements, he intended to renounce the four classes of followers and set forth on his journey.

Shi Jianghui primarily prioritized the precepts and prohibitions. Once, while preaching the *śīla* at Chongzun Temple in Handan, there were over a thousand followers in the assembly, all of whom were his regular disciples.

On the thirtieth day of the fourth month, during the *poṣadha* ceremony, as the voting sticks (*śalākā*) were distributed according to their seating positions, sixty individuals appeared who were not among the usual count.
They sat at the very head of the rows, causing him to marvel deeply at this anomaly. Since there was no...
The assembly outside remained in doubt throughout the night. At dawn, they questioned him again. Some saw him coming from the west of the city of Handan;
they were all eminent virtuous monks of extraordinary character, their robes properly adjusted and their gait dignified and elegant.
Others saw him coming from the eastern side of Mount Gushan. Those who encountered him along the way all said he was going to attend the Venerable One to hear the monks recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
In this manner, through successive stages of calculation, when their ages were verified and the number of people was counted, it exactly reached sixty; thus, the spirits descended from afar.
Later, by imperial decree, he resided at Rongjue Temple in the capital of Luoyang. Its corridors and halls were vast and extensive, spanning three *li*.

He was most skilled at widely propagating the teachings and had a profound mastery of the *Nirvāṇa* and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras. With a community of a thousand monks, his daily activities were constant and tireless.
Dai (Zhiyi). When the Indian śramaṇa Bodhiruci saw him, he prostrated before him and titled him the "Bodhisattva of the Eastern Land.

He once read the *Mahāyāna-yìzhāng* (Treatise on the Meaning of Mahāyāna) composed by Zhì, and every time he snapped his fingers in praise, saying, "Excellent! He then transliterated it into Sanskrit characters and sent it to be transmitted to Da-xi (Central Asia).
Those who read it there all faced the east to prostrate to him as a sage. Nevertheless, he [Bodhiruci] always considered [Zhì] to be one who propagated the Dharma.

This was the occasion. In the first year of the Zhengguang era of the Northern Wei dynasty, Emperor Ming donned his court robes and issued a general amnesty. He invited representatives of the two traditions of Buddhism and Daoism to ascend the dais.

Upon the conclusion of the fast, the Palace Attendant Liu Teng proclaimed the imperial decree, requesting that the various Dharma masters engage in a debate on the principles of doctrine with the Daoist practitioners.
At that time, the Daoist Jang Bin of Qingtongguan engaged in debate with Paramārtha. The Emperor asked whether the Buddha and Laozi were contemporaries.
Jang Bin replied, "Laozi entered the West to convert the barbarians and become a Buddha, and the Buddha served as his attendant;
this account appears in the *Laozi Kaitian Jing*. Based on this, it is clear they were contemporaries. Paramārtha then asked, "Under which king was Laozi born?"
Regarding the year he entered the West, Bin said: "It was in the third year of King Ding of the Zhou dynasty.

He was born on the night of the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the village of Qu-ren, in Li-hang, Ku-xian, Chen-zhou, within the state of Chu. In the fourth year of King Jian, he served as the Keeper of the Treasury.
In the first year of King Jing, at the age of eighty-five, seeing that the virtue of the Zhou was declining, he subsequently departed westward with Yin Xi, the Magistrate of San-guan."

The account of [the Buddha] entering the conversion of the barbarians (*hu-hu*) becomes clear through this. Zuì stated: "The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhaowáng of the Zhōu dynasty.
He entered *nirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Zhaowáng. Calculating from his entry into *nirvāṇa*:
Three hundred and forty-five years passed until the third year of King Ding, when Laozi was finally born.
Having been born at the age of eighty-five, he reached the first year of King Jing after a total of four hundred and thirty years, at which point he fled westward with Yin Xi.
This represents a vast discrepancy in dates; is it not erroneous? Bin asked: "If it is as you say, from what text does this account derive?"

Huiji said: "The *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies from the Book of Zhou) and the *Han Fa Ben Neizhuan* (Inner Biography on the Origin of the Dharma in the Han) both contain explicit records [of this].
Sengbin asked: 'If Confucius established the laws, the Sage should have made them clear. Why is there no mention of the Buddha at all in those texts? Huiji replied:

'Confucius’s Three Collections and Ten Classics include the Buddha’s words within the *Zhongbei* (Middle Collection). Your reverence perceives only a narrow range, like looking through a tube; your vision does not extend far. "

"How can he possibly reach [the truth] on his own? The Emperor then sent Yuan You, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to proclaim an edict: "The Daoist Jiang Bin’s discourse lacks any fundamental principle; he should be ordered to leave the assembly.
Furthermore, it was discussed that the *Kaitian jing* (Scripture of Opening Heaven) must be debated: by whom was it spoken? Wei Shou, the Vice Director of the Central Secretariat, [was appointed].
Zu Ying, Lang of the Secretariat; Xiao Zong, Grand Marshal; Li Shi, Grand Tutor; Xu Bo Tao, Commandant of the Imperial Guard; Xing Luan, Minister of Personnel;
Wen Zisheng, Attendant Censor, and others—numbering one hundred and seventy persons—consulted the scriptures at the observatory.
Having finished their reading, they submitted this report: "Laozi composed only the Five Thousand Words; there are no further discourses. This is what we, your servants, have deliberated."

Jiang Bin’s crime was that he sought to delude the masses. At that time, the Emperor was about to inflict the ultimate punishment upon him, but the Tripiṭaka Master from the Western Regions, Bodhiruci, earnestly remonstrated, and the execution was halted.
He was instead banished to Mawei. His learning surpassed that of the Wei historians, and his fame spread far and wide.

Consequently, eminent Confucian scholars and court officials descended from their steps to pay him respect, prostrating themselves at his feet in refuge. It was solely due to his efforts that the Buddha-Dharma was revived.
He devoted himself to his duties, and later his end remained unknown.
Shi Zhixuan was a native of Chengdu in Yizhou; his surname was Xu. At his birth, the room was filled with radiant light. He left home to become a monk in his youth.

He entered the capital to study, and within a few years, he had established a reputation throughout the regions of Jing and Luo. It happened that Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty abolished Buddhism and intended to preserve Daoism;
he consequently issued an edict to assemble all monks and Daoist masters to test them, retaining those deemed superior and excelling while abolishing those found mediocre or shallow.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to summon eminent monks from Huayen and Daoist masters from the various provinces, as well as practitioners of occult arts from a thousand li away, to assemble in the capital.
High seats were arranged in the Taiji Hall, and the Emperor himself attended in person. He commanded the Daoists to ascend first.
At that time, there was a Daoist named Zhang Bin, who climbed to the high seat and proclaimed: "Originally, the Way of Man is pure and void, simple and without admixture. I pray—"
I respectfully entreat for blessings. May [this teaching] ascend to the celestial bureaus so that one may rise as an immortal in broad daylight, with a lifespan coextensive with heaven and earth.
Its transformative influence first reached the Central Lands; it is without beginning and without end, and all living beings rely upon it to attain longevity.

How could it be like the Buddhist teachings, which are illusory and whose claims exceed reality? Unable to find a home in their own land, they dwell as guests in the Middle Kingdom. The common people, being ignorant, believe in these deceptions.
He said, "Today we wish to determine right and wrong; you may step forward and look.

When the Duke of Xiangcheng, He Tuo, personally took the seat of honor at the head of the assembly, the Meditation Master Dengxing of Shaolin Temple rose in indignation. The monks restrained him, saying, "The matter today is of great importance.
The Heavenly Emperor is present here; one must not act rashly. In responding to him, one must also possess quick wit and eloquence. The assembly...
They deliberated together, saying, "If it were not for Shu Xuan, there would be no one capable of responding to and upholding [the teachings]. Together they recommended Ruyi to be entrusted to Xuan.
Once Xuan had taken charge of Ruyi, he said to Zhang Bin, "The Great Way you have presented, O Master, is pure and void, simple and without admixture."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the teachings of the wind [Confucianism] were first received in the Central Xia," it is unknown when these teachings originated or from what time they arose;
as for the teachings spoken, in what place did those teachings exist? Moreover, you say that the Buddha-dharma could not be accommodated in its own land and thus resides as a guest in China.

One might ask: at what time was this [Confucian] debate produced, and at what time did the Buddha appear? The Guest replied: "When a Sage appears in the world, how can there be any fixed [time or place]?"

"At that time, when the teachings were proclaimed and put into practice, what fixed location was there? The Way of the Teachings (Daojiao) has existed fundamentally from of old; the Buddha-dharma has only recently come from the West. Xuán said:
'If one says it did not exist at that time, then it should likewise have no origin. If there were no fixed location, then there should likewise be no preaching.

That which has existed fundamentally from of old is not something newly empty and void. If one petitions the Celestial Bureau for longevity, how could it possibly be without admixture? Longevity is coextensive with Heaven and Earth.'"
[The debate] concluded. [The Emperor asked: "How can it be that there is neither beginning nor end? The Guest replied: "The Daoist speaks in vain.
It was because the former kings lacked discernment that they retained people like you until the present day. Today, under the Sage Emperor, all must be put to death.

The Emperor loathed this defeat in argument and ordered an attendant to say to him: "Guest Master, please descend. Once the Guest had withdrawn, the Emperor ascended the high seat himself and said: "Buddha..."
Within the Dharma, there are three kinds of impurity. First, taking Yaśodharā as his wife and fathering Rāhula constitutes the impurity of the master.
Second, within the Sūtras and Vinaya, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to accept the three kinds of pure meat; this constitutes the impurity of the teaching.

Third, the members of the Saṃgha frequently commit transgressions and take pleasure in licentiousness; while the Buddha was in the world, his disciples were not in harmony and instead attacked one another.
"This assembly is impure; this is the third [point]. Both the presiding master and the assembly are impure. It is my intention to remove them to extinguish these empty illusions.
Within the Way and its teachings, such a thing does not exist. I shall instead retain them to assist in the transformation of the state.

He then turned to the Dharma Master Xuan and said, "One who can resolve these three difficulties is truly a good man. Xuan replied immediately, saying, "That which Your Majesty has set forth is entirely..."
The citations from the sutras and śāstras are indeed not erroneous words. However, within the teachings of the Way (Dao), there are three kinds of impurity that are even more extreme than this.
According to the records, when the Celestial Honored One resides in the Palace of Purple Microcosm (Ziwēi Gōng), he is constantly attended by five hundred maidens;

this mastery over impurity far exceeds that of Yaśodharā alone. Furthermore, in the Daoist teachings, when performing incantations and offerings to pray for blessings, one must necessarily use [deer...].
There were a hundred platters of dried meat and ten *hu* of clear wine. This teaching is even more impure than the three kinds of pure meat.

Transgressions by Daoist masters have existed in every generation; for a thousand ages they have disrupted the constant order. That Jiang Bin violated the law was even worse than that of the assembly of monks.
The monastic community has committed transgressions of its own accord, yet they claim that the Buddha-dharma can eliminate them.
This is like a sovereign who, while ruling the realm with strict laws and regulations, cannot prevent rebellious sons and treacherous ministers from appearing one after another.

Would one, because of such treacherous ministers and rebellious sons, wish to vacate the throne of great sovereignty? Indeed, the throne of great sovereignty cannot be abandoned simply because of the rebellion of ministers or sons.
"The Buddha-dharma is empty, correct, and true; how could it be abandoned simply because the Sangha has committed an offense? Xuan’s tone was refined and modulated, his voice clear and resonant.
Although he stood before the sovereign in a moment of great gravity, he never showed even a trace of fear.

After a long while, the Emperor looked on in astonishment and asked Xuan, "Regarding what you said about the Celestial Honored One being attended by five hundred maidens—where does this appear in the sutras? Xuan replied, "It appears in the *Sanhuang jing* of the Daoist tradition. The Emperor said:
"Where in the *Sanhuang jing* has such a statement ever appeared? Xuan replied, "It is simply that Your Majesty has not seen it; it is not that there is no such text in the scripture.
To now wish to abolish Buddhism and preserve Daoism is like attempting to replace the legitimate heir with a commoner. The Emperor’s expression changed, and he withdrew into the inner palace.
The assembled ministers and the monastic community were all alarmed, saying, "His words have offended the Son of Heaven; how can he protect himself? Xuan replied, "The King has been insulted."
"Your servant shall die; to face execution is like returning home—what is there to fear? It would be better to perish early so that my spirit may roam in the Pure Land;
how could I wish to share this world with an unrighteous ruler? The assembly was moved by his words. The following morning, an edict was issued abolishing both religions.
The Dharma Master and three of his fellow students proceeded to the capital of Qi. At that time, the borders between Zhou and Qi were all covered with spears and pikes.

There was a wealthy old woman surnamed Zhang who spread out felt rugs for thirty *li* so that Xuan could pass through. He eventually reached the Qi capital and became a Tripiṭaka Master, his fame resounding throughout the eastern lands.
When Emperor Wu conquered Ye, he first dispatched messengers to seek him out. The Emperor’s younger brother, Prince Yue, had been close with the Dharma Master;

fearing that the Emperor might vent his wrath and impose arbitrary punishments upon him, he whipped the Master’s back until it bled and dressed him in lay clothing before presenting him to the Emperor. Prince Yue...
The King first spoke, saying: "I regret that he fled for his life, so I have already administered sixty lashes and ordered him to strip off his clothes to appear before Your Majesty.
The Emperor changed countenance and said: "I fear he may feel such shame that he flees far away and even dies. That is why I pursued him so urgently; I truly had no intention of harming him.
He then rebuked the King of Yue, saying: "How can a great man insult another with the scourge of a whip? Thereafter, he treated him with even greater courtesy and generosity.

He returned to the capital. After Emperor Wu passed away, Emperor Wen of Sui assumed the regency and greatly propagated the Buddha-dharma; he was the sole individual to whom both capitals turned for refuge.

As the year drew toward autumn, he felt a deep longing for his native land and, further reflecting that the remote region of Shu had not yet seen the profound teachings proclaimed there, he became concerned.

Daoyuan returned westward, his mind intent on spreading the Dharma; yet Prince Xiu of Shu was unaware of this. At that time, the Regional Inspector Zhou Xuaming was entering the capital for an official examination.
Emperor Wen of the Sui addressed him, saying, "Is Master Xuan healthy? Xuaming was struck with alarm and did not know how to respond.
The Emperor said, "A renowned monk of the entire realm, and you do not even recognize him? How can you fulfill the duties of an inspector?"

Xuānmíng bowed his head in prostration and offered a formal apology for his transgressions. Upon returning, he went first to the monastery to pay his respects. The monastery had originally been located to the east, bordering the imperial gardens;
furthermore, it was the site where Prince Poyáng had buried his mother. Because the prince had been exceptionally filial, the monastery was named "Xià'ài" (Filial Affection) Monastery.

Xuānmíng moved the establishment [to its current location] and maintained the offerings without fail. As the Dharma Master’s propagation of the teachings grew weary, he entered Sanxué Mountain. He encountered...

Mudu was deeply moved and subsequently traveled to the mountains. He composed a poem, saying: "Stately ridges meet with layered mists; The precipitous peaks reach halfway to heaven. The sheer cliffs seem lower yet rise higher;
The perilous crags are severed yet linked again. Slanted rocks lean over the cascading ravines; Whirling currents pour forth from the winding springs.

Wild reds reveal the grasses are frozen; As spring arrives, the birds naturally proclaim it. The trees are like brocade, blazing without artifice; The wild cries need no borrowed strings. [The leaf...]

The secret winds are difficult to traverse; with sparse branches, shadows easily pierce through. Embracing my books, I rely on the quiet pond; leaning on my staff, I wander through the desolate fields. My mind roams beyond the clear Milky Way;
my thoughts rest upon the white clouds. Fame and glory are not my wish; I let my will cease, remaining serenely detached.
At the age of one hundred, he passed away without illness.

Shi Huisi’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Wujin. From his youth, he was renowned for his magnanimity and compassionate upbringing. He once dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the secular world.

He took leave of his parents to enter the path of cultivation and frequently experienced the presence of divine monks who instructed him to observe the fasts and precepts. Thus, he devoted himself to maintaining his fundamental purity.
His pure conduct was refined and prudent, and he received full ordination. His resolve for the Way grew ever more lofty as he dwelt in remote seclusion.

He practiced constant sitting meditation and concentrated on his religious duties; he ate only one meal a day and refused separate offerings. He completely cut off all social interactions such as welcoming or seeing off guests.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures totaling over thirty fascicles; within a few years, he completed a thousand recitations. Furthermore, he dreamed of several hundred foreign monks whose forms—
He wore garments of rare and extraordinary beauty. The presiding elder addressed him, saying: "You have previously received the precepts; your discipline is already superior.

I shall now pray to the forty-two teachers and monks to perform the *karmavācanā* ceremony for you, so that you may achieve full accomplishment. Later, he was suddenly startled into awakening and realized it had been a dream-reception. From that time forward, his diligent labor became even deeper;
he disciplined his thoughts with focused devotion, never neglecting the transition from dusk to dawn. He sat in meditation and engaged in recitation in constant succession. Using...
He made this his constant practice. Through these ascetic disciplines, he was able to perceive the events of the paths traversed during three lifetimes.
Furthermore, in a dream, he beheld Maitreya and Amitābha preaching the Dharma and awakening him. Consequently, he fashioned two images and offered them equal veneration.

Again, in a dream, he followed Maitreya and his retinue to the assembly at the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) tree. He thought to himself: "During the final dharma-age of Śākyamuni, I have upheld the Dharma."
Huā now encountered the Compassionate Honored One; moved by deep emotion, he wept, whereupon he attained sudden awakening and redoubled his diligent practice.

Auspicious omens occurred in succession: the water in his flask remained perpetually full, and his offerings were prepared with solemnity. There was even a celestial youth who attended him as his protector.

Because he read the *Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi* and marveled at the merit of dhyāna, he immediately resolved to cultivate meditative concentration. At that time, the Dhyāna Master Huìwén [was attended by] both monastics and laypeople...
He was noble and upright. He went to take refuge [in the Triple Gem] and received the True Dharma. Day and night he restrained his mind.

Furthermore, during the coming winter, he bound his body and sat upright, binding his mindfulness before him. After only twenty-one days, a slight degree of calm observation arose, wherein he saw the signs of the good and evil karma accumulated throughout his life.

Because of this, he was struck with awe and admiration, becoming twice as courageous and diligent. Thereupon, the eight tactile sensations were stirred, and he gave rise to the fundamental first dhyāna. From this point on...
Obstacles to meditation suddenly arose; my four limbs became slack and weak, such that I could not bear to walk, and my body no longer followed my mind.

I then observed for myself: "This illness of mine now arises entirely from karma; karma is produced by the mind, and fundamentally there are no external objects. Thus, I turned back to perceive the source of the mind.

Karma cannot be grasped; the body is like a cloud or a shadow, possessing appearance yet empty of substance. Having contemplated thus, perverted perceptions were extinguished, the nature of the mind became pure, and all suffering was eliminated.
Furthermore, he lamented that his life had been spent in vain and felt deep shame and remorse.
As he leaned his body against a wall, before his back even touched it, he suddenly attained awakening to the Lotus Samādhi and the Mahāyāna Dharma-gate. Ten...

He attained the six special victories (*ṣaḍ-abhibhv-āyatana*) and realized them through his own penetration. Later, he went to masters such as Jiaozui and recounted what he had realized; they all expressed their sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
As his refinement continued for a long time, his prior contemplations increased further. His reputation and conduct became widely known, and his virtue was revered from all quarters.

His disciples grew numerous day by day, and those with spiritual capacity and awakening multiplied daily. He then expounded and illustrated the teachings of the *Sthiramati* school within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
He gathered his disciples and others. At that time, a voice resounded from the void, saying: "If you wish to cultivate meditative concentration, you should go to Mount Wudang or Mount Nanyue;
these are mountains for entering the Way. At the beginning of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, he turned away from this region of Songyang and led his followers southward.

Upon first arriving at Guangzhou, he encountered the collapse of the Liang dynasty under Emperor Xiaoyuan and the ensuing chaos of civil war. With the roads ahead blocked, he temporarily stayed at Mount Dasu for several days.

Within a year, people flocked to him like a marketplace. That region lay on the border between Chen and Qi; where the armies clashed, the Buddha-dharma was said to have collapsed and the fivefold assembly had scattered and fled.
Among them, those who were outstanding and resolute all held life lightly and the Dharma dear, crossing perilous terrain to reach him.
He gathered [disciples] in the mountains and forests, intending to provide for them with material necessities and instruct them in the flavor of the principles.

Furthermore, through the meritorious offerings of both the clergy and the laity, he commissioned twenty-seven fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in golden script and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in golden script, housed within a magnificent and dazzling casket of lapis lazuli.

His meritorious achievements were exceptionally outstanding, greatly inspiring the minds of the multitude. He was further requested to lecture on two sutras, which he immediately composed and structured.

Later, he commissioned Zhiyi of Jiangling to take his place in lecturing on the *Golden Sutra* (the *Lotus Sūtra*). When they reached the section on "one mind encompassing all practices," Zhiyi harbored a doubt. [Huisi] reflected upon how to resolve it, saying:
"What you have just doubted is merely the sequential meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; it is not yet the perfect and sudden teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*."

This is the essential point. In the summer of the past, while practicing ascetic discipline, I contemplated this; then, in a single thought during the latter part of the night, all dharmas suddenly manifested.

Having personally realized this myself, there is no need for you to harbor doubts. Zhiyi then consulted him and received the *Lotus Sūtra*, practiced its rites for twenty-one days, and further inquired about the stages of the spiritual path.
"This refers to the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi). Sengsi said, "No; I am merely at the stage of the Iron Wheel of the Ten Faiths.

At that time, he took more than forty monks and proceeded directly to Mount Nanyue. On the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the second year of the Guangda era of the Chen dynasty, he arrived and announced, "I shall reside on this mountain for exactly ten years.
After this period, I will certainly travel far away. He further said:
"In a previous life, I once walked this very path. Traveling as far as Hengyang, I came upon a particularly fine and bright spot where the woods and springs were sparse and pure;
those who saw it found their hearts gladdened. I thought to myself, 'This is an ancient temple where I once resided.

Following these words, I dug there and indeed discovered the foundations of chambers and halls, as well as the utensils used by the monks. Later, I went to Yanxia, where I sat in meditation; there, bandits cut off my way."
Upon his passing away, his entire body remained intact. Everyone searched for it together and found a heap of withered remains; searching further down, they obtained his skull.

Desiring to enshrine it upon the crown of their heads and erect a magnificent stupa, they received a divine response. Consequently, they brought the relics down to the capital and enshrined them at Xi-xuan Temple.
Once, when he went to Wa-guan Temple, he was not wetted by the rain, nor did his feet become soiled by the mud. The monks...
Zhenghui Gaofa encountered his disciples on the road and said, "This is a person of divine and extraordinary power; how could he have come here?

The entire court turned their eyes toward him, and both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with reverence. The Grand Commandant Wu Mingche held him in the highest esteem and presented him with a reclining pillow.
The separate general Xiahou Xiaowei went to the temple to pay his respects; while on the way, he thought to himself, "By the Honorable Wu..."
Regarding the person who presented the pillow: how was he to be seen? When [Faxian] arrived at the residence of Sengsi, he performed his respects while traveling with vigor and said to Wei:
"I wish to see the rhinoceros horn pillow; you may go and look for it. On another day, there was suddenly a voice announcing, "Sweep and clean the courtyard and halls.
Sengsi soon arrived, exactly as had been said. Wei looked up at him in awe. He provided him with men and boats to escort him.
He departed for the rivers and marshes. Sengsi said, "I shall reside at Mount Nanyue for only ten years; when the term is full, I must move on.

Every year, the Chen ruler sent three messengers to inquire after his well-being and provide provisions that accumulated in great abundance, such that no other could surpass him in honor and prosperity. His preaching of the Dharma was twice as frequent as usual.

As he approached the time of his passing, he descended from the mountain peak to the practice hall halfway down the slope, where he gathered his disciples in a great assembly and preached the Dharma for several days with earnest and piercing admonitions.
The reproach was such that those who heard it were struck with cold dread. Consequently, he withdrew his attendants and concentrated his mind; he passed away in a state of profound stillness.
The novice Lingbian saw that his breath had ceased, so he wailed and cried out loudly. [Sengshao] immediately opened his eyes and said: "You are an evil demon.
I am about to depart, and many holy beings are coming to welcome me in great numbers. For what reason do you cause such alarm and agitation to obstruct and disturb me? [Lingbian] was bewildered.
The person departed. Thereupon, [the practitioner] further gathered his mind and sat attentively until the end of the session. Everyone smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
On the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Taian era of the Chen dynasty, this was verified ten years later; it matched perfectly, like two halves of a tally.
Shi Zhiyi, whose courtesy name was De’an, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Yingchuan. During the relocation of the capital by the Jin dynasty, his family resided in Huāróng in Jīngzhōu;
he was the second son of Yìyáng Gōng, a *sànqǐ* (Attendant Gentleman) under the Liáng dynasty.

His mother, Lady Xú, dreamed that five-colored incense smoke entered her bosom. On the night of his birth, the interior of the room was brilliantly illuminated, and suddenly two monks knocked at the door.
He said, "Excellent, child, your virtue! You shall certainly leave the household life. Having spoken, he vanished. His guests marveled at this.
He had double pupils in his eyes; when lying down, he would join his palms; and when sitting, he invariably faced west. From the time he reached adulthood, he never ate recklessly;

upon seeing an image, he would prostrate himself; and whenever he encountered a monk, he would show him respect. At the age of eighteen, he entered the service of the śramaṇa Faxu at Guoyuan Temple in Xiangzhou.
He left the household life. Xu bestowed upon him the ten precepts and the stages of the path (mārga), and he remained bound by the monastic discipline (vinaya).
He then went to the Vinaya Master Huikuang, where he sat facing north with his scriptures spread out before him; there he received full instruction and guidance.

Consequently, he retired to Mount Daxian, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra, the Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings, and the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra. Before twenty days had passed, he had mastered all three texts. He then proceeded to Mount Dasu in Guangzhou.
Master Huisi received his formal training from Master Wencong; Wencong received the Dharma from Master Daojue; and Daojue, in turn, received the Dharma from Master Zuicheng.
As for these three men, none could be fathomed as to their spiritual rank. Master Si often sighed, saying: "In the past, at Vulture Peak, we listened to the Lotus Sutra together.

Pursued by our karmic affinity from former lives, we have come here once again. He then pointed out the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded for them the Four Kinds of Peaceful Joy.
Zhiyi then practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* on this mountain. After only three nights had passed, he reached the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" while reciting the sutra;
as his mind focused on the practice of asceticism, he arrived at the phrase "This is true diligence," whereupon sudden awakening arose, and he saw himself together with Master Si.
On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, in the pure land of the seven treasures, he listened to the Buddha preaching the Dharma. He thought to himself: "Were it not for you, this would not have been felt;
were it not for me, this would not have been recognized. This was the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvayoga*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Furthermore, while at Mount Baiśa in Xizhou, whenever he entered meditative contemplation and encountered doubts regarding the sutras, he would invariably see Zhiyi appear before him, who would secretly unravel and explain them for him. Thereafter, [Zhiyi] constantly had him lecture on the teachings in his stead, and those who heard him—

He submitted to him. Only regarding the wisdom of the three samādhis and the three contemplations did he consult him for verification; for all other matters, he acted according to his own understanding and judgment, never paying them further heed.
When it was time for Xi to depart after completing his studies, Zhiyi thought to himself, "You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen; if you go there, you will surely bring benefit.
Once Zhiyi had traveled to Mount Nanyue, Guanding then proceeded to Jinling, where he stayed with Faxi and over thirty others.

At Waguan Monastery, he first propagated the Dharma of Chan. The Vice President Xu Ling, the Minister Mao Xi, and other eminent figures of the enlightened age—whose learning encompassed both Buddhism and Confucianism—received his instructions in meditative wisdom and together transmitted the "fragrant dharma.
They revered him with deep appreciation and held him in the highest esteem, looking up to him as a source of honor and aspiration for their time.
The Great Virtuous Zhide of Changgan Temple invited him to enter Zongxi; the monk Huang of Tiangong Temple requested that he reside at Foku.

During moments of silence and reflection, he longed for the forests and marshes, and then had a dream: there were ten thousand layers of cliffs and crags, with clouds and the sun hanging halfway down;
beside them lay the vast ocean, boundless and limpid, situated beneath it. Furthermore, he saw a monk who shook his hand and extended his arm toward a fork in the path.
At the foot of the mountain, they urged Huiyi to ascend. His disciples all said, "This is Mount Tiantai in Kuaiji.
There is a monk from Qingzhou named Dingguang who has long resided on this mountain for forty years; he practices both samādhi and prajñā and is truly a divine being."
Before Zhiyi arrived for two years, he informed the mountain dwellers in advance, saying: "A great *kalyāṇamitra* will come to visit us.
Directly plant beans to make sauce, weave *phoṭṭaja* grass into mats, and build additional houses to accommodate him. He then departed for Mount Tiantai.

Having reached that mountain, he met with Guang and immediately set forth his request. Guang said, "Great Good Friend, do you remember when I was young and we waved our hands on the mountain as a sign of exchange?
Zhiyi was struck with wonder and astonishment. Furthermore, he heard the sound of bells filling the valley.
The assembly was all astonished by this. Huiguang said, "The bell is for summoning those with whom you have a karmic connection; you shall find your dwelling here.
Zhiyi then selected a superior site for his residence—north of where Huiguang lived, south of Mount Fulong, at the source of the Luoxi River. The location was both secluded and spacious.
It was easy to find a place to seek the Truth. The ground was level and the springs were clear;

as he wandered about and stayed the night, he suddenly saw three men wearing black caps and crimson robes, who held a document and requested, saying, "You may practice the Way here. Thereupon, he established a thatched hut and planted pine trees and fruit-bearing trees.
Within a few years, practitioners gathered around him, and it became a great assembly. Daoguang said, "For now, settle here as best you can until we reach the capital."

In a time of clarity, when the three regions were unified as one, there shall be a person of noble status who will establish a monastery for the Meditation Master (Chanshi), its halls and buildings filling the mountains.
At that time, Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an edict stating: "The Meditation Master is a heroic and eminent figure in the Buddha-dharma, revered by his contemporaries.

His instruction extends to both the clergy and the laity; he is a national hope. It is fitting to allot the tax revenue of Shifeng County to provide for the expenses of the assembly, and to exempt two households of commoners."
He provided him with a salary. In Tiantai County, there was a place named Le’an.

The magistrate, Yuan Zixiong of Chen Commandery, held profound faith in the True Dharma and regularly lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* every summer. Suddenly, he saw three jeweled staircases descend from the sky.

Several dozen Brahma-monks descended the stairs and entered the hall to prostrate themselves. Holding incense burners in their hands, they circumambulated Huiyi three times. This lasted for a long time.
Thereupon it was extinguished. Xuéxióng and the great assembly all witnessed this and were filled with wonder and admiration.

When Prince Yongyang Bozhì went out to govern Wuxing, he and his retinue went to the mountain to request the precepts and further established the Seven-Night Vaipulya Repentance Rite. During the day, the Prince attended to his administrative duties.
That night, he practiced meditation. Zhiyi said to his disciple Zhiyue, "I wish to urge the King to cultivate further merit to avert this calamity;

would that be appropriate? Zhiyue replied, "The court officials have no long-standing ties to you; they will surely feel resentment. Zhiyi said, "To quell worldly criticism and suspicion is also a form of goodness.

Shortly thereafter, while out hunting, the King fell from his horse and was on the verge of death. At that moment, he realized the truth of Zhiyi's intent and personally led a multitude [to the monastery].
He performed the ritual of repentance for Avalokiteśvara. Before long, the king awoke slightly and sat up, leaning against his armrest.

He saw a foreign monk holding an incense burner who walked straight toward him and asked about the king’s ailment. The king, covered in sweat, could not answer. The monk then circumambulated the king once, and immediately the pain ceased.

Thereupon, the king personally composed a text of vows and passed away. His remains were moved to Haishan (Fuzhou), where he governed the regions of Min with the Dharma. Chen Yi requested [his teachings].

The Master ascended the mountain seat. Emperor Chen, wishing to pay his respects in person and extend his veneration, consulted his ministers, asking who was the most eminent figure in the Buddhist community.
Chen Xuan replied: "The Chan Master of Waguan Monastery possesses a virtue that surpasses the wind and frost, and a realm of meditation as deep as the ocean.
Formerly in the capital, he was revered by all the wise; now he walks with lofty steps at Tiantai, where the clouds of the Dharma gather in the east. I pray that Your Majesty..."

Upon his return to the capital following the issuance of the imperial edict, he caused both monastics and laypeople to bear [the burden of his influence]. Consequently, an imperial letter was bestowed upon him, summoning him back repeatedly;

seven such missions arrived in succession, each with a personal note from the Emperor’s own hand. Zhiyi, recognizing that the Way is universal and that the King of Men alone serves as the vessel for the Dharma, eventually departed for the capital.
He was invited into the Eastern Hall of the Taiji Palace to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

By imperial decree, the "Young Child of the Ram-Cart" (Yangche Tongzi) led the way before him, while the Secretaries and Attendants followed as he ascended the steps; the ritual protocol was identical to the precedent established by National Preceptor Cui Ācārya.

Once the Chen Emperor had descended to the Dharma assembly, all the officials paid their respects. Having heard what they had never heard before, they received the Dharma and upheld the Way. Consequently—
An imperial edict was immediately issued to establish the Zen community at Lingyao Temple. Students gathered in great numbers, and the assembly appeared as imposing as a dense forest.

The Emperor repeatedly issued decrees from the Taiji Palace for him to lecture on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. The Son of Heaven attended in person, and the Chief Monks Hui-keng and Hui-k’uang, along with the great virtuous ones of the capital, all raised formidable challenges.
Zhiyi received their questions and provided responses, grandly opening the gates of the Dharma; Hui-keng held [his position].

Lu He said, "In this kingdom, there have been over ten assemblies [of lecturers], yet I alone have presided over four lectures. I have analyzed the texts and dissected their meanings, believing I had reached the ultimate truth.

Today, with the stars emerging and being withdrawn, I see my cleverness exposed as meager. The Chen Emperor issued an edict of thanks from the Guangde Hall, saying, "I now entrust the Buddha-dharma to you;
I also hope you will demonstrate what I have not yet attained. At that time, the monks and nuns were scrutinized, and those who lacked official registration were [expelled].

The number reached ten thousand. The court deliberated that those who had failed their examinations were all required to cease their monastic practice. Zhiyi submitted a memorial in remonstrance, stating: "Tie-da recited sixty thousand *xiangjing* (elephant-sūtras) yet could not avoid hell;
Pan-te recited but a single verse and attained the fruit of an Arhat. This speaks to the earnestness of the Way; how can it depend on the volume of what is recited?
The Chen ruler was greatly pleased and immediately halted the search and screening. Later, he became the disciple of Lingyao.

He sought a more secluded and quiet place. Suddenly, he dreamed of a man with a solemn and dignified retinue who introduced himself, saying, "I am Guanda. Zhiyi asked, "Guanda is the Dharma-name of Emperor Wu of Liang; is 'Sanqiao' not Guangzhai? The man replied, "It is indeed so. Zhiyi then said, "If that is the case, I shall stay here. He subsequently built a small hermitage at Sanqiao and resided there for several years. Later, when he was about to depart for Mount Tiantai, he again dreamed of the same person, who said, "The time has come; you must go quickly. Zhiyi then left Sanqiao and traveled to Mount Tiantai. It was on this day that he first received the imperial summons from Emperor Wen of Sui. Thus, it is known that the dream of Guanda was a divine omen. Furthermore, the monk Huiming of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Ming replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over twenty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Ming then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Ming subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Southern Palace. This is another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Moreover, the Master of the Three Stages, Xinxing, once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Xinxing replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over thirty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Xinxing then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Xinxing subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Northern Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huixiu of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huixiu replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over thirty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huixiu then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huixiu subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Eastern Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Huishou replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over forty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huishou then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huishou subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Western Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Huiguan replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over fifty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huiguan then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huiguan subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Central Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response.
