Huicheng replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over sixty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huicheng then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huicheng subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Northern Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huiren of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huiren replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over seventy years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huiren then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huiren subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Southern Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huizhi of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huizhi replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over eighty years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huizhi then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huizhi subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Eastern Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huixian of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huixian replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over ninety years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huixian then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huixian subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Western Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huibian of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huibian replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over one hundred years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huibian then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huibian subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Central Palace. This is yet another instance of Guanda’s divine response. Furthermore, the monk Huishan of Mount Tiantai once dreamed of a person who called himself Guanda and said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. Huishan replied, "I have been practicing the Way for over one hundred and ten years, yet I have not yet attained anything. The person said, "You have already attained it; why do you doubt it? You will soon receive an imperial decree. Huishan then dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around his body. Upon waking, he reported this to Zhiyi, who told him, "This is Guanda. You should go to the capital. Huishan subsequently went to the capital and was appointed as the *shamen* (monk official) of the Northern Palace. This is yet another
He then moved his residence there. In the fourth month of that year, the Emperor of Chen visited the temple and performed a great act of charity (*mahādāna*).

He also lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), during which the Emperor rose from the midst of the assembly to pay him reverent obeisance with great earnestness. From the Crown Prince downward, all held his disciplinary model (*śīla-vinaya*) in high esteem.

At that time, Yang Dao, the future Emperor Yang of the Great Sui, was serving in the provinces, with jurisdiction over the Huai and Hai regions. Having received his influence and cherished his virtue, he maintained a continuous admiration for him; desiring to follow his monastic discipline and uphold it, [he sent an envoy].

Acting as his teacher, [the King] sent repeated letters with earnest invitations. Zhiyi established a *sahasra-bhikṣu* assembly at Jincheng, the headquarters of the Yangzhou Governor-General, respectfully requesting that he deign to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts.
Thereupon, within the royal palace, Zhiyi personally transmitted the fragrance of the precepts and conferred the ritual of the Vinaya. The King received these instructions upon the crown of his head.
When Zhiyi wished to return to his former forest retreat, the King entreated him firmly; Zhiyi rose from his seat shaking out his robes. The King did not dare to invite him again. Together—
Hui-zhang escorted him to the city gate. When he reached it, the King gazed at him until his sight failed; choked with tears, he returned.
Hui-zhang then followed the current upstream on the river and once again sought out Mount Kuang. There he gathered disciples and practiced the Way, frequently receiving auspicious omens.

Monks from the borders of the Hundred Yue regions, hearing of his reputation, arrived one after another. Consequently, he established a vihāra on Mount Yuquan in Dangyang County. Previously, that place was merely...
The terrain was rugged and perilous, and divine beasts and snakes were violent. After the temple was founded, however, there was no longer any anxiety or distress.

That spring, a severe drought occurred; Fayi went to the source of a spring and led the assembly in reciting the sutras. Immediately, clouds arose and rain poured down. Wang Ji, the Governor-General and Duke of Yiyang, came to the mountain to pay his respects;

he was so overcome with trepidation that he could not remain at ease. He remarked, "I have frequently passed through military ranks, and I am even more courageous when facing danger. Yet I have never..."
He was struck with sudden terror as if it were this very day. That year, the Prince of Jin again sent a personal letter requesting his return.

Later, when Lady Xiao fell ill and no medical treatment could cure her, the Prince dispatched the *Kaifu* (Governor-General) Liu Guyan and others to deliver a letter, entreating him to save her life by curing her ailment.
Zhiyi then led his companions to establish a seven-day fast and perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual. On the evening of the sixth day, a voice suddenly descended.

A strange bird flew into the altar of the purification ritual, writhed about until it died, and then departed in an instant. Furthermore, the sound of a pig’s groan was heard; the entire assembly gazed at this together.
Zhiyi said, "As for these omens appearing, the Consort shall surely recover. By the following day, her illness had indeed been cured. The King was greatly rejoiced.
At that time, he encountered [the Emperor] entering court; Zhiyi then returned to Mount Tai, personally leading the Chan school to once again practice [the rites].
He performed his prior repentance and further made a vow, saying: "If there is benefit for the Triple Gem, I shall devote my remaining years to this purpose.
If my disciples are born [into the world], I pray that they may quickly follow my transformation. After a short while, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I shall pass away at this very site.

Therefore, whenever I wished to return to the mountains, I now receive a divine summons; my life-force is about to end. After my death, you must place me upon the southwestern peak. He repeated this several times.
They surrounded the corpse with stones, planted pine trees to cover the pit, and erected a white stupa so that those who saw it would be inspired to resolve their minds [for awakening].

Shi Huiyuan, whose secular surname was Li, was a native of Dunhuang. Later, he resided in Gaodu in Shangdang. Heaven had bestowed upon him an exceptionally brilliant nature, and his deportment was serene and harmonious.
Having lost his father at a young age, he lived with his uncle; whenever he encountered śramaṇas, he treated them with deep affection, esteem, and reverence. At ten...

He declined his uncle’s offer three times and went to Guxian Valley Temple on Mount Dongshan in Zhezhou. At that time, there was the Dhyāna Master Sengsi, a śramaṇa from Huayin, who saw him and took him as a disciple.

Initially, he had him recite the scriptures and instructed him according to the circumstances. During the six periods of daily practice, he never required the exertion of being called upon or exhorted.
When he reached the age of sixteen, the Master sent him to follow the Ācārya Zhàn, a Vinaya Master, at Ye. There, he studied the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras.

He was universally well-versed in all fields of learning, yet he placed particular emphasis on the Mahāyāna as the foundation of the Way. Upon reaching the age for full ordination, he again received the precepts under the Superior Patriarch.

He further studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* under Master Dayin, analyzing its provisions and prohibitions with such thoroughness that his interpretations were both logically consistent and textually harmonious.
His insights were so sharp and profound that students gathered around him in great numbers, carrying their books; he then led his fellow scholars back to the seclusion of Gaodu.

He transformed it into a monastery. The multitude rejoiced with great celebration, marveling at what they had never heard before. Each person contributed gold and silk to establish lecture halls for him;
thus, the temple buildings were all at once grand and spacious. The officials and commoners of Han and Wei all shared in this glory.

In the spring of the second year of Chengguang, when the Zhou dynasty conquered Qi, they immediately carried out the suppression of the teachings. An imperial edict was issued for all the eminent monks of former times to assemble in the palace hall. Emperor Wu...

Having ascended the high seat, he expounded the principles for the abolition and establishment [of teachings]. He proclaimed: "I, the Emperor, have received the Mandate of Heaven to nourish and raise the myriad people.

However, although the three teachings have flourished throughout the world and their influence has spread far and wide, upon examining them to determine the ultimate truth, I find that most deviate from the transformative Way. Therefore, I now abolish them all."

However, as for the Six Classics and the Confucian teachings, their texts extensively treat the methods of governance, and their rites, righteousness, loyalty, and filial piety are appropriate for the world;

therefore, they must be preserved and established. Furthermore, since the True Buddha is formless and dwells in the great void, one expresses the heart of reverence from afar, as the Buddhist scriptures praise at length.

The ignorant masses believed with fervor, exhausting their precious wealth to extensively construct temples and stupas. Since these were but hollow inducements for the expenditure of resources, they could not endure;

consequently, all scriptures and images were utterly destroyed. They failed to honor the profound kindness of their parents, yet showed no respect for śramaṇas—this was the height of perversity and rebellion.
"According to the laws of the state, how could this be tolerated? You must all return home to honor the beginning of filial piety.

At that time, more than five hundred people, including the Great Steward (Dastong) of the śramaṇas, Fazheng and others, all considered the Emperor to be acting with royal force. They attempted to remonstrate with him resolutely, but their advice was not followed. Consequently, they all remained silent.

An imperial decree was issued repeatedly to urge them to submit a response to the edict, yet they looked at one another with pale faces; no one offered a reply. Fayuan reflected upon the Buddha-dharma...

[The Emperor] sent [a message]. The fourfold assembly is that upon which he relies. Thereupon, he emerged from the assembly and replied: "Your Majesty presides over the great realm and, having attained the One, dwells in supreme honor.

You employ conventional language in accordance with worldly custom, yet your statutes and precedents follow the Three Teachings. Your edict states that 'the true Buddha has no image. This is indeed consistent with your sincere intent.

However, living beings who possess ears and eyes rely on the scriptures to hear of the Buddha and depend on images to manifest the Truth. If these were abolished, there would be no means by which reverence could be inspired. The Emperor—

Huiyuan said, "The True Buddha is empty space; all know this of themselves, without depending on scriptures or images. Huiyuan continued, "Before the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, scriptures and images had not yet reached this land.
Why, then, did sentient beings not know the True Buddha who is empty space? At that time, the Emperor had no answer.

Huiyuan said, "If one could know the existence of the Dharma by oneself without relying on scriptural teachings, then before the Three Sovereigns, when written characters did not yet exist, people ought to have known it."

[The Emperor] himself knew the five constant virtues and other such dharmas. At that time, why did these people recognize only their mother and fail to recognize their father, being no different from birds and beasts?
The Emperor also gave no answer. Yuan again said:

"If you claim that because images are insentient, serving them brings no merit and thus they must be abolished, then how can the images in the state’s seven ancestral temples be sentient? Yet they are falsely honored and served."

Emperor Wu did not answer the preceding challenge; instead, he evasively shifted to subsequent remarks, saying: "The Buddhist scriptures are the laws of foreign lands and are not used in this country.
The seven ancestral temples were established by our predecessors, yet I do not consider them correct either, and I intend to abolish them both. Daoyuan said:
If you were to discard and cease using the scriptures of foreign lands because they originate elsewhere, then what was spoken by Confucius originated in the state of Lu;

the lands of Qin and Jin should likewise be discarded and not studied. Furthermore, if you consider the seven ancestral temples to be improper and intend to abolish them, [then you must apply the same logic to other traditions].

This would mean that one does not honor one’s ancestors; when ancestors are not honored, the order of the *zhao* and *mu* lineages is lost. When the order of the *zhao* and *mu* lineages is lost, the Five Classics become useless.
If the former Confucian teachings no longer exist, where would their meaning lie? In that case, the Three Teachings would all be abolished; how then could the state be governed? The Emperor said:
"Although the territories of the states of Lu, Qin, and Jin differ, they are all without exception subject to the single transformation of the King."
Therefore, this does not resemble the difficulty regarding the seven ancestral temples in the Buddhist scriptures. Yuan said:

"If you claim that Qin and Lu equally honor a single transformation and that the scriptural teachings are universally practiced, then although the territories of China (Zhendan) and India (Tianzhu) differ, they both equally lie within the four seas of Jambudvīpa under the transformation of a single Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
Why, then, do they not all equally follow the Buddhist scriptures? And why are they now uniquely discarded? The Emperor spoke again.
The Emperor did not answer. Huiyuan said, "Your Majesty previously stated that you would allow monks to return home to honor filial piety. Yet the Confucian classics also say:
'Establish oneself and practice the Way to bring glory to one's parents. This is itself the act of filiality. Why must one return home before it can be called filial?"

The Emperor said, "The kindness of one's parents is profound; they provide for one another through physical care and nourishment. To abandon one's kin and turn toward strangers does not constitute supreme filial piety.
Tanyuan replied, "Your Majesty’s attendants all have their own parents; why do you not release them, instead subjecting them to five years of long-term labor so that they do not see their parents?
Emperor Wu said, "I also follow the rotation of shifts and am able to return home to serve them. Tanyuan replied, "The Buddha also permits this."
"Monks practice the Way according to circumstances during the winter and summer; they return home to serve and support their parents during the spring and autumn.
Thus, Maudgalyāyana begged for food to send to his mother, and the Tathāgata carried the coffin to the burial site. This principle is universally applicable and must not be unilaterally discarded.

The Emperor again gave no reply, whereupon Huiyuan raised his voice and said, "Your Majesty now relies on the sovereign power of the king to destroy the Triple Gem. The Avīci Hell makes no such distinctions!"
"Between the noble and the lowly, how can Your Majesty not be afraid? The Emperor became violently enraged;

Huiyuan replied, "Your Majesty transforms the people through false teachings and thus plants the seeds of suffering in the present life. You shall surely share the same destination as Your Majesty in the Avīci Hell; where in that place is there any joy?"
[The Emperor] was able [to respond], but his principles were exhausted and he had no answer. He then issued an edict saying: "Let the monks return for now; we shall assemble again later.

The Duke invited him to return to his native region. In the spring of the seventh year, while residing in Dingzhou, he traveled via Shangdang and stayed for the summer lecture session.

On the twelfth day of the second month in the first year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Dazhuangyan Temple. Spring.

Shi Fachang’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Baishui in Nanyang. His great-grandfather, Long, served as an official under the Wei dynasty and subsequently moved the family to Hexi Commandery.

An edict was subsequently issued ordering him to confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon the Crown Prince, whom he honored with the utmost reverence.
She was universally revered by all. In the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, she was again summoned by imperial decree to serve as the Precept Master for the Empress.

The Master’s family had long heard of his devout veneration and yearned to behold his teachings. Consequently, they crossed mountains and sailed across the sea to reach the capital.

Shi Daoji was a native of An-yi in Hedong. His surname was Xiang; his ancestors were the descendants of Zichan, the Grand Minister of Zheng.

He addressed his subordinates, saying: "Times wax and wane, but the Dharma neither flourishes nor declines. A śramaṇa is a guest from beyond the mundane world;

Shi Xuanyuan’s surname was Yang; he was a native of Huayin in Hongnong. He resided in Xinfeng, Yongzhou. Having attained awakening while still wearing the blue scholar's robe, his conduct was profound and luminous.

He shook the collar of the Great Standard; Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty held him in high esteem and established a monastery for him to reside in. Yuan occupied the position of a disciple within the inner circle, maintaining a heart of reverent diligence.

Regarding the *Fahua*, *Daji*, *Lengqie*, *Shengman*, *Didi lun*, *Zhongbian lun*, and others, he drew from their flourishing substance while refining his mastery of new insights. During the lifetime of his teacher, he vowed to create a sixteen-foot statue of Śākyamuni.
Before his plans were fully realized, he suddenly passed away. Vowing to restore the work, he succeeded in completing it according to the original model.
In the second year of the Renshou era, when the conditions were ripe, he began the casting process. At that time, the air and colors were clear and bright, and the brilliant sun shed its radiance.
From above, flowers rained down like mica, drifting and scattering through the sky before finally falling before the statue. This occurred after the mold had been opened.
Her refined features became increasingly perfect. Every calm night and clear morning, the sounds of the eight musical instruments would drift forth.

Furthermore, on the eighth day of the second month, the morning of the Great Sage’s ceremonial bathing, she opened a lecture hall and established a vegetarian feast. This continued until the beginning of the Zhenguan era, when she completed the governance of the *Wan* [monastery] through her pure precepts.
He was looked up to by both the court and the common people. By imperial decree, he was summoned to confer the Bodhisattva Precepts upon the Crown Prince and various princes;

She was invited to enter as Empress, where she conferred the precepts upon the six palaces, the consorts, and the ladies-in-waiting. Within the inner chambers, she inquired after their virtues; within the forbidden precincts, she bestowed the wealth of the Dharma.

Furthermore, she maintained rigorous self-discipline, and her words served as a model for the age. Among the monks and nuns who received full ordination from her, [she was their preceptor].
More than three thousand people—ranging from princes, dukes, and officials down to servants and slaves—numbered over two hundred thousand who followed the Dharma and returned to the precepts.

Shi Falin’s secular surname was Chen. A native of Yingchuan, he left the household life in his youth and traveled extensively to explore both Confucianism and Buddhism, mastering their terminology and meanings.

He sought guidance from the Way throughout Jinling, Chu, and Ying. Dwelling in the wilds and subsisting on wood-gathering among the mountains such as Qingxi, he would study Buddhist scriptures by day and recite and examine secular classics by night.
During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he temporarily set aside his monastic robes; however, with the commencement of the Wude era, [he returned to the Dharma].

He returned to serve the Śākya lineage and resided at Jifa Temple in the capital. In the fourth year of the Wude era, the followers of the Yellow Turbans harbored deep animosity toward the Buddha-dharma;

they submitted eleven articles petitioning for the abolition of Buddhism, claiming that the Buddhist scriptures were extravagant and false, their words were demonic and their matters obscure, and that they damaged the state and ruined families without ever being heard to benefit the world.
They requested that the heterodox teachings of the barbarian Buddha be sent back to India. All such [petitions]...
"O Śramaṇa, if you are released to return to your native land, then both family and state will flourish, and the teachings of Li (Confucius) and Kong (Mencius) will prevail.
Emperor Wu put this into practice and issued an edict asking: 'In what interval does your benefit lie, and beyond what emotion does your advantage reside?
Regarding these two matters of loss and gain, I request a subtle explanation. Faling was moved by indignation."
The messenger’s words: "I have listened attentively to Your Majesty’s clear decree and received this inquiry. I shall immediately respond: Senglin has heard that the Ultimate Way transcends words;

how could it be discerned by the Nine Schools? The Dharma-body is formless; it cannot be expounded by the Ten Wings [of the Book of Changes]. Yet, the four realms of existence are vast and desolate, drifting and drowning in the ocean of desire.
The three worlds are teeming with life, tumbling down the mountain of heterodoxy. The various sons of the Buddha are deluded and burn themselves, while ordinary beings are submerged."
Yet [the truth] does not manifest on its own; thus the Great Sage arises in the world, and the Perfected Being descends with his numinous spirit.
He subsequently opens the gate of liberation and reveals the path of peace and security. Thereupon, those of the celestial and royal lineages renounce affection and leave the household life;
the nobility and elites of the Eastern Land weary of glory and splendor and enter the Way. They vow to transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death, and resolve to seek the single, wondrous Nirvana.
They cultivate extensive goodness to repay the four debts of gratitude; they establish virtue to provide sustenance for the three realms of existence—this is their benefit.

They alter their physical appearance to fulfill their resolve; thus they discard their hair and beard and abandon the beauty of worldly adornment, transforming their customs to harmonize with the Way.

Thus they set aside the formal robes of ruler and minister; though their outward form lacks the means to serve their parents, they inwardly cherish filial piety. Though their rites differ from those used to serve a sovereign, their hearts remain focused upon loyalty.

His grace extends to both enemies and kin, thereby achieving great harmony; his blessings moisten both the hidden and the manifest, so how could they be constrained by minor contradictions? Thus, Daolun composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies).
To examine its origins: the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is profound and mysterious, and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is concentrated and still.

Only our Great Master, measuring the Dharma-realm to give rise to compassion and gauging the void to establish his vows, manifested birth in this defiled land and was born in the palace of a sage king, displaying a golden hue.

Manifesting his body, he revealed the mark of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*). Spreading the clouds of compassion upon Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), the flames of the burning house were extinguished;

fanning the wind of wisdom at Chicken Foot Mountain (*Kukkuṭapāda*), the mists of the dark path were rolled away. When walking, golden lotuses supported his feet; when sitting, precious thrones sustained his form.

When going forth, the Lord of Devas (*Indra*) led the way; when entering, the King of Brahmā (*Brahmā*) followed behind. Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas stood in solemn attendance, as if at a court assembly.
The eight classes of beings and ten thousand deities stand in solemn array as his retinue. When he proclaims the *Nirvāṇa*, the earth manifests six kinds of tremors;

when he expounds the *Prajñā*, the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers. Adorned with a hundred blessings, he resembles the full moon descending upon the blue sea; his thousand rays of light shine brilliantly.
It is like the sun gathering its light upon a mountain of jewels: with a single roar, the lion destroys the vanguard of the non-Buddhists;

with a brief peal, the Dharma drum causes the celestial Māras to bow their heads. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Dharma King. Yet, because the timing of the era had not yet fully harmonized, the Han and Indian peoples experienced different realizations;
thus, the Western lands first honored his voice and form, while the Eastern land later benefited from seeing and hearing him.

When the compassionate clouds withdrew their moisture and the sun of wisdom retracted its light, a golden deity appeared in a dream during the Yongping era, and sacred relics were beheld in the year of the Red Bird (248 CE).
Thereupon, under the regimes of the Han, Wei, Qi, and Liang dynasties, the teachings of the Image-Period flourished;

from the periods of Yan, Qin, Jin, and Song onward, eminent monks appeared one after another. Some saved the world through supernatural powers, some inspired others through miraculous traces, and some [possessed] wisdom...

Jiewen Shen, whose spiritual resonance was pervasive and whose transformations were timely; and Bazu, who remained unharmed when facing the blade, causing the Bequeathed Dharma to begin anew through his deeds.

Zhi Shang’s division of his body filled the quarters of the world, and the emperors thereby increased their faith. May these merits together reach into the future, transmitting the lamp for eternal kalpas.
I respectfully present one scroll of the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Heresies) to serve as a model for the transmission of words. Submitted by the Palace Attendant of Dongshu, Yu Shiji.

Nan. Xianglin composed a treatise, for which [the Emperor] wrote a preface. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor established Longtian Temple at the former residence of the Dahuangong Palace in the Southern Mountains.
Because Fali was by nature fond of seclusion and tranquility, he went to reside there. He was appointed to oversee the affairs of the temple;

clad in mountain robes, he lived with ease, chanting and singing amidst the forests and wilds. In the winter of the thirteenth year, there was a man named Qin Shiying, who wore yellow headcloths and...

Seeking honor through his mastery of occult arts, he was subsequently employed as an official in the household of the Crown Prince. Having long harbored animosity toward the Śākya lineage, he secretly presented the *Linlun* (Discourse by Lin), slandering the imperial clan.
His crime amounted to subverting the sovereign; the Emperor, provoked, issued an edict to purge the monks and nuns, and then sought out Lin’s person.

According to the legal investigation, Senglin clenched his fists in indignation and rose up with vigor; without waiting for further summons, he went alone to the public court, disregarding his life to seek justice.
He was consequently bound in fetters, and an imperial edict was issued questioning him: "In the ancestral alliances of the Zhou dynasty, those of different surnames were ranked last.
To honor one's ancestors and value kinship is truly a practice from antiquity. Why do you pursue their shortcomings, waver like a rat between two ends, and extensively cite superficial similarities?"

[The Emperor] spoke these words, setting forth in full detail disparaging metaphors that insulted my ancestors and defamed my forebears. To thus attempt to manipulate the sovereign is a crime for which there can be no leniency.
Senglin replied: "King Wen was a Great Sage and the Duke of Zhou were Great Worthies. They honored the distant past and were careful in their funeral rites, yet the vast heavens gave them no answer.
When filial piety and fraternal devotion reach their ultimate, they penetrate to the divine spirits. Although the House of Zhou was the ancestral dynasty, in principle they did not contend."
Long. Why is this? The August Heaven has no partiality; it ultimately depends upon the cultivation of virtue. The ancients sided with principle rather than kinship.

They did not place themselves first, nor did they place themselves last. Even if a kinsman had committed a crime, they would surely punish them; even if an enemy had performed a service, they would surely reward them.
When rewards and punishments accord with principle, the world attains peace and harmony. Furthermore, it is said: "The name of my teacher is Buddha. Buddha means one who awakens all people.
The Ancient Sovereign of Gandhāra has ascended to the West and departed. One may still trace the origins and development of the Laoist teaching.

[Laozi] daily bestowed the *Zhongjing* (Central Scripture) and instructed his disciples, saying: "He whom I call my Master has skillfully entered nirvāṇa; he exists eternally in a continuous state. I have now departed.
Now, the accounts provided by Liu and Li slander the Master of Laozi, yet the world is unaware of this; therefore, I have composed this work to provide clarification and rectification.
The treatise consists of eight fascicles. It briefly addresses more than sixty points raised by the Daoist practitioners, citing historical records and ancient precedents;

it is certainly not intended as a slander against the state or the imperial house. Having submitted a detailed report on these matters, the Imperial Edict stated: "Regarding the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing and Correcting) you have authored, it is said that faith and slander bring corresponding retributions.

One chapter states that those who contemplate Avalokiteśvara will not be harmed even when facing the blade. Grant him a seven-day reprieve so that he may practice this contemplation himself; let us see what happens."

Regarding the execution: could it be that there is no injury? Lin was externally bound by shackles and fetters, while internally pressed by the deadline for his execution; fire and water were intermingled within his breast, and he had no way to express his longing [for deliverance].
He therefore relied upon the scriptural teachings he had heard since birth, as well as the names of the Three Honored Sages, which he engraved and recited within the chambers of his heart.

He intended to manifest a divine response. When the deadline was reached, his spirit suddenly became buoyant and courageous; his mind overflowed with joy and celebration, such that he instantly forgot the fear of death.
He stood waiting for the interrogation. In a brief moment, the imperial decree arrived, stating: "The period of grace has now expired;
you are about to face execution. What do you have on your mind? Do you have any spiritual awareness? Senglin took up his brush and replied: "Since the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty..."
The four seas were in turmoil; pestilence and poison spread abroad; weapons rose up in competition; armies were raised to strike one another down; each lord monopolized military might;
ministers were sycophantic and their sovereigns were negligent, failing to govern with rectitude; they blocked the royal road and stubbornly clung to a single corner.

Since the August Sovereigns went forth to punish the rebellious and restore order, the lands and seas have been thoroughly cleansed. This is truly the power of Avalokiteśvara and the grace of Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Their virtues may be compared [to those of the Buddhas].

[The monk] Lianzong stated: "I have followed in the footsteps of the supreme sages to rescue those facing untimely deaths in the imperial court and to spare them from cruel punishments in the marketplace.
For seven days now, I have not called upon Avalokiteśvara, but have only thought of Your Majesty. [He then addressed] the Censor-in-Chief for Scrutiny of Documents, Wei Cong, with an edict.
The Emperor asked, "I have issued an edict ordering you to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. For what reason do you not recite it, but instead say only that you recite the name of Your Majesty?

Falin replied, "I humbly acknowledge that the holy discernment of Avalokiteśvara pervades the six realms of existence; from the heavens above to the earth below, all take him as their teacher and model.

Yet, the Great Tang now dwells in glory throughout the four seas; the nine provinces attend to their duties, the eight directions enjoy the clarity of law, and with a sage ruler and worthy ministers, there is no injustice."

Excessive! Now Your Majesty nurtures all beings like children; as this accords with the scriptures, it is precisely Avalokiteśvara who manifests. Since his spiritual discernment corresponds with this, he thus contemplates only Your Majesty.
Furthermore, the *Zhenglun* (Treatise on Orthodoxy) composed by Lin is comparable to the classics and histories.

Should there be even a single phrase that deviates from them, I am ready to face the executioner’s axe. If Your Majesty follows this loyal treatise and rectifies [the teachings], then Lin will not lose so much as a single hair. Your Majesty...

He further reported that if the punishments were excessive and innocent people were harmed, he would suffer the pain of having corpses buried beneath him. His report was submitted in full, and consequently, no charges were brought against him.
An imperial amnesty was issued, and he was transferred to a Buddhist monastery in Yizhou. While traveling to Pútí Temple at Bǎiláo Pass, he passed away due to illness at the age of sixty-nine.
He then summoned the monastics and laypeople from the vicinity of the pass and was buried on the summit of Mount Dōngshān.
A white stupa was erected on a high tree; an inscription was engraved there to commemorate it.

Shi Zhixi, whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Yingchuan. From his childhood, he was extraordinary among his peers; even as a youth, his mind dwelt beyond the mundane world. Having witnessed old age, sickness, and death, he became disillusioned with the cycle of existence.

Realizing that the world is transient and precarious, he felt a profound sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*) and sought out a sublime environment. I have humbly heard that the Venerable One has set his aspirations upon Mount Tai;

my sincere heart has long yearned for him. At the age of twenty, I first had the fortune to meet him. Having been fully ordained in the Vinaya precepts, I received from him the secret instructions of Chan meditation.

Those who delighted in samādhi all turned to him with reverence. During the intervals between his seated meditations, he would occasionally direct the construction of monasteries, halls, and chambers, all of which were made magnificent and orderly.

Only the scripture platform remained unbuilt; just as he was about to begin the work, there was Mount Xianglu (Incense Burner Peak), where the mountain crags were steep and perilous and the forest trees were exceptionally beautiful. However, the deities dwelling there possessed great spiritual efficacy, having been so since ancient times.
No one dared to look upon its peaks and cliffs. As those who ascended it to gather wood for construction deliberated, they said:

"Now that we have established this terrace to make offerings to the Dharma-treasure, we must seek only the finest and most exquisite materials; how can we proceed with such casualness? The juniper and cypress of Incense Burner Peak (Xianglu Feng) are the most refined and superior among woods;
let us gather them together to provide for our offerings. Once their detailed discussion was concluded, they went to consult [the Master].
Xi replied after a long silence, "The mountain deity has taken offense; one must not act rashly. That night, he dreamed of a person delivering a memorial which stated:
"The *shing* and cypress trees on Fragrant Incense Peak are all granted for the sake of the sutra platform. Having received this divine revelation, he immediately began the work of clearing the site.
He divided the laborers and sent them into the mountains to harvest timber. An attendant consulted him, saying, "Yesterday you did not permit it;

why do you have them take it now? He replied, "Yesterday it was due to another; today it is due to me. Simply take it; there is no harm. Following his instructions, they went to fetch it—*cinnamomum* and cypress trees.
They were born solely in perilous places, yet all were successfully captured without a single obstacle. The former master Zhiyi once remarked:

"I exhorted the common people to transform all rivers and streams from the shores of Mount Tiantai down to the edge of the sea into ponds for the release of living beings, forever severing the practice of hunting and fishing.
After the fall of the Sui dynasty, the subsequent generations of the populace vied with one another to establish *liángzhú* (fish-releasing shrines), filling the land with them.

In the Jiangxi region, many aquatic creatures were being killed and injured. Consequently, [the master] went with Master Ding to the meditation cell of the late teacher to burn incense and offer prayers.
At that time, some fishermen saw a monk standing atop a stack of *zhū* (bamboo mats), and thinking he had fallen into the water, they took a boat to rescue him;

however, by the time they arrived, he was already gone. From then on, none of the bamboo mats in the Jiangxi area yielded fish, so the fishermen ceased their hunting. At that time, there was a monk named Fayun who wished to...
When Wǎngxiānglúfēng went to practice *dhūta* austerities, Xi advised him, saying, "The mountain deity there is fierce and stubborn, while your power of the Way is weak;
you will certainly find no peace there. Be careful not to go. Yún did not accept this advice and proceeded to the mountain.
Before two nights had passed, the deity manifested his form and drove Yún away, ordering him to return. Only then did Yún recall the previous instructions, and he felt a deep sense of reverence.
Yang had a disciple named Daoxun who was reciting sutras in his room. Yang went to call him, saying, "Tonight there will be a monk coming.
Having finished speaking, he headed toward the gate. Immediately, he saw a monk dressed entirely in patchwork robes (*kaṣāya*), holding a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) and carrying an alms bowl.

His appearance and spirit were so refined and transcendent that they far exceeded those of ordinary men. He approached from outside, and when he was about thirty paces away, he entered the path to the east.
He vanished from sight. In a mere moment, the sound of a bronze bell was heard from the eastern mountain;
its great resonance shook the valley, and he said, "Aha! It calls for me. Within a few days, he told his disciples, "My life is nearly at its end.
Just as they had finished bathing him with fragrant water, the birds and beasts of the mountains—those of extraordinary colors and strange forms that were not usually seen—all [gathered together].
They all gathered by the side of the room; some treading upon the ground, others soaring through the air, wailing and calling out until they dispersed after passing before his mouth.

On the night of the seventeenth day of the twelfth month, he sat upright in the full lotus posture, still holding his *cintāmaṇi* staff while preaching the Dharma. His words and principles were profound and far-reaching. When he had finished, [he passed away].

He addressed his disciples, saying: "I have met you all in this transient encounter; now we must part forever. There is no appointed time for our reunion. Having spoken thus, he became silent and still.
After a long while, as the disciples were wailing and weeping, he opened his eyes and admonished them:
"In human life there is death; all things that begin must end. Such is the nature of the world—why should it be a cause for grief? I am now departing; do not disturb yourselves with such clamor."
"Regarding me: since I began practicing meditation until this very day, forty-nine years have passed, during which my back has never touched a bed.

I have not failed those who offered me alms, nor have I failed those who burned incense for me. You all should diligently exhort yourselves to practice the Way; do not let your efforts fail those who rely on you.
When his disciples asked where he would be reborn, he replied, "As I see it in my dreams, my report is that I shall be in Tuṣita Heaven."
The palace was blue in color and situated to the northwest of the heavens. I beheld the Great Master Zhizhe, surrounded on all sides by various devas and humans, all seated upon jeweled thrones;
yet one throne alone remained empty. I asked the reason for this, and he replied, "It is for the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Six years hence, he shall come to ascend here and preach the Dharma. He was seventy-two years of age. This occurred in the twelfth month of the first year of the Zhenguan era.
On the eighteenth day of the month at the hour of the horse (noon), he sat cross-legged in meditative equipoise as if entering *dhyāna*.

At that time, the sound of stringed and wind instruments arose in the void, heard by the entire assembly; after a long while, it ceased. He was seventy-two years of age. This is the location of his burial niche and tomb.
More than two hundred paces in front of Master Guǎngzhì’s stūpa was the monk Shì Yìbāo, whose surname was Xué.
He was a native of Jìnlíng in Chángzhōu and a descendant of the Qi Prime Minister Mèngchángjūn. He was also a scion of Zōngyíng, a renowned minister of Wú.
His spiritual nature was lofty and far-reaching, and his character was bright and lucid. After he entered the monastic order, he traveled about, engaging in discourse.

He diligently traveled throughout Kuaiji to preside over Dharma assemblies. Initially, he received instruction in the *Avataṃsaka* and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* sutras from Master Xiaoming at Yongding Temple in Suzhou;
subsequently, he took his leave to go to Master Kuang at Yong’an Temple on Mount Jinyun in Wuzhou.

He transmitted the scriptures and expounded the treatises for over thirty years, his fame spreading throughout the Three Commanderies. Later, he resided at Fanchang Monastery in Jinhua, Dongyang, where he propagated the Way with tireless diligence.
The capital city followed his example, and the matter was reported to the throne. An imperial decree was issued summoning him, and he immediately entered the court.
At that time, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang was at Cien Monastery, where he had recently begun to elucidate the profound principles of the Great Vehicle regarding existence and emptiness.

When both [subject and object] are dispatched and both medicine and disease are simultaneously eliminated, one might instead harbor a haughty spirit and glare with defiance, acting with arrogant and chaotic gestures.

Bao [Sengbao] provided the guiding thread for resolution and thoroughly brushed away the impurities of the divine mind. He interrogated him on the three barriers and investigated the five propositions; he meticulously encompassed the textual meanings and synthesized the insights regarding delusion.

At that time, all the eminent scholars present at the head of the assembly marveled at the extraordinary brilliance of his incisive penetration and were humbled by the comprehensiveness of his erudition.

His sharp and incisive [wisdom] caused the high officials and eminent scholars to look up to his virtuous reputation with reverence; they lingered over their conversations, and the dispatching of letters to him was never-ending.

In the winter of the third year of the Xianqing era, during the period for praying for snow through *yu* rituals, a merit-field (*fuchang*) was established within the palace. By imperial decree, he was summoned to enter the palace to debate the principles of doctrine with the Daoist masters of Dongming Guan.
There, a Daoist named Li Rong established the principle of the "Ultimate Limit" (*benji*). Bao [the Master] questioned him, saying: "Since this principle is designated..."
"Is the ultimate limit (koṭi) the basis for the Path, or is the ultimate limit based upon the Path? He replied, "They are mutually established.

Again he asked, "If the Path is based on the limit and the limit is the basis for the Path, may it also be said that the limit is based on the Path and the Path is the source of the limit? His reply was likewise comprehensive.

It was further asked: "If the Way (Dharma) and the primordial limit (ādi-koṭi) are allowed to be mutually contrary, then might it also be that spontaneity (svabhāva) and the Way are mutually capable of being each other's laws?
The answer was: "The Way takes spontaneity as its law; spontaneity does not take the Way as its law. It was further asked: "If the Way takes spontaneity as its law..."
"By nature, the Dharma does not rely on the Way; yet the Way may also be rooted in the ultimate limit (*koṭi*). That ultimate limit is not itself rooted in the Way.
Having been thus rebuked, Rong was unable to offer a rebuttal and immediately descended from his seat. The Son of Heaven was delighted, and the ladies of the inner palace sighed in admiration.

Śramaṇa Weixiu was profoundly learned, versatile, and capable; he devoted himself to the task of lecturing and proclaiming the Dharma. Resolute in his commitment to bear the burden of the teaching, he was both courageous and dignified in demeanor.
Regarding his literary style and eloquence, he was particularly esteemed for his brilliance and agility. Not long after, the Emperor ascended the throne.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the second year of Longshuo, an imperial edict was issued decreeing that monks and Daoists alike must perform secular prostrations. At that time, the monastic community was filled with confusion and did not know what to do.
Zhi Shouxia lamented the subtle decline within the Way of the Teachings and sighed over the arrogance of sovereigns and ministers toward the Dharma.

He subsequently submitted a memorial stating that śramaṇas ought not to perform prostrations. He cited various historical records spanning successive dynasties and invoked the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras as the standard for judgment.
The phrasing is elegant and refined, while the principles are profound and clear. As it says: "In leaving home, one does not maintain the rites of a householder;
in departing from the secular world, one does not receive the protocols of worldly society. This Way is manifest; it is an enduring and unalterable code for a hundred generations.

An edict was issued to the officials to assemble at the Central Secretariat to deliberate upon this matter. At that time, five hundred and thirty-nine ministers and officials submitted a petition [requesting...].

He did not bow. Three hundred and fifty-four people requested that he bow. At that time, more than two hundred monks from the capital went to the Penglai Palace to submit a memorial requesting [the Emperor] to grant his wish.
Thereupon, they gathered in great numbers at Ximing Temple to deliberate together and jointly submit a petition.
The various high officials and noble relatives were as frantic as those whose hair was already on fire; [Dao]xiu’s defiance of authority was what is meant by "staking one's life for the cause."
This is the Dharma.

Shi Faming was a native of Jingchu. He was extensively versed in the sutras and śāstras, and proficient in secular literature. His eloquence flowed like a stream, and his observance of the precepts was firm and upright.

During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, he entered Chang’an to visit and seek out various eminent masters. It happened that an imperial edict had been issued to determine the status of the monastic community.

Regarding the authenticity of the *Huahu chengfo jing* (Sutra on Laozi Converting the Barbarians to Buddhahood), at that time, the officials and attendants were gathered in the inner palace to listen;

the various eminent monks and nuns (*nāga-śrī*) were contending with the Daoist practitioners (*huángguān*). The matter was unsettled and unstable, wavering and difficult to resolve. Mingchu was not selected for the debate, yet as he left the hall, he asked the Daoists:

"In the *Laozi huahu chengfo*, does 'lão' mean 'to act' (*zuò*)? Does 'huà' mean 'to act' (*zuò*)? Does 'huà' mean 'to transform' (*huà*)? Does 'huà' mean 'to act' (*zuò*)? Does it mean 'to transform' (*huà*) into the Hu language?"

[The Master] transformed [the text]. If he had transformed it into the Chinese language, the Hu would not have understood; if he had transformed it into the Hu language, this scripture, upon arriving in this land, would have required translation.
I do not know at what year and month, in which dynasty, who recited the Hu language, or who recorded it in writing.
At that time, the Daoist practitioners were utterly unable to offer a rebuttal. The high officials all sighed in admiration. The first year of the Shénlóng era.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month, an imperial edict was issued stating: "I command all local officials to abolish this spurious scripture.
An inscription was carved upon stone at the Baima Monastery in the capital of Luoyang.
Śramaṇa Yixing, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Julu. From his youth, he was extraordinary; he did not need to read a book twice to master it, and he realized the world to be an illusion.
He took Master Ji as his teacher. Having left the household life and donned the dyed robes, there was no scripture or dharma he recited that he did not master through precise chanting.
Master Ji once convened a great assembly; śramaṇas from near and far arrived according to the appointed time, numbering more than a thousand. At that time, there was the scholar Lu Hong.

Retreating to live in seclusion on a separate peak, he was eminent in his realization and rich in learning. As the presiding master of a great assembly, he first requested Master Hong to compose a preface for the liturgical text and a eulogy for the monastic community.
On that day, Master Hong produced the text from his sleeve and placed it upon the table.

Once the bells and chanting had commenced, Master Hong said to Master Ji, "I have composed several thousand words; moreover, the characters are archaic and the style is ancient. I request that you recite them with clarity and elegance."
When it was time to proclaim [the text], Master Ji called for Xing to unroll the paper; having read it, he smiled slightly and placed it back upon the desk.

Hong found this act of levity strange. When the monks had gathered in the hall, Xing stepped forward with his sleeves rolled up and recited with a resonant voice and elegant phrasing, without a single error.
Hong stared at him in astonishment for a long while, sighing in admiration that could not be contained.

He further said to Master Ji, "This is not something you can instruct him in; you should instead allow him to travel for study. From then on, there were few renowned masters of the Three Studies who did not seek his counsel.
Consequently, he went to Dangyang, where he encountered Sengzhen, who was completing the preface to the *Vinaya-piṭaka*.

[Sengzhen] had a profound mastery of the *Vinaya* and was also well-versed in the books of *Yin-yang*, *Chen*, and *Wei*; [Huiyuan] investigated all of these in detail. He then sought out the art of calculation (*suan-shu*), which...
He traveled downward for several thousand *li*, inquiring of those who were knowledgeable along the way. Finally, he arrived at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
He saw a courtyard with dozens of ancient pines; its gate rested against a flowing stream, appearing serene and secluded.

As he stood before the screen at the entrance, he heard the sound of someone calculating within the courtyard—a rustling, *susu* sound. A monk said to his attendant, "Today there shall be a disciple."
"He has come from afar seeking my methods of calculation. By my reckoning, he should have arrived at the gate; surely there was no one to guide him here? Thereupon, he struck out one counting-bead.
He further said to his attendant, "The water in front of the gate shall flow westward again when the disciple arrives.

As the words were spoken, the disciple entered, prostrated himself, and requested the teachings. [The Master] bestowed the entire secret upon him. The water in front of the gate then flowed eastward once more. From that time on—

This reputation resounded far and wide, and the high officials spoke of him with great acclaim. When Emperor Xuanzong heard of this, he issued an edict for him to enter the palace and asked Xing, "What abilities do you possess?
Xing replied, "I am somewhat capable of memorization, but I have no other special talents. The Emperor then ordered an official of the inner court to fetch the palace registers to show them to him.
After Xing had finished perusing them once, he closed the original text; yet his memory was so precise and fluent that it was as if he had been practicing the recitation for a long time.
After several volumes [of consultation], the Emperor unconsciously descended from his couch and prostrated himself, saying, "The Master is truly a sage. He sighed in admiration for a long while.

Subsequently, the Emperor summoned him for frequent audiences to divine matters of calamity and fortune; [Yixing’s] prognostications were as clear as looking at one's own palm, and his words were often full of benefit.
At that time, there was one named Xing Hepu, whose mastery of the arts of the Way was such that no one could fathom its limits. He once said to Yin Yin: "Master Yixing is truly..."
He was a sage. Luo Xia Hong of the Han dynasty, while creating the calendar, said: "In eight hundred years, it shall differ by one day; then a sage will rectify it.
Now that the term has expired, the Da Yan Calendar has appeared, correcting its errors.
Thus, the words of Luo Xia Hong can be trusted. Who but a sage could act in such a way? Furthermore, he studied *dharma* under Vajra Tripiṭaka.

Having ascended the altar of the former Buddha and received the treasure of the Dharma King, he further translated the *Vairocana Sūtra* together with the Tripiṭaka Master Wufei, thereby opening the way for future Buddhist realms.
Both Emperor Ruizong and Emperor Xuanzong invited him to enter the Jixian Yuan (Academy of Scholarly Worthies).

Soon after, by imperial decree, he was stationed at Xingtang Monastery. He subsequently composed seven fascicles of commentaries on the translated scriptures, as well as the *She tiaofu zang* (Compendium of the Vinaya Pitaka) in sixty fascicles, the *Shishi xilu* (Genealogical Record of the Śākya Clan) in one fascicle, and the *Kaiyuan Dayan Li* (Kaiyuan Great Derivation Calendar) in fifty-two fascicles.
This calendar was incorporated into the "Calendar and Music" section of the *Jiu Tang Shu*, where it was regarded as an unalterable classic. There was a woman named Wang, an old neighbor, who...

The old woman said, "In the past, when I was poor, I often received your generous assistance. Now that you have attained such renown and fortune, I have always thought of repaying your kindness. One day, I went to pay my respects and said:

'My son has committed a murder and is about to be executed. Furthermore, since you, Master, are highly esteemed by the Emperor, I beg you to petition for a reduction of his sentence so that he may avoid death.'"

"To provide for my mother’s remaining years. She wept thus several times. The four [attendants] said, "Regarding the laws and punishments of the state, how could one possibly obtain exemption through pleading?
They ordered an attendant monk to provide a certain amount of money and goods, allowing her to leave and seek other means of support.

The old woman raised her hands like a halberd and cursed them fiercely, saying, "I lived as a neighbor to you, providing for you in turn with swaddling clothes and changing your diapers; I suckled you and raised you to adulthood."
"It has been accomplished. How could you forget this kindness? My mind was filled with compassion, and I found no joy throughout the entire night.

Thereupon, having finished his calculations, he summoned the attendants and instructed them, saying: "You all shall take cloth bags and wait, seated at noon, in a secluded spot in such-and-such a ward."
"Once you have captured the sow, cast it into the sack and return quickly. The next day, a sow indeed led seven piglets; the attendants drove them away from different directions.
The mother sow fled, and they captured the piglets and returned. Having prepared a large jar, they placed each piglet inside one by one and closed the lid.
They sealed the opening with *liu-yi* (six-ethereal) clay and recited several mantras in the local dialect before ceasing. At dawn, the palace eunuch arrived.
The Emperor summoned him to inquire, saying: "The Directorate of Astronomy has reported that last night none of the seven stars of the Northern Dipper were visible.
Why is this? He replied: "In the past, during the Later Wei dynasty, the planet Mars (Venus) once vanished; even until now, the 'Celestial Chariot' (the Northern Dipper) has remained invisible.
This is Heaven’s great warning to Your Majesty. Indeed, if even a single man or woman does not find their proper place, it results in frost falling out of season or drought."
"Moved by his profound virtue, he was able to cause [the dragon] to retreat. Nothing is better than to grant a general amnesty to the empire. The Emperor followed this advice.
That night, it was reported that one star of the Big Dipper had appeared; after seven nights, it returned to its original state. The efficacy of his arts was unfathomable.

Furthermore, during the Kaiyuan era, there was once a severe drought. The Emperor ordered him to pray for rain. He said, "One must obtain a vessel upon which the form of a dragon appears; only then will it be possible."
He brought forth rain. The Emperor ordered an eunuch to search through the inner treasury; they all reported that none were suitable.

Several days later, he pointed to a dragon coiled upon the handle of an ancient mirror and said with joy, "This is a true dragon. He then brought it into the ritual arena, and within a single day, it rained.
Shi Chengguan’s secular surname was Xiahou. He was a native of Shanyin in Yuezhou. He was brilliant, noble, and detached, not concerned with minor details.
He traveled extensively to seek out famous mountains and searched everywhere for secret treasuries. During the Qianyuan era, he relied upon Vinaya Master Li of Qixia Temple in Runzhou.
He studied the *Vinaya* according to the *Xiangbu* (Dharmaguptaka) school; originally following the tradition of Fatai, he later affiliated with the Nanshan Vinaya lineage.

He visited Dharma Master Xuanyi of Jinling to transmit the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) of Guanzhong and Heshang. During the Dali era, he studied the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) and the *Nirvana Sutra* at Waguan Temple.

Furthermore, from Fazang of Huainan, he received the commentary and meaning of the *Qixin lun* by a Korean master. He subsequently returned to the school of Dharma Master Zhen of Tianzhu to further refine his studies.
He spent seven years at Mount Shanxi studying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. From Dharma Master Huiliang of Chengdu, he revisited and investigated the *Three Treatises* (*Sanlun*).

For ten years, he studied under Dharma Master Zhanran in Suzhou, training in the Tiantai methods of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) and the commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and other scriptures.
He further visited Master Zhong of Niutou Mountain, Master Qin of Jing Mountain, and the master known as Wuming of Luoyang to seek their instruction.
He resolved upon the Chan method of the Southern School and further encountered Chan Master Huiyun, through whom he fully realized the profound principles of the Northern School.

In the eleventh year of the Dali era, he vowed to travel to Mount Wutai, visiting each site in turn; there, auspicious signs became increasingly frequent. He then proceeded to Mount Emei to seek an audience with Samantabhadra.

Ascending its precipices and lofty heights, he beheld the sacred images in their entirety. Returning once more to Mount Wutai, he resided at Dahuiyan Monastery, where he devoted himself exclusively to practice.
Regarding the Vaipulya Repentance Method: At that time, the temple master Xianlin invited [the Master] to lecture on the Great Sūtra and expound upon various treatises.

Consequently, he lamented that the old commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* were prolix in wording yet concise in meaning; overcome with deep reflection, he considered that Mañjuśrī presides over wisdom while Samantabhadra presides over principle.
The two sages combined constitute Vairocana; that all myriad practices are simultaneously perfected is precisely the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka*.

This commentary was begun in the first month of the first year of Xianqing (760 CE) and completed in the twelfth month of the third year of Zhenyuan (787 CE).

Shi Zhenbiao was a native of Baekje; his family resided at Mount Jinshan and had been hunters for generations. Zhenbiao was exceptionally agile and most adept with the bow and arrow.
During the Kaiyuan era, while resting in a field after pursuing game, he broke off willow twigs and strung them together to catch shrimp.

He had prepared a spit by skewering frogs and placed them in water to prepare as food. He then entered the mountains to hunt, chasing deer and returning home via the northern path of the mountain. He forgot to take the skewered frogs with him. When spring arrived the following year, while out hunting, he heard the croaking of frogs; approaching the water, he saw that thirty or so frogs from the previous year’s skewer were still alive. At that time, he sighed in lamentation and reproached himself, saying: [The remainder of the text follows: "I have been negligent and failed to heed my own words. I have caused these creatures to suffer for a full year. How could I not feel remorse? From this day forward, I shall never again kill living beings. Having spoken thus, he returned home and built a small shrine. He offered incense and prayed daily, vowing to abstain from eating meat for the rest of his life. After some years, he passed away peacefully. It is said that when his body was cremated, a fragrant smoke rose up and did not dissipate for several days. His remains were subsequently enshrined at the temple of Mount Zhongnan. This is the origin of the tradition of abstaining from meat on the six fasting days. Furthermore, it is said that those who eat meat on these days will suffer from indigestion and illness. Thus, one should know that the merit of observing the precepts is vast and profound, and the retribution for violating them is swift and severe. One must be cautious and diligent. This concludes the account of the Elder of Mount Zhongnan. It is also recorded that the monk Sengshao once visited the Elder’s shrine and offered incense. He then took a single stalk of incense and threw it into the fire. Suddenly, a frog emerged from the ashes and leaped onto the incense burner. Sengshao was startled and asked, "What creature is this? The Elder replied, "This is a frog from the previous year. Because you threw the incense into the fire, it has come to repay your kindness. Sengshao was deeply moved and wept. If the affliction stick departs from the "nine-eight," it is called the medium grade of precepts. If the various sticks remain buried and cover the "nine-eight," then the transgression is not extinguished, and the precepts are not obtained.
