and he mastered the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* under Master Yin at Folin Temple.

Later, he again dreamed of a foreign monk who presented him with a crystal vessel filled with śarīra relics and made him swallow them, saying, "The great teachings of the Tripiṭaka are now all stored within your belly. From that time on, regarding the scriptures...
In both Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises, he was peerless in his time. He once visited Mañjuśrī at Mount Qingliang, where all the holy sages appeared before him.

Later, at Taiyuan, he expounded a Great Sūtra, drawing a vast assembly from the entire capital. Emperor Dezong, hearing of his reputation, summoned him; upon meeting him, the Emperor was greatly delighted.

He frequently entered the imperial palace to discuss matters with the Confucian and Daoist scholars. The Emperor bestowed upon him a purple robe and a square-cut cassock, and subsequently issued an edict for him to serve as an attendant to the Sovereign.

The Crown Prince [Xianzong] at the Eastern Court held Emperor Shunzong in deep esteem; he treated him as a brother, sharing both bed and rise with him, and his kindness and courtesy were exceptionally profound.
Emperor Xianzong frequently visited his temple and received him as a guest or friend, often seeking his counsel.
Even in the midst of hurried exchanges, he never failed to make it his primary concern to propagate the teachings. Consequently, the Son of Heaven...
I further realized that the Buddha was a Great Sage and that his teaching contained great and inconceivable matters.

On the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away reclining on his right side facing west. His body was cremated, and over three hundred śarīra relics were obtained.
He was posthumously granted the title "Great Attainment" (Dá-dá), and his stupa was named "Mysterious Secret" (Xuánmì).
Shi Liangjia was a native of Kuaiji. In his youth, he followed a teacher and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.

When he reached the passage, "No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind," he suddenly touched his face with his hand and asked his teacher, "I, this person, do possess eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth."

"Why does the sutra say 'non-existent'? The Master was startled by this and took him to visit Nanquan. It happened that it was the anniversary of Mazu’s death, and they were performing a vegetarian feast.
Nanquan asked the assembly, "Tomorrow we shall hold a memorial service for Mazu; I wonder, will Mazu come or not? No one in the assembly could answer.
The Master stepped forward and replied, "He will come when he has a companion. Nanquan said, "Although this boy is young, he is truly remarkable."
[The Master] carved [the wood]. The Teacher said, "Venerable Sir, do not degrade the noble to the base. Next, he visited Mount Huai (Weishan).

He asked about National Teacher Nanyang Zhong’s discourse on "insentient beings preaching the Dharma. Weishan held up a fly-whisk and said, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not understand. I beg the Venerable Sir to explain it.
Weishan said, "The mouth born of one's parents shall never speak for the sake of a son. The Master said, "Is there anyone who is equal to the Teacher?"
At that time, a seeker of the Way was hesitant. Baizhang pointed him toward Yunyan and raised the previous question: "Regarding 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,' who is it that can hear it?
Yunyan said, "Insentient things themselves hear it. Baizhang asked, "Does the Master hear it as well? Yunyan said, "If I were to hear it, you would not."
"You did not hear me preach the Dharma. The Master asked, "Why did you not hear it? Yanguan held up his whisk and said, "Do you hear it now?
The Master replied, "I do not hear it. Yanguan said, "If you do not even hear me preach the Dharma, how much less can you hear the preaching of the insentient?
The Master asked, "In which scripture does the preaching of the insentient appear? Yanguan said, "Have you not seen that the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:"
The water birds and the trees all recollect the Buddha and the Dharma. At this, Master [Zhaozhou] attained a realization and composed a verse, saying:
"How wondrous! How wondrous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable. If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand;
Only when hearing through the faculty of sight does one finally know."
Shi Xi-yuan, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Gusu. Although his clan was wealthy and powerful, he alone renounced the household life and received the full precepts.
He then traveled among lecture halls, never remaining in one place, and diligently cultivated the Three Studies. At that time, he was widely acclaimed for his superior talent and refinement.
During the Guangqi era, he resided at Baolin Mountain Monastery in Kuaiji. He seldom harmonized with those of his time; when asked about this, he replied, "I roam freely within the formless."

This was the site where he practiced; it was merely like the lion’s play. During the Jingfu era, while expounding the sutras and treatises at the mountain temple, he authored several fascicles of the *Xuanchong chao* (Excerpts on the Profound).
He exhorted people to urgently cultivate the practices for rebirth in the upper realms, saying: "It is not difficult to know; it is difficult to practice.
He completed the six-period liturgy and repentance ceremony without ever missing even a single instance. He lived in a small room atop Langya Mountain. This is...
It is a mountain. Tradition says it flew here from Langya Terrace. This place was formerly a slaughterhouse, and thus the mountain deities were all enshrined beneath it.
The mountain’s household has a well that is full of many supernatural wonders. One account says this is where Yu chained the dragons, crocodiles, and other such creatures of the Zhejiang River;
their name is *jū*. The *jū* have two ears and are a pale yellowish-green color; whenever they climb bamboo or trees, [it is an omen]. It must...

When wind and rain arrived, [the creature] would sometimes emerge from stone crevices and enter the monks' quarters. Seeing people in the ditches and channels, it was not startled; yet if one tried to seize it, it would leap about as if in a rage.

It entered Huìyuǎn’s circular room alone; when Yuǎn grasped it with his hands, it would curl up and submit. Thereupon, he administered the precepts of taking refuge to it, commanding it not to act as a demon of wind and hail.

Following Huìyuǎn’s death, violent winds and rains became frequent. This was because of Huìyuǎn— *Note: The original text appears to be a fragment. The translation provided reflects the available portion.*
He practiced diligently, vowing to behold Maitreya. During one lecture, he sat upright and passed away upon his Dharma seat.
At that time, the assembly smelled a wondrous fragrance and heard celestial music for seven days thereafter.

Shi Zhixuan was a native of Hexi. He specialized in the esoteric mantras of the Five Indias. Clad in garments of hemp and coarse cloth, he traveled through various prefectures and counties, never dwelling in urban monasteries but lodging only in the wilds and thickets on the outskirts.
Zhixuan was intent on visiting famous sites of sacred traces; upon reaching Jizhou, he stayed overnight in a cemetery forest.
That night, the moonlight was as bright as day, and he saw a fox emerge from beneath the trees. It was about to...
She placed a skull upon her head; she wore it as long as it shook without falling off. She further took weeds and leaves to conceal her body.
In an instant, she transformed into a seductive young woman, dressed entirely in plain white silk, standing by the left side of the road.
She heard faintly from the northeast the sound of a horse with a saddle approaching. The woman wept piteously, overcome with grief. After a short while, [a rider] arrived on horseback.
A horseman encountered her. He dismounted and asked, "Madam, why are you wailing so bitterly in the deep of night out in the wilds?
The woman covered her tears and deceived him, saying, "My humble home is by the Yi River. Two years ago, my parents betrothed me to the Zhang family of this land as a wife.
Unfortunately, my husband passed away last year; the household affairs have fallen into ruin, and I have no..."
She was supported by her parents at home; they did not know that their concubine was so solitary and suffering. Her heart was pierced with such pain that she could not help but be moved to grief.
She thought of returning to her family for a visit, yet it was impossible. The groom said, "I had thought my lady’s sorrow and resentment were due to some other matter.
If you wish to return to your hometown, I am currently on leave from my duties as a soldier of Yiding Command and shall return to the River Yi. My lady—"
The son was about to mount his coarse carriage when the woman, wiping away her tears and expressing her gratitude, was just about to climb aboard.
At that moment, Xuan emerged from the cemetery grove and said, "Gentleman, this woman is not human; she is a fox transformed.
The man replied, "How could a monk make such an accusation against me? Do you perhaps wish to plot something else? Xuan said, "If you do not believe me, please wait a moment. I shall—"
He said to the man, "I shall transform you back into your original female form. Xuang then shook his monk’s staff and chanted several phrases in a foreign tongue;

the woman immediately turned back into a fox and fled, her skull and tattered grass still clinging to her body. The horseman prostrated himself in repentance, saying, "Had it not been for the Master's rescue, I would have perished along with the demon."
Shi Chonghui, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Hangzhou. From his youth, his character and disposition were transcendent.
He traveled to pay homage to National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing, where he applied himself diligently to meditative contemplation and made the practice of the Three Mysteries his constant task.

Initially, at the summit of Qianqing Zuifeng Peak in Changhua, he constructed a thatched hut as a hermitage and devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī* for several years. He subsequently traveled to Xiashiji in Yanguan.
On a mountain, he stayed in a small, pointed-topped grass hut. Suddenly, a deity appeared and said to Huì: "Master, you hold the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa* [sūtra], yet you have omitted the word *svāhā*.
This causes the secret mantra to be incomplete. *Svāhā* signifies 'accomplishment. Now, in the capital, the Buddha-dharma is being trampled by non-Buddhist teachings;
its peril is such that it is like a dangling thread. It awaits your salvation. Huì then hurried his journey westward, and after three years—

On the twenty-third day of the ninth month in the year Wushen, the Daoist priest Shi Hua of Taicong Palace submitted a memorial requesting a contest between the Buddhist and Daoist traditions to determine the superiority of their respective doctrines and practices.
At that time, Emperor Daizong held the Buddhist school in high esteem.

The followers of heterodox paths were indignant at his widespread veneration; they consequently constructed a ladder of blades before the altar of the Dongming Pavilion. Shi Hua climbed it as if it were an ordinary path.
At that time, the assembly of monastics looked on at one another, none daring to step forward. When Huai heard of this, he visited the Minister of State Yu Cha’en.
Yu submitted a petition requesting that a ladder be erected against the courtyard trees of Zhangxin Temple, with its rungs fashioned from sharp-edged weapons. As if... [the text continues].
It was as if covered in frost and snow. The height increased by a hundred *zhang*, making the ladder of Dongming extremely low.

At that time, high officials of the court and residents of the marketplaces crowded together, their feet side-by-side and shoulders brushing, to witness this feat. Then, Hui climbed the steps barefoot from the lower level.
It was as if traversing a level road, without any expression of difficulty. He further stepped upon blazing fires and reached into boiling oil with his hands;

he continued to eat iron leaves called *bàtóu* (noodles), or chewed nails and wires that sounded like brittle taffy. Shi Hua was struck with fear and shame, covering his face with his sleeves and withdrawing.
At that time, the assembly snapped their fingers in admiration, the sound like the roar of thunder. The Emperor dispatched the eunuch Gong Tingyu to proclaim [the decree].

After being comforted and exhorted several times, he was presented with a set of purple robes and a square-cut cassock. By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Tripitaka Master Huguo" (Protector of the Nation) and ordered to reside at An Guo Temple.

Shi Guichen’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Changshan. From childhood, he sought to distance himself from worldly life, observing the vegetarian diet and maintaining [his vows] for a single meal.
His mind was solely resolute. Bound by affection for his two parents, he followed the example of the prince who left the city to become a monk.

He served National Master Wuxiang of Wansui Temple in the local prefecture and ascended to the stage of ordination, where he studied the Vinaya. Thereupon, he admonished himself, saying: "To restrain the body through the observance or violation of precepts is not liberation."

To provide an interpretation based merely on the literal text—how could that possibly give rise to the realization of a sage? Thereupon, he vowed to seek out the Southern School, traveling nearly ten thousand *li*.

He first visited Yunju and later went to Xuefeng, where he questioned the masters with diligent devotion. He attained the essential meaning from Master Zongyi; regarding luminosity and darkness, form and emptiness, his mind became vast and free of delusion.
He practiced in secret for many years, concealing his realization while remaining among the multitude. Eventually, he served as the former Governor of Zhangzhou, Taizhou, and Taiyuan.
The Prince requested that he establish a lotus palace at West Stone Mountain (Xishan) in Min City and reside there.

He remained there for thirteen and a half years, with a community of two hundred followers coming and going. Because [Dao]chen regarded the secret and profound Dharma as too weighty to be shown lightly to ordinary disciples, he would only expound it upon request from those who had mastered the esoteric studies.
Later, when Longxi was under the military administration of Qinzhou, the Great Protector Langlang Gong [established a monastery]. His aspiration...
He was requested to preach the Dharma for the assembly at Luohan Monastery, whereupon he opened up skillful means. Within a few years, disciples from the north and south emerged like towering peaks.
Cao Shan Wenyi of Fuzhou and Dongchan Linfu Xian of Jiangzhou both transmitted the profound instructions of Chanben, each becoming a masterful "Dharma Eye" of their own school.
In the autumn of the third year of the Tiānchéng era (the Wuzi year), he suddenly manifested illness; after several days, he passed away while sitting peacefully.
Shi Chengchu’s surname was Zong. On the evening of his birth, a brilliant light filled the room. When he reached the age of seven, his relatives took him into a temple;
upon seeing the Buddha image, he would immediately sigh in admiration and prostrate himself. Returning home, he asked his father, "Only the Buddha is like this; what of others?
His father replied, "All living beings are Buddhas, how much more so human beings. Chengchu said, "I wish to study the Buddha. For a moment...
He sought to repay the diligent labors of his two parents, and his father granted him permission. When he reached the age of ten, he went to Xiangguo Temple and took Zhiming as his teacher.
There was a group of children playing together who lured him toward them. He rebuked them, saying, "Why do you take pleasure in such games?
Even Shancai of the Snowy Mountains was but a child; is he not also like this? A bystander who heard this marveled at him, saying, "This boy will achieve greatness in the future."
He was surely a great vessel for the Dharma-gate. Since receiving full ordination, he had studied the new Vinaya texts and frequently entered the caverns of the *Vinaya* (Vina-yaya).
His refutations were so difficult to answer that he was known at the time as a "Tiger of the Vinaya," baring his fangs and extending his claws.

As those who sought his instruction among princes, dukes, and high officials grew daily more numerous, the Jin High Ancestor heard of him and held him in profound admiration, issuing an edict to admit him into the inner chapel and bestowing upon him a purple *kāṣāya*.

He was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenfa. From this time on, among the imperial consorts and princesses who aspired to the Dharma, those who shaved their heads and received ordination under him were appointed by him as masters of the new chapter of the Vinaya.
He passed away without illness on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Xiande era.
The army of Chu clearly adhered to the laws. Why was he called the "Patriarch" at that time? There are three schools of law. Lü Sù proclaimed these:
there are human laws, which consist of the prohibitions and the majestic deportment; there are celestial laws, which consist of radiance and pure meditative concentration.

Essentially, it does not go beyond morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These three serve as the path by which one departs from the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Single-mindedness serves as the gate through which one enters the domain of *nirvāṇa*. If one relies on these for immediate application, they reside in the *vinaya* (discipline).

By guarding the three karmas, all three karmas become pure; the six sense objects are naturally dispelled. Among the practices cultivated by the sages and worthies, what is there that does not rely upon this?
From this, we may infer by extension: if one seeks the principle through the words, it is the *vinaya*; if one seeks the cause, it is the scriptural teaching of the *prātimokṣa*.
As for the fruit, it is the *prātimokṣa* itself. To speak in terms of time, all Buddhas of the three periods have established these same precepts.
To speak in terms of spatial boundaries, they are practiced together throughout the pure lands of the ten directions. This is why Upāli...
The seven Buddhas of the past all entrusted the precepts to him.

Shi Xindo was the son of the Xu family from Meizhou; he received the full ordination at the age of thirty. He went to Chengdu to study *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, believing that he had reached the ultimate understanding.
A fellow monk in his quarters challenged him, saying: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Now, with your own eyes—"
Suddenly, the myriad phenomena before him were in a state of total stillness; where did his conscious mind reside? The Way seemed vast and boundless, and he thus departed the pass.

He wandered through the Yangtze and Huai regions until he reached Tàipíng in Shū Prefecture, where he heard Fójian’s night discourse. Fójian raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” and cited Jue Tièzuǐ, who said, "The former master did not say such words;
do not slander the former master. Because of this, a great doubt arose within him. After he had maintained this inquiry for a long time, suddenly—
At dawn, his mind suddenly opened up. He immediately hurried to the master’s chamber, intending to recount what he had realized.
As soon as Foyan Jian saw him, he closed the door. Xuedou said, "Master, do not deceive me. Jian replied, "The ten directions have no walls; why do you not enter through the door?
Xuedou then broke the window paper with his fist. Foyan immediately opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak! Xuedou then struck Jian with both hands.
He struck his head with his hand, made a "tsui" sound with his mouth, and departed. He presented this verse: "Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree;
Zen practitioners have passed it down throughout the world. Most merely pluck at the leaves and seek out the branches, Unable to realize the root-source directly beneath them.
Master Jue says there is no such thing; This is truly like reviling me to my face with foul words. If Zen practitioners possess the eye that penetrates all quarters, They should look well toward—"

In this, he distinguishes between the true and the false; let us examine it clearly. In the first year of the Xuanhua era of the Song dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to change the title of "monk" (*seng*) to "Virtuous Man" (*deshi*).
Consequently, he opened the Dharma at Tianning Temple and ascended the hall, saying: "The matter of the Patriarch’s coming from the West is, today, especially new.

Formerly I had the appearance of a *bhikṣu*; now I take the form of the Old Lord (*Laojun*). A crane-feather cloak over a silver-brown robe, with a banana-leaf turban wrapped around my head. In the forests and springs there is no..."
Serving guests, I have twice received the Lord’s grace. Therefore it is said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season.
But tell me, what is the season right now? Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest the conventional within the absolute;
the old man Mañjuśrī dons a crane-feather cloak simply to conform to the exigencies of the times. One person...
Since this is so, it is likewise for all people. When a great master establishes a monastic grove, he joyfully welcomes a gathering of immortals.

Together they sip the wine of the Immortal-Intoxicated, and in unison they chant the *Buxu* verses. Sometimes they read the *Lingbao Duren Jing*; sometimes they discuss the elixirs of longevity and immortality.
Under the moon, lutes are played, their fingertips emitting the sounds of antiquity; before the eaves, chess pieces are laid out, their subtle moves emerging from the board.
Beyond divine mechanism: take one step forward and you reach the heavens of the Great Brahma; take one step back and you enter the city of the Nine Shades.

As for the phrase "neither advancing nor retreating," how would you explain it? "Even if one transforms into an immortal on the path of the Three Clarities, in the end it remains but a delusory body within saṃsāra.
In the ninth month of the second year, an imperial edict was issued to restore the monastic community. He ascended the hall and said:
He did not wear the field-clothing (kāṣāya) but donned feathered robes; this appearance suited the Old Lord quite well. For over a year and a half he reflected idly upon the matter:
generally speaking, rise and fall each have their own time. My Buddha, the Tathāgata, had previously prophesied that the Dharma would encounter difficulties;

when calculating the years, it was precisely at this point. Māra took advantage of the situation to delude and confuse the True Teaching; monks altered their secular forms, and the Buddha [was further obscured].

Regarding names, they gave rise to false interpretations at will; they excised passages from the scriptures and altered the wording of the *nīradanda* (cymbals). They added feet to the *pātra* (alms bowls) and practiced many forms of deceit.
Fortunately, my sagely brilliance did not forget the sacred entrustment and did not allow its teachings to fall into ruin.

I have specially bestowed imperial verses and granted permission for the monastics to undergo re-ordination. This is truly like cold ashes catching fire once more, or withered wood flourishing again. [The text here] transforms the wine of delusion...

It is the ambrosial jade nectar. The *Buxu Ci* (Verse of the Void-Walker) has been turned into a "Song of Returning Home. Setting down the silver wooden tablet, he picks up the *niśīdana* (sitting mat).
Yesterday he prostrated; today he bows. Only the outward appearance has changed, not the person of old.
He asks the assembly: "Is the person of old one, or two? After a long silence, he says: "The autumn wind."
Some may also resent the messiness of it all; it has blown away the ashes of the Way from those years.

In the spring of the third year of the Jianyan era, he addressed the assembly, citing the occasion when Linji entered nirvana and entrusted [the Dharma] to Sansheng. He said: "The treasury of the true Dharma eye was extinguished by a blind donkey.
Where did Linji ever say such a thing? People of both past and present have all spread this falsely. Do not believe them; simply wait and see after three months. When [the time came],...
In the intercalary third month, there was a rebellion. The assembly requested that the Master flee southward, but he said, "The purpose of studying the Way is to bring an end to birth and death;
what is there to avoid? When the rebels arrived, he said, "Kill me quickly to satisfy your hearts.
The rebels then raised their spears and struck him; white milk flowed upward from his body. The rebels were struck with awe, spread their mats over him, and departed.
Shi Dingxu, whose style name was Lan’an, was surnamed Lin. In his youth, he studied Confucianism and passed the jinshi examination; he was well-regarded for his administrative achievements.

At the age of twenty-five, while reading the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (Yijiao jing), he suddenly attained realization, exclaiming: "How nearly have I been misled by the scholar’s cap! He immediately desired to renounce the secular life.

When her mother found it difficult for her to go to the groom’s house for the wedding ceremony due to her mourning period, she laughed heartily and said, “The peach blossoms and apricot flowers shall all be entrusted to the spring breeze at once;
from now on, the green bamboo and yellow chrysanthemums shall forever be my companions on the Way. She then followed Master Le of Baoshou as a full monk (*bhikṣu*).
Having traveled extensively to consult with renowned masters, she returned to her hometown to build a hermitage on Qiang Peak. There, she once asked about the saying, “This very mind is Buddha.”
At that time, Xu Need was staying at Miaoxi Hermitage on Yangyu Island with Huian Guangzai in attendance. Need specifically sent a letter inviting him, saying:
"The methods of the abbot here are different from those of other quarters; would you come for a brief visit? Need did not reply. Guangzai used a stratagem to invite him there.
It happened that Miaoxi was conducting a formal session (*ru shi*) for the assembly; Need intended merely to join in the appreciation of the occasion. Consequently, Miaoxi...
The Record relates: A monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu replied, "Mind itself is the Buddha. [The Master] said, "How do you understand this? Give me your response!

Xiu [the monk] spoke, and Mazu scolded him, saying, "With such a view as yours, how dare you presume to act as a teacher to others? He then had the drums beaten to proclaim Xiu's erroneous interpretation.
With tears streaming down his cheeks, Xiu did not dare look up. He thought to himself in silence, "Since I have been treated thus by him..."
He set aside the teachings that had not been transmitted since the West’s arrival. Could it have stopped there? He then sought to enter the ranks of the disciples.
One day, Miaoxi asked him, “When there is no letting out from within and no letting in from without—just at such a time, what is it like?
As Xu was about to open his mouth, Miaoxi took up his bamboo staff and struck him three times across the spine. Xu attained great enlightenment and cried out in a stern voice, “Master!”
“Already too many! Xì struck him once more. Xuī bowed in prostration. Xì laughed and said, “Only today do you know that I did not deceive you.
Yìn spoke in verse: “The Eye of Mahesvara stands erect upon the crown of the head; A life-snatching talisman hangs askew from behind the elbow.
Blind the eyes! Cast off the talisman! Zhaozhou hangs his gourd on the eastern wall. From this time forth, his fame resounded throughout the monastic community.
His influence spread to distant regions. Later, when he opened the hall for teaching, he was acclaimed as a master of the "eye" (the true Dharma eye).
Shi Wunian, whose secular surname was Xiong and who hailed from Macheng, traveled to Mount Wutai and Mount Funiu, visiting and questioning renowned elders everywhere.
Upon reaching Mount Lu, he went to attend upon Da'an. An asked, "What is your name? The Master replied, "Wunian. An said, "Which one is it?"
"Non-thought. The Master was at a loss. Returning to the mountain, he spoke to his companion about his experiences traveling on pilgrimage for several years.

His companion said, "Why do you not ask about your own self? The Master asked, "What is this 'self'? [The companion] replied, "Picking up objects is not with the hands; eating food is not with the mouth.
One night, hearing the sounds of laughter and weeping meeting one another, he attained realization. He entered Longhu and, together with Layman Zhuowu, arrived at Si...
At Masan, a lecturer arrived. The Master asked him, "The fundamental nature is pure and still; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
After the lecturer finished his discourse, the Master said to him, "Try to explain this. As the lecturer was about to respond, the Master gave him a push on the knee and said, "What about this?
At this, the lecturer was suddenly enlightened. He spoke a verse: "For over forty years I did not rest my efforts; I investigated and investigated until I reached the end."
Its turning leaves no trace. Now, having reached the point of total destitution and having nowhere to rely, I finally regret my previous misapplication of effort.
A monk asked, "What is the essence of the Way? The Master said, "It fills the mouth, yet words cannot reach it. The monk asked, "What happens when the four elements disperse?"
The Master raised his fist and said, "This does not belong to the four great elements.

Shi Wuming was the son of Pei of Chongren. When he was first born, there were complications with the delivery; his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the child was delivered safely, so this was his name.
At the age of nine, he entered the local school and immediately asked, "What is this 'vast and boundless qi'? He was then given his lessons.

The Master regarded this as extraordinary. When he grew up, he read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and it felt as if he were encountering it for the first time despite having practiced it previously.

He then followed Chong of Im-san to receive the tonsure, but after some time, he took his leave and went into retreat at Mount Oe. While there, he was reading the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* and came across the passage where a monk asks Xingshan, "What is the Way?

to which Xingshan replies, "A magnificent mountain. He remained stuck in doubt and unable to resolve it. One day, while exerting himself to push a massive boulder, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He spoke in verse: "Those who wish to enter the path of unsurpassed Bodhi must swiftly clear away the great mountain. Only upon knowing the Way does one realize the mountain is not good;
then, turning the body around, one leaps out of the Patriarch’s barrier. He presented himself to Namsan, who certified him as a vessel of the Dharma.
From that time on, having shaved his head and donned the monastic robes, he labored his body and endured physical hardship, never venturing beyond the mountains for twenty-four years.
In the *jiawu* year of the Wanli era, while residing at Baofang, a monk asked the Master, "Since you have lived on this mountain, whom have you ever met?

The Master replied, "I have not yet traveled anywhere. The monk said, "How can one view the world as small from the perspective of a single corner? The Master appreciated these words and subsequently took up [his staff].
The veteran masters who traveled afar to study under him all praised and extolled him. Recently, he went to Mount Wutai to visit Master Ruifeng and inquire about the teachings of Zhaozhou.

The Master requested a verse from him. Ruifeng said, "When you understand this kind of matter, simply let it be. The Master prostrated and presented his verse: "The spring colors are hidden in the dark; The autumn light is revealed in the bright.
Though one has eyes, they cannot discern it; Even with wisdom, it is difficult to measure. Having reached home, I do not ascend Chang'an."
On the road, let the wind, flowers, snow, and moon rise as they will. "The peaks are deep"—these are the words of Master Ken; they harmonize wondrously with the Dongshan school.
The Master himself also took it upon himself to continue the lineage of the Dongshan school. Before long, he returned to Baofang. Later, he presided over the two monasteries of Dongyan and Shouchang.
Entering the hall, he said: "Clouds do not rely on the mountain; the mountain does not rely on clouds. When the mind is unstained by objects, objects are devoid of mind. Clouds and mountains..."
Pure as the state of mind, a single path of empty brilliance illuminates the Great Clarity.

Although it is thus—pulling out the sinews without moving the skin, changing the bones without seeing blood—the tendons and bones are all at once empty; one wanders about without falling or stumbling.
Bodhidharma the Great Being understood extinction but did not understand birth; Śākyamuni the Elder understood birth but did not understand extinction. To truly know birth and extinction—
"It has nothing to do with it. It is simply this year’s dried-up dung pellet.

In the winter of the Ding-si year of the Wanli era, the Master returned from the fields and said to the assembly, "From now on, I shall no longer lay stones. The assembly was astonished. On the third day of the following spring, he manifested a slight ailment.
On the seventeenth day, he composed a verse for his funeral pyre and commanded his attendant to chant it. He then wrote again, saying: "Today..."
He gave clear instructions, then cast aside his brush, sat upright, and passed away. At his cremation, his cranial bone and various teeth remained unburnt;
these were enshrined in his home temple, where a stūpa was constructed.

Master Mùyún once gave a small lecture (xiǎocān) at the residence of the Zhang family of Chángshú, saying: "Along the shores of the great sea by Lóujīng, the tides of faith gather and subside in turn.

Because the land is numinous, auspiciousness must surely concentrate here, and thus an eminent layman has emerged from among the multitude. Each of you has a home for sustaining life, with children gathered around you;
yet you remain unstained by worldly dharmas, like lotus flowers in the water. I, this mountain monk, have come at this opportune time to bear witness."
The ultimate meaning is not non-existent when proven. But tell me, by what means is it verified? He then planted his staff upright and said:
"When a son of the Buddha dwells in this place, it is the very enjoyment of the Buddha; he is constantly within it, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
If one discusses this matter, it is like a family living by the seashore catching fish: it is simply because they know that there are fish in the great ocean that they think of them.
Wishing to catch them, he devised a plan. He constructed a boat, rigged a sail, and secured the tiller.
He invited a man well-versed in sea routes to serve as the helmsman. They sailed out into the open ocean to wait for the fish to arrive;
then, casting a single net, they returned home with a full cargo of both large and small fish. Upon arriving at the market, he sold them to support his family.
Grandson, one never exhausts its enjoyment. It is the same for those who study the Way:
first, they must know that within the body of an ordinary person there definitely exists the great matter of the vast, luminous Buddha and Patriarchs—like fish in the sea.

Without giving rise to doubt or hesitation, and refusing to let themselves be deluded, they then contemplate Zen meditation and strive urgently to bring it forth. This is like seeking fish in the sea; do not engage in petty calculations, but cast aside worldly concerns.
Therefore, rouse your diligent effort. Travel thousands of miles to seek out wise teachers and draw near to virtuous friends, seeking their guidance and earnestly receiving their instruction.
Like following the directions of a skilled navigator, you will suddenly awaken within your own being to the great matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Then, returning home to nurture this realization, you shall enter the marketplace with hands extended, flourishing the Dharma gate and thereby repaying [your debts].
The Buddha’s benevolent virtue can, at the very least, serve as an inspiration for those to come; its enjoyment is likewise inexhaustible.
Nevertheless, even so, within the great ocean, how could there be no wind and waves? How could there be no peril and alarm?

Yet, one who does not give rise to fear and presses straight ahead is driven by the intense resolve to catch fish. Why should it be any different with the practice of Zen? One must seek to bring forth realization.
Regarding the great matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must disregard danger and ruin, and remain indifferent to whether circumstances are favorable or adverse.
Through a thousand demons and myriad hardships, one must proceed directly without retreating; then there will be no need to worry that the Buddha-dharma will not reach one’s hands.

Although the Buddha-dharma is a ready-made reality, if one does not exert oneself with the ferocity of a man catching fish, how can it be obtained? Therefore, those who study the Way must examine themselves and turn toward—
Come and investigate: Can you be as urgent as one catching a fish? Can you go straight ahead without turning back?
When encountering minor circumstances within the monastic community, can you remain free from alarm and not take them to heart?

If you have not yet reached this level, then ultimately your resolve for Zen practice will not be as urgent as your resolve for catching a fish. How can the Great Matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs [be neglected]?
One must be able to penetrate through to the root. Therefore, the ancients said: "To lead a person by the hand, they cannot go;

only when the person themselves is willing can there be intimacy. They also said: "The Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment everywhere: he attains equal and perfect enlightenment upon mountains of knives and trees of swords;
he attains equal and perfect enlightenment within boiling cauldrons and glowing embers; he attains equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the staff."

"Awakening. He attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; he is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker who does not deceive, and the speaker who does not speak otherwise.
Is there anyone here now who can provide witness to such a matter? After a long silence, he said:
"If one lacks such an eye for selecting the Buddha, what would even a thousand years of practice avail?"
Shi Ru, whose style name was Wufeng, was a native of Shaanxi. He maintained a strict discipline over his person and applied himself with diligent effort in all matters.
One night, while conversing with Tiantong, Tiantong suddenly extended his leg and asked, "What do you do? The Master kicked it with his own foot. Tiantong laughed and said, "Not there, not there.
The Master said, "Tell me, Venerable Sir. Tiantong lay down on his back. The Master said, "It’s just that you are tired."
The boy said, "You have gone off in that way again. The Master bowed. One day, as he was taking his leave, the boy held up a whisk and said, "To call it a 'whisk' is to encounter it;
not to call it a 'whisk' is to turn one's back on it. You may neither pick it up nor set it down."
"One must speak; one must not remain silent; one must not speak erroneously. If you do not speak erroneously, I shall entrust this to you.
The Master leaped twice, saying, "No, no! The Boy said, "That was still just shouting and jumping about.
Try speaking again. The Master turned around and said, "I am going. Thereupon, the Boy entrusted him.
Shi Fazang, styled Hanyue, was the son of the Su family of Liangxi. At nineteen, he shaved his head at Deqing Hermitage;

at twenty-nine, he encountered doubts while reading the *Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng*. After more than ten years had passed, upon hearing the sound of a bamboo being snapped, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
In the spring of the Jiazi year of the Tianqi era, when Tiantong Wu was propagating the Way at Jinsu, the Master went there to seek instruction. He arrived just as Wu was ascending [the hall].
The Master raised this case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then? The worthy replied, "You are still a man standing on the steps.
The monk said, "I ask the Master to lead me up the steps. The worthy said, "We shall meet after the moon has fallen. Thereupon, the boy looked at the Master and said:

"Furthermore, tell me: after the moon has fallen, how do you see one another? The Master then went out. When the novice ascended the hall, he raised his staff and said, "If you raise one, you must not raise two;
to let pass one move is to fall into the second. He then threw down the staff and said:
"Fall twice and go. [The Master] asked, "And as for 'one'—how do you raise it? He then descended from his seat. The Master snatched up his staff and walked away.
The attendant returned to the abbot’s quarters; the Master presented the staff to him, saying, "This is the staff that has beaten everyone under heaven.
Today, I return it to you, Master. The attendant took it and struck him, saying, "I shall beat you first to get things started. The Master said, "Fortunately..."
He managed to get back the handle of the preceptor’s ladle. The boy said, "I still find this insufficient," and struck him several more times. The Master prostrated himself and departed.
Later, while presiding over the assembly, he said in his hall discourse: "Unable to hold on, one suddenly turns back; thus the ultimate barrier of our school is shattered."
"Only a pair of impoverished companions remain; / Only then does one know there is no dharma to entrust to the world.
Shi Daomen, styled Muchen, was a native of the Lin family of Chaozhou. He received the tonsure at Mount Lu and entered the presence of Master Wu as a seat-counselor at Tiantong.
Having served as head of the secretariat for many years, he was invited to succeed to the abbacy. A monk asked: "What is the realm of Tiantong?"
The Master said: "Twenty li from the Pine Pass, the journey is nearly over; the green mountains cradle forth the Palace of the Brahma King. [The student] asked:
"What is it like to be a person within this realm? The Master said: "Leisurely shifting my staff, I stand at the foot of a pine tree, smiling as I ask the guest:

'From where have you come? [The student] asked: "As for the matter of the Supreme Vehicle (the *zongchengl*), what is it like? The Master said: "Look beneath your feet. [The student] asked: "What is the emergence of all Buddhas?"

[The Master] was at his dwelling. The Master said, "Have you eaten your congee yet? The monk hesitated. The Master said, "The Buddhas have long since passed away. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said:
"Śākyamuni Buddha said, 'When one engages in such reflection, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear.

An ancient worthy said, 'As soon as one enters into reflection, it immediately becomes a superfluous dharma. Now tell me: since the names are the same, why is there benefit for some and harm for others?"
A woman of upright countenance may easily apply her rouge; a fine young man is hard to find without wealth. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"There is one person with three heads and eight arms; there is another person without a back and without a face. Both arrive at the gate of Tiantong—tell me, where shall they lodge?
One evening, he entered the hall and cried out loudly: "I have not seen the ox from the pen since this morning!"
"Everyone, let us go up the mountain with torches to search for the ox! The assembly was stunned. As soon as one monk stepped out, the Master returned to his quarters.
He often cited the saying, "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts," and offered this verse: "My straw sandals have trodden through the snows of Jiangnan;
Returning, I gaze upon the clouds on the stones of Mount Lu. I laugh that my idle body is still not old, Yet I have searched for plum blossoms many times."
Passing through the Pine Gate.

Compiled by the Layman of Wuyuan, Xu Changzhi (Jin Zhou):
The monk Shi Tanhuo practiced vegetarianism and asceticism. He frequently resided among tombs and beneath trees, specializing in converting sentient beings through his supernormal powers.
At that time, Lili Gu, a Xianbei from Hexi, had usurped control of Xiping and proclaimed himself king, naming his era the second year of Huanxi.
In the eleventh month of that year, Huo came from Henan, arriving from Xiping carrying a single *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), saying, "This is the Eye of Prajñā;
by revering it, one may attain the Way. When people offered him clothing or other items, he would accept them and immediately cast them to the ground.
Or he would cast it into a river; after a short while, the robe would return to its original owner, not stained by anything at all.
He traveled as swiftly as the wind and spoke of people’s births, deaths, nobility, and lowliness without the slightest error.

If someone hid his staff, he would close his eyes for a brief moment and immediately know its location. All marveled at his spiritual wonders, and because of this, many people came to follow the Buddha. Lu Gu had—

His younger brother, Tuotan, was temporarily appointed as General of Chariots and Cavalry; his influence dominated the puppet state. By nature he was suspicious and jealous, committing many acts of murder and harm.
Huo repeatedly said to Tan, "You ought to cultivate goodness and practice the Way to serve as a bridge for future generations.

Tan replied, "Since my ancestors' time, I have reverently served Heaven and Earth, as well as the famous mountains and great rivers. If I were now suddenly to embrace Buddhism, I fear it would violate the intentions of my forebears."
"If you, sir, can remain without food for seven days while your complexion remains as usual, this would prove that you possess the spiritual power of the Buddha-way;
I shall then honor you. He then had someone keep Huo secluded for seven days. Yet Huo showed no sign of hunger or thirst.
Tán dispatched the śramaṇa Zhìxíng to secretly bring him cakes as a gift. Huo said, "Whom have I ever deceived, that I should deceive the King? Tán was deeply amazed.

He treated him with profound reverence and respect; consequently, he converted his faith, curbed his killing, and promoted compassion. As the people of the state received his protection, they all called him "The Great Master.
Whenever he entered or left the streets and alleys, the common folk would come out to welcome and honor him. In the third year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Ju-tan was defeated by Bo-bo;
the territory of Liang fell into turmoil, and [the Master's] whereabouts became unknown.
Guṇavarman—translated into Chinese as "Armor of Merit"—was originally of the Kṣatriya caste. For generations his family had been kings, and they ruled over the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
At the age of fourteen, Varman was already exceptionally brilliant and perceptive, possessing profound foresight. He was compassionate and devoted to doing good.
Once, his mother desired some wild meat and ordered Varman to procure it. Varman replied, "Among all living beings, there is none that does not..."
"Born of greed, you have brought about his premature death; you are no benevolent person. His mother said in anger, "Even if you have committed an offense, I shall take your place.
When Guṇavarmā was boiling oil in his mouth, he accidentally spilled it on his own finger and said to his mother, "Take my place and endure this pain.

His mother replied, "The pain is in your body; how can I possibly take its place? Guṇavarmā said, "If you cannot even take the place of this suffering before your eyes," [how much less could you endure the future retribution?].
"How much more so for the three miserable realms! Thereupon, her mother repented and awakened; she vowed to abstain from killing for the rest of her life.

When [the son] reached the age of eighteen, a physiognomist saw him and said, "When you reach thirty years of age, you shall rule over a great kingdom and face south as a sovereign. If you do not delight in worldly glory,"

He was destined to attain the fruits of sainthood. By the age of twenty, he left the household life and received the precepts. He thoroughly mastered the nine divisions of the scriptures and had a broad understanding of the four Āgamas.
He recited more than a million words of sūtras, deeply penetrated the categories of the Vinaya, and wondrously entered the essentials of dhyāna.

People of the time called him the Tripitaka Dharma Master. When he reached the age of thirty, the King of Kaśmīra passed away, leaving no heir to the throne. The assembly all deliberated, saying: "Bhadra..."

He was a descendant of the Mātṛceṭa clan; moreover, his talent was brilliant and his virtue was esteemed. The ministers, numbering several hundred, repeatedly and earnestly petitioned that he be permitted to return to lay life so that he might succeed to the throne.
Guṇavarman did not accept this, and thus he took leave of his teacher and went against the will of the multitude, dwelling in the forests and drinking from the mountain streams.

He traveled alone through mountains and fields, concealing his traces from the world of men. Later, he arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala, where he observed the local customs and propagated the teachings;

those who saw him were moved to resolve their minds for enlightenment. Subsequently, he reached the Kingdom of Śrīvijaya. On the eve of his arrival, the mother of the King of Śrīvijaya dreamed of a Taoist master at night.
A flying vessel entered the kingdom. The next morning, Guṇavarman arrived. The Queen Mother received him with the rites due to a holy one and accepted the five precepts from him.
She then exhorted the King, saying: "Through karmic conditions from past lives, we have become mother and son. I have already received the precepts, yet you do not believe;
I fear that the cause for future births will forever sever the fruit of the present. Pressed by his mother’s command, the King immediately obeyed her order and received the precepts.
Shortly thereafter, the neighboring troops violated the border. The King said to Guṇavarman, "The external invaders rely on their strength and wish to commit aggression and insult us.
If we engage them in battle, the casualties will surely be many; yet if we do not resist them, our peril and ruin will be imminent.

Now I can only take refuge in the Venerable Master; I do not know what plan to adopt. Guṇavarman replied, "When violent raiders attack, it is necessary to provide defense. However, you should simply give rise to compassion."
"Have compassion; do not harbor thoughts of malice. The king personally led his troops against them. As soon as the banners and drums clashed, the rebels retreated and dispersed.
However, the king was struck by a stray arrow and wounded in the foot. Guṇavarman performed a consecration with water and washed it; after two nights, he was fully restored.

The king’s respectful faith grew increasingly fervent, and he desired to leave the household life to cultivate the Way. Consequently, he addressed his ministers, saying, "I wish to personally dwell within the Dharma-gate."

"You ministers may now choose a wise sovereign. The assembly of ministers all prostrated themselves and entreated him, saying, "If Your Majesty abandons the kingdom, then the subjects will have no one to rely upon.

Furthermore, our enemy's state is fierce and powerful, and they face us from their strategic heights. Your Majesty’s heavenly compassion—how can you not pity our lives? We dare to entreat you with our very deaths.
The King, unable to bear their persistence, would not flatly refuse; he then approached the ministers and requested three vows. If these were granted—
"You must remain to govern the kingdom. I have three vows: first, that all within the realm of my rule shall likewise serve the Upādhyāya;

second, that throughout the entire territory under my governance, all killing shall be abolished; third, that all accumulated wealth shall be distributed to the poor and the sick. The ministers joyfully and respectfully assented.
Thereupon, the entire kingdom followed suit and received the precepts. Later, the King established a vihāra for Guṇavarman; while he was personally carving the timber, he injured his toe.
Guṇavarman again performed a mantra-ritual to treat it, and after a short while, it was restored to health. The fame of his spiritual transformation spread far and wide.
Hearing of his reputation, neighboring kingdoms all sent envoys to invite him. At that time, the renowned and virtuous masters of the capital, Huìguān and Huìcōng—
[Dao]guan and others, from afar admiring his character and conduct, personally petitioned Emperor Wen in the ninth month of the first year of the Yuanjia era, requesting that he welcome Guṇavarman.
The Emperor immediately granted him the rank of Governor of Jiaozhou and ordered him to dispatch a ship to invite [the master].

[Dao]guan and others further sent the śramaṇas Fachang, Daochong, Daojun, and others to that region to entreat him, while also delivering letters to Guṇavarman and the King of Śrīvijaya, expressing their hopes.

Upon reaching the borders of the Song territory, he found that Daoism was prevalent. Guṇavarman, believing that the holy teachings should be propagated widely, did not hesitate to travel through various regions.
His route led through Shixing, where he stayed for about a year. In Shixing there is Mount Hushi, its form towering and majestic, with peaks and ridges rising loftily and steeply.
Bamó remarked that the mountain vaguely resembled Gṛdhrakūṭa, and thus he renamed it Lingjiu (Vulture Peak).

Outside the monastery, he established a separate meditation hall several li away from the temple, where the sound of the *khaṇḍi* could not be heard. Yet whenever the mallet was struck for the assembly, Bamó would already have arrived.

At times he would walk through the rain without being wet, or tread through mud without becoming soiled. Among the monks and laypeople at the time, there were none who did not feel a profound sense of reverence. The temple possessed precious treasures...

In the Moon Palace (Candraprāsāda), Guṇavarman personally painted with his own hand on the northern wall an image of Rāhula, as well as the figure of the youth Meghadatta offering his hair to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
After the images were completed, they emitted light every evening. This mountain was originally plagued by many tigers;
however, since Guṇavarman resided there, he would walk about during the day and go out at night. Whenever he encountered a tiger, he would press its head down with his staff and drive it away.
He was a guest of the mountains and a visitor of the waters; his coming and going were never obstructed. Emperor Wen issued a second decree, earnestly inviting him once more.

Thereupon, he embarked on a boat and traveled down to the capital, arriving at Jianye in the first month of the eighth year of the Yuanjia era. Emperor Wen received him in audience, greeting him with profound courtesy and inquiry.
He then said, "I, your disciple, have long desired to observe the fasts and refrain from killing, yet I have not been able to fulfill this wish. Master..."
"Since you have not come from afar across ten thousand *li* to transform this kingdom, with what will you instruct us? Guṇavarman replied, "The Way resides in the mind, not in external affairs;
the Dharma arises from oneself, not from others. Furthermore, the cultivation practiced by an emperor and that of a commoner differ according to their respective stations."
An ordinary man is of humble station and inferior reputation; his words lack majesty. If he does not overcome himself and subject his body to hardship, what purpose will they serve?
A sovereign takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children; when he utters a single virtuous word, both men and women rejoice.
When a single virtuous administration is established, humans and spirits harmonize; punishments do not take premature lives, and labor does not exhaust strength.

This causes wind and rain to arrive at their proper times, cold and heat to correspond with the seasons, the hundred grains to flourish, and mulberry and hemp to grow luxuriantly. To maintain such a state through fasting is truly great, and to refrain from killing is likewise manifold.
It is surely better to omit half a day’s meal than to deprive a single bird of its life; only in this way can one truly act for the greater good.

"Is it for the sake of great salvation? The Emperor then leaned on his desk and sighed, saying: "Ordinary people are deluded regarding profound principles, while śramaṇas are hindered by superficial teachings.
Those deluded regarding profound principles claim that the Ultimate Way is but empty talk; those hindered by superficial teachings remain bound and attached to mere literary compositions."
As for what the Dharma Master has said, he is truly awakened and profoundly insightful; one may indeed discuss with him the boundaries between the celestial and the human.

Consequently, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Zhihuan Temple, where provisions were granted in great abundance. Among the princes and eminent scholars, there were none who did not revere and follow him.

Shortly thereafter, he began lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* at the temple. On the days of these dharma assemblies, carriages and parasols filled the streets as people flocked to witness his teachings and returned home.

They followed one after another like shoulders touching shoulders and heels meeting heels. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of that year, before his meal was finished, he suddenly passed away at the age of sixty-five.

Shi Daojin, also known as Fa-jin, was surnamed Tang and a native of Zhangye in Liangzhou. From his youth, he applied himself with rigorous devotion to recitation and possessed a spirit of transcendent excellence.
He was highly esteemed by Juqu Mengxun. After Mengxun passed away, his son Jinghuan was defeated by border raiders.
Jinghuan questioned Daojin, saying, "I now wish to advance and take Gaochang; do you think it can be conquered? Daojin replied, "Victory is certain. However—"
There was only distress, calamity, and famine. Upon the withdrawal of the army, things were immediately settled. Three years later, Jinghuan died, and his younger brother Anzhou succeeded him.

In that year, there was a great famine, and those who perished were beyond counting. Since Zhou had come to power, he had repeatedly requested relief for the poor; consequently, the state's stores were gradually exhausted.
He no longer sought anything further. He then bathed himself clean, took up a knife and salt, and went to a deep, remote cave where hungry people had gathered.
There he conferred the Three Refuges upon them one by one, hung his robes and bowl on a tree, and threw himself before the starving ones, saying, "I give myself to you;
let us eat together. Although the multitude was famished and exhausted, they could not bear it out of a sense of righteousness. Jin then cut his own flesh, applied the salt, and ate it.
The flesh of both thighs was exhausted; his heart grew faint and he could not cut it himself. He then said to the starving man, "Take my skin and flesh; it will suffice for several days.
If the king’s messenger arrives, you must surely take me away. The starving man was filled with grief and lamentation, yet none dared to take it.
In a short while, his disciples arrived, and the king’s men followed. The entire nation rushed there, their cries of wailing following one after another, as they carried him away on a litter.
Upon his return to the palace, Zhou issued an edict to provide three hundred hu of wheat to be distributed to those suffering from hunger.

He also opened the state granaries to relieve the poor, until the supplies were exhausted at dawn the following day. The body was taken out through the northern city gate and cremated; the smoke and flames reached the heavens and only subsided after seven days.
The remains were entirely consumed, except for the tongue, which did not decay. Thereupon, a three-story stupa was erected at that very spot, and a stele was set up.

The above [concerns] Shi Tanyuan of Yanmen. His family resided near Mount Wutai, where divine traces and numinous wonders abound. Even before he had reached the age for formal study, he went there to seek them out.
Having fully beheld the sacred remains, his heart and spirit were filled with joy, and he immediately left the household life to study the Mahāyāna sūtras. He felt regret...

The meaning of its words was profound and subtle, difficult to comprehend. Consequently, he provided a commentary; however, when more than half of the text had been written, he was stricken by a wind-illness.
He set down his pen to seek medical treatment. Upon traveling to the old ruins of Qinling in Fenzhou, he entered through the eastern gate of the city.
Looking up toward the azure heavens, he suddenly beheld the Celestial Gate opening wide, with the six realms of desire stacked one above the other, all clearly visible at once. Because of this—
His illness was cured. Previously, he had gouged out his own eyes; it was only after this that he began to revere the Buddhist teachings.

Hearing that Tao Yinyu of Jiangnan was a master to whom all practitioners of arts and techniques turned—a man of vast learning and profound erudition who was honored as a patriarch throughout the realm—he went to follow him.

Upon arriving at the Liang court during the Dàtōng era, he announced himself as "the foreign monk Tánluán from the northern lands" seeking an audience. At that time, the officials in charge suspected him of being a spy.
Upon investigation, no conflicting testimony was found, and the matter was reported to the Emperor. The Emperor said, "This is not one who spies upon the state.
He was then ushered into the Chongyun Hall via the Qianmi Road. The Emperor had already taken his seat upon a rope bed in a corner of the hall;

he wore a *kāṣāya* robe and covered his head with a monk’s cap. When Luan arrived before the hall, he looked around but saw no one to receive him, until he noticed a high canopy set up [in the corner].
He ascended the seat, upon which a small table and a fly-whisk were placed; it stood alone in the center of the hall with no other seats nearby.

He proceeded directly to mount it and established the meaning of Buddha-nature. Three times he addressed the Emperor, saying: "Great Donor, the meaning of Buddha-nature is profound; I have briefly set forth its outline. If you have any doubts, please grant me the opportunity to question you."
The Emperor withdrew his cap and engaged in several rounds of exchange. He then remarked, "It is already late today; we must meet again tomorrow.
Luan rose from beneath the seat and proceeded directly forward as before, passing through more than twenty winding and overlapping gates without a single error.

The Emperor sighed in extreme amazement and said, "This is the 'Path of a Thousand Delusions. From time immemorial, this has been the old route where travelers have always encountered uncertainty and obstruction;

how is it that upon passing through it once, one is suddenly free from delusion? The next morning, he was ushered into the Taiji Hall. The Emperor descended the steps to receive him with courtesy and asked about his origins.

Sengluan replied, "I wish to study the Buddha-dharma, but I regret that my allotted lifespan is short and diminishing. Therefore, I have come from afar to visit Master Tao Yinyu to seek [instruction]."

Regarding the various arts of the immortals, the Emperor said, "This man is one who haughtily secludes himself from the world; though he has been repeatedly summoned, he has not complied. You may go to him as you please.

Lüan subsequently sent a letter to establish contact. Upon arriving at the mountain retreat, the hermit received him with great joy and immediately presented him with ten scrolls of immortal formulas.
To repay his distant intention, he returned to the Zhejiang River. There was a deity named Baolangzi who surged the waves at the stroke of a drum;

it had been raining for seven days and had just begun to subside. Finding no means to cross, Sengluan went to the temple and prayed with sincerity, vowing that if his request were granted, he would build a shrine for the deity.
In an instant, the deity manifested its form and said to Luán: "If you wish to cross," [the deity provided a way].

"I shall obtain it tomorrow morning; I pray you do not break your word. When the following dawn arrived, the waves were still surging and raging, but as soon as he entered the boat, they became perfectly calm and still.
Arriving at the imperial court on schedule, he related the circumstances in detail. An edict was issued to build a spirit temple for the river god.
Thereupon, he took his leave and returned to the territory of Wei, intending to travel to a famous mountain to cultivate himself according to the teachings. Upon reaching Luoyang, he encountered...

The Chinese Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci was approached by Seng-luan, who asked: "Within the Buddha-dharma, is there perhaps a method for longevity and immortality that surpasses the *xianjing* (immortal scriptures) of this land?
Bodhiruci spat upon the ground and said: "What kind of talk is this? It is not even comparable.
Where in this region could there be a method for longevity and immortality? Even if one were to attain a long life, it would merely be a brief period before death."
They merely undergo the cycle of rebirth within the three realms of existence. He then bestowed the *Amitābha Sūtra* upon him, saying, "This is the prescription of the Great Sage;

if you practice according to it, you shall surely attain liberation from birth and death. Daoluan then received it upon the crown of his head. He burned all the prescriptions he had previously carried as sages' formulas.

He traveled through various regions to transform others, spreading the teaching widely and extensively. The Wei ruler held him in high esteem and titled him "Divine Luan" (Shenluan). This was in the fourth year of the Xinghe era.
In his [seventy]-eighth year, he passed away at a mountain temple in Pingyao due to illness.
Shi Fajin was a native of Xinfan in Shu. While still a layman, he was diligent in his practice and abstained from pungent and raw foods. He worked as a farmer in the fields.
He used the blades of his plow as bells and chimes. He maintained his fasts by measuring the time according to his shadow. Once, when the food was being delivered late, he simply drank water.
On the field where he had plowed, he did not harm insects or ants. Suddenly, a voice from the air said: "Advance, Ācārya! The time for you to leave the household life has arrived."

Thus, for four or five times, the entire household heard him together. Sengjin subsequently went to Mount Luokou to leave the household life and practice *dhūta* austerities, refusing to reside in monasteries.
At that time, Prince Xiu of Shu of the Sui dynasty, having heard of his reputation, knew he would be difficult to entice and dispatched the military aide Yu Jiulü Changqing to invite him.

Changqing took ten attendants with him and, upon meeting the Master, said to the Prince: "I have heard that you possess the Way and its Virtue; if you do not grant me leave to go, I shall not return."
"Come; we shall observe the worldly rites. The King said, "There is no need for intimidation; simply extend the invitation with reason. Tomorrow you shall arrive here.
When Changqing emerged from the city gate, he looked back and said, "Today I am taking you all to the Tuṣita Heaven to invite Maitreya Buddha;
I hope to succeed there as well. How much more so for a mountain-dwelling practitioner—why would they not come? Upon first arriving at the foot of Mount Jiyang, night fell.

Seeing a tiger crouching on the road, he ordered his men to shoot it; however, his horses all retreated and fled. He wished to head toward a village, yet feared disobeying the King’s command. Suddenly, he saw a monk carrying a bundle up the mountain.
Changqing ordered him to stop and become his companion, while the rest of the followers were left behind. They proceeded on foot to the monastery.
He summoned the monk inside and led him to the bed, where he again saw the tiger beneath the bed. Terrified and unable to remain at ease, he advanced to drive the tiger out. [He then] prepared...

He recounted the King’s sentiments. Although he offered a reply, his fear was manifest in his physical demeanor. [The King] pressed him, saying: "When you first left the city gate, how heroic and bold you were!
Now that you have arrived here, why are you so timid and apprehensive? Changqing prostrated himself in silence.

Because they had stayed overnight, [the King] ordered him to go on ahead, while he, the poor monk, would follow later. When they reached Wangxiang Terrace (Gazing-at-the-Hometown Platform), he looked back as they continued their journey.
Then, together with King Tongjian, he entered the inner quarters to receive the precepts. On that very day, he took his leave and departed, refusing to accept any of the alms offered to him.
He was instructed to stay at Fajusi Monastery. The king turned to his attendants and said, "Seeing this monk makes my hair stand on end;
he is protected by the deities of the precepts. Later, the king summoned him back into the city. Upon seeing him from afar, the king prostrated himself and advanced to say, "The King himself..."
"You are at ease; you yourself are at ease. Why do you trouble yourself with such suffering and perform useless deeds?
The monks admonished him, saying, "The King is the lord of the land; you should inquire after his welfare kindly. Why do you rebuke him? Utpalaka replied, "Venerable sirs, you fear death."
One must seek the King’s intention. Seeing evil deeds with one's own eyes, yet failing to offer any admonition or encouragement—how can this be called propagating the Teaching?

To advance without fearing death, how could one begrudge being held accountable for one's faults? Although he provided sumptuous bedding and seats and rich, heavy delicacies, he sat only upon a simple rope-couch and ate nothing but coarse cakes.
After his consort and concubines had received the precepts, he again took his leave to enter the mountains; though they earnestly invited him to stay for three more days, the time limit was reached.

He then returned. Various lay devotees all prepared food and invited him; when the time arrived, each household claimed that he had come to their house, and upon gathering together to calculate the accounts, it was found that he had manifested his body in dozens of places simultaneously.
On another occasion, while traveling with the monks out of the mountains to attend a meal, he suddenly laughed.
When people asked the reason for this, he said, "The temple attendants at the mountain monastery have broken through the wall to steal honey. Upon returning, the result was indeed as he had said.
As it was said: The first master of the royal gate, Cizang, served as the state prelate for the monastic community. His administration was severe and fierce;

if even a slight deficiency occurred regarding his water jar, robes, incense, or flowers, he would inflict beatings. The monks suffered under him, yet because he was held in high esteem by the king, no one dared to remonstrate.

They reported the matter to the Emperor, requesting that he intervene to provide relief. The Emperor replied: "His power and influence are such as this; how could he possibly accept my words? Thus they suffered.
He did not cease his pleading. He proceeded to the door of the storehouse, where the *zàng* (treasurer) came out and said to him, "The Dharma-gate should not be treated in this manner;

you too possess great power" (*dàlì*; the people of Shu used *dàshèn* for "great power"). [Huiyuan] then returned and entered the room. From that time on, the *zàng* ceased speaking, and the monks were thereby at peace.
He passed away on the mountain during the Kaihuang era at the age of ninety-six.
No one could discern the identity of this wealthy elder. He constantly stayed overnight at Jingde Temple and buried a large straw hat on the road.

During the day, he would sit upon it to read the scriptures. Although people passed by, he did not call out to them to solicit alms; even when someone threw money his way, he offered no prayers of blessing.

He always kept his hands still as he walked along the path and never entered into crowds. Though he appeared to be about fifty years old, he had lived there for many years without any record of wrongdoing.
There was a person with faith who said, "To the west and north of the city, the population is dense and alms are plentiful; what are you doing staying here?
He replied, "One or two coins are sufficient to sustain my life; why would I need more? This was Zhao Zhongshu, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Lingzhou.

The three dynasties had cruel historians. [The man] was utterly lacking in faith and reverence. Hearing of this, he went to test him. He rode his horse straight past and feigned a fall, dropping a string of coins.
Fu merely continued reading his scriptures; his eyes never glanced back. When they had gone far away, the magistrate of Shu ordered someone to retrieve the money, but Fu still did not look at it.
Shu then turned back and said, "Did you see my coins fall to the ground? He replied, "I saw them. Shu asked, "Where are the coins now?
He replied, "I saw a person pick them up and take them away. Shu said, "You spend all day on the road begging for a single coin;
how could it be that you did not take the string of coins lying on the ground? When you saw someone taking them, why did you not stop him? He answered, "It was not because I was poor..."
[The monk] said, "These are sacred objects. Why do you recklessly claim them? Zhongshu replied, "I wish to have the *kāṣāya* on your person.
Furu said, "I merely wished to test you. If you can take it away, I shall give it back to you; one may say that gain and loss are of one kind. He then folded the robe and handed it over.
Zhongshu dismounted, bowed in thanks, and said, "I, your disciple, am a man of the Zhou dynasty; my official career has spanned three reigns. [I have served alongside] the assembly of monks..."

He traveled back and forth. One who was not greedy from his youth went to visit him upon hearing his name; he had no ill intent at all. [Hui]fu requested to go to Lingzhou, and [Hui]shu said, "Very well.
However, I, a poor monk, wish to establish many karmic connections. I hope you will assist the state in bringing peace and stability; this is how we shall meet for a long time and receive offerings.
Hui-shu took his leave and sighed, saying, "This man must not be treated with contempt. After that, they were never seen again. —From the *Yizhou* [section].
Regarding the person from Ji who was a physiognomist: he saw him while returning from Yangzhou and likewise buried his hat by the side of the road;

his facial features remained as they were before. Shi Fazang’s secular surname was Sun; he was a native of Yingyin in Yingchuan. He lost his father at the age of three and lived with his mother in seclusion. At ten, his mother passed away, and he stood alone.
Because of this bitter calamity, he gained a profound realization of impermanence. At the age of twenty-two, [he traveled] throughout the heavens...

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Harmony (Wahé) era, Emperor Ming ordained monks and subsequently left secular life. In the fourth year of the Heavenly Harmony (Tianhé) era, a prince was born;

an imperial edict was issued to select those of eminent virtue to proceed to Liquan Palace. Emperor Wu personally hurried to the foot of the hall and called out in the Xianbei language to inquire after their welfare.
The assembly of monks remained motionless, and no one responded. [One monk] was hiding in the back row; he stepped forward from the crowd and stood alone, and composed—
He replied in the Xianbei language. The assembly of officials in the palace courtyard all rejoiced at this response.

The Emperor commanded the various ministers: "This man’s body is small, yet his spirit is great; he alone transcends his peers. To report these words to me—can he not be called a 'robust practitioner'? An imperial decree was issued to grant him two hundred and ten thousand coins.

Consequently, their relationship became harmonious, and he frequently received the Emperor's inquiries and consolation. Although his body resided within the monastery, his mind remained focused on [the world].
In the second month of the second year of the Jiande era, he took his alms bowl and carried his case into the deep forest, casting himself upon Mount Zigai—a peak of Zhongnan Mountain.
There he dwelt alone in a meditation cell beneath a high crag, wearing robes of patched rags and subsisting on pine needles and wood.
On the eighth day of the first month of the third year, while walking upon the mountain summit, he suddenly encountered ten sweet apricots; he immediately [took them].

He consumed it. Having received this spiritual assistance from the unseen realm, he merely redoubled his diligence in his religious practice. On the twenty-third day of the fourth month of that year, the Emperor destroyed the images, burned the scriptures, and ordered the monks to return to lay life.
Sengling remained in seclusion in the mountains, following the Way and concealing himself; eight years passed as he constantly contemplated the restoration of the Dharma.
In the ninth month of the first year of the Daxiang era of Emperor Xuan, he descended the mountain to visit the Emperor, intending to honor the Triple Gem. Upon arriving—

At the South Gate of the City, facing the residence of the Marquis of Wuhou, the Senior Grandee Tuowang Meng said: "In the second year of the Jiande era, he abandoned his monastery and entered the mountains.
In the fourth month of the third year, the Emperor finally proscribed the clergy; with the exception of Sengzang, who remained in the mountains, all others were required to return to lay life.
Zang alone remained in the mountains, making the forests and valleys his home, birds and beasts his companions, and grasses and trees his provisions. Thus it was.
