He reflected: "Under heaven, there is no land that does not belong to the King. Since you reside under the Purple Canopy and consume the provisions of the mountain, these supplies shall be considered as bestowed by the Most Honored One.
When Meng and the others submitted this memorial, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "I desire to govern and transform beings as a Bodhisattva.
Since this monk has come from Mount Zigai, he perfectly accords with my intention. You should order him to grow his hair long and wear the robes of a Bodhisattva."
Wearing his official cap and robes, he served as the abbot of Zhuhu Monastery. The Grand Secretary, Da-da Tang Yi-yuan, submitted a memorial stating:
"To universally require all monks in the realm to return to lay life while ordaining only a single individual violates the late Emperor’s edict.

In the tenth month, at the eastern side of the city, he had a private audience with Emperor Xuan, who asked about the names of the three teachings. [The Emperor] said: "I desire for a Bodhisattva to govern and transform the people; perhaps manifesting in a celestial body, or..."
They emerge from the earth, sometimes taking the form of deer or horses; by means of such transformative manifestations, they gather in sentient beings. How so?

The *Zang* (Treasury) cites the account of the two sons of King Miaozhuang who exhorted their father. It further states: "Your Majesty, when you were formerly our subject and son, you were unable to provide corrective counsel."
This ultimately led Your Majesty’s predecessor to burn the sacred scriptures and cast holy images into coinage. Considering such rebellious harm, how does it differ from that of Qin Shi Huang?
The Emperor said in anger, "Since you have disobeyed my late sovereign’s clear edict, you may be executed immediately. Sengzang replied, "I have presumed to offend Your Majesty’s august countenance."
He requested that his execution take place in the capital city so that both the living and the dead might witness it together, for this was his sincere intention.

At that time, his life hung by a thread like a dangling vine, yet his speech and demeanor remained undaunted. He underwent the interrogation nine times, and his composure grew even more steadfast with each repetition. When the tenth petition reached the Emperor, the Emperor asked, "Is the monk afraid?
The Grand Scribe, Duke Pei, replied, "Of all things a person values, none is more precious than life. To stand in a place of the ultimate punishment—"

"How could he not be free from fear? Upon hearing this, the Emperor’s countenance grew somber and he said, "A true man who protects the Dharma and brings blessings to all living beings—this is indeed the 'Goose-Protecting Bhikṣu.
I shall not kill an innocent person; his punishment should be commuted. There is no need for further inquiry.
I grant him the robes and cap of a Bodhisattva and appoint him as the abbot of Shizhu Temple as before. Having repeatedly bestowed such imperial favors, he was able to continue the lineage of Śākya.
Having attained rebirth, he took his leave of the Emperor to depart for forests, springs, mountains, and marshes, seeking to live in seclusion.
The Censor Bao Hong submitted a memorial to the Imperial Decree: "In the five counties of Wannian, Chang'an, Lantian, Zhouzhi, Hu, and Du, he may wander at will.

Yet Your Majesty must see him; he must not remain hidden. Although he had received this gracious decree, [the Master] ultimately did not open himself to the world. His spirit remained constrained and unsettled, and he pondered...
Cherishing the Holy Way, the virtue of the Zhou dynasty declined while the mandate of the Sui was about to arise.

On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Daxiang era, the founder of the Sui served as Chancellor at the Humen Gate. On the sixth month, [Dao]zang again descended from the mountains to discuss the Three Jewels with the Great Chancellor.
Having stayed overnight, he was immediately granted the tonsure; the Chancellor bestowed upon him a set of dharma robes and fifteen pieces of multicolored silk from Qingzhou.

One *shí* of dates was given. Soon thereafter, [Fazang] returned to the mountains. In the seventh month, he was summoned down from the mountains to further deliberate upon the propagation of the teachings.
On the fifteenth day, he ordered Fazang and Lord Jingling to inspect the ordination of one hundred and twenty-eight monks; all were granted Dharma robes and returned to their respective residences.
Fazang alone stayed overnight at the Prime Minister’s residence, where they discussed the origins of the Teachings. The second month of the first year of the Dading era.
On the twelfth day, the Chancellor ascended the throne and immediately changed the era name to the first year of Kaihuang.

On the fifteenth day, he received an imperial decree to summon those who had previously attained [realization], establishing them at Daxingshan Temple to perform rites for the state. From this point on, the teachings gradually flourished and spread throughout the realm.

His treasury of precepts was pure and luminous, and his meditative mind was lush and profound. He frequently entered the gates of nobles and repeatedly ascended the imperial couch during the Kaihuang era.

In the second year, the Palace Secretary and Attendant Zhao Wei proclaimed an imperial decree providing a monthly allotment of *fuling* (poria cocos), dates, apricots, ghee, oil, firewood, and charcoal as his regular provisions.
However, as his nature inclined toward emptiness and stillness, he did not seek honor or profit. In the fourteenth year, he submitted a petition to discontinue these provisions.

He provided him with whatever offerings were required. General Wuhou, who had long been a harmonious practitioner, harbored pure faith in his heart; he invited [the Master] to his residence, hoping to pay him honor and provide for his needs.
Influenced by his accumulated merit, the General eventually relinquished his own dwelling to establish it as a Buddhist temple.

He personally oversaw the secular affairs and encouraged the monks, establishing a vegetarian feast for ten thousand monastics. Whenever the Right Vice-Director Su Wei came to pay his respects, they together constructed a great hall and installed sacred images.
The palace attendant Pei Ju proclaimed the imperial decree, and Master Zang was tonsured. The presiding monk then hosted a grand vegetarian feast;

the magnificence of this propagation of the Dharma was beyond compare. In the second year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Guantai in Hu County and was interred on the southern slope of the hill.
The śramaṇa Xiaocai of Yunji Monastery composed an inscription, which was engraved upon a slab of true stone beside his niche.
Seol Wŏngwang’s family name was Pok. His ancestors originally resided in the Three Han—Jinhan, Cheonhan, and Mahan—and he himself was a native of Silla within Cheonhan.

His family had been established in Haedong for generations, yet his spiritual vessel was vast and expansive; he scrutinized the profound teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism and investigated the rival schools of the *Zi* and *Shi*.

At the age of twenty-five, he boarded a merchant vessel and traveled to Jinling. Upon hearing of the Buddhist tradition, he submitted a memorial to the Chen Emperor requesting permission to return to the Dharma;

an imperial decree granted his request. Having shaved his head, he immediately received full ordination. He frequented lecture halls and mastered the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, internalizing them within his mind.
He extensively studied and investigated the Abhidharma and the various numerical treatises (*saṃkhyā-śāstra*). Finally, he went to Wu.

He went to Mount Huqiu. There, a multitude of those who had stilled their minds gathered like clouds around the groves and springs; they all mastered the four Āgamas and their merits flowed through the eight dhyānas.

Deeply fulfilling his long-held aspiration, he eventually conceived the intention to remain there for the rest of his life. He immediately severed ties with worldly affairs and wandered among the sacred traces.

At that time, there was a lay devotee living at the foot of the mountain who invited Sengguang to come out and lecture. He began by expounding the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (*Cheng lun*), but before he had finished teaching the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [he passed away].
If [he were there], all would have attained a profound and penetrating understanding through reflection; those who heard him would have rejoiced as their minds harmonized with his inner treasury.

His fame would have spread far and wide throughout the regions south of the passes, and those who came to him—picking their way through the brambles and carrying their satchels upon their backs—would have followed one after another like scales of fish. At that time, however, the Empress of the Sui dynasty was presiding over the throne, and her authority extended to the southern lands.
Consequently, he was encountered by a band of rebel soldiers and was about to be executed. A great general, seeing from afar the temple pagoda engulfed in flames, [acted].
He ran to rescue him, but there was no sign of fire; he saw only light before the stupa. As the man was about to be executed while bound, they marveled at this anomaly and immediately released him.
Guang’s learning was pervasive throughout Wu and Yue, and he desired to observe the transformation [of the Dharma] in Zhou and Qin.

In the ninth year of the Kaihuang era, he came to travel within the imperial domain, arriving just as the first assembly of the Buddha-dharma had begun and the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) was first being promoted. He reverently upheld these great words and spread them abroad.

Continuing his illustrious legacy, his reputation reached far abroad; the Sovereign repeatedly sent petitions requesting him, and by imperial decree, he was granted generous inquiries and allowed to return to his native land.
Over several decades of his travels, both the old and the young rejoiced. King Kim of Silla personally expressed his profound reverence, regarding him as a sage.
As his age advanced, he was carried in a palanquin into the inner palace, where the Queen herself provided all his clothing, medicine, and food.
He prohibited the establishment of funeral monuments and did not permit others to assist in them, desiring that the merit be dedicated exclusively [to his own liberation].

Prior to his passing, the King personally attended to him with consolation and entrusted him with the legacy of the Dharma, charging him to provide universal relief for the people. He then explained the auspicious omens that had appeared throughout the coastal regions.

Because he had cultivated merit for fifty-eight years, he felt a slight ailment; after seven days had passed, he issued his final instructions with profound clarity and sat upright until his end at his residence.
He passed away in Long Temple at the age of ninety-nine.

Shi Mingzhan’s secular surname was Du; he was a native of Shiyi in Hengzhou. From his youth, he possessed extraordinary character. He resided in Longgui Village, where over two thousand households all held him in high esteem.
At fourteen, he mastered the sutras; at seventeen, he was proficient in history. Thereupon, the prefecture and county officials recommended him for advancement.
The Master was by nature inclined toward the transcendent and did not accept official summons. He entered the monastic life at Yingjue Temple on Mount Feilong.

His teacher, perceiving his extraordinary spiritual capacity, wrote a letter to the Dharma Master Daochang of Daji Temple in Ye, requesting that he be taken under his guidance to specialize in the study of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Soon thereafter, encountering the destruction of the Dharma, he went into hiding in Dongjun. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, when the Dharma was restored, he returned to reside there.

At Fazang Temple in Xiangzhou, he was internally well-versed in both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings and externally proficient in the Confucian classics. Intending to observe the state of the realm, he traveled to the capital.

In the third year of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, he was summoned to perform translations and resided at Daxingshan Temple. As the assembly beheld his virtue and reputation as worthy of veneration, they appointed him to oversee the affairs of the temple.
In the second year of the Daye era, when the Emperor returned to the capital and was stationed at the southern suburbs, he arrayed his military forces in great display. At that time...

There were those who, having corrupted the monastic order, defiled the imperial laws; this matter was reported to the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly incensed and summoned the various monks, placing them all in a row before him.

They stood firm and maintained their ritual decorum, refusing to bow. He issued an edict of reprimand, stating: "Regulations have been promulgated for a long time; by principle, one must pay due respect.

At that time, the followers of Huang-Lao, both men and women, bowed immediately upon hearing the command; only the Buddhist community remained solemn and did not yield. At that moment, [the Emperor] took Zhan as his model.

Daowang, who was revered by all as a preeminent master, replied: "If Your Majesty truly intends to follow the principles of Buddhism, it is logically impossible for the monastics to perform acts of reverence.
If we were to return to the secular way according to the imperial decree, then our dharma robes would not permit us to show respect to laypeople.

The Emperor asked: "If wearing dharma robes makes such respect improper, why did Song Wu Di pay obeisance to them? Zhan said: "Song Wu was an unrighteous ruler; he did not prostrate before those who were his equals."
"Summon him to be executed! Your Majesty possesses a governance that preserves the righteous; you do not ensnare the innocent. Therefore, I dare not prostrate.

The Emperor did not yield to his words and immediately dispatched a palace attendant to speak with the monk, asking, "Why do you not prostrate? This occurred five times. [The attendant] was of the Huangzhong clan.

He prostrated himself repeatedly without ceasing; only Zhan and the monk remained standing, bowing with long salutations as before. Furthermore, they addressed the Emperor with raised voices in their discourse, showing no sign of fear or intimidation.
The Emperor then asked who had been the one that answered the decree regarding the monks, and upon having their names recorded and reported, he immediately ordered them to be executed.

The following morning, the officials recruited those willing to die to go to the palace gate to offer their apologies; Zhan again went forward first, even though he had already submitted his humble petition.

The Emperor remained indifferent and made no further comment; he merely issued an edict for both monasteries, Chanding and Shouning, to each provide vegetarian feasts for all the monks in the capital, and sent a gift of silk bolts, treating them with exceptional honor beyond their usual standing.
Later, as he turned his carriage back from the western suburbs, he looked toward the capital and said to his ministers:

"I thought there were no monks within my realm; now it is proven that one person is sufficient. From then on, he issued an edict ordering them to reside at Chanding Monastery. The assembly [thereupon]...

Sengzhan maintained a dignified countenance and was resolute in his administration; he did not shrink from powerful adversaries. He was subsequently appointed as the *upadhivāra* (administrative senior monk) to manage monastic affairs.

During the reign of the Great Tang, the office of monastic official (*sengguan*) was established. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, because Sengzhan was well-versed in the methods of governance and had gained a reputation at court, he was summoned to the inner palace.
There, he personally ascended the imperial throne; after the meal, he received an imperial edict and extensively recounted the history from ancient times onward.

The enlightened ruler explained the methods for governing the people, while also presenting the teachings of the Buddhist school, whose primary principle is salvation through compassion. The Emperor was greatly pleased;

consequently, on the sixth day of the third month, he issued an imperial edict universally prohibiting slaughter. Furthermore, he ordered that Buddhist temples be established at all military encampments.

At one time, seven sites were constructed simultaneously: Shaoren in Bingzhou, Ciyun in Jinzhou, Pujie in Lüzhou, Hongji in Fenzhou, Shaofu in Mingzhou, Dengci in Zhengzhou, and Zhaojue in Luozhou; in each case, the government provided the craftsmen and laborers.
Those sent from the capital to serve as laborers were all inspired by his awakening. As his final years approached, he retired to dwell among the mountains;
he subsequently entered Zhiju Temple on Mount Taiyi to live in seclusion. Those who placed their faith in him flocked from the imperial capital to the forest.

After a short time, he fell ill and said, "My life has reached its end; it can be extended for one more month. Fearing that his withered remains would burden others, he then summoned the great [monks].
Master De went to Xingshan Temple to prepare a vegetarian feast as a parting offering. The Vice Directors Fang and Du, along with the entire court, assembled there;

they brought abundant provisions for the offerings, and the gifts and alms piled up like mountains. Zhan and Tong made great sacrifices, performing repentance and bidding him farewell. That very day, Master De departed from the capital on foot with a staff and returned to Zhiju.
There he dwelt with utmost sincerity and diligence, contemplating the Western Pure Land. His mind and insight were clear and sharp, and he said to his attendant: "A..."
"Amitābha Buddha has arrived. After a short while, he further said, "The two great Bodhisattvas have also arrived.
His countenance suddenly faded, and he passed away instantly at the age of seventy.
Shi Huian, whose secular surname was Wei, was a native of Zhijiang in Jingzhou. Huian was by nature broad-minded and did not soil himself with worldly dust.

In his cultivation and study of the Dharma-gates, there was nothing he did not master. During the Daye era, when the Tongji Canal was being excavated, laborers were conscripted in great numbers and those who died of hunger were seen everywhere.

Huian traveled about begging for food from many alms-bowls to relieve their illness and deprivation; those whom he saved and sustained were numerous. When Emperor Yang heard of this, he issued an edict [summoning him].

An eventually entered Mount Taixi in secret. When the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu and the realm was in turmoil, he took up his staff and ascended to Hengyue Temple, where he practiced the dhūta austerities.
During the Zhenguan era, he went to Qizhou to pay homage to Master Ren and traveled to the Stone Cliff of Zhongnan Mountain, where he stayed.
At that time, between the plains and valleys where he resided, an early frost damaged the crops; [he remained] at his place of dwelling.

He alone was exempt. For forty *li* around, all suffered from the calamities of the Blue Maiden (*Qingnü*). When the Great Emperor, the Heavenly Sovereign, heard of this, he summoned him; however, Dao’an did not comply with the imperial decree.
In the second year of the Yongchun era, he arrived at a thatched pavilion in Huatai and took up residence there.

He sat upon a rope bed in the open air, exposed to the four directions. An imperial edict was issued to construct a temple for his dwelling, which was named Zhaoti. Later, he returned to his hometown at Yquan Temple. At that time...
Master Shenxiu had recently passed away. Everyone requested that Dao’an take up the position as abbot, but he did not comply with their request.
In the fourth month of the second year of the Shengli era of Empress Wu Zetian, he informed his disciples and students, telling them each to return to their quarters and close their doors.

At the third watch, a group of Chan practitioners arrived, accompanied by a dense retinue of guards and the jingling of ceremonial bells. As wind and rain set in together, the spirit of the deceased master circled the monastery several times before Dao’an.
He spoke with him, offering earnest instructions and admonitions, and after performing two prostrations, he departed.

Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied, "I am a deity of Mount Song who has received the Bodhisattva precepts. Empress Wu once asked him about his age, and he replied, "I do not remember.
She asked, "Why do you not remember? He said, "The body of birth and death is like a cycle; it has neither beginning nor end. What use is there in remembering it? Furthermore, as for this mind..."
The continuous flow has no interval between its stages; even seeing the arising and ceasing of bubbles is but a deluded thought.
From the initial consciousness until the movement-characteristic ceases, it is exactly like this—how could one record it by year or month? Empress Tianhou bowed her head in prostration.
In the ninth month of the second year of the Shenglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict ordered the eunuchs to bestow upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and silk, and grant him the title Anbing.
Master Jing entered the inner palace to receive offerings for three years, during which he was granted a set of monastic robes (*māṇava*). He then took his leave to return to Shaolin Monastery.
On the eighth day of the third month in the third year of the Jinglong era, he closed his door, lay down, and passed away at the age of one hundred and thirty.
His body was cremated, and eighty *śarīra* relics were collected; five of these were red and purple, which were presented to the imperial court.
There were other miscellaneous offerings. He built stupas according to his means.

Shi Zhikuan, surnamed Yao, was a native of Hedong in Puzhou. His father served as the Prefect of Qingzhou during the Sui dynasty. From childhood until adulthood, Zhikuan was renowned for his purity and frugality.
He attended lectures on various sutras throughout his life, taking the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) as his core essentials. To the east...
In his travels westward seeking the Way, he did not let even a moment’s time go to waste. Throughout his life, he always practiced faithfulness; his words and deeds never contradicted one another.
Once, while traveling to study in Chang’an, he went to the market to buy silk. A man said to him, “You may pay the price now; I shall deliver the silk tomorrow.

Thereupon, he paid the money and returned to the monastery, where he was ridiculed by the other monks. Hui-kuan said, “As far as I can recall, I have never failed anyone. How could there be such a person [as you]?”
His faith was unwavering. When the appointed time arrived, he indeed obtained it. Daokuan constantly recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
In the dwelling where he resided, there was always a vibration and the sound of armored troops at night. Those who peered out secretly all saw extraordinary divine beings walking around the room.
On another occasion, during the middle of the night, there was the sound of something being struck on the upper story of his room. His fellow student Baotong heard it.
Startled and bewildered, he could not remain settled on his mat. Hui-kuan went to him to comfort him, yet [the patient] continued to strike objects as before.

When dawn arrived and he examined him, it was found that a beam in the room was about to collapse; he immediately ordered it to be propped up, thereby saving the man’s life. By nature, he delighted in visiting the sick, showing no regard for distance.

Furthermore, because both monastics and laypeople knew there was no one else who could treat them, they all brought their patients to his room in litters, and he personally attended to their care and management.
Later, during the middle of the night, the interior of the room became brilliantly illuminated; looking outside the chamber, it was no different from daylight. This phenomenon appeared repeatedly.

Sengkuang took the encouragement of worldly affairs as a means to lead others, making the great salvation of sentient beings his vocation. It coincided with Emperor Yang’s promotion of the Way, during which a nationwide search for talent was launched.

Because Sengkuang’s practice and understanding were deemed peerless, he was summoned to this honorable command. However, the rebellion of Xiao Ji ensued, and Sengkuang became entangled in the affairs of the Qi dynasty. Thereupon, Sengkuang...

He was imprisoned to await his sentence. Whenever anyone brought him food or gifts, he would not take any for himself; instead, he distributed it all to the fellow monks in prison, who laughed and conversed with him as they had in the past.

Later, both were assigned to the ranks of common laborers to serve on the "Celestial Road" (the road to the capital). They were constantly ordered to carry earth, required to fill their baskets to capacity, and then to haul them along with all their strength.
Zhi寬 never showed the slightest sign of weariness or rest. A fellow laborer said to him, "There is no supervisor here; you ought to stop for a moment. Kuān replied, "This is my karma..."
The retribution is such as this; how can one deceive oneself? To act contrary to one’s heart is truly not at peace. Later, he was again exiled to Xishu.

Upon reaching Shan Prefecture, there were those who sent wealth and silk as parting gifts for his journey, yet he distributed them all immediately, leaving behind only a donkey to carry his scriptures.
On the road at Tongguan Pass, there was a wandering monk named Baoxian, a man of profound understanding and great virtue, whose feet were so worn that they were broken.

He did not proceed further. When Kuan saw him lying by the side of the road, he wept in sorrow. He immediately gave up his donkey and mount, carrying the scriptures and treatises himself on foot as he traveled to Shu.
This greatly moved the hearts of the people, who all felt deep reverence and joy. At that time, tigers were rampant in the riverside towns and villages, cutting off the paths of travelers;
they would roam in packs of several hundred through the hamlets and cities, injuring both people and livestock. Among them was a "king of beasts" whose—

His head was the largest, and he was endowed with all five colors. His majestic presence subdued all other beasts. When Zhang Xun, the Prefectural Governor of Suizhou, heard of his compassionate virtue from afar, he dispatched messengers to welcome him.
Daokuan then ordered the prefectures and counties to establish assemblies for the practice of the Way, and everyone received the eight precepts.

That very night, the calamity of the tigers dispersed, and no one knew where they had gone. The people of the time were moved by this; they revered him as a divine sage, and offerings and almsgiving followed one after another.
Whether it amounted to one hundred thousand or two hundred thousand [coins], he would immediately distribute it all until nothing remained for his own use.
He told his donors: "Wealth is like a seed; when accumulated, it is difficult to multiply. Therefore, I distribute it so that it may serve a purpose.
Furthermore, I hold my life lightly and wear simple, coarse, and tattered clothing. Yet, once these have been worn upon my feet, I cherish and protect them more than my own flesh. At such times...
In years of famine, he personally boiled congee and gruel to provide for those who were hungry and emaciated. Weeping as he spoke of the Dharma, he urged them to recite the names of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, from the robes he wore and his felt blankets, he would cut or diminish portions to provide for the poor and destitute. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, when he returned to the regions of Pu and Jin, both monastics and laypeople rejoiced;
they gathered like clouds in joyful song. He frequently established dharma assemblies, once again proclaiming the teachings that lead to successful crossing over. At that time, the Prefecture...
The district encountered a drought; none of the various prayers brought success. Sengquan established an altar and made a personal vow:

"If it does not rain, I shall no longer dwell in my hall or rooms. He exposed his body to the sun for two days. After three days, dense clouds gathered and spread, and the entire region was flooded with torrential rain.
The people relied upon him for their revival, and he was hailed as the "Sun of the Buddha" for an entire era.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month of the summer in the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan period, he passed away at Renshou Temple at the age of seventy-eight.
Śramaṇa Cizang’s secular surname was Kim. He was a native of Silla, whose ancestors were among the Three Han states; specifically, they belonged to the kingdom of Chinhan in the east.
Cang’s father, named Wulin, served as a *su-p'an* (an official equivalent to the first rank of the Northern Tang), enjoying a high position, yet he had no male heirs.

Deep sorrow constantly accumulated within her. Having long revered the principles of the Buddha, she sought his protective grace and extensively practiced great renunciation, directing her heart toward the Buddhadharma.

She also commissioned one thousand images of Avalokiteśvara, hoping for the birth of a child. She further vowed that if the child grew up, he would resolve to seek the Bodhi-mind and deliver all living beings.
There were both hidden auspicious signs and manifest responses; she dreamed that a star fell into her lap, and thereupon she became pregnant. On the eighth day of the fourth month, [she gave birth].

Dàn was born with a spiritual intelligence that was clear and refined, having surpassed the age of elementary schooling. He had perused almost all the historical records and chronicles of successive dynasties.

When both his parents passed away, he grew increasingly weary of worldly splendors and deeply realized the truth of impermanence and its ultimate return to emptiness and stillness. Thereupon, he renounced his wife and children, as well as his manor, houses, fields, and gardens;
providing for their needs as required, he remained solitary and alone, casting himself into the mountain forests. Clad in coarse garments and wearing straw sandals, he dwelt by himself.
While practicing the dhyāna of stillness, he occasionally succumbed to heavy sleep. He subsequently moved to a small room, which he surrounded on all sides with thorny brambles.

He sat upright in the nude so that any movement would prick his flesh; he hung his hair from a beam to dispel his mental dullness. As he became an object of universal esteem, he was destined for the rank of prime minister. Despite repeated summons, he did not comply, which provoked the Great King’s great anger.
The King issued an edict to detain him at his mountain retreat and intended to put him to death by the hand of execution. Huìcáng said, "I would rather maintain my precepts."
One day he died; he had not wished to live even a single lifetime having broken the precepts. The executioners were terrified of him and did not dare to apply the blade.

They reported the matter to the king, who was filled with shame and submission. He released the man to leave the household life, allowing him to follow his practice of the Way as he pleased, whereupon he again went into deep seclusion.

He cut off all external contact and lived in utter poverty regarding food and grain, making his very life dependent on death. Thereupon, he was moved by supernatural birds, each carrying various fruits, which came to his hands to offer them to him.
The birds would hold the fruit in their beaks while he took it from them and they ate together. This occurred whenever the time arrived; it never failed to happen according to its appointed season.
He was constantly filled with sorrow and felt compassion for all sentient beings, wondering what skillful means he might employ to enable them to escape birth and death.
Consequently, while sleeping, he saw two men who asked him, "You dwell in such seclusion; what benefit do you seek? Puṇyālaṅkāra replied, "I seek only to benefit sentient beings.
Thereupon, the two men conferred upon him the five precepts and said, "You may take these five precepts and use them to benefit sentient beings. Puṇyālaṅkāra then—
Upon leaving the mountains, within one month, the men and women of the kingdom all received the five precepts. He then reflected deeply, saying:

"I was born in a remote land where the Buddha-dharma had not yet spread widely. Were it not for my own direct observation, there would have been no way for me to receive and uphold it. He then petitioned his original king to travel westward to observe the Great Transformation.
In the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era, he led more than ten followers, including the monk Sengshi, and took his leave from the East.

Upon arriving at the capital, he received an imperial decree to be comforted and settled at the Shengguang (Victorious Light) Monastery. There, he was provided with lavish gifts and extraordinary provisions;

people gathered in great crowds, and as his wealth accumulated, a thief intended to take it. Terrified and struck with alarm, the monk returned to confess his transgression and immediately received the precepts.

Furthermore, there was a man suffering from congenital blindness who went to the Tripitaka master to perform repentance; later, upon his return, he regained his sight. Because of such auspicious responses, those who received the precepts from him increased day by day.

He numbered in the thousands. By nature he delighted in seclusion and tranquility, and having petitioned for an imperial edict to enter the mountains, he built a dwelling upon a precipitous cliff to the east of Yunjì Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
Morning and evening, people and spirits returned to him for the precepts; he spent three summers traveling back and forth, always remaining on this mountain.

When he was about to depart for the eastern regions, he took his leave at the foot of Yunjì and beheld a great host of ghosts and spirits, their number beyond counting, clad in armor and bearing weapons, who said:
He brought out this golden carriage to welcome Cizang, but he saw a great deity fighting with him and refusing to allow the welcome.
The deity said to Cizang, "You shall not die now; you have already reached over eighty years of age. Subsequently, he entered the capital and received an imperial edict of consolation and inquiry.

He was granted two hundred bolts of silk to provide for his clothing. In the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era, he requested to return to his own country; having petitioned the Emperor, he received permission.
He was escorted into the palace, where he was granted a set of patched robes (*nāṃśaka*) and five hundred pieces of variegated silk. The Crown Prince also granted him two hundred pieces.

Furthermore, at Hongfu Monastery, a great vegetarian feast (*mahā-pūjā*) was held on his behalf for the sake of the state, a great assembly of virtuous monks was convened, and eight persons were ordained. Moreover—
An imperial edict was issued for the Nine Departments of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to provide offerings.

As the scriptures and images of his own country had fallen into decay and were incomplete, he obtained a complete set of the Tripitaka, along with various exquisite images, banners, flowers, and canopies—all fit to bring merit and benefit—which he then carried back to his native land.
Upon his arrival in his native land, the entire kingdom came out to welcome him. There, the Buddha-dharma of the era flourished and became manifest.

The King, admiring the Great Country (China) and desiring to propagate and uphold the True Teaching, realized that without a person of capable governance, there would be no means to ensure its solemn purification.

He therefore decreed that Saṃghabhadra be appointed as the Overseer of the Great Country and assigned him to reside at Wangfen Monastery. Furthermore, he constructed a separate cloister and ordained ten individuals specifically to serve as his constant attendants. He then requested—
He entered the palace for one summer to lecture on Mahāyāna treatises. Later, at Kōryū-ji Temple, he lectured on the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* for seven days and seven nights.
Heaven sent down sweet dew, and clouds and mists gathered thickly, shrouding the lecture hall. The fourfold assembly sighed in admiration, and his reputation spread even further.
Hōzō, belonging to this auspicious era, offered all his clothing and possessions as alms; he devoted himself solely to the practice of *dhūta*.

Lanruo oversaw the entire undertaking. Since the Buddha-dharma first flowed eastward from the Green Mound (Qingqiu) for a hundred years, he, together with various ministers, conducted a detailed evaluation to establish the correct record.

He maintained that all Buddhist teachings must have established regulations and protocols, and thus entrusted the matter entirely to the *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Monks), ordering him to manage the five divisions of monks and nuns.

Each [monastery] was to increase its traditional practices and establish further administrative oversight to maintain discipline. The *śīla* (precepts) were to be recited every half-month, and transgressions were to be expiated according to the Vinaya.

Comprehensive examinations were to be conducted during both spring and winter to ensure that the monks understood what constituted an offense and what did not. Furthermore, itinerant inspectors (*xunshi*) were appointed to travel throughout all the monasteries, earnestly exhorting and instructing the practitioners in the Dharma.
He adorned Buddha images and managed various monastic affairs as a constant practice. Furthermore, he separately constructed more than ten temples and stupas. Daozang then made a vow, saying:
"If what I have created possesses spiritual power, I hope it will manifest extraordinary signs and cause śarīra relics to appear within these cloths and bowls.

The great assembly was moved with both grief and joy; offerings accumulated like mountains, and they immediately received the precepts. Consequently, the practice of goodness became widespread. Moreover—
Regarding customary dress and insignia, though they differed between China and the outer regions, Tibet alone remained devoted to the Emperor’s calendar;
now that the entire nation has attained peace, all frontier attire shall be universally reformed to conform strictly to Tang protocol.

Shi Mingdao, surnamed Yao, was a native of Wuxing. From childhood, he possessed refined and elegant qualities that set him apart from the common crowd. During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, his parents passed away;
he resolved to leave the household life, intending to protect the Dharma. He traveled everywhere in search of Maitreya’s monastic discipline.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, while traveling to Chenzhou, he encountered an imperial decree to select monks, with only one guide to be retained. Because his virtuous reputation had long been widespread, he was consequently chosen for this appointment.
Although he received this honor and fame, it was not what his heart desired; he sighed and said, "The purpose of leaving the household life is to propagate and save others."
How could he remain confined to one region? He instead turned his steps toward a distant journey, abandoning the monastery to seek instruction at the feet of the two masters Yan and Li.

There, he consumed their profound and esoteric teachings. Before even a single summer had passed, his reputation for erudition was preeminent; consequently, they ordered him to recount what he had learned, and he delivered it with such thoroughness that nothing remained unmastered.
Among his fellow students and spiritual companions, there were none who did not hold him in the highest esteem. In the second year of the Longshuo era, his virtuous conduct was already manifest;

by imperial decree, he was granted a separate residence at Tiangong Temple in the Eastern Capital. In the first year of the Linde era, the Emperor commissioned a statue of Laozi and ordered it to be sent to Mount Mang, with instructions that all the cultural and ceremonial trappings of Luoyang be arrayed before it.
At that time, the local magistrate Han Xiaowei, falsely invoking the Emperor’s majesty, incited the masses through the deceptive influence of the "Yellow Turbans."

I entrust this to the monks and nuns, commanding them all to escort [the remains] together. Wei then issued a decree for the twenty-two counties of the prefecture, ordering the fivefold assembly to gather at Luozhou.

Each was to prepare banners and streamers, and on the appointed day, they were to set them up in unison. Leading the procession out, the multitude declared: "The two gates of the Buddha-way and the Way of the Sages..."

"From the beginning, the heavens have been severed [from the earth]; the positions of the heterodox and the orthodox are distinct. They have fundamentally been vastly different; how can they be mixed together as if they were identical?

Since there is no separate imperial decree to lead you [to this], I dare not obey your command. Wei then said in a great rage, "What kind of Daoist practitioner are you, to dare to refuse the sovereign's mandate?"
He then sent men to strip Dao of his *kāṣāya* (monastic robe) and take him away for interrogation and punishment. Dao said, "The *kāṣāya* is that which one wears by virtue of an imperial decree;
it cannot be removed arbitrarily without such a decree. I have sent the monk to the authorities because there was no decree to do so, and thus I did not disobey the mandate of the state. Wei Nu said:
When there was a Daoist who did not escort the Celestial Venerable out, Xuandu immediately stood up alone. The monks and nuns all went together to where Xuandu was;
he spoke with a look of fierce anger, saying, "The Daoist intends to rebel.

Xuandu replied to the officials of the Six Ministries at once, saying, "If the high officials have summoned the monks and nuns and they proclaim a rebellion, then it is the high officials themselves who are rebelling, not the assembly of monks. It must be...

He informed the Censor. At once, Dao and the others collapsed and fled. Wei was greatly alarmed and fearful; he descended from the steps, bowed his head in submission, and withdrew after offering an apologetic thanks.
Because of this great assembly of monks, an examination was held to ordain new members. Heavenly palaces sent down food, which arrived even after midday.
Among the monks were those who did not gauge the time; they took the food and ate it. Dao said, "All you Great Virtues are the entrusted legacy of the Buddha’s Dharma throughout the world."
He was a model of integrity. When eating at improper times in the presence of laypeople, he openly violated the laws and precepts, thereby destroying the conditions for the present Dharma.

He had presumed upon his status as both a sage and an ordinary person to such an extent that the entire assembly felt ashamed. Consequently, they sought water for him to rinse his mouth; for over a month he did not eat.

Lamenting that the True Dharma was reaching the point of decay, he finally accepted some steamed buns only after the monastics and laity urged him with great earnestness. He was over sixty years old when, in the East...
Xia Yingmao presided over the assembly, and everyone gathered there for the occasion.

Shi Daoxing, whose secular surname was Liu, originally resided in Qinzhou. When he was eight or nine years old, he constantly thought of leaving the household life; at the age of nineteen, he [entered the order].

He resolved to go to Daguang Temple. The monastic community took pity on him, and his two parents pleaded with him earnestly. The assembly offered him counsel and persuasion, and he finally consented to tonsure.
At that time, the world was in great turmoil, and bandits were rampant in every direction; the dead lay piled like mountains.

Having become a śrāmaṇera, Daoxing said to his fellow students, "A human body is difficult to obtain; the upholding of the precepts is paramount. His mother was then plundered and taken away by bandits, six *li* from the city.

They pursued him for ten *li*. Xing gave his life to continue the chase until he reached the thief, who had already been wounded but was not yet dead. Seeing this, the thief said, "This monk is truly the height of filial piety;
he has followed his mother all the way here. He then spared Xing's life and carried his mother on his back back to the city. Everyone in the city marveled at this.
The rebel roads were treacherous and perilous; by what means could he return? Seeking refuge in Shu, he reached Hechi County, where he encountered Duke Zhanhuang.

Having received his comfort and reassurance, the Duke escorted him to Liangzhou. When his age was reached, he received full ordination and constantly dwelt in aranyas, practicing the dhūta ascetic practices and begging for alms.
Master Zhishun was a preeminent lecturer on the Way. Having heard [the teachings] five times from him, [Daoxuan] was already able to recite them from memory.

Whenever Zhishun encountered a divergent view, he marveled at Daoxuan’s profound insight. Later, Daoxuan returned to the region of Shu, where he extensively studied the sutras and śāstras, never wasting a moment of his time.

Furthermore, under Master Jiang, he received instruction in the path of Chan, taking it as the essential method for verifying the mind. After Zhishun passed away, Daoxuan continued the lecture series on the Vinaya.
Whenever he lectured on the Vinaya-piṭaka or exhorted others to generate the bodhicitta, he used these means to encourage the assembly, causing those who listened to weep profusely.
People from afar came to seek refuge with him; at that time, the local authorities were strict and did not permit guests to stay, so there was no temple where they could find lodging.

They all came to him for comfort, but the abbot said, "In accordance with government regulations, it is not permitted; how can you allow them to stay? Daoxing replied, "The officials do not permit even a needle to be harbored."
"I am using your carriage and horses; have you, the Abbot, not heard this? The Abbot became furious and said, "This youth does not heed my words. Daexing replied, "These are the Three Jewels.
If one respects them, one sees what is good; if one dislikes them, one perceives evil. The Abbot, filled with indignation, returned to his quarters;
when he looked at his own *kāṣāya*, he could no longer see it. He then went to the three gates to attend a banquet at the Wang family's house, where he perceived the food as being blood.

The man offered him food, but Daoxing would not eat it; he returned to the temple and performed a repentance ceremony. He subsequently went to live in an araṇya (forest hermitage). At that time, a ghost came to harass and disturb him.

Daoxing stepped out from his rope bed, whereupon the ghost retreated. After Daoxing had received the Three Refuges for the ghost, he recited the names of the Buddhas, and the ghost followed along in the prostrations.
During the Zhenguan era, Dai Ling of Qingcheng arrived late in the evening and wished to stay in the same room as Daoxing to sleep. In the middle of the night, while sleeping...
Startled, he went out of the room and said that he saw a monk dressed in red holding a staff and striking his back.

[The monk] asked, "Why are you staying here overnight? He then used fire to illuminate his back; it was the size of three fingers and a deep, vivid crimson. Because he sought repentance for his transgression, his illness became extremely severe.
He heard the sound of music coming from within the room, and from that moment on, he recovered. He regularly prostrated before the Thousand Buddhas, doing so once every day, forevermore.

In the third year of the Huichang era, Dharma Master Xuanzang sent śarīra relics for veneration. Having received them, Master Xing established a dharma-assembly hall within his quarters and made this solemn vow:
"If throughout my life I have propagated the Dharma and paid homage to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa in accordance with the holy intention, may you please emit a radiance.
As he spoke, the entire room became golden in color. This occurred on a certain day of a certain month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era.
He ultimately attained the merit of victory. He was sixty-seven years of age. Shi Guangyi’s secular surname was Li;
he was originally of the Tang imperial clan. His father, Prince Langye, raised troops together with the Prince of Yue, intending to restore the original dynasty and revitalize the Way of the Emperor.
This failed, and Empress Wu executed his entire clan. Guangyi was still in his swaddling clothes at the time; his nurse...

The mother carried him on her back and fled. Several years later, Empress Wu secretly heard that a son of Langye was among the common people and increased the rewards for his capture with ever-greater urgency.
When the wet nurse reached the borders of Fufeng, she sold her handicrafts to support herself. Boyi was then eight years old;
his appearance was extraordinary, and his spiritual insight was transcendent. The wet nurse feared he would be captured because of his looks and fell into deep anxiety.
Feeling apprehensive, she fashioned a cloth tunic and placed money between her waist and abdomen. Beneath a mulberry grove, she instructed him to depart.
She commanded that he search for her without negligence, adding, "I fear we shall both die; it would be of no benefit to the cause. You are intelligent and will surely establish yourself;

should you ever attain wealth and honor, do not forget this old woman. Having finished speaking, they wept together. Zhiyi was so overcome with grief that he could not control himself. From this time on, the wet nurse...

He passed away. Zhixi was bewildered. When he reached an inn, the sun was setting; he sought a path, intending to seek shelter at a village dwelling. He encountered an old monk who called out to him, "You young man!
Now that you are but a single person and your family has already perished, where do you intend to go? Zhixi stood there in respectful astonishment.
The old monk spoke again, "The life of a renunciant is spacious and leisurely, and moreover free from sorrow and fear. Young man, you should go there."
Yi said, "This is indeed what I have long desired. The old monk then took him by the hand and led him to the shade of a great tree.

He had him prostrate before the Buddhas of the ten directions and take refuge in the eternal Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Having done so, he shaved his hair. He then brought out a *kāṣāya* robe and clothed him;
it fit his body perfectly, both in size and proportion. His manner of holding and adjusting the robes was just like that of a bhikṣu with several years of seniority. The old monk—
Xi said, "This is due to the influence of habitual tendencies. Maintain your monastic conduct well. He then pointed toward the northeast and said, "A few *li* from here is a monastery.
Go straight there and visit the abbot, saying: 'I have sent you to be his disciple.

Having finished speaking, the old monk suddenly passed away; only then did Xi realize he was a holy monk (*ārya*). Following the instructions exactly as given, he went to that place. The abbot was struck with amazement.
He spoke thus, and [the Emperor] detained him there for ten years. By then, Huikai had thoroughly mastered the sutras and vinaya and was proficient in dhyāna meditation.

It happened that the Zhongzong ascended the throne and the Tang dynasty was restored; an imperial edict was issued to seek a descendant of the Prince of Langye. Huikai then informed the monks of the temple about this matter.
The crowd was greatly astonished. Thereupon, he went to visit Li, the Prefect of Fufeng—who was the elder brother of Zhiyi’s paternal uncles.
Upon seeing him, Li was filled with both grief and joy, and he took him into his home. Just as he was about to report the matter to the authorities, Zhiyi firmly declined, saying it could not be.
Li had a daughter whose age was similar to his own; she took a liking to Zhiyi at first sight and wished to offer her affection. Zhiyi, however, was terrified and sought to avoid her. Later...
One day, the Prefect’s wife sent her daughter out, gorgeously adorned and wearing magnificent robes, accompanied by a vast retinue.

She approached him with intent to seduce him, but Huiyi resolutely resisted her with every means at his disposal and ultimately refused to yield. He deceived her, saying, "My person is not pure; please allow me to bathe and await your command. The girl consented.
Just as he ordered the bathwater prepared, the girl went out; he then locked the door. When the girl returned and pushed against the door, she found it would not open. Not having gained entry...

He was able to enter. Peering through the window, he saw that [the man] was just then holding a razor for shaving hair. Looking up, the man said, "Because this organ exists, one is thus oppressed by desire.
If it were removed now, what would there be to oppress? The woman, terrified, tried to stop him, but it was not possible;
he then severed his member and threw it to the ground. The official also fainted. Since the door would not open, shortly thereafter both the Magistrate and his wife arrived together.
Upon arriving, the woman told him the full truth of the matter. He then broke down the door and looked inside; she had gradually regained consciousness.

He ordered medical practitioners to carry her back to the silkworm room, where they burned the ground and doused it with bitter wine (acetic acid). They seated her upon it and applied medicinal ointment to her wounds. After more than a month, the sores were healed.

The Prefect submitted a memorial stating that Yi was the son of the Prince of Langye. By imperial decree, he was escorted by relay station to the capital, where he was granted an audience and received inquiries of comfort.

He was bestowed with abundant and generous rewards, and an edict was issued for him to inherit his father’s rank. However, Yi earnestly declined, vowing to become a monk; his resolve was firm and unshakable.
Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict permitting him to lead disciples and establish hermitages at will to transform the regions. Yi’s natural inclination was toward Mount Zhongnan, and consequently—
He resided at Faxing Temple and constructed hermitages and *āraṇyakas* at various mountain passes, numbering some dozens in total.

His reputation for the Way spread far and wide, and his discourses moved people’s hearts. Even when he traveled ten *li* into the mountains, his monastic and lay attendants would always number several thousand.
They welcomed and waited upon him with reverence. His demeanor was always abiding in silent concentration. Sometimes he would speak of future events to determine good or ill fortune;

his predictions were invariably without error, and people increasingly turned to him for refuge. On the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era, he entrusted his disciples with these words:
"You must carefully guard your body and speech, and do not engage in clamor or frivolity. The Master’s intention is nothing other than this: when one is still, that is the Truth."
The Dharma manifested before him. Furthermore, his outward proclamations were all uttered out of necessity; his words were exceedingly urgent and poignant.
Consequently, he lay down facing north, resting his head on his right arm with his right side against the mat, and passed away.
Shi Zhixian’s secular surname was Jiang. A native of Jianyang, he possessed a naturally firm and upright mind from an early age and established his principles while still young.
Having entered the monastic order, he subsequently received full ordination. He maintained his integrity and cultivated his mind, never deviating from the monastic precepts.

In the first year of the Dabao era, at Fotie Rock in his home prefecture, he served Chan Master Daoyi, fetching water and gathering firewood, devoted solely to diligent toil. Later, while traveling, he visited Jinhua.
Mount Chisongdong is the place where Huang Chuping commanded the stones to become sheep. Its dense forests and steep ridges stretch for about a hundred paces toward the springs and lakes;
its secluded and wondrous character is deeply pleasing. Having taken up residence upon the summit, a rustic elder carries fragrant rice and vegetables to provide for him.
At that time, there was a great drought. Hui-xian gazed into the sky and struck a stone, then rebuked the dragons, saying:

"If you dragons are powerless due to your karma, why does the Bodhisattva Dragon King not obey the Buddha’s command to save the common people? As soon as he finished striking the stone, rain poured down.
The people of Wu were all filled with joy. Later, while traveling to Chang’an, eminent officials and men of great virtue lined up to invite him to establish a great monastery.
The Master Gongde was startled and looked back with apprehension; the next day he set out and ascended Mount Wutai, eventually settling at Ganshui Temple in Taiyuan.
Monastics and laypeople who requested instruction in the principles of Chan arrived one after another.

Shi Yuanguan resided at his home in Luoyang. By nature he was simple and unpretentious; while he sometimes applied himself diligently to Buddhist studies, he also enjoyed managing his livelihood and profited from his fields and gardens, earning him the contemporary nickname "Yiduon of the Empty Gate.
Beyond this, his conduct was extraordinary, and he was moreover proficient in musical theory.
Toward the end of the Dali era, he became a bosom friend with Li Yuan. At the end of the Tianbao era, Yuan’s father, Li Cheng, had served as the Guardian of the Capital.
Having fallen among bandits, he subsequently took his family estate and donated it to Hui-lin Temple north of Luoyang.

He provided only one vessel of food daily, eating and drinking together with the monastic community. After three years had passed in this manner, he suddenly planned a journey to Shu to seek medicinal herbs in mountain caves such as Qingcheng and Emei.
While Dao-guan wished to travel to Chang’an by way of the Xie-gu Pass, Li wished to enter from Jingzhou.
At the Gorges, they debated these two paths for half a year without reaching a decision. Huineng said, "I have already ceased serving kings and lords;
I do not wish to travel the road through the two capitals. Huinong said, "In action, there is no fixed necessity; I request to follow your command. They then proceeded from Jingzhou up the Gorges.
While traveling, they stopped their boat at Nanpu and saw several women wearing silk sashes and brocade aprons, carrying jars to draw water. Huinong lowered his head and...
He wept and said, "The reason I did not wish to pass through here was that I feared encountering this woman. Li said, "Since coming from the upper gorges, you have encountered many such people;
why do you weep alone? Guan said, "That pregnant woman, Lady Wang, was the place where I entrusted my life.
It has been over three years, yet she has still not given birth. It was only because I had not yet arrived that she remained safe; now that I have seen her—"
"Indeed, destiny has its own destination. Observe how death gives rise to life: a pregnant woman shall give birth. On the third day, Li went to visit the newborn child.
As he was wrapped in swaddling clothes and brought into the light, the infant indeed gave a smile. Li wept and informed Wang Shi of this occurrence. Wang Shi performed a grand burial for Guan.

Li constantly remembered his promise with the girl from Hangzhou; when the appointed time arrived, he went to Tiantzhi Mountain Temple. That night, as the moon shone with brilliant clarity, he suddenly heard the sound of a reed flute.
Beside Hongjing, there was a cowherd singing a *zhuzhi* song, riding a cow and striking its horn, with his hair in two topknots and wearing short clothes;
he slowly approached the front of the temple, and it was revealed to be Guanzhi. Li stepped forward and bowed, saying, "Master Guan, are you well? He replied, "Master Li, you are a true lay devotee.
My path and yours are different; be careful not to draw near me. Your worldly karmic ties are not yet exhausted; simply continue to practice diligently so that you do not fall. Thus he spoke.
They eventually met. Li had no way to initiate conversation; he gazed at him with tears in his eyes. Guan then sang a *zhuzhi* song, its melody drifting away as it proceeded.
The lyrics were poignant and the tune lofty, such that no one knew their meaning. He sighed and said, "Truly a monk who has attained the Way.

Though we are but a few feet apart, we are worlds apart—sages and worldlings follow different paths. Yuan subsequently renounced alcohol and meat, did not marry, and did not employ servants, constantly relying on wisdom.
At the Linsi Monastery, he occupied a single room and partook of his meals with the monks.
Shi Xuansu, whose courtesy name was Daoqing, was surnamed Ma and was a native of Yanling in Runzhou. He possessed extraordinary character from birth and sought to enter the Buddhist order;
his parents granted him permission. He left home to rely upon the Pure Realm (the Sangha), and in the Ruyi era, he first received the monastic regulations and was enrolled on the registers.
He received full ordination at Changshou Temple in Jiangning. In his later years, he entered Qiuqi Temple on Mount Qingshan, where he served under Master Wei.

He concealed his form and practiced ascetic discipline, remaining unchanged through both cold and heat. Whether encountering the noble or the lowly, the resentful or the kin, he never experienced joy or anger;
at that time, people called him the "Infant. When kings and lords prostrated themselves before him, he remained unmoved. Thus did he regard worldly fame.
He was like a phantom. One day, a butcher came to pay his respects; he experienced a spontaneous awakening and repented of his past transgressions.
He requested that Huisu partake of the midday meal as a *bhikṣu*. Su accepted with joy and descended to the man’s house. The officials and commoners were struck with awe and marveled at the wonder.
Su said, "The Buddha-nature is the same for all; how could there be distinction between the born and the unborn? However, those who can be saved, I shall [save]."
He delivered them across. What difference was there? At the beginning of the Tianbao era, those of Wuyue looked up to him with reverence, as if he were about to manifest a descent from heaven.

A monk named Xihuan from Yangzhou requested that he come to the north of the river; however, [the Master] secretly fled by night. The moonless night made crossing difficult, and the river waves were vast and surging.
As the boatman steered against the wind, suddenly a single white light appeared, leading the oars straight across. Tongbo was thus saved. The people of Chu...

They congratulated one another, for the Sun of the Buddha had shone forth once more. People from across the province rushed to the ferry crossing, where the throngs of men and women blocked the roads so that there was no space to stand between them.

They stripped their garments and offered them as alms, piling up like hills and mounds; yet he took no personal interest in these offerings, ordering that they all be used to provide for those who cultivate the field of compassion.

Shi Wuzhuo was a native of Yongjia. His intellectual capacity was broad and clear, and his moral integrity was steadfast and firm. He devoted himself to the Great Way and resolved to travel abroad to seek it.
Arriving at Yunhua Temple in the capital, he studied the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* under Dharma Master Chengguan.
In the second year of the Dali era, he entered Mount Wutai, desiring to behold the realm of the Sage. In the fifth month, he arrived at Huayan Temple and hung [his robes].
Xī was drinking tea in the hall when he saw an elderly monk of humble appearance reclining on the northern couch. He asked, "Have you come from the south?
I have brought a rosary for you; please examine it. As the monk put it on and began counting the beads himself, Xī looked away for a moment, and the monk had vanished.

At that time, his spirit was dazed and bewildered, and a mixture of doubt and joy arose within him. He said, "In the past, the monk Sengming entered here and beheld a stone mortar and a wooden pestle;
later, he entered the Holy Monastery and was able to see the sages and worthies. I wish to dwell here—how joyful that would be!
Next, from the pavilion of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, he saw an auspicious bird with brilliantly colored plumage flying in pairs above his head; he gazed toward the northeast.
He flapped his wings and departed. The following day, two stalks of white light entered the room, drifting and lingering for a short while.
His fellow monk Fǎděng and others saw this and were struck with wonder, saying, "What auspicious omen is this? We pray that it may appear again to sever the doubts of sentient beings.
Immediately, they beheld the light as before; they then went to the Vajra Cave, paid their respects from afar, and while sitting down to rest, they heard the sound of someone shouting at an ox.

Three times he called out, "I am thirsty for water. An old man of ancient appearance and extraordinary form, wearing coarse short trousers and dragging hemp sandals, with a most unusual turban wrapped around his head, came forward and took his hand.
He asked where he had come from. The old man replied, "I have come from outside the mountains seeking provisions.
When asked where he was staying, he said, "I am seeking provisions at Mount Tai. Zhe then questioned him in turn, saying, "Why has the Master stopped here? He answered, "I heard..."
"There is a Vajra Cave here; that is why I have come to join you in your appreciation. The old man asked, "Are you weary, Master? He replied, "No.
The old man said, "If you are not exhausted, why do you sleep so abruptly? He replied, "Ordinary people are subject to dullness (*styāna*); how can it be considered strange?

The old man said, "If you are indeed drowsy, you may go and drink some boiled *chuan* tea. The old man pointed toward the northeast, where a vihara was visible at a distance of several paces. The old man led [him there].
The ox walked ahead, and he followed, treading along the path. Upon reaching the temple gate, he called out "Kunti" three times. A youth responded with a single "Yes," opening and closing the gate.

He was about fourteen or fifteen years old, with hair hanging down to his eyebrows, wearing a coarse tunic. He led the ox into the temple and saw that the ground was entirely made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
The halls, chambers, corridors, and verandas all shone with a golden luster; their splendor and magnificence were unlike anything in the human world.
Regarding the protocol for this, the old man sat cross-legged upon a white ivory couch, pointed to a brocade cushion, and bade him take his seat. A youth presented two bowls of tea;
after they had finished drinking them together, he lifted a tortoise-shell vessel filled with cream and curd, and each took a spoonful and swallowed it.

As if having attained some realization, [the Master] suddenly awakened to his past lives. The old man asked, "Since you left home to become a monk, what have you sought and what have you worried about? He replied:
[The Master] said: "There are those who cultivate but do not realize; they merely dip their fingers into the waters of both the Great and Small Vehicles.

[The Master] asked: "When you first left home, what state of mind did you seek? He replied: "I sought the Mahāyāna bodhicitta. [The Master] said: "If you cultivate with that initial resolve, you will attain it immediately.
He asked again: "How old are you? He replied: "Thirty-one. The Elder said: "Your age is thirty-eight; such is the depth of your roots of merit."
"Plant these trees so they may flourish, and descend the mountain slowly. Take care to find the path and do not injure your feet. I am old and infirm;
having come from outside the mountains, I am utterly exhausted and wish to rest. The traveler said, "May I stay for one night? He replied, "No.
It is because you have two companions following you. Tonight, when they do not see you return, they will be filled with grief and anxiety."
[The Master] said, "This is merely because the teacher still harbors attachments. Zhe said, "What attachments do the disciples of Gautama have?
Even though they have companions, they feel no lingering attachment to them. [The Master] asked again, "Do you carry the three robes? He replied, "I have carried them since receiving the precepts.
[The Master] said, "This is a point of attachment. Zhe said, "There is also sacred teaching on this matter: if one intends to stay overnight, one should mentally relinquish [the robes]."
If there were compelling circumstances, the Buddha would indeed grant permission. He said: "If, according to the Hīnayāna, there is no obstacle, one must not discard one's robes;

one should instead maintain them with urgent care. The old man brushed his lapel, threw back his sleeves, and composed [a verse]. He put it on and walked away at once. The old man said: "Listen as I proclaim this gāthā."

"A single thought of pure mind is Bodhi; it surpasses the construction of seven-jeweled stupas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Though those jeweled stupas may eventually crumble into dust, a single thought of pure mind achieves Perfect Enlightenment.

[The Master] spoke thus, looking down and listening with focused concentration. [The attendant] said, "Having been granted the proclamation of this secret verse, I am like one who has drunk the *amṛta* (clarified butter);
my countenance has entered the gateway of wisdom. How could I dare forget your instructions? The Elder called for Junti and said, "You may escort the Master away. As they were about to depart—

Zhuo patted him on the back and said, "Go well. Zhuo bowed twice and walked shoulder-to-shoulder with the boy until they reached the Vajra Cave. Turning to ask the boy, he said, "What cave is this? The boy replied, "According to the oral tradition of former generations, it is named the Vajra Cave. The boy asked, "What character follows 'Vajra'? Zhuo reflected for a moment and said, "Below 'Vajra' is 'Prajñā' (Wisdom). The boy said: [He was right. Zhuo said: [I knew it. The boy said: [How did you know? Zhuo said: [Because I have studied the scriptures. The boy said: [If that is so, then you already know the Buddha’s mind. Zhuo said: [I do not yet know the Buddha’s mind; how could I know the Buddha’s body? The boy said: [If you do not know the Buddha’s mind, how can you know the Buddha’s body? Zhuo said: [I am merely a man of the world who has not yet attained the Way; I cannot know the Buddha’s mind. However, I have heard that the Buddha’s body is like empty space, and I have heard that the Buddha’s mind is like empty space. Since both body and mind are like empty space, how can there be a distinction between them? The boy said: [If you say the Buddha’s body is like empty space, then empty space itself has no body. If you say the Buddha’s mind is like empty space, then empty space itself has no mind. Since there is neither body nor mind, what is it that you call the Buddha? Zhuo was speechless. The boy said: [The Buddha is not a person; a person is not the Buddha. You must not seek the Buddha outside yourself. If you seek the Buddha outside yourself, you will never find him. You must seek the Buddha within yourself. If you seek the Buddha within yourself, you will immediately see him. Zhuo said: [If I seek the Buddha within myself, how shall I recognize him? The boy said: [If you seek the Buddha within yourself, you will see that your own nature is originally the Buddha. You need not seek elsewhere. Zhuo said: [If my own nature is originally the Buddha, why did I previously not realize it? The boy said: [It is because you have been deluded by false thoughts for countless eons. Because of these false thoughts, you have failed to recognize your own original nature. Now that you have encountered me, you should cast away your false thoughts and see your own original nature. Zhuo said: [I have cast away my false thoughts, but I still do not see my original nature. The boy said: [If you have cast away your false thoughts, where is your original nature? Where is your original nature? Zhuo said: [I do not know. The boy said: [Since you do not know, how can you say you have cast away your false thoughts? False thoughts are originally non-existent; they arise from nowhere and cease into nowhere. Your original nature is also like this—it arises from nowhere and ceases into nowhere. Since arising and ceasing are both non-existent, what is there to be seen? Zhuo said: [I understand your meaning, but I am still confused. The boy said: [Confusion is precisely the Buddha. Non-confusion is precisely the Buddha. Confusion and non-confusion are both the Buddha. There is no other Buddha apart from confusion and non-confusion. Zhuo said: [If confusion and non-confusion are both the Buddha, then all sentient beings are the Buddha. The boy said: [All sentient beings are indeed the Buddha. But you must not take the Buddha to be sentient beings, nor take sentient beings to be the Buddha. If you take sentient beings to be the Buddha, you will fall into the error of eternalism. If you take the Buddha to be sentient beings, you will fall into the error of nihilism. You must transcend both eternalism and nihilism, and then you will see the Buddha. Zhuo said: [I have transcended eternalism and nihilism, but I still do not see the Buddha. The boy said: [Transcending eternalism and nihilism is precisely the Buddha. What else is there to see? Zhuo was speechless. The boy said: [You have now seen the Buddha. You should go quickly and tell others of this. Do not let them remain in delusion. Zhuo bowed and departed. He returned to his monastery and told the monks: "Today I went to the Vajra Cave and met a young monk. He taught me that the Buddha is not a person, and that one must seek the Buddha within oneself. I have now realized the Buddha. The monks said: "That young monk must be an incarnation of a Bodhisattva. You should go and visit him again. Zhuo said: "I have already seen the Buddha; what more is there to see? The monks said: "Even if you have seen the Buddha, you should still go to pay your respects. Zhuo said: "I am a man of the world; how can I meet a holy sage? The monks said: "The holy sage is not a holy sage; he is just an ordinary child. An ordinary child is not an ordinary child; he is a manifestation of the Buddha. Zhuo said: "I understand your meaning. I shall go. Zhuo went to the Vajra Cave and found the boy sitting alone under a tree. Zhuo prostrated himself before him and said: "I have come to pay my respects. The boy said: "Why have you come? Zhuo said: "I have come to pay my respects. The boy said: "Respect is not respect; it is just a formality. A formality is not a formality; it is the Way. You must not take the Way to be a formality, nor take a formality to be the Way. If you take a formality to be the Way, you will fall into the error of attachment. If you take the Way to be a formality, you will fall into the error of emptiness. You must transcend both attachment and emptiness, and then you will see the Way. Zhuo said: "I have transcended attachment and emptiness, but I still do not see the Way. The boy said: "Transcending attachment and emptiness is precisely the Way. What else is there to see? Zhuo was speechless. The boy said: "You have now seen the Way. You should go quickly and teach others. Do not let them remain in ignorance. Zhuo bowed and departed. He returned to his monastery and told the monks: "Today I went to the Vajra Cave and met the young monk again. He taught me that the Way is not a thing, and that one must not seek the Way through forms. I have now realized the Way. The monks said: "That young monk is truly a great teacher. You should go and visit him once more. Zhuo said: "I have already realized the Way; what more is there to realize? The monks said: "Even if you have realized the Way, you should still go to pay your respects. Zhuo said: "I am a man of the world; how can I meet a holy sage? The monks said: "The holy sage is not a holy sage; he is just an ordinary child. An ordinary child is not an ordinary child; he is a manifestation of the Buddha. Zhuo said: "I understand your meaning. I shall go. Zhuo went to the Vajra Cave and found the boy sitting alone under a tree. Zhuo prostrated himself before him and said: "I have come to pay my respects. The boy said: "Why have you come? Zhuo said: "I have come to pay my respects. The boy said: "Respect is not respect; it is just a formality. A formality is not a formality; it is the Way. You must not take the Way to be a formality, nor take a formality to be the Way. If you take a formality to be the Way, you will fall into the error of attachment. If you take the Way to be a formality, you will fall into the error of emptiness. You must transcend both attachment and emptiness, and then you will see the Way. Zhuo said: "I have transcended attachment and emptiness, but I still do not see the Way. The boy said: "Transcending attachment and emptiness is precisely the Way. What else is there to see? Zhuo was speechless. The boy said: "You have now seen the Way. You should go quickly and teach others. Do not let them remain in ignorance. Zhuo bowed and departed. He returned to his monastery and told the monks: "Today I went to the Vajra Cave and met the young monk again. He taught me that the Way is not a thing, and that one must not seek the Way through forms. I have now realized the Way. The monks said: "That young monk is truly a great teacher. You should go and visit him once more. Zhuo said: "I have already realized the Way; what more is there to realize? The monks said: "Even if you have realized the Way, you should still go to pay your respects. Zhuo said: "I am a man of the world; how can I meet a holy sage? The monks said: "The holy sage is not a holy sage; he is just an ordinary child. An ordinary child is not an ordinary child; he is a
"Zi, you are right. As they entered, they reached Baoyue Temple. Zhe took the boy’s hand, bowed, and looked back at him before parting.
The boy stared wide-eyed at Zhe as if wishing to speak. Zhe said, "To see me off, can you offer words in place of a white silk sash and a jade pendant?
The boy then recited a verse for him, saying: "No anger on the face—this is the offering; No [harshness] in the mouth..."
