"Anger emits a wondrous fragrance; a mind free from anger is a precious treasure. Untainted and stainless, it is the true eternal.
When the verse ended, in an instant of daze, both the youth and the holy temple vanished. Only the mountains, forests, earth, and stones remained.
Grief filled his breast, and he could not stop his sobbing.

Shi Fenggan cut his hair so it reached his eyebrows and wore a coarse cloth robe to cover his body. When people asked where he was staying, he replied, "Just the two words 'according to circumstances,' and nothing more.
He once rode a tiger straight into the Songmen Gate; the monks were struck with fear, yet he sang a dharma song aloud, and everyone came to revere him.
Later, during the Xuan Tian era, he traveled through the capital of Jingzhao to propagate the teachings, his appearance resembling that of a madman.
He was eccentric; his speech was often prophetic. Previously, at Guoqing Temple, there were two practitioners of asceticism in the monks’ kitchen known as Hanshanzi and Shide.
They frequently attended to the cooking fires in the kitchen. Once the cooking was finished, the two would converse with one another;

those who listened in secret could rarely understand their meaning. At that time, Lü Qiuyin was appointed as the governor of Danyou. As he was about to set out in his carriage, he suffered from a headache, and a physician...
It was of little efficacy. Qian Zao said, "I have come from Tiantai to pay my respects to the Prefect. Master Liu has informed me of his ailment. Qian said, "What need is there for you to worry?
He then requested a clean vessel, consecrated water with mantras, and sprayed it [upon the patient]. In a short while, he felt that his body was considerably better.

Lu Qiu was amazed by this and requested a word from Qian to determine whether his upcoming journey would be auspicious or inauspicious. Qian said, "When you arrive at your post, remember to visit Mañjuśrī."
Liu Qiu asked, "Where is this Bodhisattva? [The monk] replied, "He is in the kitchen of Guoqing Temple; he is the one who tends the hearth and washes the utensils.
When [Liu Qiu] entered the mountain temple, he asked, "Has there ever been a Chan Master Fenggan at this monastery?
[The monk] said, "There has. "Where is his courtyard located? And who are Hanshan and Shide? At that time, the monk Daoqiao replied, "Master Fenggan’s former quarters are the Sutra Repository."
Later, the place was now silent and deserted; there were only tigers and leopards that would occasionally come here to roar. Hanzhu and Shishi were seen serving as laborers in the monastic kitchen.
When Lü Qiu entered the dry storehouse, he saw only tiger tracks crisscrossing the floor. He asked again, "What kind of spiritual practice do you two perform here?
They replied, "We only attend to the task of husking grain to provide rice porridge for the monks. At night, we sing songs and recite scriptures."
He did not stop. Thus he sighed and marveled at this a second and a third time before entering the kitchen. There he saw two men burning firewood, appearing as if they were gathered around a brazier.
Lüqiū bowed to them, but the two men repeatedly shouted "Du-ta! They then took Lüqiū by the hand and stripped him, laughing "Ying-ru-zu-he" incessantly.
As they walked away, one said, "Fenggan is too talkative. From then on, the two men went out hand-in-hand.
At the Pine Gate, he no longer entered the temple.
As for Hanshanzi, he was a man of eccentric character who lived in seclusion seventy li west of Shifeng County in Tiantai.
He was known as the "Cold and Dark" pair of cliffs; he made his permanent dwelling within the secluded caves of the Cold Cliff. At that time—
He came to Guoqing Temple. There was a man named Shidi, whom the temple monks had appointed as the supervisor of the refectory.

He would constantly collect the leftover food and vegetable scraps of the assembly of monks; he would cut large bamboo into tubes and cast his finds inside them for storage. Whenever Hanshanzi arrived, [he would find the contents].
He would then carry them away. Sometimes he would stroll slowly along the corridors; sometimes he would shout and roar, intimidating others; or he would hurl insults into the air.
The monks of the monastery could not tolerate this and pursued him with staffs, but he would turn around, clap his hands, and retreat slowly with a "ha-ha" laugh.
Yet, the tone and spirit of his words always returned to the Buddha. Initially, when Lü Qiū entered the monastery, he went to inquire about Hanshan with the śramaṇa Dàoqiáo.
Startled, he said, "Great official, why do you pay such courtesy to a madman? The two men linked arms and went out of the temple laughing and mocking.
Lü Qiū went again to Han-yán to visit and inquire after him, bringing him clothes and medicinal herbs; however, [Huiyuan] spoke out in a loud voice, saying:
The thief thought, "I am being discovered," and immediately shrank his body into a crack within a rock cave. He cried out once more, "Tell all of you people to each exert yourselves!
Then the fissure of the rock cave closed up seamlessly, leaving no trace whatsoever. Thereupon, he ordered the monk Daoqiao to [inform the authorities].
In searching for his遗物 (remains), I found only verses inscribed by attaching them to leaves amidst the forest, as well as those transcribed on the walls of village houses and dwellings;
more than two hundred pieces were thus collected. These have now been compiled into a single anthology, which many recite and chant.
Later, Chan Master Ji of Caoshan provided commentaries on them, titled *Verses Responding to Han Shanzi*.
The one who found him was the Chan Master Fenggan. Previously, while wandering through the mountains, he came upon the side of the road at Chicheng and heard the crying of a child.
He went to search for it and saw a boy about several years old; at first, he thought he was a cowherd’s lad.
Upon questioning him thoroughly about his origins, the boy said he had been abandoned alone with no home. Fenggan took him to Guoqing Temple and entrusted him to the head cook.

A monk, or perhaps someone who came to claim [the image], would surely have had it returned. Later, the śramaṇa Lingyi took charge of it and ordered him to attend to the incense and lamps in the dining hall.
Suddenly one day, he saw him ascend the seat and eat from a dish facing the statue.
He then called out to Kauṇḍinya, saying, "Little-fruit Śrāvaka! You act as if there were no one beside you! He grasped his chopsticks and laughed loudly. The monk then...
He drove them away. Lingyi consulted with the venerable elders and others to relieve him of his duties in the hall and instead ordered him to wash the utensils in the kitchen.
As soon as the washing was finished and the food scraps had been strained and filtered, they placed the refuse in a tube and sent Hanshan to carry it away.

Furthermore, at the shrine of the Protector of the Monastery (Galan Shen), every day when the monks' kitchen served food, it would be snatched up by crows and birds until it lay in a messy heap on the ground. Han Shan picked it up.
He struck an earthen statue with a staff two or three times and scolded it, saying, "If you cannot even protect your own food, how can you protect this monastery?
That evening, a deity appeared in a dream to the monks of the entire temple and said, "Shikoku has beaten me. The next day, the dreams recounted by all the monks were identical.
The whole temple was in an uproar, and they finally realized he was no ordinary man. At that time, a report was sent to the prefectures and counties.
The district magistrate issued an edict stating: "This worthy man is a recluse; he is the manifested body of a Bodhisattva. It is fitting to honor him.
Thus, Shide was titled "Worthy Man" (Xiānshì). Furthermore, while herding oxen at the temple estate, he would sing and call out to Heaven.

Once, while the monks of the temple were performing their *poṣadha* ceremony, Shide drove his oxen to the front of the assembly hall where the monks had gathered. Leaning against the door, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying: "How vast and far-reaching! (Yōuyōu).

The assembly gathered their heads together. At that time, the head seat who maintained the Vinaya rebuked them, saying, "You wind-swept people, why do you create such a clamor and disturbance during the recitation of the precepts?
Shide replied, "I am not herding oxen. These groups of oxen are mostly the people of this monastery who are in charge of monastic affairs.
Shide then called out the dharma names of the deceased monks one by one; the oxen each responded to the sound as they passed by. The entire assembly was struck with confusion and astonishment.
All contemplated reforming their past ways and cultivating themselves for the future, moved by the Bodhisattva’s manifestation in this world to deliver sentient beings.

At that time, Daoqiao compiled and recorded the texts and phrases of Hanshan; on the wall of the local deity shrine within the monastery, he saw the verses of Shide, which he appended to the collection of Hanshan.
Shi Yize’s surname was Changsun; he was a native of Chang’an in Jingzhao. From his youth, Yize remained untainted by worldly affairs, remaining serene throughout the day without any worldly pursuits.
He initially studied cursive script under Zhang Huiguan and alone mastered the subtleties of the brush. He was also deeply devoted to the classics and histories.
He took pleasure in Buddhist scriptures and, one morning, abandoned his family estate to follow Huizhong, the Sixth Patriarch of Niutou Mountain.

He transmitted Zhong’s Way and practiced profound contemplation for a long time, concluding that heaven and earth contain no things and that he himself contains no things; yet, though there are no things, it has never been the case that there are no things.
Thereupon, he traveled south to Mount Tiantai and reached Fokuoyan (Buddha-Cave Cliff), where he lived on *pi-li* (millet) and fallen leaves.
He sat like a corpse, drinking from mountain streams and eating the fruits of trees to fill his emptiness. Tigers and leopards were his guests; deer and elk were his companions.
He was as motionless as withered wood. Later, a woodcutter saw him and told others in turn. A seeker of the Way said:
Daozhe had no disciples; they led one another to build a residence, where they depicted Buddhas and accommodated monks, until it flourished as a vihāra.
Since the Yuanhe era, Daozhe’s lineage has further come to regard itself as the "Buddha-cave school."
Shi Tianran entered the Dharma-gate in his youth and visited Master Shitou. He personally attended to the kitchen duties for three years before finally shaving his head.
Later, he received the precepts from Vinaya Master Xi at Yue Temple. He then traveled to Daji in Jiangxi, where his responses were refined and correct;
Daji regarded him with great admiration. Subsequently, he resided at Huading Peak on Mount Tiantai for three years and paid homage to National Teacher Guishan.
During the Yuanhe era, [the Emperor] ascended Mount Longmen at Xiangshan and formed a friendship with Chan Master Funiu that transcended worldly distinctions.

Later, while at Huilin Temple, he encountered a great cold; thereupon, he burned a wooden Buddha statue to ward it off. Someone criticized him, saying, "We perform *te-p'i* (cremation) for *śarīra* (relics).
What *śarīra* could a block of wood possibly have? He replied, "If that is so, why do you reproach me? — thus it was during the Yuanhe era.
In the third year, he passed by the Tianjin Bridge at dawn and lay down across it. It happened that Zheng Gong, the Regional Commander-in-Chief (Liushi), was passing out;

he scolded him for not leaving, but the man simply looked up slowly and said, "I am no temple monk. The Regional Commander-in-Chief found this strange and subsequently offered him two sets of plain silk robes and a monthly allowance of rice and flour.
The people of Luoyang were moved and turned to him with faith. In the spring of the fifteenth year, he said, "I long for the forests and springs," and thus entered the South.
Yang Danxia built a hermitage on Mount Shan. In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Changqing era, he told his disciples, "Prepare my bath;
I am about to depart. He then donned a bamboo hat and took up his staff, entering [the chamber] with one foot hanging down; before it had even touched the ground, he passed away.

He was eighty-six years old. Liu Ke composed his stele inscription; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Zhìtōng" (Wisdom-Penetrating), and his stupa was named "Miàojiào" (Wondrous Enlightenment).
Śramaṇa Qī'ān’s surname was Lǐ, a lineage of the Tang imperial house. He deeply avoided worldly glory and ultimately kept his clan affiliation secret. While Qī'ān was still in the womb...
Her mother dreamed of the sun as an auspicious omen. Upon her birth, divine light shone down from above. When she was several years old, a strange monk came to her door;

he summoned her to see him, rubbed the crown of her head, and said, "The phoenix nest shakes with dignity; the dragon palace conceals treasures. The continuation of the ultimate task rests upon this very person."

When he reached the age of childhood, he repeatedly requested to leave the household life. His parents complied with his wish, and he subsequently relied upon Chan Master Yunzong of his native commandery.

Upon reaching the required age, he received full ordination and then went to see Vinaya Master Zhiyan of Mount Nanyue. There, he externally examined the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) and internally illuminated the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Later, hearing that Chan Master Dajue of Gonggong Mountain in Nanjiang was traveling to transform and save sentient beings, he bound his feet, shook his mendicant’s staff, and set out on one day.

He constructed it there. Da Ji was delighted by his reliance [on him] and held the treatises for him without weariness. When he passed away, Dao’an exerted all his strength to conduct the funeral rites.
Toward the end of the Yuanhe era, Dao’an was already over seventy years of age, yet he traveled to Faluo Temple in Xiaoshan, Yue.

At that time, there was one named Faxin in Haichang, a preeminent figure among the monastic community. On a piece of abandoned land adjacent to a fish-releasing pond, he began to construct a Chan residence and invited Huian to preside over it.
Students from all quarters flocked to him like deer; the flourishing of his spiritual transformation caused everyone to submit with unanimous acclaim.
Huian foresaw that Emperor Xuanzong’s hidden brilliance and monastic conduct would lead to a future assembly of the Dharma, and he prepared for this duty with sincere devotion in advance.
Hui'an said, "There will surely be extraordinary people arriving here; we must refrain from idle chatter and cease all worldly affairs, for I fear they might bring reproach upon the Buddha-dharma.

The next day, several traveling monks came to pay their respects. Hui’an silently recognized the Emperor among them and ordered the *vinaya* master to seat him in a position of high honor, treating him with a distinction far exceeding that of others.
Each time Hui’an engaged him in conversation, he perceived even more clearly the Emperor’s noble bearing. He then remarked, "This poor monk has been mistakenly surrounded by a vast assembly."

He circumambulated [the assembly], concerned that the offerings for the fast-day meal were insufficient. He approached the presiding elder and requested a written list of the offerings. The Emperor took up the brush and composed the text for him. When Hui'an read it, he was struck with awe and alarm;
he realized that the offerings for the monks had been carried away and that what he had obtained was so abundant it was almost unlike any ordinary measure.

He then said to the Emperor, "The time has come; do not linger like a snake in the mud. Having entrusted the Emperor with the future affairs of the Buddha-dharma, he departed. The Emperor was originally... [text ends].
He was the fourth son of Emperor Xianzong and the uterine younger brother of Emperor Muzong. Emperor Wuzong constantly feared and resented him, so he cast him into the palace latrines.
The eunuch Qiu Gongwu secretly provided rescue and protection, causing him to shave his head and become a monk; he then released him and allowed him to escape.

He traveled throughout the empire, experiencing every kind of hardship and peril. Upon the demise of Emperor Wuzong, Yang Gong, the Commander-in-Chief of the Left Shenche Army, exhorted the Prime Ministers and the various officials to welcome and enthrone him.
When he heard that An had already passed away, he mourned him for a long time. By imperial decree, An was posthumously titled Wukong, and the Emperor composed a poem in his memory;
a stupa was subsequently erected for him.
Shi Weiyen was surnamed Han and was a native of Jiang County. From his childhood, he was resolute and spirited; his intelligence and brilliance were far beyond his peers.

At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and received the tonsure under Chan Master Huizhao. In the eighth year of the Dali era, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Hico of Mount Heng, who said to him:
"A great man should transcend phenomena to achieve self-purification. How can you deign to concern yourself with such trivialities as minor rules of conduct?"
He then went to pay his respects to Master Shitou, where he secretly realized the Dharma of the Mind. He resided at Yaoshan.
One night, under the bright moon, he ascended the mountain peak and let out a great laugh; the sound echoed for nearly ninety *li* to the east of Linyang.

That night, everyone in Linyang heard the sound and all said it came from their neighbor to the east. The next morning, they inquired from house to house until they reached Yaoshan, where the assembly of disciples [confirmed the source].
It is said: "Last night, was it not the Master laughing atop the mountain? From that time on, his reputation spread, and the news resounded far and wide.

During the Yuanhe era, Li Ao served as the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel (*Kao-gong yuan-wai-lang*). Having been demoted due to the case of Li Jingjian, he was sent out as the Prefect of Langzhou.

While there, Li Ao came to visit Huian in leisure; he subsequently attained awakening. Furthermore, when he first met Huian, the Master held a scripture volume and did not look at him; [Li Ao] attended...
The other person informed him, "The Governor is here. Hao, being of a narrow and impatient temperament, exclaimed, "Meeting him in person does not match what I have heard of his reputation.
Yan then called out, and Hao responded with a single "Yes. Yan said, "Governor, why do you value my ears while disparaging my eyes? Hao folded his hands and apologized.
A question was asked: "What is the Way? Yǎn pointed to the sky and then to the pure water pitcher, saying: "Clouds are in the blue sky; water is in the pitcher.
At that moment, Xuāo’s dark room was suddenly illuminated and the ice of his doubts instantly melted away. He immediately composed a verse: "Refined, my physical form resembles the shape of a crane;
Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture. I came to ask about the Way, but you had no further words to say— Clouds are in the blue sky."
"Water in a jar. Furthermore, there is a verse: Having chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments, throughout the year there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.

At times I ascend directly to the peak of a solitary mountain; beneath the moon, I part the clouds and let out a laugh. Yanru entered nirvana in the second year of the Dàhé era, sitting upright with palms joined.
Shi Hengzheng, whose secular surname was Zhou, was a native of Pingyuan. Before entering the Dharma, he entered the local school as a youth and encountered Buddhist scriptures;

he became so immersed in their flavor that he could not abandon them. He went to Master Shuancheng at Yanhe Temple in his home province to receive instruction in the recitation of the sutras and the Dharma.

Once he had received full ordination, he sought out the Way on Mount Song and Mount Shao, resolving all doubts without obstruction. He then withdrew to the Three Peaks, living in carefree seclusion for some time.

He entered Mount Taiyi. As he had only recently begun to propagate his teachings, students flocked to him like ants. During the Taizhong era, Emperor Wenzong was particularly fond of oysters and clams.
One day, when a platter full of them was served as part of the imperial meal, there was one that would not open its shell even after being pried.

The Emperor, observing this anomaly, immediately burned incense and offered prayers; suddenly, it took the form of a Bodhisattva, with all the features of a Brahmanic deity perfectly complete and its appearance most majestic.
The Emperor’s affection led him to provide it with gold-dust sandalwood and to cover it with jade-cotton and brocade, bestowing it upon Xingshan Temple to be treated with ritual reverence.

He then inquired of his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this? Prime Minister Li Gongmin replied, "Your servant is not worthy to know such things, yet I do know that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue has manifested in response to the principles of the Buddhas.
I have heard that on Mount Zhongnan there is a Chan master named Hengzheng."

The Master was profoundly enlightened in the Buddha-dharma and possessed vast learning and a powerful memory. When the Emperor summoned him to inquire about the administration of the state, he replied:
"I, a poor monk, have heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is merely to inspire and awaken Your Majesty’s faith. Thus, it is said in the sūtras:

'For those who are to be saved by means of this body, one shall manifest this very body and preach the Dharma for them. " The Emperor said: "I have already seen the Bodhisattva’s body, but I have not yet heard [the Dharma]."
He preached the Dharma. Wonjeong said, "Does Your Majesty perceive this as permanent or impermanent? Is it true or not? The Emperor replied, "This is a rare and marvelous thing;
I believe it with deep conviction. Wonjeong said, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma. The Emperor’s heart was filled with joy, such as he had never experienced before.
He issued an edict to all temples throughout the land to each establish an image of Avalokiteśvara in gratitude for this extraordinary grace, and consequently, he retained Wonjeong in service.

Within the inner precincts of the monastery, he repeatedly declined to enter the mountains and was instead appointed to reside at Shengshou Temple. Upon the accession of Emperor Wuzong, he suddenly departed for Zhongnan Mountain.
When someone asked the reason for this, he replied, "I am avoiding an enemy; how could I stop? Later, he passed away in his mountain retreat at the age of eighty-seven.
His body was cremated, and forty-nine śarīra relics were collected on the fourth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Huichang era.
The Sun Enters the Stūpa.
Chuanzi Decheng’s integrity and conduct were lofty and remote; his capacity was peerless.
Having personally received the seal of mind from Yaoshan, he shared the Way with Daowu and Yunyan. After departing from Yaoshan, he said to his companions: "You gentlemen should each..."
Based on one perspective, he established the school of Yaoshan. He was by nature simple and rustic, delighting only in mountains and waters;
he took pleasure in his own disposition for diversion and possessed no specialized skills. Later, if you come across a sharp-witted presiding master at the place where I reside, [inform him].
He pointed to a man and said, "If he is capable of being refined, I shall entrust him with what I have attained throughout my life to repay the kindness of my former teacher.
He then departed and reached Huating in Xiuzhou, where he traveled by small boat, spending his days according to circumstances to receive those coming and going from all quarters.
No one knew of his lofty transcendence, so he was called the Boatman Monk. Later, when Daowu arrived at Jingkou, he encountered Jiaoshan presiding over the assembly.
A monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body? Jiaoshan replied, "The Dharma-body is formless. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-eye? Jiaoshan replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw.
Daowu could not help but let out a laugh. Jiaoshan immediately descended from his seat and inquired about the reason for his laughter.
"Regarding what I just said in response to this monk, there must have been something incorrect, which caused you, Venerable One, to laugh. I hope you will not withhold your compassion.
I replied, "Your Reverence is equally one who has appeared in the world, yet you still do not have a teacher. He asked, "In what way was it incorrect?"
Feng hoped that I would explain and refute this. I said, "There is no need to explain it. I ask that you, Master, go instead to where the Boatman Master of Huating resides.
Feng asked, "What is this man like? I replied, "This man has not a single tile above him and not a needle’s point of ground below him."
"If the Master goes, you must change your robes before departing. Baizhang then dispersed his assembly, packed his belongings, and went straight to Huating.
As soon as Chujiang saw him, he asked, "Virtuous One, in what monastery do you reside? Baizhang replied, "I do not reside in a monastery; if I were to reside, it would not be like this.
Chujiang said, "It is not like this—what is it like? Baizhang said, "It is not the Dharma Master from the past. Chujiang asked, "Where [have you been]?"
"Learned it," said Shanshan. "It is not something that can be reached by the ears or eyes. The Master said, "A single phrase that fits the mark is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.
The Master asked again, "The line hangs down a thousand feet; the intent lies in the deep pool. It is three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak?
As Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him with a pole and knocked him into the water. Just as he climbed back onto the boat, the Master spoke again:
"Way, Way. As Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him again. Shanshan attained a sudden and great enlightenment, nodding his head three times.
The Master said, "The silk line on the tip of the pole is for you to handle as you please; yet, without disturbing the clear waves, its meaning is naturally distinct.

Shanshan then asked, "As for casting the line and throwing the hook, what is your intention, Master? The Master replied, "The line hangs in the green water; whether it floats or sinks is beyond the reach of thought. Shanshan said: [End of excerpt]

The words carry the profound mystery yet leave no path; the tongue speaks, yet there is nothing spoken. The Master said, "The waves of the river have been fished through until at last the golden-scaled fish is encountered.
Shanshan covered his ears. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, you must ensure that where you hide your body, there are no traces;
and where there are no traces, do not hide your body. For twenty years, I remained at Yaoshan."

"I have clarified this matter for you. Now that you have attained it, simply go into the deep mountains; by the side of your mattock, seek out one or two others to carry on the lineage, so that it does not cease.
" Shanshan then took his leave, looking back again and again. The Master called out, "Upādhyāya! Shanshan turned his head.
The Master held up his oar and said, "You thought there was something else; it is just the overturning of the boat. Shanshan entered [the mountain].
He departed by way of water.
At that time, when Chan Master Jiufeng Daomin heard that Chan Master Shishuang Qingzhu had entered nirvana, the assembly requested the Head Seat to succeed him on the seat.
Jiufeng said, "One must clarify the late master’s meaning before one may do so. The Head Seat asked, "What meaning did the late master have? Jiufeng replied:
The former master said: "Rest, cease; go into a state of cold stillness; go for ten thousand years in a single thought; go like cold ashes or withered wood;
go like an incense burner in an ancient temple; go like a single length of white silk. [The Master] asked, "I do not ask about the rest; how is it to go like a single length of white silk?
The Abbot replied, "This merely clarifies the matter of the 'one color' side. Yuanfeng said, "So it was all along."
"I have not yet grasped the meaning of the former master's intent. Zuo said, "Do you not agree with me? Just bring some incense.
When the incense smoke breaks, if you cannot depart, then you have not grasped the former master's intent. He then burned incense; before the smoke had even faded, Zuo had already passed away.
Feng patted Zuo’s back and said, "To die while sitting or standing—this is certainly not lacking, yet it is not even a dream of the former master's intent."

Shi Jiankong, whose secular surname was Qi, was a native of Wujun. Having suffered from poverty and hardship since his youth, he devoted himself solely to his studies. At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, he traveled to Qiantang;
encountering a period of famine and scarcity there, he planned to seek food at the Tianzhu Monastery. Upon reaching the west of Gushan Monastery, he was famished.
He was deeply distressed. As he stood by the stream, he wept and chanted several verses in grief. Suddenly, a monk from India appeared, sitting by the water.
Looking into the sky, he smiled and said, "Dharma Master, you scholar: have you had enough of the flavors of your travels? The monk replied, "As for the flavors of travel—"
"That is already sufficient. Why is it that the Dharma Master’s address is so erroneous? It is because when I was not yet a monk, my name was Junfang.
The Indian monk said, "Do you not remember lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Tongde Temple? Kong replied:
"Since my birth, forty-five years have passed. I have wandered between the regions of Wu and Chu and have never set foot in Jingkou;
how then could I know the accounts of Luoyang? The monk said, "You must be consumed by the fires of hunger, leaving you no leisure to recall past events.

He then reached into his bag and produced a jujube fruit about the size of a fist, saying, "This is a product of my country. Those who eat it possess superior wisdom and recognize their transgressions."

He had departed from matters of the future; his inferior wisdom merely ceased at knowing the events of his previous life. Externally exhausted by hunger, he ate jujubes and drank from his cupped palms of spring water.
Suddenly, he let out a yawn and groan, and leaning against a stone, he fell asleep. After a short while, he awoke and remembered preaching the sutras at Tongde Temple.
It was as if it were yesterday; he shed even more tears and asked the monks, "Where is Master Zhen? They replied, "He was so single-mindedly diligent that he has not yet arrived;

he has become a monk in Shu once again. As for him now, he has severed all攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging attachments). "Where is the Venerable Shen? they asked. They replied, "His former vows have not yet been fulfilled.
"And where is Dharma Master Wu? they asked. They replied, "Do you not remember how, before the stone statue at Mount Xiangshan, he playfully made a great vow?"
"Alas! If you do not realize unexcelled bodhi, I vow that you shall surely become a valiant and noble minister. I heard yesterday that you have already attained the rank of Great General.
At that time, among the five traveling companions, only I attained liberation; only you were left to suffer from cold and hunger.
Kongri said, "For some forty years, I have had but one meal a day; for over thirty years, I have worn but a single garment."

Coarse cloth. Regarding worldly and superficial matters, one must decisively sever their root source. Who would have expected that blessings would remain incomplete, leading one to sit in hunger and cold? The monk said:

"It is because you preached heterodox views from the lion’s throne, causing those who study emptiness to harbor doubts in their hearts. The pearl of the precepts has been marred, and a trace of impurity remains.
When the sound is muddled, a clear resonance can never be achieved; when the substance is crooked, the shadow will be bent. Such is the law of karmic retribution."
"It is indeed so. Haikong asked, "What should be done about this? The monk said, "As for what must be done today, I have no plan.
However, regarding matters of future lives, I shall warn you, my son. He then reached into his alms-bowl bag and took out a mirror, both sides of which were perfectly clear and translucent.
He said to Haikong, "If you wish to know the distinction between noble and base, the span of long and short life, the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma, and the flourishing or decline of our Way—"

"You should examine this mirror once. After the monk had gazed into it for a long time, he said in thanks, "I have now clearly understood the matter of karmic retribution and the principles of prosperity and decline.
The monk took the mirror and placed it in his bag, then departed with it. After walking some ten paces, he suddenly vanished without a trace.

In the evening of that day, [Dao]kong went to Lingyin Temple to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Later, he traveled to famous mountains, further increasing his austere discipline.
Shi Hengchao’s secular surname was Feng; he was a native of Fanyang. His grandfather practiced Confucianism, and the family possessed wealth amounting to tens of millions. Chao was born...

He was intelligent and wise; at the age of fifteen, he had already mastered the Six Classics and was further adept in the *Fengsao* (the style of poetry). One day, while reading Buddhist scriptures, he attained a sudden and clear awakening.
He then sighed, saying: "Human life, with its wealth and nobility, is like a phantom or a bubble.

Only the True Vehicle can provide transport across the sea of existence. Thereupon, he entered the Zhubi Temple to leave the secular world. Day and night he applied himself to his practice, until his teacher passed away, whereupon he followed the teachings of Śākyamuni.

Regarding his funeral rites, he observed the protocols with unwavering diligence. In the third year of the Qiánhuà era of the Liáng dynasty, he resided at Mount Wǎitái and received the *mokṣa* (full) precepts.
Thereupon, he traveled afar in search of renowned masters; however, being obstructed by the two rivers, he settled instead in his home province between the regions of Wèi-bó, Bìng, and Fén.
There, he studied seven texts of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras. In the second year of the Lóngdé era, he hung up his monk’s staff at Wúdí.
Daochao said, "This place is entirely the old territory of Qi and a good neighbor to the lands of Zou and Lu.

He then settled in the northeastern corner of Kaiyuan Monastery and established a cloister there to lecture on various sutras and treatises for over twenty years. He expounded them more than thirty times each.

Among the people of Qi and Lu, those who came to seek excellence did not travel more than several hundred li; they would come to his gate to pose difficult questions. As soon as the gentlemen beheld Daochao...
Dong listened in on their discussions, consulting the *Zizhi tongjian* and other historical records while corroborating them with the scriptural traditions.

When someone questioned him regarding *hetuvidyā* (logic), he responded with a poem whose diction was fresh and its principles profound; everyone sighed in admiration and submission. At that time, the Prefect Li, who had long esteemed his lofty character, [was deeply impressed].
When he wished to submit a memorial requesting the bestowal of purple robes, Chao heard of it and was struck with alarm. He then took up his brush and composed a poem, saying:
In vain I wear these coarse brown robes, an old man; Floating in my bowl, the Way remains unfulfilled. I vow to transmit the sutras and śāstras unto death;

I shall not be stained by profit or fame in life. I weary of trees that obscure the mountain colors; I cherish the window facing the moon’s brightness. In another time, I shall follow Fan Li, With a single oar upon the clarity of the Five Lakes. —Li Junfu.
He exhorted others to persevere, wishing for them to form karmic conditions that would be firm and unshakable.
Shi Fachong’s secular surname was Mei; he was a native of Xinye in Nanyang. He left home to become a monk at the age of eight, standing out as exceptionally brilliant and refined.

His character was upright and pure, and his physical form was like jade. He delighted in simple greens and herbs, having no desire for rich delicacies. As he grew to maturity, his integrity and conduct were exemplary.

He was exceptionally diligent in his pure giving and provided great benefit; those who followed him were all supported by his provisions. He dedicated these resources toward the creation of more than three thousand scrolls of the Sūtra-piṭaka, thoroughly exhausting the depths of the Agamas and Śāstras.
At the age of twenty-five, he traveled east to Mount Song and west to Mount Wudang. Wherever he passed along the main thoroughfares, he dwelt only in quiet seclusion.
Consequently, he went to Umbrella Canopy Mountain and White Horse Spring in Xiangyang, where he built a chamber of one square zhang to serve as his dwelling.

Regarding the "Abode of the Mind": he established two *āraṇya* hermitages in the valley. Initially, when the Prince of Jin’an of the Liang dynasty came to the capital at Xiang-yong, he heard of [the Master’s] reputation and went to inquire after him.
As he was about to reach the meditation chamber, his horses and attendants inexplicably retreated; the prince returned in shame.

That night he had a bad dream. He went there once more, but the horse retreated as before. The King then purified himself through fasting and, with the utmost personal devotion, was finally able to enter and see [the deity].
Upon first arriving at the side of the temple, he saw only a valley where a fierce fire blazed intensely. After waiting for a long while, he gazed out.

Suddenly, it transformed into water. After remaining thus for a short while, the water subsided and the hall reappeared. When he inquired about these events, he learned that at that time [the Master] had entered the meditative absorption of fire and water (*tejodhātu-āpasamādhi*).
Inside the hall sat a rope bed, with a tiger on each side; the King did not dare to advance.
Daocong then pressed their heads to the ground with his hands, closed both their eyes, and summoned the King to come forward, whereupon he was finally able to approach.
Li informed [the Master] that his territory was frequently beset by tiger disasters and requested rescue. Sengcong immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In a short while, seventeen large tigers arrived; he then conferred the Three Refuges (*triśaraṇa*) upon them and commanded them not to harm the common people.

He further instructed his disciples to tie old garments around the necks of the tigers and told them that they should return there after seven days had passed. When the appointed time arrived, the King...

On that day, a vegetarian feast was prepared and the assembly gathered; the tigers also arrived. [Cōng] immediately gave them food and untied the cloth [bound around their necks), whereupon they ceased to cause harm.
That day, as the King approached the White Horse Spring (*Baimaquan*), there was a white tortoise within it. It came to Cōng’s hand to take food, and said to the King: "This is the male dragon.
Again, as he approached the Spirit Spring (*Lingquan*), there was a five-colored carp. It likewise came to his hand to eat, saying: "This is the female dragon. The King—

Together with his subordinates, he praised and commended this deed. After making these great offerings, he was returning when a band of some dozens of criminals approached at night intending to plunder the donated goods.
They encountered a tiger that roared and blocked their path;

furthermore, they saw a Great Being standing by a meditation hall, beside which stood a pine tree reaching only to his knees, holding a vajra-pestle as if to provide protection. Thereupon, he reported the matter.
He reported this to the throne. By imperial decree, Xu Chi was ordered to build Lingquan Monastery at his place of residence.

Sengcong resided in the meditation hall, where white deer and white sparrows would tame themselves to his presence, settling there to dwell. In all his movements and travels, he prioritized compassion and salvation.

Once, he unexpectedly encountered a butcher driving more than a hundred pigs. Sengcong called out three times, "Liberation! Śūraṅgama! and the pigs subsequently broke their ropes and fled. The butchers...

He became greatly enraged and placed his hands upon the objects, yet they remained entirely motionless. He then returned to acknowledge his transgression and repent for his sins, thereby severing his karmic ties to killing.
Furthermore, at a place where fishermen were casting nets in the Han River, he repeated the previous three requests;

the nets could not be pulled in, and only then did the fisherman turn his heart toward the Dharma, returning with the nets empty. Moreover, when Jingzhou suffered from a severe drought, a monk was sent from Changsha Temple to Huicong’s location to request rain.

When the envoys returned, there was a great downpour, and all the ponds and reservoirs were filled to the brim. The High Ancestor sent the Prince of Luling to entreat him to descend to the capital, but he remained firm and refused.
Later, he arrived at Mount Lu; the Prince of Weiwang, the General of the Flying Cavalry, followed him there to receive the precepts and urged him to return to the palace.

However, his enlightened will was set upon emptiness and stillness, so he secretly traveled upstream to the west and went into seclusion at Mount Shen in the Jing region. When the Prince of Xiangdong heard of this, he hurriedly set out for him.
At the mountain gate, he performed the rites of Master Xiang with full prostration. He repeatedly invited [Sengshou] to descend to the capital, but the latter firmly declined and would not permit it.

When [Sengshou] traveled up to Shu, he received the *śaraṇagamana* (refuge) precepts from him. During the final years of Emperor Xuan’s reign, he likewise maintained his former reverence. Whenever Sengcong entered the dharma hall, his tears would flow and he would gaze upward with devotion.

Thereupon, Samantabhadra bestowed a prophecy upon him; celestial flowers and extraordinary fragrances appeared, and music resonated mysteriously. This was in the fifth year of the Dading era of the Liang dynasty.
In the ninth month, he passed away without illness.

Shi Zhenbian was a native of Zhongshan. From his youth, he knew how to transcend the mundane; as he grew older, he vowed to cultivate his studies. In his leisure time, he would prick his own blood to transcribe the sutras.
Furthermore, he drew images of Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, and others using his own blood as ink.

Once, while resting from his practice of the Way, two celestial maidens came to disturb and vex him. He made a solemn vow, saying, "My heart is not of stone," and he repelled them with divine mantras.
From this point on, his Way prevailed and Māra left no trace. Bearing his book-cases upon his back, he traveled to the city of Taiyuan to study.

At that time, the territory of the Wang family of Zhongshan bordered that of the Li family of Later Tang; fearing that he might be a spy sent to incite internal strife, they [restricted him] within the walls of the city of Bingzhou.
Foreign monks were not permitted [to stay], so Daoben was driven out because of this. He consequently stayed overnight among ancient tombs in the wilds.

It happened that Emperor Wu was on a hunting excursion, and the tombs were within the hunting grounds. Daoben did not know this at all; he was just about to enter the city to attend a lecture when he saw banners, standards, and cavalrymen, whereupon he shrank his body and crawled back into a hollow.
Emperor Wu became suspicious and ordered him to be seized and brought before him. When questioned as to the reason, the truth was thus verified.
Within the tomb, he spread out a grass mat and set up a desk and inkstone; he then arranged his commentaries and sub-commentaries in order.

He was subsequently summoned to the palace to receive offerings. At that time, Empress Dowager Cao held him in profound esteem. He petitioned the Empress Dowager, saying: "I have always cherished the study of the Dharma.
Having resided in the royal palace for so long, I find it as unpleasant as being bound by shackles. Emperor Wu granted him his freedom, whereby he was able to complete his scholarly work.
Shi Miaopu, whose style name was Xingkong, was a native of Hanzhou. Having long relied upon Huanglong Sixin, he received the seal of the mind in secret.

His character and integrity were lofty and ancient, and his spirit was vast and far-reaching. Out of admiration for the legacy of Chuanzi, he traveled to Xiushui and built a hermitage in the wilds of Qinglong.
He possessed no possessions other than what was necessary; he merely played the iron flute to amuse himself. He delighted in composing poetry and once wrote a mountain verse:
A verse on dwelling [in seclusion] says: "When mind and dharmas are both forgotten, one is still separated by delusion; When form and dust are non-dual, a trace of dust still remains.

The hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more; I know not who is the person dwelling in the hermitage. A verse shown to the assembly says: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city:
By day, guard against the six thieves; by night, remain alert. If the commander-in-chief of the central army can carry out his orders, He need not move a blade of grass or a weapon."
During the Taiping era of the Song dynasty, at the beginning of the Jianyan period, the rebel Xu Ming passed through Wuzhen on his way to commit widespread slaughter.
The people were terrified and fled. Fahu普 heard of this and sighed, saying, "The sentient beings are mired in suffering; why should I not rescue them? Thereupon, he took up his staff and set out.

He went straight to where the bandits were. When the bandits saw him, they found him extraordinary and suspicious that he must be a deceiver. They inquired about his place of origin, and he replied, "I am a practitioner of meditation.
When they asked where he was going, he said, "To Miyin Temple. The bandits grew angry and intended to execute him.
Baopu said, "If you want my head, take it; why be so angry? My death is certain; I only wish to have one meal as a parting gift. The bandits...
He offered meat. Pu made offerings to the Buddha according to the usual ritual and said, "Who should I commission to compose a text for this sacrifice?

The thief laughed but did not answer. Pu searched for paper and brush and wrote in large characters: "Alas, O Spirit! That you have caused me to undergo the toil of life is the fault of the Great Mass (the Earth).
That you have employed me with the burden of longevity is the error of Yin and Yang. That you have deprived me of wealth through poverty is the irregularity of the Five Elements."

To constrain me with the limitations of life is for the days and times to be inauspicious. Alas! How profound! Fortunately, there is the Way that transcends the mundane, which awakens my nature and its wondrous mind.
As for this wondrous mind, with whom could it share its neighbor? Above, it accords with the true transformation of all Buddhas;
below, it merges with the ignorance of ordinary beings. Not a speck of dust stirs; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. How wondrous indeed!
How marvelous! The sun and moon are not sufficient to serve as its illumination; heaven and earth are not sufficient to serve as its magnitude.

Magnificent and expansive, it is without obstruction or hindrance. For over sixty years, it has blended with the light and mingled with the mundane; for forty-two years since ordination, it has wandered at ease and in freedom.
It rejoices upon meeting people, yet does not bow before the Buddha. How joyful! How joyful! What a pity for this young man.
"His refined elegance is so radiant! He returns with ease, entrusting himself to the spring breeze. His body is like empty space; it shall never perish. [He added,] "Enjoy the offering!

Thereupon, he took up his chopsticks and ate heartily. The bandits laughed loudly. When he had finished eating, he said, "Since we have encountered this era of calamity and chaos, I am a man of spirited joy.
Now is precisely the time to act; let me be cut in two with one stroke! He then raised a great shout.

"Chop! Chop! The bandits were struck with awe and wonder; they bowed their heads in apology for their transgression and ordered his guards to escort him out. Consequently, among the people’s dwellings, none suffered harm, whether young or old.
A monk asked, "Since you have already seen the Buddha, why did you not prostrate? Foyan Pu slapped him and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand.

Foyan slapped him again and said, "There are no two masters in one house. In the winter of the Shaoxing era, he personally constructed a large basin, bored a hole in it, and sealed it shut. He practiced... [text ends].
In that letter, he sent word to Chan Master Chih of Xuedou, saying: "I shall undergo a water burial. When Chih arrived in the year Renxu, Fuping was still alive.
Chih then composed a verse in jest, saying: "Alas, you old Xingkong! You insist on feeding the fish and turtles. Why do you not simply depart as you wish, instead of merely talking to people?
Fuping laughed and said: "I waited for my brother to provide witness. He then announced this far and near until the assembly had gathered.

He universally demonstrated the essentials of the Dharma by speaking these verses: "To die while sitting or standing is not as good as water burial. First, it saves the need for firewood; second, it avoids the excavation of a grave.
To cast off the hands and depart immediately is truly swift and unimpeded. Who knows this melody? It is the Boatman Monk.
His lofty style is difficult to emulate after a thousand years; few can sing this one song of the fisherman. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged within the basin and blew into his mouth.
Taking up his iron flute, he followed the tide downstream. The multitude all followed him to the seashore. He removed the plugs everywhere and bailed out the swirling water;
the crowd pressed forward to watch, yet not a single drop entered. Thereupon, he rode the current and came to a halt, singing: "For over sixty years I have returned to my native land;
The place where my traces vanish is wondrous beyond measure. The true wind is sent everywhere to those who understand; I cross the iron flute, blowing it freely."
The assembly dispersed; as people gazed after him until their vision failed, they still heard the sound of the flute wailing amidst the vast, desolate expanse.

From afar, they saw him cast his flute into the air and vanish. The multitude wailed and wept, vying with one another to paint images of him. Three days later, he was seen sitting cross-legged upon the sand as if alive.
Monastics and laypeople welcomed him back and kept him for five days before performing cremation. The *śarīra* relics were as large as beans.
Two cranes circled in the air; only when the fire was extinguished did they depart. He was enshrined at Qinglong Hermitage.
Shi Liaoxing, styled Dalin, was the son of the Wu clan. His surname was derived from the posthumous title of Song Wugong.

From his youth, he was fond of learning, possessing a natural brilliance and wisdom bestowed by Heaven. Initially, he relied upon Master An to shave his head and receive the full precepts, subsequently attending various lectures.
Xī devoted himself to the profound study of the Tripiṭaka. Later, he encountered National Teacher Zhēnjué, who enlightened his mind.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively through Guānshǎn, Héluò, and Xiānghàn, visiting various venerable masters. Among them were Bólíntán, Huái of Guānfǔ, and Cí of Nányáng;

all of these gentlemen were renowned at the time for their learning in the tradition of Xuánzàng (Xiànxíu). Xìng visited each of their doors to receive their instructions. Upon his return, he once again...

From Zhenguang to Mount Wutai, not long after, Zhenguang passed away. He then traveled north to Yan and Ji, concealing his traces beneath the gates of Wei and wandering leisurely through the lands of the rivers and seas.
He seemed as if he had forgotten the world. During the reign of Emperor Chengzong, he was summoned to reside at Wanningsi, where his reputation resounded both within and without the court.
During the Zhida era, the Empress Dowager founded Puning Temple on Mount Tai and invited him there.
He remained as the first generation of abbots; his footsteps never entered the city walls, nor did he pay court to the powerful and influential.
Some people grew envious of him. Xingwen once said: "I am originally but a solitary bhikṣu who was graced by the Son of Heaven with the appointment to this great monastery.

I do nothing but strive tirelessly day and night to propagate the Dharma, finding no leisure to repay the bounty of the state. Beyond this, what else could I seek? Even though I possess storehouses and granaries..."
Such disparaging words are like blue flies alighting upon a thorny hedge. Considering that my destiny has not been met and my Way cannot be practiced, I shall put on my sandals and depart;
where could I not go? At that time, during the Yuan dynasty, Western monks were held in high honor and favor, and their followers were exceedingly numerous.
When they went out or entered [the palace], their mounted retinues were as grand as those of princes and dukes. Among the renowned and virtuous masters of the world...

There was no one who did not offer him formal courtesy, yet the Master merely performed a long bow (*changyi*) in return. He looked at the assembly and said, "I have heard that a gentleman loves others with propriety (*li*).
How could I bend my will and bring humiliation upon myself? If I were to yield to them, it would be either flattery or sycophancy."
Those who understood him held his principles in high esteem. On the third day of the ninth month of the first year of the Zhizhi era, he entered nirvana.
He was interred in a grove of bamboo, and his posthumous title was bestowed as Hongjiao (Great Teacher).
Shi Datong, courtesy name Yiyun, was the son of Wang Youqiao of the Wang family from Shangyu in Yue. His father was a friend of [the Master]. His mother was of the Chen clan.

When she had been pregnant for ten months, his father was sitting in the hall during the day when he suddenly saw a strange monk with bushy eyebrows enter, shaking his mendicant’s staff. The father rose and bowed, asking, "Where have you come from, O Monk?
The monk replied, "From Mount Kunlun," and then pushed open the door and hurried inside. His father pursued him in haste and heard the sound of a child in the room.
At the sound of his weeping, his father said with a smile, "Is it not that my son is one who has come again? His mother sighed and said, "This child possesses the seed of *prajñā*.

She ordered him to enter Chongsheng Temple in Kuaiji to have his hair shaved. Hearing that Dharma Master Chundu was lecturing on the essential tenets of the Qingliang school, he went to rely upon him and mastered all of his transmissions.
He further visited the Venerable Gaohuai Zhao and refined his understanding of the Contemplation of the Four Dharmadhātus. Consequently—
Chuntang moved his residence to Baolin Temple and said to the Master, "Your studies are both refined and extensive; yet I fear you may allow your mind to stagnate in coarse attachments.
Merely increasing your erudition binds you to intellectual views, which is truly not the foundation for seeing one's nature.

You should retreat into seclusion to cultivate yourself and wash away these impediments. He then sent him out to Qiantang to pay his respects to the Chan Master Huiji Xi, who was at that time brandishing a fly-whisk.
In an instant, the Master’s long-standing habits of perception and learning were all swept away; only a solitary clarity remained, shining steadily within him.
He continued in this state for six years, during which time Huìjī deeply admired his resolve.

Hearing that the Dharma path was flourishing at Tiānmù Zhōngfēng, he went there to study with the intention of remaining there for the rest of his life. One day, Zhōngfēng summoned him and exhorted him, saying: "Worthy one,"
"One school has become increasingly distant and its teachings increasingly faint. Your capacity is sufficient to restore it; do not let yourself linger here for long.

He specially wrote a verse, read it before the image of Qingliang, and entrusted it to him to send him on his way. The Master was greatly pleased and said, "Only now do I understand that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally rooted in the one mind.
I did not know who was practicing Chan and who was teaching the Dharma. He returned to Baolin Temple and once again served [his teacher].
Chungu then informed Zhongfeng of his intention. Chungu immediately ordered him to share the seat and lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

At that time, the Song officials Xu Tianyou and Wang Yijian jointly honored and promoted him, so that his reputation shone brightly. Prefect Fan, taking pity on Chungu’s advanced age, wished to encourage him to yield the seat;
he thus prepared a vegetarian feast (*īpupu*) and spoke personally with the Master. The Master responded with resolute determination.
Rong said, "That which is most precious in the Way lies in the distinction between teacher and disciple. This clarity can serve as an instruction for future students.

If one were to take advantage of his old age to usurp his position, how could that be considered human conduct? Your Excellency surely loves me, yet you cause me to fall into a breach of name and principle;
this truly causes me pain. Fan unconsciously rose from his seat and apologized, saying, "My teacher is indeed..."
He was no ordinary man; how could he be known by me? At the beginning of the Yanyou era, he went forth to preside over Jingtu Temple in Xiaoshan, and subsequently moved to Jingde.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Dongta in Jiahe, which was later renamed Baolin.

Thereupon, following the precedent of the Caotang hermitage in Zhongnan, he cleared a secluded dwelling and summoned men of talent. Thus, among the scholars of the realm, there were none who did not carry their staffs and travel on foot to seek him out.

[He] gathered [offerings] beneath his sandals. At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he was granted the title "Buddha-mind, Compassionate Aid, Wondrous Eloquence" (Fǔxīn Cíjì Miàobiàn) along with a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe.
When the Yuan official Taibuhua governed Yue and suffered from a severe drought, he earnestly requested the Master to offer prayers.

The Master burned incense from his own arm beneath the Xuandu Pagoda, and rain immediately poured down in great torrents. Upon the ascension of the Great Emperor Taizu to the throne, he established the *wu-zhe* (unrestricted) assembly.

A great assembly was held at Mount Zhong, where the Master was summoned to have an audience in the Wulou Hall. At that time, the Master was eighty years old; he was exempted from prostrating and kneeling.

On the following day, he was granted a banquet within the imperial palace. Upon the conclusion of these affairs, he was presented with several ingots of white gold from the Inner Treasury, along with various precious objects, to honor his departure.
The Master upheld the Vinaya with great strictness; he possessed nothing beyond a single alms bowl, save for some five thousand scrolls of books and historical records.
In the twelfth month of the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. On the tenth day of the spring of the following year, he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
He took leave of the assembly and returned to his quarters. Sitting upright, he passed away. His secular age was eighty-two, and his years of monastic seniority were sixty-five.

After his cremation, many extraordinary signs were observed, and a stupa was erected at Zhushan. Among his writings were the *Tianzhu Gao* and the *Baolin Leibian*, each consisting of several volumes.
Shi Huiri was known as Dongming. He was the son of the Jia family of Tiantai and a descendant of Jia Sidao, the Chancellor of the Song dynasty.

While Jia Sidao was under sentence of exile, Shi Huiri was still young; he resolved to seek ordination and relied upon Master Pingshan of Guangyan Temple in the county to shave his head and receive full precepts.
At the age of twenty-two, he heard Master Boziting lecture on the Tiantai teachings at Chicheng.

The Master hurried down from his seat. Before long, [the boy] was able to grasp the great meaning. His son, Ting, sighed and said, "Casting a ball down a steep slope is not sufficient to illustrate the swiftness of his spiritual faculty.
Will my Way rely on you to flourish greatly? One day, while dozing, he had a vivid vision of bamboo lying across the ground;
upon the bamboo, there was white congee, glistening brightly. The Master lay on the ground and ate it. Upon waking, he found it was real.
Yanzi said to Ting: "Ting, let me explain this for you. 'Zhú' (bamboo) and 'zhōu' (congee) share the same pronunciation. Thus, you may eat while remaining on the ground.
It seems your karmic connection lies with Upper and Lower Tiantai. Thereupon, he crossed the Qiantang River and visited Master Jing of Zhuyu at Upper Tiantai.
Jing appointed him to the Guest Office and charged him with overseeing the monastic registers. When Zhuyu passed away, Master Cheng of Zantang succeeded him.
Regarding his seating arrangement: the Chief Preceptor resided in the Rear Hall. After more than a year, he went to preside over Shengshui on Mount Wu.

In the fourth year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he took up residence at Jianfu Temple. After three years had passed, Tianzhu was ravaged by fire. The Yuan official Gao Nalun requested the Master to rebuild it;

when the temple buildings were completed, Wang Min composed a commemorative record for them. In the fourth year [of the following cycle], he moved to Upper Tianzhu. The Master, knowing that his karmic conditions were still present, worked tirelessly day and night.
He was indolent. Generally, whatever was prescribed within the monastery, he would perform it with single-minded diligence.

When Emperor Shun of the Yuan dynasty heard of this, he specially bestowed upon him the title "Compassionate Light, Wondrous Response, Universal Salvation" (*Ciguāng Miàoyìng Pǔjì*) and sent him a golden-embroidered robe as a token of summons.

In the sixteenth year, he withdrew into seclusion among the crags and gorges of Kuaiji, where no one recognized him. The Yuan Chancellor Daśi Temür dispatched messengers to search for him and found him; [the Chancellor] exerted great effort...

He was requested to return to the mountain. He resided at Upper Zhu for twenty-five years in total. Upon reaching the Ming Dynasty, in the second year of Taizu Hongwu, he was summoned by imperial decree to the Buddhist assembly at Mount Jiangshan;
the Ministry of Rites was ordered to provide him with meals. The following day, he was summoned for an audience in the Fengtian Hall.

The hundred officials assembled; the monks followed one after another like a string of fish. Only the Master was of the highest seniority (*vassa*); with his ruddy complexion and white eyebrows, he took his place at the head of the ranks.

The Emperor personally questioned him regarding the Way of delivering those submerged in the darkness of ignorance. The Master presented a comprehensive exposition that accorded with the Emperor’s wishes. Emperor Taizu turned to the assembly of monks and said:
"Lately, those who study Buddhism have merely eaten their fill and lived in leisure, wasting their years. As for the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*..."
The *Gāthā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is a fundamental scripture for the essential practice of gathering the mind; why not investigate its meaning thoroughly?

Should there be points that remain unclear, one should consult the Dharma Master Bai-mei. Thereafter, whenever he was summoned for an audience, Taizu addressed him simply as "Bai-mei" and did not call him by his personal name.
He once partook of a meal in the imperial palace together with the Dharma Master Tong of Bie-feng, the Chan Master Jin-bi-feng, and others.
He subsequently memorialized the throne regarding Waguan Temple. The Sui Emperor, who was well-acquainted with the Master, decreed that the site where Śramaṇa Fahua had resided must not be abandoned.

The Taizu ordered that a separate monastery be constructed at Tianjie Temple to preserve those traces, and issued an edict for the Master to be the founding patriarch (*kaishan*) and preach the Dharma there.

In the first month of spring in the fifth year, he again established a Great Water-Land Assembly (*shuilu daizhai*) on Mount Zhong, commanding the Master to expound the Vinaya precepts. The Taizu personally [attended].

He led a hundred officials to attend his lectures. When the affairs were concluded, he returned to Shangzhu (Upper Bamboo) Monastery to resign from his administrative duties. There, he daily practiced the Amitābha Repentance to perfect his pure karma.
In the seventh month of the autumn of the twelfth year, one night he dreamed of a blue lotus flower growing in a square pond, its fragrance overwhelming the senses.
Upon waking, he told the assembly: "The auspicious sign of my rebirth in the Pure Land has appeared. Four days later, he sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away in silence with his palms joined. His worldly age was eighty-nine, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was seventy-three.
Ten days later, his entire remains were enshrined in the Miaoying Stūpa Courtyard on the western peak of the monastery.
Shi Ying was able to falsely claim the surname Yang; he was in fact Prince Jianwen, the eldest son of the Heir Apparent Yiwen and the legitimate grandson of Taizu.
He was enfeoffed as the Imperial Grandson (Huangtaisun) and his name was Yunwen. At birth, the crown of his head was somewhat tilted, whereupon Taizu stroked him and said, "A half-moon child.

Later, when he studied, he proved to be exceptionally intelligent. One night, while the Heir Apparent Yiwen was with him... [the attendant]... Taizu... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the extant portion.)
The Patriarch commanded them to compose poems on the new moon. The Crown Prince recited: "Yesterday at Yanling, the fishing hook was lost;
Who has now placed it atop the azure clouds? Though its round form is not yet fully attained, Its clear light nonetheless pervades the nine continents.
The Grandson recited: "Who has taken these jade-like fingernails And scratched through the scars of heaven? Its reflection falls upon rivers and lakes; Even the dragons dare not [stir]."

[The Emperor] swallowed it. When Taizu read this, he was displeased; for the characters were neither complete nor round, and their reflections falling upon rivers and lakes were both inauspicious omens.

In the thirty-first year of the Hongwu era, as Taizu’s condition grew critical, he entrusted him with a small casket, its seal and lock extremely tight, instructing him not to open it except in times of urgent distress.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month of that year, he ascended the throne at the age of twenty-three. Ming.
In the year [1399], the reign title was changed to Jianwen. Fang Xiaoru was summoned and appointed as a Palace Attendant (Shijiang) in the Hanlin Academy and a member of the Wenyuan Pavilion.
He lectured daily on the *Rites of the Zhou Officialdom* (*Zhouguan Li*) and revised the old regulations established by the Taizu. Consequently, many of the princes became increasingly insolent.
Thereupon, the Court Attendant and Grand Master of Ceremonies Huang Zicheng and the Minister of War Qi Tai proposed a plan to curtail the power of the princes.
Regarding this strategic maneuver, the plotter first turned toward Yan. He commanded Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhang Bing and Commander-in-Chief Xie Gui to observe the movements of the Prince of Yan.

Subsequently, they pressured the Prince to raise the "Jingnan" army to campaign southward against Huang Qi. On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of Jianwen, the gates of Jinchuan were breached.
The Emperor set fire to the palace and burned it down; opening the late Emperor Taizu’s sealed casket to examine its contents, he found Yang Ying...
Taking his ordination certificate, a razor, and a black cassock, he then shaved his hair and departed from the Imperial Canal to wander the four quarters.
Starting from Huxiang, he entered Shu and Yunnan, then returned to Min, and proceeded into Guangxi, arriving at Shoufu Temple on the south gate of Hengzhou.

After fifteen years had passed, he ascended the seat to expound the Dharma; those who returned to him were very numerous, and wherever he went, he established great assemblies for the Dharma, such that people did not realize he was the Emperor.
He traveled again to Nanjing and stayed in a humble temple, where monastics gathered like clouds;

the Master provided teachings according to their needs, and the entire assembly was filled with joy. After a long time, he arrived at Sien Prefecture and stood by the roadside, just as the Prefectural Governor was coming out.
His attendants rebuked him, but the Master said, "I am Emperor Jianwen. Having traveled from Yunnan through Fujian to this place, I am now old.
I wish to have my remains sent back to the imperial capital. When the Imperial Intendant heard of this, he reported it to the court, who bestowed upon him the title "Old Buddha."

He ordered a courier to escort him back to the capital. Upon arrival, he composed a poem, saying: Forty autumns have passed in exile upon rivers and lakes; Returning home, I find snow already filling my hair.
Heaven and earth harbor grievances, yet where is my home? The Yangtze and Han rivers are heartless, their waters flowing on alone.

Cloud-shadows darken within the Changle Palace; Rain-sounds bring sorrow to the Zhaoyang Hall. The new rushes and slender willows turn green year after year, But the wild... (Note: The final line of the provided text fragment appears incomplete.)
The old man choked back his sobs and wept without ceasing. Upon arriving at the capital, the court had not yet ascertained whether the report was true or false;

since the eunuch Wu Liang had once served as an attendant at the imperial meals, they sent him to investigate. As soon as the Master saw Liang, he called out, "Are you not Wu Liang? Liang replied, "I am not.
The Master said, "In the past, when I was in the private audience hall, I dropped a piece of meat on the ground. You prostrated yourself on the floor and licked it up."

"How could I have forgotten this? Liang prostrated himself and wailed with great grief. He subsequently brought [the relics] into the Western Palace for veneration, where they passed away within the palace.
Shi Daguan was the son of Shen of Jigu. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and traveled to various regions. There, he heard the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse, which reached—
To sever delusive thoughts is to increase one’s illness; to pursue True Suchness (Tathatā) is likewise a deviation—a great doubt.
One day during a meal, he suddenly attained awakening and said: "Had I been under the seat of Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me; what need was there for 'how' and 'what'?
While traveling through the capital, Emperor Shenzong personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his perspiration soaking the paper.

Suspecting that the case might require further investigation, the Emperor sent his close attendants to question the Master. The Master presented this verse: "A single drop of the Imperial sweat serves as a bridge for ten thousand generations;
from this point on, the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury shall radiate its light. The Emperor was greatly pleased. In the autumn of the Gui-mao year, a seditious book suddenly surfaced.
When the Emperor saw the memorial, he felt great pity for him; yet the law could not spare him. Consequently, he was arrested and subjected to interrogation.
At that time, his countenance remained composed, and he did not yield even unto death. On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he entered prison. The judicial authorities sentenced him to death.

The Master spoke a verse, saying: "A single laugh has long had its own cause; Who would have known that the Great Mass of Earth cannot tolerate a speck of dust? Henceforth, I shall gather up my mother..."
He was born with feet already formed. When the iron stake flower blossomed, he did not wait for spring. Having finished his bath, he instructed his attendant, saying, "I am going now.

Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors of Jiangnan. He spoke a verse and passed away while sitting upright. (He visited Mount Wutai and brought back woodblocks for the Tripitaka over many years to be re-carved at Jingshan.
He then sent the printed volumes to Lengyan Temple for circulation; this was truly a monumental achievement.)
Shi Hanshan Deqing was the son of the Cai family of Quanjiao, Jinling. His mother conceived him after experiencing a miraculous dream.
At the age of twelve, he received the tonsure from Master Xilin at Baoguan Temple in Jingzhou. At nineteen, he received full ordination.

While listening to lectures on the "Ten Mysterious Gates" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained realization at the point concerning the "Ever-Abiding Sea-Seal Array. He subsequently traveled to various regions and became a close friend of Miaofeng.

When Biànróng first went to visit [Huineng], he requested instruction. Huineng received him by gazing directly at him in silence. Biànróng subsequently read Sengzhào’s *Treatise on the Emptiness of the Mind* (*Zhàolùn*).
Upon reaching the passage concerning the Brahmin who left home and returned with white hair, a neighbor saw him and said, "Is that man from before still here?

Zhào replied, "I am the same person as before, yet I am not the person of before. At this, he suddenly attained awakening and exclaimed, "Today I have finally realized that my nostrils point downward!"
At that time, Miaofeng saw this and said with joy, "What have you obtained? The Master replied, "Last night two iron oxen fought and entered the water;
to this day there has been no news. Miaofeng laughed and said, "I am glad you now have the capital for staying in the mountains."

He also visited Xixian (Xiaoyan). Xixian asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the South. Xixian asked, "Do you remember the path by which you came? He replied, "Once passed, it is simply over.
Xixian said, "You, however, have a clear understanding of where you have come from. The Master then prostrated himself. He resided at Laoshan on the East Sea, where his reputation was most eminent.
Empress Dowager Li treated him with exceptional courtesy and honor. Later, he encountered [the persecution of] the Huichang era.

Falsely slandered, he submitted a memorial to Emperor Shenzong through a Daoist official. Many of the ministers and high officials in the court deeply regretted this, yet the Master subsequently received an imperial decree for interrogation.
On charges of privately founding a temple, he was sentenced to military exile in Leizhou. Upon reaching Shaoyang, he paid homage to the Patriarch, composing a verse which said:
"The drop of water at Caoxi is from the Spirit Source; It flows into the vast ocean where waves strike the heavens. How many..."

Fish and dragons vied with one another in their transformations, yet a single stream at the source remained cool and clear. Eleven years later, in the year Bingwu, the Emperor’s eldest grandson was born;

by imperial grace, [the Master] was pardoned from military service and remained at Caoxi. He traveled back and forth between Caoxi and Duanzhou for nine years before finally returning to his monastic robes.
In the winter of the Bingchen year, he crossed to Shuangjing in Jiangyou to serve as the torch-bearer for Master Da; monks gathered there in dense crowds.
The mountain valleys were stirred with clamor at this. Later, he arrived at Mount Kuang. The Prefect of Shaozhou earnestly requested that he reside at Caoxi.
The Master said, "Caoxi is where I wished to repair and restore in the past. He then set out immediately with his staff, crossing the ridges and chanting:
"A single glance at the five clouds leads into Nan'an; ten thousand folds and a thousand bends through the Sixty-six Rapids. Walking until the water ends and the mountains..."
"At the end of all things, one views countless plum blossoms atop the ridges. The following year, in the *guihai* (10th) year, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:

"My karmic conditions conflict with the times; where shall my transformation be entrusted? Having completed the affairs of this one period, I shall return. He requested a bath, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Nanhua Temple in Shaozhou, two li south on Tianzi Hill. [They] welcomed him back to Kuang...
He remained on the mountain for over twenty years. Because the ground was damp, insects and ants had half-eaten away his meditation niche. He requested to return to Caoxi;
along the way, his disciples peered through a crack in the niche and saw that the Master’s features were as if he were still alive, with his hair and nails having grown long.
They lacquered his body with gold, built a temple to enshrine him, and called him the "Flesh Patriarch."
Shi Xueqiao Yuanxin was the son of the Zhu family of Yinqian County. He left home at the age of twenty-nine and traveled as a wandering monk (*yújiǎo*) to places where no one else had been.
Later, he visited Master Miaozhen on Mount Qinwang. The Master cited the karmic occasion regarding a "mind-reading monk" (*tāxīn sēng*):
A monk went to visit him and asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from India. The mind-reader said, "I hear there are three Indias; from which one have you come?"
"From where does that one come? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! At this, the Master’s doubts were suddenly resolved.

The following day, he took up his staff and went to Shitou, where he raised it high and said, "From where does that one come? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Suddenly, his past and future limits were severed. He returned to Tiantai;
