looking up, he saw the three characters for "Ancient Yunmen" and attained great enlightenment. On the road, he composed a verse, which begins: "Once ascending to heaven..."
The mountain clouds deepen further; the heels have cut through the shoelaces. Of the five hundred bhikṣus, not a trace remains. When you see him, you will break your sinews.
Consequently, he entered Shuangji to clear away the weeds. Subsequently, he visited Yunqi and Longchi. On the day he appeared in the world [as a master],...
He offered incense to Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen Yan. Later, when he opened the hall at Dongta, he also made offerings to Longchi.

When he fell ill, he wrote a verse, saying: "Little children! On the road of birth and death, one must be carefree. Under the bright moon and frosty dawn, let us drink a cup of tea and depart while sitting.
He was enshrined with his entire body in a stupa at Yunmen.
Chan Master Wanyu said: "Body and mind are as one; there is nothing else beyond them. Whether in the human realm or the heavens, they are fundamentally not bound by anything.
This very thing is not some other thing; north, south, east, and west do not differ by so much as a hair’s breadth. Since time immemorial, the thousand sages have shared this same single pulse.
If you laboriously pursue it outwardly, you may run until the year of the donkey and yet fear you will never find rest. Turn the light back and reflect within."
There are not many such sons. Huangbo’s staff-head has already leaked the secret. One who knows the sound must be one of these people;
if you are not a knower of the sound, do not wag your tongue. Deshan would strike as soon as one entered the gate; Linji would shout as soon as one entered the gate.

They cut off the rotten vines of all quarters and pointed out the person within as lively and alert. It is valued that one should accept it directly right here and now. The Buddhas and Patriarchs—straightforwardly!
This teaching is but a speck of dust in the eye. As for that single phrase which directly points to one's own fundamental portion—how would you say it?
"At midnight, azure clouds shroud the ancient hall; at daybreak, the golden sun bursts forth from the seashore."
Shi Linye, surnamed Cai, was a native of Changle. From birth, he abstained from meat. He followed the two uncles Dao Ran and Ben Ran of Jinzhong Temple in his home district into the monastic life.
With his aspirations set upon the Buddhist scriptures, he traveled from Shu to Jiangnan to enter lecture halls.
In the *dingmao* year of the Great Ming Tianqi era, he settled at Danghu, where he met with figures such as Mao Yu at the residence of Dezang to discuss the *Lengyan jing*.

Yan then remained in seclusion behind closed doors to read the Tripitaka. It happened that he was returning the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Miyun; as he opened the volume, he reached the verse on practicing Chan:
"Before the single thought has arisen, try to look at its form. Suddenly, a fierce state of doubt arose within him, such that he forgot both sleep and food.
In the spring of the Gengwu year, when the Elder Master Miyun visited Danghu, he sent a gatekeeper to deliver a message and offer his instructions.
He said, "Tell him not to engage in false conceptualization in Guanzhong. This further increased his doubt; before he knew it, he lost his footing and fell from the tower.

Like waking from a dream, he suddenly realized the principle of the state prior to the arising of a single thought. He then broke through the barrier and went to Suzhou, where he met Master Mi at Qingliang Hermitage. He applied himself with great effort to investigation.
At that time, the Elder cited the story of the World-Honored One’s first birth, pointing and saying: "At this moment, I am the Buddha. He immediately attained realization.

The Master pointed toward the ground and said, "You people, what kind of bowl do you still intend to seek from this old monk? He then dragged his staff and struck everyone down at once, dispersing them.

From that moment on, he was completely liberated and deeply penetrated the essential meaning of the blows and shouts. In the winter of the Yihai year, within the Huang Gong Garden at Suli, he transmitted the whisk to him.
Shi Tongcheng, whose secular surname was Zhu of Jinhua, became a monk at the age of twenty-six under Tianzhen.
He received full ordination from Yunmen. Upon reading the *Sixth Patriarch’s* koan regarding "not thinking of good," he attained realization.

He traveled extensively to consult various masters before visiting Tiantong at Jinsu. Tiantong asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Yunmen. Tiantong asked, "When did you set out?"
The Master drew a circle. The youth said, "Do not confuse the fundamental. The Master said, "A thousand miles of the same breeze; you have come today specifically to receive this severe blow.
The youth said, "Since it is a thousand miles of the same breeze, why did you come? The Master raised his left foot. The youth said, "Not yet.
The Master raised his right foot. The youth said, "It is wrong. The Master said, "The wind blows through a different tune. The youth then withdrew.
Upon entering the room, the attendant raised his hand and said, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Later, while presiding over the assembly at Jingu Temple, he ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition.
Bodhidharma came from the West to point people toward seeing their nature and becoming Buddha. I, Jingu, am not familiar with the 'granny's Zen'; I simply want everyone to see blood under the staff."
If you can understand it in this way, you will encounter Him at every turn; there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation.

Extending your hand into the human world, you harmonize with the light and transform beings. Since you encounter Him everywhere, tell me: who is this "Him"? A hair’s breadth of error, and heaven and earth are as far apart.
(He lets out a shout.)
Shi Tongren, whose courtesy name was Chaozong, was the son of the Chen family of Changzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of twenty.

He went to visit Tiantong at Jinsu, but he remained utterly bewildered and made no progress. He subsequently traveled extensively, paying respects to masters throughout various regions. Later, he accompanied Tiantong to respond to an invitation from Yuyang Monastery.

On a stele at the temple, there was an inscription of the words left by Chan Master Daqian, which said: "The fierce tiger in the mountains takes meat as its life; for what reason does it not eat its own?"
The Master was oppressed by the boy; he could find no peace whether sitting or lying down for two days. Suddenly, the thing that had been choking his chest was removed.
He hurried down to see the boy and said, "Only when one consents within oneself does one become intimate. The boy replied, "That is still not it.
The Master laughed and said, "The Master has only managed to become a grandson of the Great Thousand Worlds," and then he left. Shortly thereafter, he heard the boy answering himself: "By oneself."

He did not finish his meat dish, at which point he suddenly attained realization of the meaning of "not yet having arrived. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, a monk asked, "The dog has Buddha-nature;
why did Zhaozhou say it does not? The Master said, "Once a single character enters the gates of officialdom, even nine oxen cannot pull it out.
A lay practitioner asked, "What is meant by 'the common people use it daily without knowing it'? The Master said, "Shang Daren Qiu Yiji."
The scholar could not help but laugh. The Master then laughed loudly and said, "So, this has all along been your family’s daily fare. The scholar was speechless.
Later, as the layman was reading the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), he came to the passage where [the Master] folded his hands and wailed to the blue heavens.
He asked with a smile, "Why did he weep at that time? The Master replied, "Why do you laugh now? The layman said, "I understand the meaning of this one cry."
"No," [the monk] replied. The Master said, "Do you now understand this laugh of yours? He replied, "I laughed at his crying.
The Master said, "He was crying precisely because of your laughing."

Shi Tongxiu, whose style name was Yulin, was the son of the Yang family from Rongcheng. When Chengjiang invited him to join Qingshan, he did not go; instead, the Master broke through the barrier to see him.
With hands joined in reverence, he said, "In the realm of a wild child, even his father cannot pass. Is this peak-head still the dwelling place of the old man?
Qingshan said, "Stand your ground for a moment, and I shall speak with you. As the Master spoke, he overturned the incense burner.

As he was about to leave, the Mountain Master raised his voice and said, "Bring me my staff! The Master responded from afar, "The sword has long since departed. Later, after taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said:
"There is a phrase that the Buddhas of the three periods throughout the sands of Ganges-dust lands cannot speak;

that the ancestral masters of the West and the East throughout successive generations cannot speak; that the good spiritual friends of the world cannot speak; and that even the former master could not speak it."
"I have never spoken of this before. Since the Venerable Xu now occupies this position, I shall clearly set it forth for the sake of the assembly.
After a long silence, he said: "The New Year begins its reign; all phenomena flourish. A monk asked, "What is concentration? The Master said, "Utterly topsy-turvy. The monk asked, "What is wisdom?
The Master said, "Utterly foolish and deluded. The monk asked, "What is the union of concentration and wisdom? The Master said, "Utterly foolish and deluded."

"Total Retention. The Master said, "Again you are inverted; again you are ignorant. He ascended the hall. After the assembly had vied with one another to pose questions, the Master said, "One who wishes to catch the giant whale must clear the vast depths;
yet here you sigh over the toad’s steps, hindered by mud and sand. He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
Shi Tongyun, whose style name was Shiqi, commented on Xuedou’s “Retreat” (Jiezhi) verse:

"As for the retreats held in various quarters, the kitchens and storehouses are abundant, everything proceeds in orderly succession, and every object is in surplus; within the ninety days, one sits peacefully through the entire period and finally achieves a semblance of a practitioner.
But here at Xuedou, there is not a single tile above and not a needle-point of space below; it is such that not even a single thing exists."
[The Master] suddenly held up his whisk and said: "Right here, you must urgently realize it. Do not bind yourself with no ropes.
As it is said: 'Originally there is no wound; do not injure it. Otherwise, you will rely on others' gateways and lean against others' walls, only to be called a 'lord' by the people of the age.
On New Year's Day, he addressed the assembly, saying: "In a year of three hundred and sixty days, this day is the most..."
On the first day: if one can grasp the first phrase, then there is newness in the year, newness in the month, and newness in the day;
it is new day after day, new moment after moment, and new at every instant. In this ever-renewing state where nothing abides, within that non-abiding, heaven remains heaven.
The earth is earth; the mountains are mountains; the waters are waters; the monastics are monastics; the laity are laity. Not a single hair’s breadth has ever been shifted.
Thus it is said: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. In the informal discourse (xiao can), he said:
"Today is the thirtieth night of the twelfth month, at the moment when the year ends and the age concludes. Fortunately, there is not the slightest thing to do. Now, in this state of nothingness..."
Regarding this matter, I, this mountain monk, shall deliberate for you. Great assembly, since there is nothing to do, tell me, what else is there to deliberate upon?

If you can understand and master it, then throughout spring, summer, autumn, and winter; through birth, abiding, change, and extinction; and through the waxing and waning of human affairs—[you will find it all].
As time flows on, the Way of things and self is the same; past and present are not two. Have you not seen when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the year ends and the season passes, what then?
The worthy replied, "The old Wang at East Village burns paper money at night.
Observe how this ancient one, having attained clarity and realization, gave such a response from within the interlacing of the lattice-pattern. Is he not more than sufficient?
Ah! He further addressed the assembly, saying: "The single stroke of the present moment stands alone, revealed without obstruction. It is brilliant on all eight sides and vast in the ten directions.

With clear eyes as witnesses, how could one dare to conceal it? It is such that the jade towers and crystal palaces are fully manifested upon the tips of a hundred blades of grass, and the thousand-fathom transformation body suddenly appears amidst a heap of rubble.
It is thus in every atom, thus in every world-realm—suddenly emerging, without..."
The True Man occupies his station, revealing the public case that is already perfected.

Even if the Buddhas of the three periods and the ancient masters of successive generations were to arrive, each would have no choice but to step back. At such a moment, what is it like? When waters return to the great ocean, the waves and billows are stilled;
when clouds reach Cangwu, the atmosphere is at ease.
Shi Tongxian’s style name was Fushí. He was the son of the Zhao family of Pinghu and received the entrustment of Old Man Mi.

He resided at Ba’en Temple. On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he spoke as follows: "Since leaving the imperial palace to enter the Snowy Mountains, I sat coldly for six years, cutting off all pursuit and attachment.
Who would have known that tonight, upon this grass mat, my dark-blue eyes have, for no reason, developed spots of cataracts? When I, this mountain monk, announce this, it is simply because—"
If you all cast off your hats of dripping fat and strip away your stinking cloth shirts, you will immediately see that Śākyamuni of old was not first, and Maitreya of today is not last.
At all times, do not rely on a single thing; utterly naked above, there is nothing to grasp or look up to;
starkly bare below, one's own body is cut off. A thousand sages cannot know it; how can ten thousand spirits fathom it? All...
Seated in cessation, not a single thread of thought leaks through. Furthermore, in the New Year’s address upon the conclusion of the retreat, he said:

"No sooner has the wild horse of the mind been tethered than, in an instant, the deep winter has passed away. By the ears one hears only the clamor of gongs and drums; every sound strikes the heart until the hair at the temples turns white.
O Great Assembly, is there anyone who does not shift with sounds and forms? If you can casually recognize the face of the east wind..."

"Tens of thousands of purples and thousands of reds are all but spring. When one reaches such a state, it can be called "knowing where to return. If someone asks, "From where have you come? do not say, "I have come from Baoen. Why is this so?

It is because one does not respond with something ordinary and straightforward; rather, one precisely intends to cause them to doubt. Thus it is said: "When there is great peace, the Son of Heaven’s edict is not transmitted;
when the times are clear, do not sing the Song of Great Peace. He then raised the following case:
One day, as the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, they saw an ancient stupa along the way. The World-Honored One then paid homage to it.
Ānanda asked, "Whose stupa is this? The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stupa of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda asked, "Who were their disciples?"
The World-Honored One said, "I am his disciple. Ānanda said, "It should be so, Great Assembly. [The assembly asked:
"Since he is a past Buddha, why is he also a disciple of the present World-Honored One? Since he is a disciple of the World-Honored One, why does he pay homage?
Thus they investigated, finding each point to be contradictory. Why, then, did Ānanda say, "It should be so"?
It is so. One who can turn toward this point and clearly penetrate it will realize that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are, in their very essence, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Shi Xingyuan, whose style name was Baichi, was the son of the Cai family of Zhangpu in Min. Having studied Confucianism from his youth, he lost both parents in succession and lived with his elder brother.
At the age of twenty, having failed to achieve success in the civil service examinations, he was resting at a guesthouse in Tong’an when he dreamed of a person one night.
He called out, "The time has come; go on quickly. We shall travel tomorrow morning. There, he met the Master of True Precepts (Zhenjieshi) and entered Longtai Shishiyan together to request tonsure.
In the spring of the Jiaxu year of the Great Ming Chongzhen era, he went to Huangbo to attend upon Master Feiyin.
Whenever he asked a question, he was struck with a severe blow of the staff. Before long, he realized the profound mysteries and was appointed to oversee the office of the Secretariat (Jishu).

In the year Wuyin (1638), the Elder Fei became the abbot of Jinsu Temple; the Master served as the West Hall Preceptor and was entrusted with the robe and whisk. He returned to Lianfeng in Jianning to dwell in seclusion.
In the winter of the year Xinsi (1641), he entered the monastic world (*chushi*), subsequently moving between the two monasteries of Baofeng and Baishan, as well as Taiping and Changqing in Zhejiang.
At the beginning of the summer in the year Wuzi (1648), the Dharma-protectors Xu Jinzhou and others of Haiyan gathered because the seat at Jinsu was vacant.
The assembly requested him to serve as abbot. The Master remained serene and composed. He occupied the seat for six years, exerting his strength and laboring his mind;

even his modest possessions, such as robes and alms bowl, were entirely dedicated to the community. In the eighth month of the year Gui-si, he went to the imperial court to escort the Tripitaka into the monastery.

That very morning, he retired from the abbacy and ascended the hall, saying: "I have served as abbot for six years, yet it has been utterly devoid of flavor. When scrutinized, what leisurely spirit could there possibly be in this?"

How wonderful it is beneath the long pines, amidst a single stone, carefree and detached. With head resting on hands and legs sprawled wide, let the shifting tides of the Dharma and the clamor of the flies’ buzzing be as they may.
For now, let us perform a song before departing. How should it be sung? He strikes the whisk and says: *La la li.
La la lan.* White hair urges one toward old age with ease; A broad mind and no affairs—this is the immortal. Then he stops.

[He] traveled to visit his fellow patrons and supporters, welcoming them into the *Brahmavijaya* [Hall]. Now, at dawn, he departs. The Master has a record of his teachings (*yulu*) in sixteen volumes that circulates in the world.
As he said on the New Year’s Day of the Golden Grain year: "If the Buddha-dharma is not expounded by someone, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it.
How much more so when encountering the New Year; how could one remain in such profound silence? When the drum is beaten and one ascends the hall, clouds of incense rise in all directions."
He circumambulates; leaning on his staff, he drags his head along. He forgets whether the inner or outer side of his *kāṣāya* robe is facing out.
When questioned, his mouth has no reply; from afar in the empty sky, he points at a white bird. The assembly, tell me: when Jin-sul acts in this way, is it joy? Or is it haste?
If you say it is joy, every year is a good year—what is there to be joyful about? If you say it is haste, I am the Dharma King.

Having attained mastery over all phenomena, why do you allow yourself to be so flustered? If you can distinguish between the clear and the turbid within this, it is precisely the right time to wave your hand at the mountain gate and bow your body before the jeweled hall.
Seeing a monk, greet the monk; seeing a layperson, greet the layperson; seeing a white ox or a wildcat, greet the white ox or the wildcat.
If you do not act thus, you will merely be following the seasonal ordinances of the Lord of the Year, striking out amidst flashes of lightning.
Roll it away! As Fànshèng showed: "Forged from lazy bones, one reclines idly on a single mat to pass the bright days;
washed from a withered gut, half a couplet of oblique rhymes stirs the cold tide. Whether Buddhas or Patriarchs come, what does it matter?
Whether called 'ox' or 'horse,' life’s livelihood is complete in every instance, and my treasure-store is revealed everywhere. If you people can truly...
If you see thus and resolve with faith thus, you may then let the mind rest and cease discursive thought. Hang up your alms-bag and dwell together with this mountain monk;
walk together, eat together, and drink together. Plowing through the clouds and tilling the moon, sing your tuneless songs; naturally, the Way will be secure and the times will be clear.
Should you, however, follow your own changing whims or rise and fall with external objects, I dare say that even at year’s end you will never find the time to lay down your tools.

It is as clearly revealed in the *Mingfa*: "The conduct of a patch-robed monk has no fixed pattern; wherever he rests his body, there he finds leisure. Gazing upon the white lotuses filling the pond is never enough;
again, he takes up his bamboo staff and reaches the clouds. Having reached the clouds, right and wrong are forgotten in the distance.
The earth is vast and the heavens are high; voices harmonize with their echoes. He even comes to cherish that man of old, the Boatman, who fished alone with a single line."

Cold River. Furthermore, I hope that on this day, Vimalakīrti will extend his hand to jointly support the ancestral Way. Moreover, as for the phrase that accords with the timing of the season—how can it be explained?
"A wave upon wave of fragrant breezes comes from the palace halls; though the scorching heat presses in, there is coolness."

Abstracts of Eminent Monks Who Attained Transformation, Volume Four.
Compiled by the Layman of Wuyuan, Xu Changzhi (Jin Zhou).
Shi Anqing, style name Shigao, was the crown prince of the King of Parthia. From his youth, he was renowned for his filial conduct;

his intellect and aspirations were sharp and keen. He applied himself with diligence to learning, mastering foreign scriptures as well as the seven luminaries, the five elements, medical prescriptions, and various extraordinary arts.

He comprehended and understood everything, even down to the cries of birds and beasts. Once, while walking and seeing a flock of swallows, he suddenly said to his companions, "The swallows say there must be someone bringing them food.
Shortly thereafter, food was indeed delivered. Everyone marveled at this. Although Gao lived as a layman, [he possessed such spiritual insight].

He observed the precepts with rigorous austerity. Upon the king’s death, he succeeded to his father’s throne; however, he reflected deeply on suffering and emptiness, developing a weary detachment from the physical body.

Once his period of mourning was complete, he abdicated the kingdom to his uncle and left the household life to cultivate the Way. He became extensively learned in the Piṭaka of the Sūtras and was especially proficient in the study of Abhidharma.
He recited and upheld the Dhyāna-sūtras, mastering their subtleties in their entirety. Subsequently, he traveled abroad to propagate the teachings, traversing all regions.
He arrived in the Central Kingdom at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty. Possessing keen intelligence and quick wit, he could grasp the meaning upon hearing it once.
Not long after his arrival, he had mastered the Chinese language and began to propagate and translate various scriptures, rendering them from Sanskrit (Fan) into Chinese (Han).

He also separately translated the *Dao-di jing* (Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra) and other preceding and subsequent sūtras and śāstras, totaling thirty-nine works. Their principles were clearly analyzed and their wording was authentic and correct. Those who read them...
He was diligent and never grew weary. Initially, Daogao claimed that in a previous life he had already left the household life. He had a fellow student who was prone to anger;

whenever he encountered a donor whose offerings did not meet his expectations, he would invariably harbor resentment. Daogao repeatedly admonished and exhorted him, yet he ultimately refused to reform.
In this manner, for more than twenty years, he took leave of his fellow students, saying: "I shall reside in Guangzhou to exhaust the karmic retributions of my past lives.
You have been diligent in your mastery of the scriptures and are not behind me; however, your nature is prone to anger, and upon the end of your life, you will likely receive an evil form.
If I attain the Way, I shall certainly deliver you. Subsequently, he departed for Guangzhou, where he encountered bandits.
During a great upheaval, he encountered a young man on the road who spat upon his hand, drew his sword, and said, "I have truly caught you!

The Master laughed heartily and said, "In a previous life, I owed you a debt; therefore, I have come from afar to repay it. Why must you be so angry? He then extended his neck to receive the blade, his countenance showing no sign of fear.
The bandit subsequently killed him, and among the onlookers, there was none who did not marvel at this extraordinary wonder. Subsequently, [his remains] were taken by the King of Parthia.
The Prince traveled and transformed the people throughout the Central Kingdom, completing his mission of proclaiming the scriptures.

At the end of Emperor Ling’s reign, when Guanzhong and Luoyang were in turmoil, he took up his mendicant’s staff and headed south toward Jiangnan, saying, "I shall pass through Mount Lu to deliver my former fellow student. Upon reaching Qingtang Lake Temple, he arrived.

This shrine had long possessed divine power; merchants seeking blessings from it would pray for favorable winds above or below, and the boatmen, filled with reverence and awe, were all struck with terror.

Gao Tong traveled with more than thirty boats, offering sacrificial animals and requesting blessings. The deity then descended through the medium of the priest and said, "There is a śramaṇa on one of the vessels;
you may call him up immediately. The guests were all startled and asked Gao to enter the shrine. The deity addressed Gao, saying, "In the past..."
A foreigner and his son both left the household life together to study the Way. They delighted in practicing generosity, yet they were by nature prone to anger.

Now they have become the guardian spirits of a shrine at Quting. The territory they govern extends for a thousand *li* in every direction. Because of their practice of giving, their treasures and playthings are exceedingly abundant;

however, because of their anger, they have fallen into this retribution as deities. Seeing their former fellow students now, their grief and joy are beyond words. Their lives will end in a matter of days or nights, and—
My form is hideous and large. If I were to die here, I would defile the rivers and lakes;

I must pass away in the marshes west of the mountains. After this body perishes, I fear I shall fall into hell. I have a thousand bolts of silk and various precious objects; you may use them to establish the Dharma and build a stupa for me, so that I may be reborn in a good realm.
Gaogao said, "I came specifically to save you; why do you not show your form? The spirit replied, "The form is extremely—"
It was hideous and strange; everyone would surely have been terrified. Baogao said, "Just come out; the crowd will not find it strange. The spirit emerged its head from behind the bed;
it was a giant python, and no one knew the length of its tail. It reached as far as Baogao’s knees.

Baogao addressed it several times in Sanskrit and chanted several verses of praise. The python wept with tears like rain. After a short while, it withdrew and vanished. Baogao then took his silk goods and took his leave.
He departed. As his fellow voyagers hoisted their sails, the python again emerged from its body, climbed a mountain, and watched him.
In an instant, they reached Yuzhang. Tanqiao immediately used the temple's property to establish Dong Temple. After Tanqiao had left, the deity passed away.
At dusk, a young man boarded the boat and knelt before Tanqiao for a long time, receiving his blessings; suddenly, he vanished. Tanqiao said, "Gong!"
The deity of the shrine and temple was thus able to leave its evil form behind. Later, people saw a dead python in a marsh in Shanxi;
its head and tail spanned several li, and this place is the present-day Snake Village (Shecun) in Xunyang Commandery.

Afterward, Sengga returned to Guangzhou and found that the youth who had harmed him in his previous life was still there. Sengga went directly to his home and recounted the events of their past karmic retribution. Furthermore—
They recounted their past karmic connections and faced each other with joy, saying, "I still have residual retribution;
I must now go to Kuaiji to settle this account. The Guangzhou guest realized that Gao was no ordinary man; his mind suddenly opened to understanding, and he regretted his former transgressions.

He provided Gao with generous provisions and accompanied him on his journey eastward until they reached Kuaiji. Upon arriving, Gao immediately entered the marketplace, where he happened upon a brawl. By chance, he struck one of the combatants.

Tou died at the appointed time. A traveler from Guangzhou repeatedly witnessed these two responses and consequently applied himself with diligence to the Buddha-dharma, sighing with sorrow over how the three periods of time possess manifest signs.
Since Gao was of royal lineage, those in the Western Regions called him "Lord An" (Anhou).
Shi Kang Senghui was originally from Kangju; his ancestors had lived for generations in India. His father moved to Jiaozhi due to trade.
When Senghui was over ten years old, both his parents passed away. Out of his innate character, he devoted himself to filial piety; once his period of mourning ended, he left the household life.

His conduct was exceedingly rigorous. He was a man of broad learning and refined character, possessing great intellectual capacity. He was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and had extensively read the Six Classics.

He had a comprehensive mastery of astronomy, including the *tu* and *wei* texts, and was quite adept at literary composition. At that time, although Sun Quan had already established control over the region east of the Yangtze River, Buddhism had not yet spread there.
Previously, there was the Upāsaka Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming, who was originally a person from Yuezhi and had come to travel in the Han lands.

Regarding the region: during the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling of the Han dynasty, there was Zhi Chen, who translated numerous scriptures. Zhi Liang studied under Chen, and Yao Xian received his instruction from Liang.
Xian read widely across the classics and histories, mastering them all with great precision. At the end of the Han Dynasty, during the chaos following Emperor Xian’s reign, he fled to the Wu region.
When Sun Quan heard of his talent and wisdom, he summoned him for an audience and was pleased with him, appointing him as a *boshi* (Court Scholar) to serve as a tutor.

At the Eastern Palace, he collaborated with Wei Yao and others to provide full counsel and assistance. Although the Great Teaching had already been propagated, he observed that many of the scriptures were in Sanskrit;
he therefore collected various manuscripts and translated them into the Chinese language.

From the first year of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty until the Jianxing period, he produced forty-nine scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Dharmapada*, the *Śūramgama-samādhi* (or *Śrīkūṭa*), and the *Nidāna*.

He thoroughly mastered the sacred meanings and produced annotated versions of the *Sūtra on the Ending of Birth and Death* and other texts. At that time, the Great Dharma had only recently begun to take root in the land of Wu, and its influence was not yet complete.
Kāśyapa Mātanga wished to spread the Way throughout the region east of the Yangtze River and establish Buddhist temples; he therefore took up his staff and traveled east.
In the tenth year of the Chiku era of the Wu dynasty, he first arrived at Jianye. He constructed a thatched hut, established an image, and practiced the Way.
An official submitted a memorial, saying: "A foreigner has entered the borders, calling himself a śramaṇa; his appearance and attire are unusual, and he ought to be investigated. Sun Quan replied:
"Formerly, Emperor Ming of the Han dreamed of a deity who was titled 'Buddha. Could what this man practices be a remnant of that tradition? Thereupon—
The official summoned Hui and interrogated him: "What spiritual efficacy do you possess? Hui replied: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, more than a thousand years have suddenly elapsed.
His remaining relics and śarīras have manifested divine radiance beyond measure. In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stūpas;
for the establishment of such stūpas and monasteries is intended to manifest his bequeathed transformation. The official considered this boastful and said to Hui: "If you can obtain a relic..."
"You must construct a stupa for him. If this is false, the state has established laws for such offenses.

He then requested a period of seven days and addressed his followers, saying, "The rise or fall of the Dharma depends upon this single undertaking. If we do not act with utmost sincerity now, how can it be remedied later?

Thereupon, they collectively purified themselves in a quiet chamber, placing a copper vase upon a stand, burning incense, and making offerings with reverence. When the seven-day period concluded, there was silence and nothing [was seen].
He should have requested an extension for another two weeks, and it would have been the same as before. Zhi Quan said, "This is a deception; I am about to impose punishment upon you.

Daohui further requested another three weeks, and Quan again granted this special request. Daohui said to his followers, "The Dharma has manifested its spiritual response, yet we have felt no resonance.
Why rely on royal law? We shall simply take death as our deadline. At the end of the third seven-day period, even at dusk, nothing was seen.

Everyone was struck with awe and trepidation. When the fifth watch had passed, they suddenly heard a metallic *keng* sound from within the jar. Senghui went to look for himself and indeed obtained a *śarīra*.
The following morning, he presented it to Sun Quan; the entire court assembled to witness it as five-colored flames and radiance shone brilliantly upon the jar.
Sun Quan personally took the vessel in his hand and poured [the contents] onto a bronze platter. Wherever the śarīra struck, the platter immediately shattered.

Sun Quan was profoundly solemn and started up in alarm, saying, "This is a rare and auspicious omen. Zhihui then spoke, saying, "The majestic spiritual power of the śarīra is not merely its radiant appearance;
even the fires at the end of an eon cannot burn it, nor can the vajra-pestle shatter it. Sun Quan...

The Emperor ordered an experiment to be conducted. He placed the śarīra upon an iron anvil and had strong men strike it with a hammer. Thereupon, both the anvil and the hammer were dented, yet the śarīra remained undamaged.
Qian was deeply moved and filled with admiration; he immediately erected a stūpa for it. Since this was the first Buddhist temple ever established, it was named Jianchu Si (Temple of the Beginning).
Consequently, the area was named Fotuo Li (Buddha Village). From this point on, the Great Dharma flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
The state was subsequently established. Upon reaching the reign of Sun Hao, the administration became harsh and cruel. He abolished "licentious shrines," and this extended even to Buddhist temples.
The ministers all said, "The power of the Buddha is not like that of other deities. Kang Senghui moved Heaven by his auspicious responses, and the Great Emperor founded these temples.

If we now destroy them lightly, we fear it will lead to future regret. Sun Hao dispatched Zhang Yu to the temple to interrogate Senghui. Zhang Yu was naturally gifted with eloquence and persuasive skill.

His difficult questions were纵横 (zōnghéng—literally "horizontal and vertical," meaning pervasive and multifaceted). Hui responded by expounding his words according to the occasion; his literary principles emerged with sharp brilliance. From dawn until dusk, Sun Yù could not defeat him.
Upon returning, Yù marveled at Hui’s talent and clarity, remarking, "This is beyond my own comprehension; I pray Your Majesty will examine this.

Emperor Hào convened a great assembly of court scholars and went out in person with carriages and horses to welcome Hui. Once Hui was seated, Hào asked him: "The Buddhist teachings clarify the retribution of good and evil."
"What are these? The Duke of Wei replied: "When a sagely ruler instructs the world with filial piety and compassion, the crimson phoenix soars and the Star of the Aged appears.
When his benevolence and virtue nourish all things, sweet springs gush forth and auspicious sprouts emerge. Since goodness brings such omens,"
The same applies to evil. The *I Ching* proclaims that accumulated goodness brings forth blessings; the *Odes* sing of seeking fortune without turning back from one's path.

Though these are the orthodox maxims of the Confucian classics, they are precisely the clear instructions of the Buddha. Hu said: "If this is so, then since Zhou and Kong have already made this clear, what further need is there for Buddhism?"

The Master said: "What was spoken by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius merely indicates superficial traces. As for the teachings of Śākyamuni, they exhaustively reveal the most profound and subtle truths.
Thus, it is made clear that committing evil leads to the long-lasting suffering of hell, while practicing goodness results in the eternal bliss of the celestial palaces."
How great was his power in both exhorting and deterring! At that time, Sun Hao had no means to refute these words.
Although he heard the True Dharma, his deluded and perverse nature could not overcome its own cruelty. Later, he ordered the palace guards to enter the inner quarters to clear the gardens.
There, they found a standing golden image several feet high buried in the ground and presented it to Hao. Hao placed it in an impure location and poured foul liquids over it.

Together with his various ministers, he laughed and took it as amusement. In an instant, his entire body became severely swollen; his private parts remained painful, and his cries reached the heavens.
The Grand Astrologer divined and said, "This is caused by offending a Great Deity. He immediately offered prayers and sacrifices at the various shrines, yet there was never any recovery.
Among the palace ladies, there were some who had previously honored the Dharma; they therefore inquired after him, saying, "Your Majesty should seek [relief] from the Buddha."
Fu Bo did not believe this. Shao raised his head and asked, "Is the Buddha a great deity? The court lady replied, "The Buddha is a great deity. Shao’s heart was then enlightened.
The court lady immediately welcomed the image and placed it upon the altar in the hall; she washed it with scented water dozens of times, burned incense, and performed repentance.

Sima Hao knelt with his head to the pillow and personally confessed his transgressions. After a short while, when the pain had subsided, he dispatched a messenger to the monastery to invite Huì to preach the Dharma.
Huì immediately followed him inside. Upon meeting him, Hao questioned him regarding the causes of sin and merit; Huì expounded upon them for him, his words being exceedingly precise and essential.

Sun Hao was greatly delighted and consequently requested to see the monastic precepts. Zhihui then took the *Pratimokṣa* of one hundred and thirty-five vows and divided them into two hundred and fifty items.

He made a vow for all sentient beings during every activity—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Upon seeing that these compassionate vows were so vast and universal, Sun Hao’s wholesome resolve increased even further.
He immediately received the five precepts from Zhihui. Within ten days, his illness was cured; he then went to Zhihui’s residence.
He further embellished his residence and proclaimed it to the imperial clan, ensuring that all were required to pay their respects. During the Wu dynasty, he frequently preached the True Dharma;

because Emperor Huo’s disposition was fierce and coarse, he did not dwell upon subtle meanings, but instead recounted matters of karmic retribution and immediate consequences to open the Emperor's mind.
At Jianchu Monastery, he translated numerous sutras, such as the *Ānanda-nāma-mitāyus-sūtra* and the *Ādarśamukha-rāja-sūtra*.

He examined such works as the *Chawei Wangfanhuang jing* (Sūtra on King Brahmā Examining the Subtle), as well as the *Xiaopin* (Shorter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra), the *Liudujijing* (Collection of Six Pāramitās), and the *Zapiyuyi* (Miscellaneous Parables).
He also annotated three sūtras: the *Anban shouyi* (Mindfulness of Breathing), the *Fajing* (Mirror of the Dharma), and the *Daoshu* (Tree of the Path), and composed prefaces for them.

In the fourth month of the fourth year of the Tianji era of the Wu dynasty, Sun Hao surrendered to the Jin. In the ninth month, Zhi Dun fell ill and passed away; this was the first year of the Taikang era of Emperor Wu of the Jin.
Shi Huiyuan, whose secular surname was Jia, was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. At the age of thirteen, he followed the family of Lingfu to study in the regions of Xu and Luo.
In his youth, he served as a student (*zhusheng*) and extensively mastered the Six Classics; he was particularly proficient in the *Zhuangzi* and the *Laozi*.

At that time, the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an had established a monastery on Mount Heng in the Taihang Mountains to propagate and extol the Dharma of the Image Age (*xiangfa*). Huiyuan went there to take refuge in him. One day, he heard Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
When he suddenly attained awakening upon reading a sutra, he sighed and said, "The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are all nothing but chaff and husks.

Thereupon, together with his younger brother Huichi, he cast aside his hairpin and shaved his head, entrusting his life to the study of the Dharma and taking the Great Teaching as his own responsibility. He applied himself to profound contemplation and recited the scriptures with devotion.

He continued his studies by night as if it were day. Being a poor traveler without means, he was constantly lacking in coarse woolen clothing; yet his brothers remained respectful and diligent toward him, never flagging from beginning to end.
A śramaṇa named Tanyi regularly provided him with the expenses for lamps and candles. When Master Dao’an heard of this, he said with joy, "The Daoist truly knows people.
He further remarked, "If the Way is to spread to the eastern lands, it will surely depend on Huiyuan. At the age of twenty-four, he [left home].
He then proceeded to deliver lectures. Once, there was a guest who listened to his discourse and raised difficult questions regarding the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).

The exchange continued for some time, and the guest’s confusion and obscurity only increased further. Huiyuan then cited the principles of Zhuangzi as a parallel analogy, whereupon the deluded one became clearly enlightened.
Thereafter, accompanied by several dozen disciples, he traveled south to Jingzhou and went to Shangming Temple. Later, wishing to go to Mount Luofu, he arrived at Xunyang.
Seeing that Mount Lu was pure and serene, it was sufficient to quiet his mind. He first resided at Longquan Monastery. This place was originally far from water;
Huiyuan then struck the ground with his staff and said, "If I may find a dwelling here, let a spring gush forth from this parched soil.
As soon as he finished speaking, a clear stream surged up and formed a brook. Later, during a severe drought in Xunyang, Huiyuan went to the side of the pond and recited the *Sāgara* [Sea] Sūtra.
In the *Nāgarāja Sūtra*, it is said that suddenly a great serpent emerged from above the pond, and in a brief moment, a heavy rain fell, ensuring bountiful harvests for years to come.
Consequently, the vihāra was named Longquan Temple (Dragon Spring Temple). Huiyuan constructed this vihāra, fully capturing the beauty of the mountain;

it faces the Xianglu Peak (Incense Burner Peak) behind and borders a gorge with waterfalls on its side. He used piled stones as a foundation and planted pines to form the structures, with clear springs encircling it.

The steps were lined with white clouds filling the chambers. Furthermore, within the monastery, he established a separate Zen grove where dense trees gathered mist and stone paths were covered in moss;
all who visited were moved to spiritual clarity and solemnity of spirit.

From afar, he heard that in India there was a shadow of the Buddha, which was the image left behind when the Buddha formerly converted a venomous dragon. It was located to the south of the city of Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, in the stone cave of an ancient seer.

In the interim, he was constantly filled with a sense of joy and inspiration, his heart yearning to behold [the Buddha]. It so happened that a Daoist from the Western Regions described the Buddha’s radiant features;
thereupon, Huiyuan built a grotto cell facing the mountains and overlooking a stream. He employed skilled artisans for a marvelous design, and they painted it with subtle colors.

The hues seemed as if they were empty space, appearing like mist and clouds when viewed from afar. Huiyuan then composed an inscription, which began: "Vast is the Great Image; its principle is profound and nameless. Its substance..."

The divine person undergoes transformation; their falling shadow detaches from their form. Radiance swirls across the layered cliffs, coalescing as a reflection in the empty pavilion. Not obscured when in the shade, it becomes even more luminous in the dark.

Moving with graceful steps, they shed their mortal shell like a cicada; they become the sovereign source for all spirits. Responding to different realms, their traces vanish into the profound mystery.
Furthermore, in the past, while Tao Kan of Xunyang was stationed at Guangzhou, a fisherman saw a divine light upon the sea that shone brilliantly every evening.
The manifestation lasted for ten days and grew increasingly intense. Frightened, [Huan] Kan reported it to him; Kan went to examine it closely and found it was an image of King Aśoka.

He immediately took it back and sent it to Hanxi Temple in Wuchang. Later, when Kan moved his military command to another post, he dispatched an envoy to welcome the image because of its divine power.
As dozens of men carried it on a palanquin to the water’s edge to board a boat, the vessel capsized and sank. The envoy, filled with fear, turned back.

Hui-k’an was naturally heroic and martial from his youth and had always been skeptical of religious faith; thus, there was a popular saying in Jing-chu that went: "It can be brought about through sincerity, but it is difficult to summon by force.
When Hui-yuan had completed the construction of the monastery, he prayed with a devoted heart and invited [the Buddha] to descend; the image then floated down effortlessly and without obstruction.

Thereupon, he led the assembly in the practice of the Way, continuing without ceasing from dusk until dawn. People gathered from afar at the mere sound of the wind, including Liu Yimin of Pengcheng and [the people of] Yuzhang.
Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, Bi Yingzhi of Xincai, Zong Bing of Nanyang, Zhang Laimin, Zhang Jishuo, and others all renounced worldly glory to follow Huiyuan’s travels and reside with him.
Huiyuan then established a fast and made a vow before the statue of Amitābha in the vihāra, pledging together to aspire for the Western Paradise.
When Yin Zhongkan was in Jingzhou, he passed by the mountain to pay his respects.
Together with Yuan, he visited the northern stream to discuss the essential principles of the *Yi* (Book of Changes); they spent the time without weariness as the shadows shifted.

Wang Shi, the Minister of Education, and Wang Mo, the Commander-in-Chief, both admired his character and virtue, paying him the respect due to a teacher from afar. Shi composed a letter of praise, saying: "At the age of only forty..."
When Huiyuan reached the age of sixty, he responded to [the Emperor’s] message, saying: "The ancients did not prize a foot-long jade disc, but instead valued a single inch of shadow.
Judging by what they preserved, it seems their concern was not for longevity. When Lu Xun first descended and took control of Jiangzhou, he entered the mountains to visit Huiyuan.
In his youth, Huiyuan had studied as a scholar together with Sengxun’s father, Sengjia. When he met Sengxun, they joyfully reminisced about their past;
consequently, they maintained a constant correspondence. A monk admonished Huiyuan, saying, "Sengxun is a national rebel. To maintain such close ties with him—will you not be suspected?"
Huiyuan said, "In our Buddha-dharma, the mind has no grasping or rejecting; will this not be observed by those who possess discernment?

Later, when Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty pursued Lu Xun and established his headquarters at Sangwei, his attendants remarked, "Master Huiyuan has long presided over Mount Lu and was on intimate terms with Lu Xun.
Emperor Wu replied, "Master Huiyuan is a man beyond the mundane world; he certainly makes no distinction between self and other. He then dispatched a messenger bearing a letter to him.
He paid his respects and sent him money and rice. Consequently, those both near and far were moved by his clear insight. Initially, when the scriptures reached Jiangdong, many were incomplete;
the methods of Dhyāna were unheard of, and the Vinaya-piṭaka was fragmentary. Daoyuan ordered his disciples Fajing and Falin to travel afar in search of various scriptures.
They crossed deserts and snow mountains, returning only after many years, having obtained Sanskrit manuscripts which they were then able to translate. There was...
The Śramaṇa Saṃghadeva from Kaśmīra was widely learned in the various scriptures. In the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he arrived at Xunyang.
Huiyuan requested that he retranslate the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*; thus, these two studies flourished.

Whenever he encountered a visitor from the Western Regions, he would invariably consult them with earnest sincerity. Upon hearing that Kumārajīva had entered Guanzhong, he immediately dispatched [messengers].

He sent a letter to propose a friendly alliance. Kumārajīva replied with a letter and appended a verse, saying: "Since you have already abandoned the pleasures of defilement, has your mind attained perfect mastery?
If it does not scatter and wander, have you deeply entered the true mark of reality? Within the ultimate mark of emptiness, does your mind find no delight?"
"If one delights in dhyāna and wisdom, this Dharma-nature is without illumination; it is empty, deceptive, and lacks reality, nor is it a place where the mind can rest.
O Benevolent One, regarding the Dharma you have attained, I pray that you will graciously reveal its essentials. [He] sent a letter to Kumārajīva from afar, along with a reply in verse, which said:

"From where does the root of all things ultimately come? Its arising and ceasing lie at the boundary of existence and non-existence. A single atom, by entering the realm of movement, creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. Delusion..."

As we continue to rely upon one another, our contact with the underlying principle naturally gives rise to stagnation. Although causes and conditions have no master, the opening of the path has not occurred in a single lifetime.
Since there is currently no awakened master to guide us, who will grasp the profound seal? The inquiry remains distant; let us together look forward to the final years.
Later, Puṇyatāra arrived in Guanzhong and recited the Sanskrit text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which Kumārajīva translated into the Jin language.
The text consists of three parts; two had already been translated when Mahādeva passed away. Daoxuan often lamented that it was incomplete.

Upon hearing that Dharmaruci had arrived in the Qin territory and was well-versed in reciting this section, he dispatched his disciple Tanyong to deliver a letter of request, asking that the remaining portions be translated anew in Guanzhong.
Consequently, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) was made complete without omission. Previously, these had not [yet been available] in the Central Kingdom.
There was a teaching that Nirvana is eternally abiding; it merely stated that its lifespan is immeasurably long. Yuan then sighed and said:

"The Buddha is the ultimate reality and is therefore immutable. How could the principle of immutability ever come to an end? Consequently, he composed the *Treatise on the Dharma-nature* (*Faxing lun*), in which he wrote:
The ultimate takes non-change as its nature; attaining this nature takes the embodiment of the ultimate as its principle.
Upon seeing the treatise, Kumārajīva sighed and said, "A man from a frontier land has, without even having seen the scriptures, darkly accorded with the underlying principle. How marvelous!
Emperor Yao Xing of Qin, admiring his fame and virtue, sent him earnest letters and a continuous stream of gifts and offerings, presenting him with fine silk thread from the kingdom of Kucha.
He presented a transformed image to express his sincere devotion. Furthermore, he had Yao Song offer him a pearl-encrusted image.
As the *Śāstra* was newly translated, Xuangxing sent the treatise along with a letter, saying: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* has been newly translated.

Since this was composed by Nāgārjuna and represents the ultimate purport of the Vaipulya sūtras, it is fitting that you provide a preface to express the author's intent. He requested a distant preface from Huan Xuan while the latter was campaigning against Yin.
When Zhongkan’s army passed by Mount Lu, he invited Huiyuan to come out to Tiger Creek. Huiyuan claimed he was too ill to comply. Daoyuan entered the mountain himself;
upon seeing Huiyuan, he unconsciously paid his respects. Daoyuan asked, "The precepts state that one must not harm or injure the body;

why then do you shave your head? Huiyuan replied, "To establish oneself and practice the Way. Daoyuan praised this as excellent. He did not dare to voice further questions or objections, but instead spoke of his intentions regarding the military campaign.

Huiyuan did not answer. Daoyuan asked again, "How do you wish for me? Huiyuan replied, "I wish that you, the donor, may be at peace and secure, and that those others may likewise meet with no misfortune.
Daoyuan left the mountain and said to his attendants, "Truly, such a person as this has never been seen since the beginning of my life.

Later, Daoyuan, relying on his status as the ruler of the region, earnestly sought to invite him. Huiyuan’s responses were firm and upright, remaining steadfast and unshakable. Shortly thereafter, Daoyuan desired—
In purifying the monastic community, only Mount Lu—where those of virtue and wisdom reside—was exempt from the process of searching and screening. Huiyuan wrote a letter to Xuanshi, saying:
"The Buddhist teachings have declined, and they have been defiled by impurities for a long time. Every time I reflect upon this, my indignation fills me to overflowing.

I have privately observed that the instruction to purify and clarify the various practitioners truly accords with my own fundamental intent. However, this must ensure that those who adorn their falsehoods are cut off and that those who rely on pretenses are excluded."
The Way and Truth are such that those who embody them incur no suspicion of being worldly. When the Way and the world flourish together, the Three Jewels once again prosper.
Consequently, Daoxuan expanded upon the regulations for the profound [Buddhist teachings], and Daoyuan followed him. After a short while, Daoyuan usurped the throne and issued an edict stating:

"The Buddha-dharma is vast and grand; it cannot be fathomed. Let the various practitioners of the Way no longer offer salutations. Thereupon, Huiyuan composed the *Treatise on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings*.

Before the scroll was even half-finished, he passed away at the age of eighty-three.

He treated him with secret respect and wonder, knowing that [Hui]yi would certainly not fail the offerings of the faithful. Later, he sent a gift of a thousand *hu* of grain; Yi accepted it and distributed it among others.

Yi once took up his staff and traveled south, where he constructed monasteries. Later, when the Hu rebels escaped and plundered the region south of the Han River, the entire district of Jiangling sought refuge at Shangming.
When Yi returned to Jiangling, he restored Changsha Monastery and prayed with sincere devotion, whereupon—
He was moved by the śarīra relics, which he enshrined in a golden jar and placed upon his altar for the midday meal.

When midnight arrived, five-colored radiance gradually emerged from the jar, illuminating the entire hall. The entire assembly was struck with wonder and awe; all were moved to reverence by this divine response.
Later, he entered the Junshan Mountains of Baling to fell timber. On the mountain there was a cavern that connected to Baoshan in Wu. As the mountain was already a site of spiritual wonder, people...
He was deeply apprehensive. As Huiyi led his men in and out, they encountered dozens of white snakes lying across the path, blocking their way.

Huiyi returned to his quarters and, from a distance, invoked the mountain spirits to perform rites of repentance on their behalf. He then addressed the deities, saying, "I am felling timber to build a monastery."
"May we together perform this meritorious deed. That night, he dreamed of a divine being who told Daoyi:

"Since the Dharma Master requires these for the sake of the Triple Gem, I especially rejoice in your undertaking. However, do not allow others to recklessly clear the land. The next day, they went again; the path was remarkably clear and level.
Thereupon, they felled the timber and floated it downstream. Daoyi often sighed: "The temple is established and the monks are sufficient, yet the physical [structure]..."
The previous images were still few; those created by King Aśoka possessed such divine auspiciousness in their appearance that they were spread throughout all directions.
How could it be that there was no response and they could not be summoned? Thus, with single-minded devotion and sincere lamentation, he prayed for a truthful manifestation.

On the eighth day of the second month in the year of Jiǎwǔ, the nineteenth year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty, a statue suddenly appeared north of the city, its radiant features shining forth.

At that time, the monastic community of the Baima Monastery went out first to welcome it, but they were unable to move it. Daoying then went there to pay his respects and said, "This must be the statue of King Aśoka;
it has descended to our Changsha Monastery. He immediately ordered three disciples to receive and support it, whereupon it rose up with a whirring sound.
They welcomed it back to their own monastery, and both clergy and laity rushed there in a great throng, the sounds of carriages and horses filling the air. Later, from Jibin...
Master Bin, Sengqanata, came down from Shu to enter the temple and pay his respects. Seeing Sanskrit characters upon the halo of the image, he declared, "This is an image of King Aśoka.
He passed away the following year at the age of eighty-two. On the day of his death, the halo of the image [manifested].
Suddenly, he underwent a spiritual transformation; no one knew where he had gone.
Shi Sengjin’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Pei and the fourth son of the recluse Dai. In his youth, he was proficient in the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi.

He also studied the *Shi* (Odes) and *Li* (Rituals). Later, traveling to Guangling, he met Dharma Master Tanyin; he then bowed his head in prostration and took him as his mentor, studying the inner scriptures (*neidian*) and extensively surveying the Tripitaka.
Subsequently, he arrived at the capital, where he encountered Dao-sheng of Longguang Temple and again relied upon him for his studies. Initially, he stayed at Yecheng Temple.

Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree appointing him as the tutor to Prince Xiangdong. The Prince followed his request and received the five precepts, treating him with great respect.
He was treated with great courtesy. At that time, Xiangdong ascended the throne; this was Emperor Ming.

He subsequently issued an edict appointing Sengjin as the Patriarch of the Monks of the World, providing him with a troupe of ritual musicians, twenty personal attendants, a monthly stipend of thirty thousand coins, four seasonal gifts throughout the year, as well as a carriage and the labor of officials.
By nature, Jin did not hoard gold, but used it all for meritorious works. He founded the two monasteries of Linggen and Lingji.
It served as a dwelling place for meditation and wisdom. Toward the end of Emperor Ming’s reign, however, there was considerable suspicion regarding its recitation;
consequently, the banner of the *Nirvāṇa* and *Parinirvāṇa* temporarily ceased to fly here. Furthermore, one was not permitted to respond to any mention of death, calamity, misfortune, or aging.
Consequently, those who offended him and were executed numbered seven or eight out of ten. At that time, Zhou Yong of Runan was serving as a private counselor to the Emperor.
Sengjin said to Yong, "The admonitions and remonstrances offered regarding the Emperor's recent conduct have been of no avail; there is only the bitter retribution of the three periods of existence."
This is the most urgent matter. If you, donor, find the opportunity and the occasion appropriate, you should present this [to the Emperor].

Later, when the Emperor’s wind-illness (apoplexy) recurred frequently and he suffered from distress and despondency, he repeatedly summoned Sengyong and Yin Hong to speak of various matters concerning spirits and ghosts to relieve his mind.
Yong then studied the *Dharmapada* and the two scriptures, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*. Whenever he encountered their teachings, he invariably cited them first.
The Emperor often remarked in surprise, "Karmic retribution truly must be like this; how could one not stand in awe of it? Consequently, those who had previously offended him [were moved].
He was repeatedly granted full clemency. Sengjin passed away during the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-nine.
Shi Tanwuqie—translated as Fayong—was surnamed Li and was a native of Huanglong in Youzhou. From his youth, he served as a śrāmaṇera and practiced asceticism;
he observed the precepts and recited the scriptures, earning the high esteem of his fellow monks. He often heard of Faxian and others who had personally traveled to the lands of the Buddha.
The Master then sighed with resolve and made a vow to sacrifice his own life.

Consequently, in the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he gathered twenty-five fellow practitioners, including the śramaṇas Sengmeng and Tanlang, and together they carried banners, canopies, and various articles for making offerings.
Setting out from his native land, he reached Henan and emerged from Haixi Commandery. He entered the shifting sands and arrived at Gaochang Commandery.

He traveled through the various kingdoms of Kucha and Kashgar, ascended the Pamir Mountains, and crossed the Snow Mountains. There, obstructing mists lay in a thousand layers and tiered ice extended for ten thousand li.
Below, a great river flowed with a current as swift as an arrow; across it, they tied ropes to form a bridge between the flanks of the eastern and western mountains, sufficient for ten men to cross.
Once they had reached the other shore, they raised smoke as a signal. Those behind, seeing the smoke, knew that the predecessors had already crossed and could then proceed further.
If they did not see smoke for a long time, they would know that a violent wind had blown the rope away and people had fallen into the river.

After traveling for three days, they again crossed the Great Snow Mountains, where precipitous cliffs rose sheer with no place to set foot; on the stone walls, there were everywhere old wooden stakes.

The holes were positioned facing one another at regular intervals. Each person took hold of four stakes; first pulling out the lower stake, they grasped the upper stake with their right hand, passing from one to the next by holding onto each other.
It took three days to cross over. Upon reaching level ground, he counted his companions and found that twelve men had been lost.

Continuing on, he arrived in the kingdom of Kapiśa, where he paid homage to the Buddha’s alms bowl. He stayed for more than a year, studying Sanskrit script and the Sanskrit language, and sought out the Avalokiteśvara [Sūtra].
There is one Sanskrit manuscript of the *Ghoṣāvyākaraṇa-sūtra*. Continuing westward, he reached the Indus River (*Sindhu-nadī*; Lion’s Mouth).
Following the river westward, he entered the country of the Yuezhi, where he paid homage to the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone and beheld the "Self-boiling Water" boat.
Later, he arrived at the Śailaguhā Monastery south of Mount Dandaka, where more than three hundred monks resided, studying the various teachings of the Three Vehicles. Wujie stayed there.

He received the full precepts at this monastery. During the three-month summer retreat under the Indian meditation master Buddhatāra (whose name signifies one who has attained the fruit of sainthood), he then set out toward the borders of Central India.
As the road was desolate and vast, he carried only rock honey as provisions.
Among his thirteen companions, eight died along the way; only five remained traveling together. Although Wujie had frequently encountered perilous difficulties, he remained steadfastly focused.

He constantly recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* he had carried with him, never ceasing for even a moment. As he was about to reach the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he encountered a herd of wild elephants in the wilderness.
Aniruddha invoked the name [of the Bodhisattva] and took refuge; immediately, a lion emerged from the forest, and the elephants fled in terror.
Later, as he was crossing the Ganges, he again encountered a herd of wild oxen that came bellowing toward him, intending to harm him.
Wujie took refuge [in the Buddha] as he had done before. Soon, a large vulture flew in, and the wild oxen were startled and dispersed; thus, he was able to escape.
Later, in South India, he traveled by ship across the sea and arrived at Guangzhou, where he translated the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
This was transmitted to the capital, after which his final whereabouts became unknown.
Shi Sengti’s surname was Sun; originally from Changli, he later resided in Yingtao, Julu. His character and disposition were pure and noble.
Xiaoxin was renowned for his filial piety and integrity. He applied himself diligently to the secular classics, gaining a comprehensive mastery of the Confucian scriptures and histories.

Summoned to serve as a *boshi* (doctor) at the Imperial Academy, he examined the Buddhist sutras once and attained a profound, intuitive understanding. At the age of twenty-eight, he entered Jingming Monastery in Julu under the guidance of Master Sengshi and received the tonsure to become a monk.
There, he further sought out the sūtras and śāstras; his spiritual resolve was fierce and courageous, and he subsequently followed Master Daofang in the practice of meditation.
The Master received and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. His dwelling was that of the divine-footed (ṛddhipāda) Bhadra. He traveled north to Mount Jiayu in Dingzhou;

after concentrating his thoughts for a long time, he achieved no realization whatsoever. He then intended to leave the mountain to recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Suddenly he encountered a monk who said he had come from Mount Tai.
Hui-chou informed him of his situation, whereupon the monk earnestly exhorted him to practice *dhyāna*, warning him to be careful not to harbor other intentions. Because of this—

All sentient beings possess the *dhyāna* of the "taste of the first stage" (*prathamabhūmi-rasa-dhyāna*), which necessarily requires the binding of the object of focus; if one does not seek it, it will not be attained.

After ten days of following this practice, he focused his mind and indeed achieved meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He constantly relied upon the noble practices of *nirvāṇa* and the method of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), such that even in sleep and dreams, he perceived nothing but awakening, and was entirely free from thoughts of desire.
Having completed five summer retreats, he again went to Dao-ming on Mount Zhanghong in Zhaozhou.
The Zen Master received the Dharma of the Sixteen Special Victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*). He restricted his food and lashed his own mind, eating but once every ninety days.

Sometimes, while the food he was cooking had not yet been finished, he would withdraw his mind into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), remaining there for the duration of a full watch of the day. His previous meals were all devoured by birds and beasts. Furthermore, he constantly cultivated the perception of death;
when encountered by bandits who threatened him, he showed no sign of fear. Only then did the bandits explain their various karmic deeds to him, whereupon he shattered their bows.
Shi returned after receiving the precepts and frequently stayed in a secluded place on Mount Que. There, he was disturbed by a spirit that came to harass him;

Hui-chou resolved to die in order to test his resolve, and consequently attained profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), remaining unmoving for nine days. Later, awakening from this state, his mind and thoughts were serene and clear.
He then went to Shaoling Temple to present his realization to the Patriarch Tripiṭaka. Bodhidharma said: "To the east of the Pamir Mountains, as far as the study of Chan..."

"Excellent! You are such a person. He then bestowed upon him further profound and essential teachings. [Hui]ji immediately resided at Songyue Temple, where there were a hundred monks and the spring water was barely sufficient for their needs.
Suddenly, he saw a woman in tattered clothes holding a broom, sitting cross-legged on the steps and listening to the monks recite the sutras.
The assembly did not realize she was a divine being and rebuked her, ordering her to leave. The woman looked indignant and, with her foot, stepped upon the spring; the water immediately surged forth.
The water dried up and her body vanished. The assembly informed Sengchou, who called for the laywoman (upāsikā). After she was called three times, she emerged.

She then said to the spirit, "The monastic community is practicing the Way; you should provide protection. The woman then nudged the old spring with her foot, and the water immediately surged upward. Everyone marveled at its depth.
Thereafter, she frequently entered meditative absorption, always setting a period of seven days as her limit. [This occurred during the reign of] Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty.
In the second year of the Tenpō era, an imperial edict was issued to exhort him; only then did he finally grant his request.

On that very day, he brushed off his robes and was about to depart from the mountain retreat when both peaks suddenly shook with a start, their echoes mournful and piercing, causing humans and livestock to be thrown into alarm and birds and beasts to flee in all directions.

This continued for three days. He looked back and said: "Those who admire the Way and cherish benevolence find it present in all things. Is it not because human affections are easy to guard against? [He then departed.]

Is it difficult to maintain such detachment? He did not linger to attend to worldly affairs, but instead took up his staff and traveled toward the Zhang and Fu rivers. The Emperor personally led the imperial carriage out of the suburbs to welcome him.

Although he was over seventy years old, his spirit was clear and expansive, moving the hearts of all who encountered him; he treated all things with respectful composure and seized every opportunity without missing a beat.
The Emperor escorted him inside the palace and engaged him in discourse on the True Principle (*zhengli*), whereupon he expounded that the three realms are fundamentally empty and that all lands...
It was likewise so. The splendors of worldly phenomena cannot be maintained forever. [The Buddha] expounded the Dharma of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness in detail.

Upon hearing this, the Emperor’s hair stood on end and he broke into a sweat; he immediately received the path of dhyāna. After studying for no long time, he realized profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Thereafter, he continued to receive pure instructions with sincere and profound reverence. Consequently, he received the Bodhisattva precepts, abstained from alcohol and prohibited meat, and released hawks and falcons.

He abandoned his official post to pursue hunting and fishing, yet he established a kingdom overflowing with benevolence. Furthermore, he prohibited slaughter throughout the empire three times a month;

by imperial decree, the people were to observe the fasts and abstain from meat, and all pungent vegetables and strong-smelling herbs were removed from both public gardens and private plots. On another occasion, the Emperor remarked: "The Way is propagated by men."

"Truly, there is no empty response. I pray that the Master will set his mind at ease and maintain his mindfulness of the Way. Your disciple ventures to act as an external protector and donor (*dānapati*. Sengchou said:

"The Bodhisattva’s great vow takes the protection of the Dharma as its core purpose. Your Majesty responds to Heaven and accords with worldly custom; you occupy the position of the sovereign to establish transformation.

As a pillar for the Triple Gem and a guide for the four classes of people, since your benevolent governance has arrived, it is right that I entrust myself to you and not decline. Thereupon, he stayed within the palace precincts for four days.
After more than ten days, [Tanyou] daily offered clear instructions, which the Emperor followed without fail.
Later, as his transformation through the Way required its dissemination and he desired to dwell among the mountain forests, he took his leave to return to his original residence.

Because the hills and mounds were winding and interlaced, making it difficult to seek audience, in the third year of the Tianbao era, the Emperor again issued an edict to construct a vihāra on the southern slope of Longshan, eighty *li* southwest of Yecheng. It was named...
He was invited to reside at Yunmen Temple and concurrently served as the Abbot of Shiku Monastery. During his two terms in these administrative positions, he trained nearly a thousand monks;

the services and provisions provided were so extensive that they filled the mountain valleys. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Chan monasteries were established separately in various prefectures throughout the realm.
He caused those who possessed mindfulness and wisdom to attain full understanding. He was granted the title of "Professor" (Jiùwéi Jiàoshòu).

On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Qiánmíng era, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), he passed away peacefully in his mountain temple, free from all illness or affliction. He was eighty-one years of age.

By imperial decree, Prince Xiānglè was dispatched to offer condolences and oversee the construction of a stupa. Wèi Shòu, the Right Vice-Director of the Chancellery, composed the inscription for the stele.
Shi Yuantong left home to become a monk at a young age. He was widely loved for his broad learning and was renowned for his gentle and quick intelligence.

He went to Dazhuangyan Monastery in the capital city of Ye, where he studied and recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* with meticulous attention to its literary style and meaning. In the summer of the fourth year of the Wuping era of the Gao Qi dynasty, he began lecturing on it.

At that time, there was a visiting monk whose appearance and attire were simple and plain, yet whose conduct was broad and elegant. Because he was afflicted by illness, he sought refuge among the monastics of various temples;
however, as his ailment persisted and its foul odor wafted intensely, everyone loathed him and none dared to host him.

Yet, having observed that his capacity and discernment were vast and profound, they marveled deeply at his character and invited him into their quarters. Although it was filled with filth and impurity, from the very beginning—
Without any sense of condescension or apprehension, his sincere sentiments communicated their mutual understanding. [The host] asked what he studied, and he replied, "Nirvana.

It was evident that they shared a common background through their previous training; everything felt as familiar as an old acquaintance. He then proceeded to discuss the profound essentials of the sutras alongside the accumulated insights of past masters, narrating them all together.
The visiting monk likewise concurred with what was cited, further organizing it into chapters and verses. His analytical explanations were clear and lucid, possessing a truly elegant refinement.
Tong rejoiced in their shared affinity for the Way. He attended to his medicine and managed his care, staying by his side day and night.

Once, in the middle of the night, Tong took a cup of spring wine and urged him, saying, "It would be best if you take this. The guest then knit his brows and drank it; he stopped after a single swallow.
