When summer ended and his illness was cured, the guest took his leave and departed. Tong said, "The time for receiving winter robes is fast approaching; according to custom, officials at monasteries are entitled to a gift of robes. You may [accept them]."
"Wait for three or five days; I shall present you with a set of winter garments. The guest said, "I have already received your great kindness; why trouble yourself further?

Although Sōtō tried to detain him, he made the clothes and gave them to him. As they were parting, the guest took Sōtō’s hand and cautioned him, saying, "In the practice of the Way, do not deceive even in the dark room.
Previously, when you offered me wine, I feared it would mar your kind intentions; it was not in accordance with the True Principle. From this day forward..."
"I shall go. This matter must be settled. Have you ever visited the Stone Cave Temple on Mount Gu?

I, a humble monk, reside at a small temple in a lower quarter, located exactly five li north of the Stone Cave. There is a small valley winding along a mountain stream; exiting to the east from there is Zhulin Temple.
If you have occasion to go there, I hope you will visit me. I offer my respectful thanks for your previous instructions and shall certainly go to pay my respects. Thus he spoke.

They parted ways. When the beginning of the following summer arrived, as monks were rare at the Shiku Mountain Monastery, he reduced the number of monks from the official temples of Zhuangyan, Dingguo, Xingsheng, and Zongchi to about one hundred for a single group.

They spent the summer retreat together while staying in advance at Shiku, intending to visit Zhulin. Thereupon, they gathered a great assembly of guests and hosts and asked where the temple was located; everyone laughed heartily.
Tong cautioned [the author] not to spread these superstitious rumors. In the end, none were found in the Bamboo Grove; they were merely the common legends of the vulgar world.
Tong was a visiting monk who had been treated with exceptional hospitality; when he spoke of this matter, it was clear his words were not baseless. The assembly also regarded this with astonishment.

Thereupon, each of them took incense and flowers and traveled together with Tong. Upon reaching a small valley five *li* to the north of the monastery, they emerged to the east along a narrow path barely wide enough for a person.

After traveling about five *li*, they ascended a mountain ridge and saw an old man with a handkerchief tied around his forehead, wearing a short tunic and coarse cloth trousers, wielding a hoe to clear the land over some twenty *mu*.
Seeing the group of monks from afar, he let out his horse and came forward, saying: "What..."

The man who lived in the mountains did not follow the main paths. When the monks said they were staying in a stone cave and intended to head toward the bamboo grove, the man became furious and said, "Last year, when the government temple let its horses loose, they devoured my young crops. My son tried to protect them and was nearly beaten to death.
Have you come back with that same face now? He dragged his hoe forward to pursue them, and the dozen or so monks fled toward the valley, leaving him alone.
Futong did not pursue him. He said to Futong, "You are a capable man who does not return; let me go into the mountains to feed the tigers.

Futong then traveled east for several li until he came upon a winding stream, shallow yet surrounded by dense, lush vegetation. Following the stream further east, he heard the sound of chanting coming from atop the southern ridge.
Futong asked where the Bamboo Grove was located, and the voice replied immediately, "From where have you come?"
"Could this not be the Dharma Master Yuantong? Tong replied, "It is. Thereupon, [the monk] cleared the forest and crossed the precipices to approach Tong.

Tong briefly recounted their long separation, and his joy overflowed as he spoke of his feelings, saying, "The small temple at the foot of the mountain has monks who are like a ravening flock; their minds and natures, as well as their conduct and movements—"
For the most part, he did not deign to accept the invitation. Nevertheless, having already shown such great respect, he finally had to proceed to the monastery.

After traveling several *li* together, they suddenly beheld a pair of watchtowers and a lofty gate, with long corridors and double passageways. Tall bamboos reached the clouds, and green pines obscured the sun.

Outside the gate was a black-lacquered trough over a hundred feet long, arranged in ten rows, each lined with a hundred rings, exquisitely adorned with gold, copper, and fine embroidery, and filled with—

There were grains of millet and beans scattered about, and horse tracks nearby; yet it was swept clean and purified. He then established a gateway on the left and announced, "One must first consult the Great Master.
After a short while, he was led inside to the corridor beneath the western eaves of the lecture hall.

The Master sat upon a high couch, attended by fifty or sixty youths and clerks. The Master was about seventy years of age; his eyebrows and face were as sharp and elegant as mountain peaks. His appearance—
He resembled a monk from India; leaning upon a desk, he was occupied with documents. Beside him stood an attendant who announced his arrival and then stepped back.

The Upādhyāya commanded, "Since you reside in a state temple, it would be difficult to refuse such generous offerings; why have you deigned to come here yourself? This monastery truly has nothing worth seeing.

The attendant fully explained the reason for his visit, whereupon the Master ordered him to be settled in a room. He then led the attendant on a tour of the quarters to pay his respects, and saw two monks, each sitting in their respective rooms.
The jeweled canopy was draped with various ornaments that outshone the light of the sun. He addressed the monk, saying, "Who is this person who dares to enter here?
He shook his hand and dismissed him. The monk felt ashamed and looked back at Tong, saying, "Our dispositions are not in accord;
he has caused me to lose hope. For now, let us go to my small dwelling where we can speak freely. They then entered the room, where they recounted their past karmic connections in detail.
He also provided a midday meal; the food was of the same quality as the usual fare in Ye. After the meal, he led him on a tour.
The images were magnificent, and there were gardens, ponds, terraces, and pavilions. They traveled about and viewed them all, yet could not see everything. Tong Yin spoke from the heart, saying:

"If I might be permitted to join the ranks of the common laborers to constantly provide for the sweeping and sprinkling of the grounds, my life's wish would be fulfilled. The monk said: "I have already kept this intention in mind since we met; however, you must consult [the authorities]."
"Venerable Master, I do not yet know whether you will grant me a place or not. I stayed the night with you, and at dawn I came to consult you, saying:
'I am well aware of your intention; I would not begrudge you a single room. Generally, when one accepts an invitation from an official, the debt of gratitude is profound.

However, according to the monastic rules, one may not maintain two names simultaneously. I shall now return for the time being; once my official title has been removed, I will certainly come again and you must accept me. Do not harbor any resentment. Thus he spoke.
He was sent out and reached the side of the horse troughs; looking back with longing, he wept, lamenting that his own sins were so grave that he was not granted leave to stay.
Taking the hand of a monk to bid him farewell, he walked west for a hundred paces and still saw the gate towers standing solemnly as he looked back step by step.
After traveling another two *li*, he suddenly beheld jagged peaks and crags, no longer the monastery grounds. Despondent, he sought his way forward until he reached Kaiyuan Temple.
It was a desolate place, utterly devoid of any traces or signs, with nothing but wild shrubs.

Shi Dao-pian’s surname was Guo; he was a native of Cheng County in Caozhou. He lost his parents at the age of three and traveled to study at fifteen, gaining a broad mastery of both Confucianism and Daoism.
At nineteen, he resolved to leave the household life and sought refuge with his maternal uncle to receive the tonsure. After receiving full ordination, he...
He sought out virtuous friends throughout his travels. Whenever he read of the Buddhist teachings transmitted to the East, he lamented that he had not personally beheld its sacred sites.

Consequently, he resolved with courageous intent to reach the realm of the Buddha, vowing to behold and revere them. In the first year of the Gānmíng era of the Qi dynasty, he joined a party of twenty-one people and set forth from the capital of Yè.
As they traversed passes and barriers, which were strictly guarded, the moonlight shone upon them; yet they hesitated and turned back, for in principle, they could not proceed further.

As he was traveling, he suddenly encountered clouds rushing in and the moon disappearing; taking advantage of the darkness, he crossed a rickety plank bridge. In the second year of the Baoding era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, he arrived at the capital.
Emperor Wu received him with great honor and respect, and further ordered that he be provided with generous offerings at Dacheng Monastery.

After more than two years had passed, he submitted a memorial requesting to follow his original vow. He received an imperial decree granting him maps and books, as well as travel provisions and funds, and thus crossed the Stone Shingle (Shiqi) Pass to the west.

It was fifteen hundred *li* [in distance]. Looking in all four directions, it was desolate and vast; there was absolutely no water or grass. Traveling with urgency due to hunger, after seven days had passed, he arrived at the Kingdom of Gaochang.
This was a small vassal state of the Tujue (Turks). He again requested a letter of introduction from the state.

Upon reaching the residence of Ke Han of the western region, the local people were unfamiliar with the assembly of monks (*saṃgha*) and intended to inflict harm upon them. They increased their guard and did not provide him with provisions.

Furthermore, they were not permitted to go out to gather firewood or vegetables; they were merely left to die of hunger. A messenger from the state of Zhou remonstrated against this cold treatment, saying, "These are disciples of the Buddha.
The sovereign and high ministers of their native land revere and provide for them with offerings. Wherever they travel," [they are treated with such respect].

He was able to cause the sheep and horses to multiply, which brought great joy to Kan. [Kan] provided four sheep daily for his constant sustenance and decreed that they be released equally among the herd.

He himself cooked vegetables to eat. Having seen that he did not kill living beings and did not consume wine or meat, and observing that his conduct was so exceptional, [the official] would not allow him to go further west.
Instead, he provided him with a horse and carriage and dispatched an attendant to escort him back, arriving safely at Chang’an.
While residing at Qiansong Monastery, he encountered Dharma Master Jing’ai and consulted him on matters concerning the Way. Jing’ai’s wisdom and religious practice were profound and far-reaching;
he had already passed through five cycles [of persecution]. When Emperor Wu suppressed the Dharma, he fled westward with Jing’ai to Mount Taibai, accompanied by twenty-six fellow practitioners.

Fleeing from the turmoil, he lived in mountain caves, never ceasing his lectures and instruction. He investigated the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and the four *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikās* day and night. With humble reverence, he followed the teachings;

though there was the threat of capital punishment for his state, he disregarded the possibility of death. To the east, he traveled through the mountains as far as Mount Hua. Of all those who sought refuge with him, they came to him like the rising sun.
Thus, he relied upon and inherited Da’ai’s virtue, becoming the foremost disciple within the inner circle. From beginning to end, this lasted ten years.

For five years, he followed [Falin] without ceasing. Later, when Fa’ai cast off his body in a remote valley to manifest his protection of the Dharma, [Falin] judged that the situation was fraught with bitterness and poison;
he respectfully received the remains, erected a stupa and inscribed a stele, carving the inscription upon the cliff face.

When Emperor Tianyuan succeeded to the throne, he sought to reform the heterodox customs and established a community of one hundred and twenty people as Bodhisattva monks, assigning them to this office. Initially, [Falin] resided at Zheshu Temple.

When the Great Sui dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven, they widely propagated the Buddha-dharma and renamed it Daxingshan (Great Flourishing Goodness). [The Master] presided over the monastic community with profound harmony and served as the head of the administrative leadership throughout his tenure.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he entered the Zhongnan Mountains to the eastern ridge of Jiaogou Valley. There was a pond known as Yezhe, situated far above the clouds and overlooking the plains below.
He personally inspected the site and found it a place where one could settle the mind; thus, he thatched grass to build a hermitage and gathered a community of followers.

Regarding the lectures: In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict dispatched Li Shishi, the Vice Minister of the Department of Revenue, to bring Indian medical craftsmen to construct a vihāra for the purpose of constant imperial service.
It was known that the site for the cultivation of the Way was vast and open, so it was granted a formal name and established as Longchi Temple.
The Great General Yun Dingxing took him as his *dānapati* (donor) and provided for all four necessities of life.

The Gentle Attendant Du Guji, who revered his teachings and character, built a separate meditation hall in the garden behind his residence and invited him to stay there, where he received his instructions on the Dharma and precepts.

Duke Xue and his wife, Lady Zheng, had long followed his pure guidance; they visited the mountain once a year to consult him regarding the precepts and receive his instructions. They resolved [their doubts]...
He resolved all doubts and deliberations. At dawn on the fourth day of the fifth month in the eleventh year of the Daye era, he passed away at the mountain temple.

Shi Sengfan’s surname was Li; he was a native of Pingxiang. From his youth, he studied various books, and by the age of twenty-three, he had thoroughly mastered both the detailed commentaries and the concise summaries.
As for the seven luminaries, the nine divisions of astronomy, and the arts of divination, he consulted them but required no second realization.
People of the time said: "Li Hongfan of Xiangzhou understands the profound meanings thoroughly; Zhang Bingsheng of Ye understands everything without omission.

Furthermore, because of his youthful appearance and handsome countenance, he had no desire for marriage. He sought to attach himself to the Dharma, burning off his fingers as an act of offering. At the age of twenty—
19. While living in a small town, he heard a lecture on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Upon hearing it once, his mind was awakened; he subsequently entered the monastic order at Ye City.

He then traveled to Luoyang, where he studied the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under Master Xian. Later, he received the Way from Master Zheguang, deeply savoring the profound essence of the Empty Doctrine (*śūnyatā*).
He traveled abroad to propagate the teachings, bringing benefit and peace to the Qi and Wei regions. Whenever a Dharma assembly was convened, the audience—

There were more than a thousand [students]. Upon his arrival at the capital of Ye, he enabled Cui Jin to comment on the *Yi* by consulting him to adopt its strengths, and led Zong Jing to compile a calendar by seeking him out to discard its weaknesses.
Great scholars such as Xu Zunming and Li Baoding gained faith in his words upon their first meeting.

He received the Bodhisattva precepts, and the five assemblies flocked to him like a marketplace. He lectured on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*;
for each, he produced commentaries and records. Furthermore, he transformed these commentaries by citing the sūtras to compose them as formal treatises (*śāstra*).

Consequently, works such as the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* were all referred to as "treatises," while the ten sections of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* alone were specifically termed "expositions" (*nirdeśa*). Nevertheless, his phrasing was prolix and grandiose.

Coinciding with worldly sentiments, his words and deeds supported one another, and auspicious omens descended repeatedly. There was once Du Bi, the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhou, who requested Daofan to give a winter lecture at Xianyi Temple in Ye.
When they reached the sixth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a wild goose suddenly flew down from the east of the pagoda, proceeding along the corridor into the hall.
It settled directly facing the high seat, prostrating on the ground to listen to the Dharma. Once the lecture concluded, it slowly departed and returned.
He followed the stupa westward until he vanished. Furthermore, while delivering a summer lecture at this temple, sparrows came and sat among the assembly;

they remained crouched in the southwest corner, listening until the end of the ninety-day period. He once resided in Jizhou, where another bird also flew in to listen; it departed as soon as the lecture concluded.
Various auspicious omens moved the multitude; the Way permeated all, and there was a profound resonance with the unseen realm.
Shi Mingda, surnamed Kang, was a native of Kangju. Having left the household life while still a child, he strictly observed the fasts and precepts. Initially, he received the ten precepts.
He then guarded his five sense-faculties. Upon reaching full maturity, his conduct became even more rigorous: he did not let his side touch the mat, and he took no second meal throughout the day.
He established external decorum and ritual rules while internally cultivating the causes of the Path. With universal salvation as his heart’s intent, he made his travels his primary task.

At the beginning of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, he came from the Western Regions and arrived in the region of Yizhou. At that time, the Mian tribes of the Ba and Xia valleys were plundering and looting with great force, causing turmoil among the prefectures and commanderies.
Da was conscripted for military service. With a fixed deadline for his execution, he resolved to save others and set out alone to visit the rebels.

He comforted and enticed them, yet they had not yet become familiar with his intentions. Suddenly, wind and rain darkened the sky, and thunderbolts struck with a roar. The rebels were struck with terror and piteously sought mercy.
Da then prepared a thousand lamps and prayed with sincere devotion to the Triple Gem. As soon as his preparations were complete, the gloom and mist instantly cleared away. All at once—

However, all the states within his gaze followed the King’s transformation. Carriers with infants on their backs crowded the marshes, and otters and wild beasts rushed forward in droves, filling the wetlands.
Consequently, the river routes became clear and serene; travel back and forth was unhindered. Without the deployment of military force, ten thousand *li* were made level and peaceful.
Later, while traveling on official business, he encountered a man on the road binding a pig to the ground. The pig spoke in human voice, saying: "I pray that the Supreme Sage [will grant me life]."
"Save me! Da immediately disrobed to ransom him and set him free. When they reached Niutou Mountain in Zizhou, he wished to construct a stupa and a vihara;
yet, instead of seeking timber or stone, he went directly to look for craftsmen. Both monastics and laypeople found his words strange.

At that time, after three months, the waters receded. They went down to search for timber and found a long piece of wood in the water, which was exactly suitable for a pillar at the site of the monastery;
its length and proportions were perfect. Everyone was delighted and proceeded to erect it.

By the fourth month, the Fu River overflowed its banks, and the wood floated down, covering the river until it came to rest against the village shore, where it remained fixed without moving. Da and all his followers, both monastics and laypeople, were filled with wonder.

He gathered them all together, piling them up like mountains both lengthwise and crosswise. He first constructed a hall and erected a nine-story pagoda; people from near and far joined their efforts, completing the construction all at once.
The labor did not exceed a short time, and it was suddenly and perfectly accomplished. As for himself, he wore the three robes made entirely of coarse cloth;

when they became worn, he would mend and patch them, remaining unchanged through both cold and heat. At times, while in meditative concentration, he sat upon his meditation seat, and a brilliant fire [blazed forth].
He rose, and the crowd went to extinguish it, but he felt only a refreshing coolness. There was a śramaṇa named Sengjiu who suffered from chronic ailments, stiffness, and lameness;
he came to beg for a cure. Da immediately gave him a staff and told him to walk; before the sun had shifted its shadow, he returned with rapid strides.
Furthermore, during the uposatha ceremony, he sat at the head of the assembly. At that time, a thief broke through a wall to carry off goods; having gone outside, he became dazed and confused.
He returned to seek refuge at the monastery, whereupon [the Master] exhorted him and sent him away. In the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era, he accompanied Prince Shixing back to Jingzhou.
In the twelfth month of winter, he passed away in Jiangling at the age of fifty-five.

Shi Fazong, surnamed Duan, was a native of Taiyuan in Bingzhou. From his youth, he devoted himself to the recitation of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Having mastered the entire text, his primary interest lay in its literary phrasing and terminology.

Later, upon hearing the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning), he immediately began to lecture and propagate it. During the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, he was summoned to serve as the presiding master of the *Nirvāṇa* assembly.
Residing at Haijue Monastery, he gathered disciples from all quarters and constantly expounded the ultimate truth. At the beginning of the Renshou era—
An imperial edict was issued to dispatch śarīra relics to Zhimen Temple in Suizhou. When the foundation was excavated to a depth of three chi, a divine tortoise was obtained;
it was yellowish-green in color and its markings resembled colorful embroidery. Upon its head were eight characters which read: "For the Great King, eighty-seven thousand years."
Beneath its belly were the two characters "Wang Xing" (King Rising). By the willow trees beside the Suihou Bridge, it again rained down sweet dew;
its appearance was like falling rain, fragrant, sweet, thick, and moist. The multitude drank of it together and reported the matter to the Emperor.

The Emperor paid his respects to this auspicious omen and constantly kept this tortoise upon his imperial throne for the ministers to observe. After some months had passed, the Emperor went on a tour to the Northern Garden.
He was released into a clear pond; although he submerged and swam for a short time, he emerged again and circled the pond, following the Emperor’s person more than once.

Those in attendance and guard all witnessed this and together rejoiced at the auspicious response. In the spring of the fourth year, an imperial decree was issued again to send śarīra relics to Xiasheng Temple in Liaozhou.
They emitted light and divided into grains in great numbers; the stone casket transformed into patterns like brocade, and as for the child...
The image of the Son [of the Buddha] is within the casket facing north, appearing amidst the twin trees with a reclining Buddha beneath it.

Furthermore, to the south of the casket, there appears the form of a Vajrapāṇi holding a vajra and pointing it toward a mountain. Moreover, to the east of the casket, two Buddhas appear standing together along with a qilin.
Additionally, to the west of the casket, a bodhisattva appears together with a divine nun, who bows her body with palms joined toward the bodhisattva.
Sā. Furthermore, he emitted a great light that rose up in a chaotic swirl, dazzling the eyes of men from dusk until dawn.

Although all the lamps were extinguished, the light continued to shine without ceasing, no different from the brilliance of the sun and moon. That night, during the dark rain, a yellow light was emitted from the *garuḍa* finial (*kīrṇaka*) of the Buddha hall;
it flew and shifted three hundred paces toward the southeast. Following the source of this light, it was found to have issued from within the hall.

It emerged from the site of benefit, and the entire assembly saw it clearly, all of whom were greatly inspired to seek the Way. On the eighth day, as the image was about to descend, a five-colored cloud-canopy covered the top of the stupa.
Furthermore, a wondrous bird appeared, with a white body, black tail, and red beak; it held a fragment of cloud in its mouth, shaped like a floral canopy, and likewise manifested atop the stupa.
On the ninth day of the fourth month, light was emitted from the base of the stupa, dividing into five streams that headed straight west.
It departed. Its form was like a painted image; it was drawn for several hundred li, and those who saw it were not few. The Emperor himself attended this auspicious omen, his joy arising from within.
He commissioned a detailed illustration and presented it to the throne. By imperial decree, it was enshrined in the Secret Library (Bige).

Shi Tongzhen’s surname was Li. His distant ancestors were from Longxi, and his family resided in Puzha in Hedong. From his youth, he grew weary of birth and death and set his heart upon the eternal abiding (nitya).

He entered the service of Dharma Master Tanyan as his preceptor and model. He synthesized the profound mysteries of both Buddhism and Confucianism; his brilliant talents and outstanding conduct were exemplary.

After receiving full ordination, he returned to the fundamental principles of the Vinaya. Later, he delved into the sutras and śāstras, gaining a thorough understanding of both Mahayana and Hinayana teachings, and was particularly adept at the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the Daxingshan Monastery to translate Sanskrit texts face-to-face with the originals.

In the sixteenth year, an edict appointed him as the Director of Nirvana Affairs for All Sentient Beings. In the first year of the Renshou era, an edict was issued to construct spirit-stupas throughout the entire realm.
From the various provinces in both the front and rear regions, one hundred and eleven locations all sent śarīra relics.

Because Emperor Wen of the Sui Dynasty was a true king of virtue at that time, he issued an imperial decree ordering that they be conveyed to Yongzhou to establish a sacred stupa. Consequently, the śarīra were sent to Xianyou Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
This is the very place traditionally said in ancient lore to be where Nongyu, the daughter of Duke Mu of Qin, practiced the arts of the immortals and ascended into the clouds. At first...

In the tenth month, as [Seng]zhen traveled from the capital to the monastery, he encountered snow and rain along the way; they fell in torrents and poured down heavily, soaking both people and things.
Yet, upon the carriage carrying the śarīra alone, not a drop of moisture fell. All marveled at this anomaly. The monastery was situated in a valley pass where wind roared day and night;
yet from the moment the sacred relics first arrived until their final interment, all was serene and perfectly still. Furthermore, lamps shone brightly throughout the mountains and valleys.
As dark clouds closed in on all sides and snow and rain fell together, he hoped for clear skies and the appearance of the sun so that the appointed time limit might be met.
Truly, holding an incense burner and giving rise to a great vow, just as the final deadline arrived, the winter sun shone down. It was precisely at noon;

both monastics and laypeople rejoiced together. Once the covering was completed, the clouds closed in once more, leading the great assembly to sigh in admiration. This occurred in the first year of the Daye era.

In the [X] year, he engaged in great meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). An imperial edict was issued summoning him to serve as the master of the monastic center (*dharmapada*). In the ninth year of the Daye era, he passed away at his residence temple due to illness.
Shi Daomi’s secular surname was Zhou; he was a native of Xiangzhou. Initially, he entered the service of the Tripiṭaka Master Yaśas to study various arts and skills, and subsequently followed...

In Yecheng, he studied the Mahāyāna and mastered the Indic languages and scripts of the West. During the rise of the Sui dynasty, when the propagation of the Dharma was being promoted, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital to serve as a translator.
He resided at Daxingshan Temple, where both teacher and disciples achieved spiritual perfection, and he further propagated the Indian languages.

During the Renshou era, when the construction of the stupas began, an imperial edict was issued summoning him to deliver the śarīra relics to Daxingguo Temple in Tongzhou; this temple was the birthplace of Emperor Wen.

This was the site where his original foundation lay: the Banni Monastery. On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Datong era of the Later Wei dynasty, the Emperor was born within this monastery.
At that time, a crimson light illuminated the chamber and overflowed beyond its outer doors;

purple vapors filled the courtyard, appearing like a multi-storied pavilion, and their hue stained the clothing of those inside and out. Both within and without were struck with alarm. As the weather was sweltering, the wet nurse...

It was hot, so he approached her and fanned her. It was so bitterly cold that she nearly died; exhausted, she could not cry out. There was a divine nun named Zhixian, a woman of the Liu clan from Puzha in Hedong.
She had left home to become a nun at a young age, possessed strict observance of the precepts, and made the practice of dhyāna meditation her vocation.
On the Emperor’s birthday, she arrived without any apparent cause and said to the Grand Ancestor (Taizu), "This child is protected by celestial beings; do not worry.
The nun then named the Emperor Nārāyaṇa, saying that he was like a vajra—indestructible. She further remarked, "The origins of this child are beyond the ordinary;
his secular home is defiled and impure, so I shall raise him myself. Thereupon, the Grand Ancestor partitioned his residence to establish a temple within it.

He passed through a small gate and entrusted the child to a nun, not daring to inquire after him by name. Later, when the Empress Dowager came to embrace him, she suddenly saw that he had transformed into a dragon;
in her alarm, she fell to the ground. The nun said, "Why did you recklessly touch my child?

Consequently, [the Emperor] would later obtain the empire. When the child reached the age of seven, he told the Emperor: "I am destined for great nobility. I have come from the Eastern Country. The Buddha-dharma shall soon perish. Because of this—

Her son, Xingzhi, rose [to prominence], while the nun remained serene and spoke little. Whenever she predicted the success or failure of affairs, or their auspicious or inauspicious outcomes, there was never a discrepancy.
Initially raised in a temple, the Emperor did not return home until he was thirteen years old; for more than thirty years thereafter, she rarely left her door.

When the Northern Zhou dynasty suppressed the two religions, the nun concealed herself within the imperial palace, wearing dharma robes internally, yet her observance of the precepts remained unchanged. Later, the Emperor...
The fruition indeed came from the east; he entered the capital as the Son of Heaven and extensively restored the Buddha-dharma, exactly as the bhikṣuṇī had foretold.

After ascending the throne, he would frequently look upon his ministers and reminisce about the ācārya, making it a constant topic of conversation. He would further say: "My rise to power was brought about by the Buddha-dharma."

She was fond of eating sesame and beans. Because she had come from among the practitioners in a previous life, having been at a monastery since childhood, she took pleasure in hearing the sound of bells until her present life.
Thereupon, she commanded the court historian Wang Shao to compose a biography for her as a nun.

Regarding the forty-five provinces through which she had passed in her hidden state, they all simultaneously became Great Xingguo Monasteries; consequently, the Prajñā Monastery was renamed one of them.
In the first year of the Renshou era, the Emperor and the ladies of the inner court were both moved by the appearance of śarīras, all of which emitted radiance.

When tested with a hammer and an anvil, they remained perfectly intact without any damage. Consequently, they were distributed throughout the provinces and prefectures, and more than one hundred stupas were erected.
Beneath each stupa, the divine nun was depicted, many of whom displayed miraculous signs. Through the recommendation of those who had heard of her in secret, she was sent to this temple. At first...

When the stupa was lowered, a single courtyard was filled with radiance, alternating between yellow and white, interspersed with vermilion-tinged vapors that circled about and shone with clarity before fading after a long time.
At the end of the Renshou era, an imperial decree was again issued to secretly transport it to Jin’an Temple on Mount Huanggu in Ezhou.
When the foundation was excavated down to the water level, a golden image approximately one chi in height was discovered; its iconographic style was exceptionally unique.

At the time the stupa was being lowered into place, flocks of wild birds flew about, circling above the stupa before dispersing once the work was finished. Furthermore, three golden flowers were seen soaring into the air;
after lingering for a long while, they descended and vanished. From within the foundation, fireflies also emitted light, which subsequently expanded until it circled the stupa three times.

Although the temple was originally high and prominent, it had never possessed a spring; whenever water was needed, one had to go down to draw it. One night, however, [a spring] appeared at a distance from the stupa.
After five paces, a spring gushed forth spontaneously, resembling the famous Lang-well (Wave Well).

At the beginning of the Daye era, he was secretly transferred to the Shanglin Garden in Luoyang and placed within the Institute for Translating Scriptures (*fanjing guan*), where he subsequently carried out his translations. He eventually passed away at that very location.
Shi Tanrong’s secular surname was Zhang; he was a native of Jiumen in Dingzhou.

At the age of nineteen, he was a scholar who applied himself with great diligence to profound principles. Upon hearing Dharma Master Lingyu lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he went to listen and immediately attained thorough awakening.

He then became a disciple of Lingyu. Observing that Tanrong was diligent and self-restrained, Lingyu subsequently ordained him. After receiving full ordination, he specialized exclusively in the Vinaya.
His school took the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* as its study. Initially, during the period when the two teachings were abolished under the Zhou dynasty, he concealed his form within the secular realm;

outwardly, he conformed to the dust of the world, yet inwardly, he partook of the flavor of the Way. When the Sui dynasty first restored the teachings, he followed conditions to propagate transformation, remaining entirely free from attachment.

Upon reaching the age of forty, he set out westward in pursuit of the Way. Traveling as far as Shangdang, he took up residence among the mountains of Luceng and Licheng, constructing a dwelling by a cliff.

Yu immediately sought to go into hiding. As his sublime virtue filled him, both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with devotion. His physical presence was majestic and profound; he feigned illness and prescribed remedies.
All who partook of his food and drink were moved by his supreme grace. Ritual offerings grew ever more abundant, and those who came to seek his guidance arrived in great numbers.

Amidst the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he hoped to preserve his precepts and virtue, guarding them with all his might. He personally presided as the Master of the Dharma during every spring and summer.
He practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi for a full year, engaging in seated meditation and recitation during both autumn and winter.

Monks and nuns were housed in separate quarters, ensuring that the five assemblies gathered like smoke and the hundred offerings assembled like scales of fish. From the states of Jin, Wei, Han, Zhao, Zhou, and Zheng, members of the Śākya clan renewed their precepts;
he frequently traveled to Yansheng Temple in the district of Hanshou to establish the method of repentance, a practice which the local governor also embraced.

The Venerable [Renshou] had long been a devoted follower of the Śākya school, and his family had maintained offerings for generations. He presented three grains of śarīra to the assembly of practitioners on the pilgrimage route.
At the age of nearly eighty, he personally led a procession of three thousand monastics and laypeople, traveling twenty-odd *li* along the road to welcome them.

The grandeur of his retinue brought him renown throughout the land at that time. Upon arriving at the monastery, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The virtue of the śarīra is truly extraordinary..."

His manifestations were without fixed form. When his accumulated karma was exhausted, he requested that his wishes be fulfilled; thus, before each person, a water bowl was separately placed and incense burners added.
He prayed fervently throughout the night, and when the appointed time arrived, a total of more than four hundred śarīra relics were obtained within the bowls.
His reputation spread throughout the local villages and towns. The County Magistrate, fearing that he would gather a large following and thereby violate the regulations, suppressed his activities.

That very night, strange beasts howled at his hall and residence; both officials and commoners remained restless throughout the night. The next morning, [the Magistrate] expressed regret and finally permitted him to practice the Dharma.
In the summer of the ninth year of the Wude era, he established a site for practicing the Way at Jiaozhang Village in Lucheng. This was the hall where he resided.
The hall suddenly collapsed of its own accord, and the shrine, the image, and the śarīra emerged intact, scattered across the courtyard without the slightest damage.
Furthermore, in the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, the lay devotees Changyi, Bao, and others invited Huirong to the Fazhu Temple in the provincial seat to perform the Fangdeng Repentance Rite.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, there was a śramaṇa named Sengding from that temple who...
His conduct in the precepts was refined and firm. Within the site of enlightenment, he beheld a great radiance of five intermingling colors arising from above and descending.
In its midst were seven Buddhas, whose marks and signs were extraordinary. They spoke to the monk Sengding, saying: "We are the Tathāgatas Vipaśyin, the Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones.
Because your offenses have been extinguished, we have come to bear witness. However, we are not your original teachers and shall not bestow upon you a prophecy. Thus it was.
These six Buddhas all spoke with these same words. The last Buddha said: "I am your original teacher, Śākyamuni.
Because your transgressions have been extinguished, I have come to bestow this prediction upon you. Tánróng is your excellent condition for the eradication of sin;
within the Bhadrakalpa, he shall be named Púníng Buddha. Your physical vessel is now pure; in the future, you shall become a Buddha named Pǔmíng. If...
This was the response. A spiritual omen manifested immediately. Later, while lying ill upon his bed, tears flowed from his eyes.

His disciple Yuanzong asked, "Master, throughout your life you have cultivated mindfulness and wisdom; surely there is nothing that troubles your mind. For what reason do you weep? He replied, "The day of my death is drawing near.
I regret that I shall no longer be able to wash away the karmic burdens of the great assembly. This was in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
In the twelfth month of that year, he passed away at Fazhu Temple at the age of eighty-five.

Shi Mingjing was a native of Gaodi. He left home to become a monk in his youth and took the cultivation of meditative concentration as his primary practice. His will was pure and his devotion sincere; he was prudent, generous, serene, and solemn.
He frequently dwelt in meditative seclusion on Mount Meng by the seaside for several decades, such that no one could fathom him. Later, he traveled south.
To the east of Mount Tiantai, he dwelt among the various mountains, keeping meditative contemplation in his heart and acting in accordance with the demands of the moment.

His fellow practitioners and fellow meditators did not yet look up to him with great admiration. When provisions from the mountain ran out, he would go daily into the villages to beg for food; while returning along the road, he encountered a pack of tigers.
All of them had their mouths agape and eyes closed, appearing as if they were starving. Sengjing said, "I have traveled extensively through mountains and marshes."
Tigers and rhinoceroses have no conscious fear of him. Now that he stands by the roadside, is it not for the sake of food?
He then uses a spoon to scoop rice and place it into their mouths; the remainder he eats facing them until it is gone. The next day he went begging for alms, and the tiger was as before.

Such occurrences happened frequently, and his companions marveled at his extraordinary conduct. Once, they encountered a severe drought during which the crops were all withered. [At a place of] licentious sacrifice—
The rain flowed on. Although they offered false prayers and invitations with great earnestness and sincerity, they were ultimately unable to bring it about.

Jing said, "You may cease all these heterodox supplications; I alone can cause the rain to fall. He then observed a fast in a quiet room. At dawn on the seventh day, clouds gathered and rain was bestowed, pouring down upon the high and low lands alike.
The common people benefited from it and revered him as a sage. From the winter of the third year of the Zhenguan era until the summer of the following year, for six [months]...

The moon shone far and clear without a drop of rain. The Son of Heaven issued an edict ordering that both the traditions of Śākyamuni and Li (Buddhism and Daoism), the various temples of mountains and rivers, and even all illicit cults, should universally perform *yu* rain rituals.
At that time, for ten thousand *li*, the sky blazed with heat, yet there was no response at all. Officials and commoners looked upon one another in despair and grief.

There was a Minister of the Court named Pan, who had previously served in Mí Prefecture and knew that Jìngnéng was capable of inducing spiritual responses; he submitted a formal memorial regarding this matter.

He was summoned by imperial decree to the capital and ordered to reside there for the purpose of praying for rain. The Emperor informed him of his requirements, stipulating that not a single cent should be spent on expenses;

he requested only that he maintain quiet contemplation of the Triple Gem and compassionately deliver the four classes of living beings. He promised that after seven days, a sweet rain would surely descend.

If one wished to repay this virtue, the Emperor decreed that all deserted temples within the realm and privately ordained monks should be restored under his name, so that the holy Way might be propagated. An imperial edict granted this permission. Although...
Without being provided with any supplies, he was instead granted fragrant oil. At the Zhuangyan Temple, he sat in silent meditation in a quiet room.

When the seventh day approached dawn, he asked the guards, "There ought to be a white rainbow in the northwest of the sky; you may try to observe it. Upon hearing his words, they looked and saw it immediately.
Jing said, "Rain will surely arrive. In a moment the clouds gathered, and a torrential rain suddenly fell. By the time it reached the hour of *bú* (sunset), [the rain had ceased].

Throughout the realm, all was well-ordered. After a fresh rain had recently cleared the skies, the farmers were engaged in their labors; the seedlings had emerged from the ridges, yet as no further rain followed, they began to wither and fall, on the verge of death.
With no recourse left for their plans, Fang Xuanling, the Left Vice President of the Secretariat, personally visited the place of purification to request that he pray once more for rain.
Jing said, "The rising and falling of rain depend upon the sovereign and his ministers. What virtue do I, Jing, possess to dare to receive such sincere entrustment? Previously...

It was granted that there would be no retribution; both the hidden and the manifest shared this concern. If one cultivates purity and makes a request, rain should likewise arrive. This matter was reported to the Emperor, who again granted his permission.

He then issued an edict to temporarily suspend secular affairs and for the entire court to observe the fast. Sengjing then sat in meditation as before. At the end of seven days, the previous moisture descended once more.
The four classes of people were joyful and at peace, and the year consequently became bountiful. An edict was then issued to ordain three hundred [monks] in total.

He provided food for a thousand monks to repay his mother’s pure virtue; however, as the capital was noisy and chaotic, his nature did not favor such bustle, so he requested to return to his native village at Yisheng Temple.
There he lived among the mountains as Jieye, and in the end, no one could determine whether he was alive or dead.
Shi Daoxuan’s secular surname was Qian; he was a native of Dantu. His ancestors were descendants of Qian Rang, the Governor of Guangling, whose profound virtue has endured for a hundred generations.
When his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed that the moon pierced her womb; she further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to her, "The one you are carrying..."
He was the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty, who was formerly the monk Senghu of Yinyue Temple on Mount Shanyu during the Southern Qi.
He was suited for the monastic life from birth; his birthday was the eighth day of the fourth month. At age nine, he was able to compose poetry; at fifteen, he grew weary of worldly life.

He recited and studied various sutras under the tutelage of Vinaya Master Zhiyun. At sixteen, he shaved his head at Riyen Monastery (Dayan Daochang), where he applied himself with single-minded devotion and attained spiritual realization. He moved the hearts of those around him...
His spiritual benefit was manifested within a jeweled casket. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Zhishou.

He practiced the Vinaya, having heard it only once, before setting his mind on cultivating dhyāna. Master Ying rebuked him, saying: "One travels to distant places starting from nearby ones; one comes to know the fundamental principles through the subtle."
There are times for the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*); when one’s meritorious vows must be fulfilled, it is not yet appropriate to depart according to the Vinaya.

After suppressing [his desires] and allowing him to hear [the teachings] twenty times, he then sat in the mountain forests to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). He concealed his traces in the Valley of the Palm at Zhongnan Mountain.

His dwelling lacked water; a divine being pointed it out to him. Upon digging the earth by more than a foot, a spring gushed forth. At that time, it was called Baiquan Temple (White Spring Monastery). Fierce...
Wild beasts became docile and submissive; they always found refuge there. Fragrant, famous flowers bloomed, and rare herbs spread their tendrils.

At the end of the Sui dynasty, he moved from Chongyi Jingshe and was later transferred to Fengde Temple. Once, while sitting in solitary meditation, a Dharma-protecting deity informed him: "In that Qinggong Village..."

Therefore, at the site of Jingye Monastery, the Way may be practiced and perfected. Having heard this, [the Master] made his divination there. He burned the incense of merit and practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*.

At that time, a multitude of dragons came to pay their respects; whether male or female, they transformed themselves into human forms. A novice monk, however, allowed his mind to wander and looked back with a sidelong, lustful gaze.
The dragons were suddenly provoked to a fierce rage and were about to seize and claw him. He immediately felt remorse and spat poison into a well. [The Master] proclaimed—
He knew it was sealed, yet someone would secretly open it, and often smoke would rise from within.

Observing these divine transformations, he sometimes found a casket containing extraordinary flowers shaped like jujube blossoms, as large as elm seeds, with a most fragrant scent. He also offered him rare fruits such as pears and crabapples, which were sweet in taste and pure in color, unlike anything encountered in the human world.
There was a scholar-recluse named Sun Simiao who frequently lived in seclusion at Mount Zhongnan.
Daoshan formed a friendship with Xuán beneath the forest trees. Whenever they visited one another, their discussions would continue until late at night.

At that time, there was a drought, and a monk from the Western Regions established an altar at Kunming Lake to pray for rain. By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to prepare incense, lamps, and ritual implements.
After seven days, the water in the lake rose several feet daily. One night, an old man came to Xuán seeking rescue, appearing quite distressed.
In a state of great urgency, he said, "I am the dragon of Kunming Lake. That there has been no rain at this time is the will of Heaven;
it does not stem from me. Now, Western monks seek profit from me by deceiving the Son of Heaven, claiming they are praying for rain."
"My life hangs by a thread; I beg for the protection of the Dharma. Xuán replied, "I am unable to save you. You must urgently seek Master Sūn.
The old man went to Simǎo’s stone chamber and lamented his grievance repeatedly, saying, "Master Xuán instructed me to come here."
"Therefore, I venture to entrust myself to you. Miao said, "I know that in the Dragon Palace of Kunming Lake there are thirty scrolls of immortal formulas (*xiānfāng*).
Show them to me, and I shall save you. The old man said, "These formulas are not permitted to be transmitted recklessly in the higher realms.
But now the situation is desperate; what would I begrudge? After a short while, he presented the formulas. Miao said, "Return quickly; do not fear the foreign monks."
From that time on, the water in the pond swelled greatly; after several days, it overflowed the banks. The Western monk’s arts were exhausted.

When Ximing Monastery was first completed, an imperial edict appointed Xuanchong as its *upādhyāya*. When the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang arrived, an edict ordered him to assist with the translation work.

During the Zhenguan era, while Xuanchong was practicing the Way at Ximing Monastery, his foot slipped. There was something before him that supported him, allowing him to tread upon empty space without harm. Looking closely at it, he saw that it was—
A youth was there. Xuān hurriedly asked, "Who are you? Why are you here in the middle of the night? The youth replied, "I am no ordinary person;
I am Nàzhā, the son of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. For the sake of protecting the Dharma, I have been guarding this place for a long time. Xuān said:
"I, a poor monk, practice the Way; there is no need to trouble the Crown Prince with such matters. However, Your Highness possesses sovereign power throughout the Western Regions.
If there is anything that can serve the Buddha's work, I pray you will procure it for me. The Crown Prince replied, "I possess a precious Buddha-tooth relic," and he immediately presented it to Xuán.

He propagated the protection [of the Dharma] and was provided with offerings. Furthermore, in the courtyard, a deity came to pay his respects and said to Xuan, "The Vinaya Master shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
He gave him a bundle of objects, saying they were "thorn-forest incense" (*kaṇṭaka-vana-gandha*). Later, after sitting in meditation for one hundred days, he passed away.
His disciples interred him in a stone chamber at Tangu Valley. Subsequently, three stupas were erected there during the reign of Emperor Gaozong.
Imperial Decree: Order that [his portrait] be adorned and depicted for wide circulation (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Shi Yixiang’s secular surname was Park; he was a native of Gyeongrim-bu. He was born with extraordinary brilliance and grew up seeking renunciation. Wandering freely, he entered the Way.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he heard that the teachings of the Tang lands were flourishing and, sharing the same aspirations as Dharma Master Wonhyo, [he traveled there].

Traveling westward, he arrived at the border of Tangzhou by the coastal gateway of his own country. He sought out a large ship intending to cross the vast waves, but suddenly encountered heavy rain midway.
He consequently took shelter within a mud grotto by the roadside to avoid the wind and dampness.
When the following morning arrived, they looked around and saw it was beside the skeletal remains of an ancient tomb. The sky was still drizzling with rain and the ground was mired in mud;

not even a foot could be gained, so they lingered and made no progress. Furthermore, they were lodged within the midst of fired bricks. Long before the night had ended, a spectral being suddenly appeared as a monster.
At dawn, Master Xiao sighed and said: "My previous lodging was called an earthen niche, yet it was peaceful. This..."
At night he stayed overnight. Entrusting himself to the realm of ghosts, where veneration is abundant, he realized that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;

because the mind ceases, the tomb and the grave are not two. Furthermore, the three realms are but mind, and the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Since there is no dharma outside the mind, why seek elsewhere?
"I shall not enter Tang," he declared, and instead took his bag and returned to his country. Xiang, however, traveled alone with but a solitary shadow, swearing never to turn back even unto death.

He returned. In the second year of the Zongzhang era, he traveled by merchant ship to Denglou for alms. Upon arriving at the home of a lay devotee, he saw a woman named Xiang, whose countenance was striking and elegant;
he remained lingering at her gate for a long time. There was also a young girl, beautifully dressed and elegantly adorned, named Shanmiao, who sought to seduce him with artful charms.
However, Xiang’s heart was as firm as stone and could not be turned; when the girl’s advances went unanswered, she suddenly—
He resolved his mind upon the Way and, before [the image], made a great vow, saying: "In birth after birth and age after age, I take refuge in the Upādhyāya.
I shall study the Mahāyāna and accomplish the Great Task. As for my disciple, I shall certainly act as a donor (*dānapati*) to provide him with all necessary provisions.

Xiang then proceeded directly to Zhongnan Mountain at Chang’an, to the abode of the Tripiṭaka Master Zhiyan, where he thoroughly studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. At that time, the National Teacher Kangzang was...

They were fellow students; thus, they deliberated on the return journey. As the Dharma Master preached and exhorted them, they returned once more to the home of an old patron in Wéndēng to thank him for his offerings and support over many years.
He then recruited a merchant ship, and after some hesitation, they cast off their moorings.

His daughter, Shànmìào, had already prepared a set of monastic robes and various utensils for Xuān, filling several boxes. When the transport reached the seashore, the merchant ship had already departed.
The girl incanted it, saying: "I have truly offered this to the Dharma Master with a sincere heart; may this robe-casket leap into the boat ahead!
Having finished speaking, she cast the casket into the surging waves. After a short while, a fierce wind blew it, and from afar they saw it leap directly into the boat.
The girl vowed again: "I wish that my own body may transform into a great dragon to support the stern and the prow, so that we may reach the kingdom."

To transmit the Dharma, he rolled up his sleeves and cast himself into the sea. Indeed, his body moved with agile grace, leaping like a serpent, whereby the bottom of his boat became calm and he reached the other shore.
After entering the kingdom of Ssang (Xiang), he traveled extensively through mountains and rivers. In Guri (Goryeo) and Baekje, the land was spiritually numinous and the mountains were magnificent;
truly, it was a place where the Wheel of the Dharma could be turned. Not long after, however, the provisional schools and heterodox sects gathered their followers.
There were approximately five hundred followers. Xiang silently thought to himself, "The Great Avataṃsaka teachings cannot flourish in a land lacking merit and virtue.
At that time, the dragon Śubhavimala, who constantly followed him to provide protection, secretly perceived this thought and manifested great supernatural transformations.
In the midst of the empty sky, a massive boulder, one *li* in length and breadth, manifested and covered the summit of the monastery, appearing as though it were about to fall but did not.
The assembly of monks was struck with terror and, not knowing where to go, fled in all directions.
Xiang then entered the temple and began to expound this sutra. Like the sun in winter and the shade in summer, those who came of their own accord were many; the king held him in profound esteem.
When he lectured, the trees blossomed; when he spoke, the clusters bore fruit.
Those who ascended the hall and beheld its profound depths included Zhitong, Biaoxun, Fanti, Daoshen, and several others—all of whom were like *garuḍa* birds pecking at giant eggs and flying forth.

Whenever disciples requested instruction, he resolved their doubts and cleared their obstructions, leaving no dregs or kernels behind. From that time on, he traveled as a wandering monk without fixed residence, planting his staff [as he went].
He resided [there], and his students gathered like swarms of bees. Holding their pens and carrying their lead, they transcribed [his teachings] as if compiling a formal collection.
These recorded words constitute such gates of meaning (*arthamukha*); they follow the disciples' oral transmission, as seen, for example, in the "Chapter on the Body of the Way" (*Daoshen zhang*).

Some are titled after their location, such as the several chapters and commentaries including the "Questions and Answers on the Cone-Hole" (*Zhui xue wen da deng shu zhang*). All of these clarify the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, the boundless realization of Vairocana.
This is an example of the scriptural meaning. Xiang died in his own country, and his stupa remains there; he is titled the First Patriarch of Huayan in海东 (Haidong).
The monk Shejien (釋鑑) Yuanxiao’s conduct was exemplary and clear; he encompassed the path of the Vinaya and lectured on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which was known as the "Superior Assembly" (勝集). Daily—
He provided gruel for a thousand people; though there were only several hundred *hu* of rice and millet in his granary and bamboo baskets, they were never exhausted as he drew from them.

This mountain temple had many miraculous responses. There was Meditation Master Huiguan, who saw more than three hundred monks holding lotus lamps ascend into the air, appearing clearly like falling stars.
During the Kaiyuan era, Lord Cui Ning of Ji doubted this as being superstitious and deluded, and personally [investigated it].
From the time he entered the mountain to stay overnight, he saw flames thirty li long on each of the four sides of the mountain.

By the third night, more than a hundred lamps appeared, accompanied by a crimson light over a thousand feet high. Master Ji suddenly prostrated himself in worship, exclaiming that such a thing had never occurred before.
At that time, a golden hand emerged from among the pines, approximately seven feet in length. Two bodhisattvas appeared, their yellow-white golden complexions shimmering with radiance.
Upon a cypress tree in front of the courtyard, a single lamp manifested during the day; its brilliance was like that of the sun.

Across the Borei Mountain, a single precious jewel was suspended, one zhang in circumference, glowing brilliantly and lovely to behold. At the mountain gate on the western ridge, a great rainbow bridge hung suspended; upon the bridge—
Brahman monks, youths, and elderly men emerged from between [the trees]. There were two torches, blazing in the air like the manner of welcoming and seeing off as they passed each other.
Below were four bodhisattvas, standing in pairs, emitting light from their entire bodies that rose sixty or seventy feet high.

Furthermore, behind a great pine forest, there suddenly appeared a temple plaque with the three characters for "The Three Studies" (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*) written in seal script. Moreover, beneath the lamp, there was...
Two embroidered sashes were placed between the eastern groves. At night, he went out to Mount Jinshan when the moon was at its zenith.

Two-colored lamps, gold and silver, were arranged beside the tomb of Master Zhixuan. Whenever the Third Month arrived, Wei Nan’gang Gaos would go to the temple to perform a great vegetarian feast for three hundred bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattvas would manifest their forms and hold up lamps; the monks would carry incense and lamps to lead and welcome them. This occurred in the eighth year of the Dazhong era.
In that year, the temple’s name was changed to Kaeho (Opening Illumination).
The monk Fa-xiu resided at a temple in the capital and traveled throughout the Gyeong-ho region, making it his primary duty to exhort and mobilize the populace for meritorious causes.
Toward the end of the Kaiyuan era, he dreamed of someone saying, "Take five hundred hand towels and five hundred monastic robes; you may distribute them within Hwaengjangsa Temple."
Having made the offering, he questioned his attendants upon waking, but they all replied that there was no temple to which it had been dedicated.

He then recruited people to manufacture monastic robes and inquired everywhere among the elderly monks and laypeople: "Is there not such a monastery as this? At that time, there was a monk of robust and imposing stature.
No one recognized him. He replied, "I know the location of Huixiang Temple. When asked what was required, he answered, "Simply bring the items offered for alms and one catty of incense will suffice.
They then followed his instructions and delivered the goods. Accompanying Xiu, the monk traveled directly into Mount Zhongnan.
After traveling for two days, they reached an extremely deep and precipitous place where nothing could initially be seen; they pressed on further.
Cheng saw a set of millstones and was startled, saying, "This place is inaccessible to human footsteps; how can there be such things here?
He then burned the incense he had brought upon them, praying with repeated prostrations and deep lamentation from noon until evening.

A mist filled the valley, so dense that one could not distinguish objects even a few feet away. After a short while, it cleared, and between the cliffs appeared a vermilion gate with white walls and green windows.
From atop the jade-ornamented roof, Xiu clearly beheld a temple amidst the clouds. A large plaque hung above its triple gate inscribed with the characters "Huixiang Temple" (Temple of Dedication).
Delighted, Xiu climbed up and eventually reached it; it was already dusk. Hearing the sound of bells, chimes, and the chanting of *sādhana*, the gatekeeper questioned him regarding his origins.
After some hesitation, he was led inside. There he saw an elderly monk who greeted him with repeated inquiries and spoke, saying: "The Tang..."
"Is His Majesty in good health? He gave instructions for another monk to accompany him as they toured the quarters, distributing hand towels and *kāṣāya* robes until only one portion remained.
Pointing to an empty bed in one room where no one was present, yet which contained clothing and seating, he remarked that it seemed someone had recently departed.
Shortly thereafter, he saw an old monk who appeared like a leader of a governing body. The monk said, "Those who went out should have returned by now.
The monk and Xiu wished to go there again, so they were given hand towels and other items. However, a room that had been empty of beds was likewise devoid of people.
They recounted this in detail once more. The old monk smiled, motioned for them to sit, and looking toward the interior of that room, brought out a *shichaba* (flute) and approached.
"It is indeed a jade *shichaba* (flute). The old monk asked, "Did you see that foreign monk? He replied, "I saw him.
The monk said, "This one shall temporarily act as your master in the future. The capital will fall into chaos, and countless people will die. This monk’s name is Wang Mo-mie (King Annihilation).
That single room is your master’s quarters. Your master is currently in the temple; because he loves to play the *shichaba*, he has been punished [to stay there]."

"O human, this is that which has been blown constantly. Now its term is about to end, so it shall return immediately. Tomorrow, send it to the vegetarian feast. Once the feast is concluded, you must return it.
You may take this *shichiku* (flute), along with the *kashaya* (robe) and hand-towel, and give them to your master to keep.
Xiu prostrated himself and departed. The youth escorted him for only a few dozen paces before clouds and mist gathered from all sides.
He no longer saw the temple. He then took his hand towel, his *kāṣāya*, and his jade flute (*yùchí*) and presented them to the Emperor.

Xuanzong summoned him for an audience, and he related the entire sequence of events in detail. The Emperor was deeply moved and pleased; he concentrated his spirit for a long time, then took the flute and blew it—it was exactly the one he had previously used.
A few years later, the catastrophe of Lu Shan indeed occurred. The foreign monk whom Xiu had seen was none other than Lu Shan himself. This was Xiu’s [vision].

Moved by what he encountered, his diligent practice became redoubled and intense; he knew not where it would end. According to worldly tradition, there was a sacred temple on Mount Zhongnan, and there was also a Huixiang Temple.
Shi Lingtan’s secular surname was Wu. He was a native of Wen-shui in Taiyuan and a great-nephew of Empress Wu Zetian. His father, named Xuan, served as the Magistrate of Luoyang County.
His mother, surnamed Xiahou, initially dreamed while pregnant with Lingtan that a divine monk bestowed upon her a precious mirror, its interior and exterior both brilliantly polished, and said:
"I entrust this to you; protect it well. When he was born, his parents experienced no suffering. At the age of barely...

At the age of seven, he had completed his studies and was eligible for the examination for young scholars (*tóngzǐ*). He constantly lamented the dilapidated nature of the world and vowed to enter the Gate of Emptiness.

At that time, Chan Master Shenhui of Heze Temple was flourishing in the capital of Luoyang. Xuantan went there to pay him a visit; Shenhui provided excellent guidance and immediately perceived his mind.
In the first year of the Tianbao era, [Shenhui] summoned Tan and said: "I have a single phrase, which has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch down to..."
"Caohui, Caohui has entrusted this to me; you must receive it with earnest attention. I shall soon encounter obstacles. Thereupon, he took his leave to travel abroad.
Before long, as expected, an imperial decree was issued to transfer him to Guyang. Zhituan then proceeded to Fucha Temple in Luzhou, where he perused the Tripitaka.
Later, hearing that National Teacher Huizhong had been summoned from Nanyang, he went to pay his respects to him at the fifth year of the Dali era. (8)
As the year drew near to his departure from the pass, Zhong submitted a memorial stating: "This man is my fellow disciple under the same master, Shenhui.
By imperial decree, he was granted the title 'Great Compassionate One' (Dabei) and was carrying an official edict as he traveled to propagate the Dharma in the state of Liang.

There, the Chancellor, Lord Tian, provided him with divine offerings. As he proceeded gradually toward Wiyang and Liuhe, he was lamenting the decline of the Great Dharma when he suddenly heard a voice from the air."
Sheng said, "Open the ground of the mind. Immediately, he saw a bodhisattva appearing like Mañjuśrī, who said, "I shall give you a seal of verification.
He was told to raise his head and press it with his palm; upon inspection, there were four finger-width marks of redness. This seal-mark has remained visible ever since.
Furthermore, he stayed on Mount Jinshan in the Yangtze River at Runzhou—this is the present-day Zexin. On the northern face of that mountain, there is a dragon hole that constantly emits poison.
His breath was like a cloud; those who came near him often fell ill or died. Daotan lived there, and the poisonous clouds vanished without a trace.

Later, he built a hermitage on Mount Ding in Jiangyin. Suddenly, he heard the sound of voices praising him; looking, he saw two white tortoises, to which Daotan administered the precepts of taking refuge.
He then saw two large white snakes, several *zhang* in length, to whom he likewise administered the precepts and repentance. Afterwards...

He went to Línshān in Wúxīng and constructed an araṇya there. Three men dressed in purple-gold robes, walking with slow and dignified steps, praised the site of the practice hall as being exclusively excellent.
Many of the villagers abandoned their fishing nets and traps. In the fifth year of the Yuánhé era, the Chancellor, Duke Lí Yōng, summoned him to reside at Huálín Monastery.
Within the monastery was the former site of the Great General Zhāng Liáo, and the monks there were numerous.

He was not deluded or disturbed by ghosts and spirits; he dwelt in tranquility, profound and without trace. Furthermore, many people in Yangzhou suffered from the bewilderment caused by mountain sprites and water monsters, yet Hui-tan suppressed and warded them off all of them.
People vied with one another to seek his guidance and faith. In the tenth year, he suddenly saw two monks who claimed to have come from the kingdom of Kucha.
They said, "In that land there is no supreme teaching; we have traveled far to invite the Venerable Master to expound it. Ten...
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the first year [of the Tianping era], he addressed the assembly during the memorial vegetarian feast for Heze:

"I have accepted a distant invitation; on the eighth day of the eighth month, I shall pass away. Indeed, he entered nirvana on that very date. His stupa was enshrined on the southern ridge of Xunzhai Ward in Western Yangzhou.
Zheng Jian, the administrative assistant of Yue Prefecture, erected the stupa. He lived to the age of one hundred and eight.
Shi Daowu’s secular surname was Zhang. He was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou. From birth he was spiritually distinguished; as he grew, he became prudent and sincere.
At the age of fourteen, he sought to leave the household life, but his parents, out of affection, would not permit it. He consequently reduced his regular meals, eating but one meal a day.

His parents, having no other recourse, finally granted him permission. He then went to Dade Monastery in Mingzhou to undergo tonsure. At twenty-five, he relied upon [the master at] Zhulin Monastery in Hangzhou.
The Great Virtue of the temple, fully ordained in the precepts, threw himself at the feet of National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing. There, he secretly received the essentials of the school’s lineage;

amidst the flow of words, he recognized the pearl within his robe. His body and mind became suddenly vast and open; both truth and falsehood were cast aside, all doubts and obstructions severed, and he directly beheld his Buddha-nature.
Having served with diligence for five years, he withdrew to Mount Daiméi in Yu’ao. It was the eleventh year of the Dali era.

Amidst steep cliffs and precipitous ravines, where the natural sounds were desolate and there were no neighboring villages for miles, he went without food for seven days. Monkeys and gibbons brought him acorns and chestnuts as offerings.

When a local villager cleared away thorny brush and beheld him, he was struck with awe and drew back in trepidation, regarding him as a divine being. Those who came to visit became like a marketplace; they leaned against the overhanging crags to gaze upon him.
Qiao then constructed a perilous roof-beam. Provisions and ritual implements surrounded his quarters. A fierce tiger, with a haughty gaze, emerged from its den to roam;
upon approaching the side of his seat, it crouched and lowered its limbs in submission. In the first year of the Jianzhong era, he went to see Master Ma at Zhongling.

In the autumn of the second year, he visited the Great Being Shitou. Traveling from Mount Jing to Mount Heng, he encountered three wise masters in succession, and only then did he choose his site for residence.
In Liyang, he next resided at the mouth of the Heng River, and finally settled on Mount Chaizi in Dangyang—a place where five hundred arhats once soared.
There, cypress and pine trees grew in lush profusion, and the cliffs and peaks rose steeply and ruggedly. Sometimes he joined the shade of the woods of Wulin; sometimes he shared his hut with others.
The shoes outside his door were always numerous. Jingzhou was a preeminent province, and its inhabitants—both men and women—numbered in the tens of millions.

It was calculated that there were none who did not rise and kneel, bowing their heads in prostration as if responding to the wind. As for Tiantai Monastery, it is situated to the left of the prefecture;

its distinctiveness sets it apart from other temples, and it is renowned as a famous monastery (*mínglán*). When it was completely consumed by fire and reduced to ashes, the monastics lost the place where they could pay their respects.

During their periods of meditation and communal feasting, they encountered a divine being. The shrine stood near the river and was rich with pine and catalpa trees; [the deity] expressed a wish for them all to be toppled and offered to the Saṃgha.

Lán then cut the ridgepoles and repaired the pillars; the construction gathered like clouds at the well-frames. At that time, the waters had run dry, and the assembly of disciples stood with hands folded in helplessness.

Suddenly, one night, rain fell, and ten thousand logs were brought forward simultaneously. Setting out from the riverbank at dawn, they arrived at the temple gate by evening. During the process of carving and joinery—
As for those who were active and lacked for nothing: the rest of the corridors, pavilions, beds, and desks were all provided through his profound assistance.
Śramaṇa Yuanxiao’s surname was Xue; he was a native of Xiangzhou in Donghai. He was profoundly versed in the Three Studies, such that his compatriots regarded him as a "match for ten thousand men.
At that time, the King established a hundred-seated Great Assembly for the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and searched everywhere for men of eminent virtue. His home province [thereupon]...
He recommended that [the physician] be promoted, but the king would not accept it. Before long, the king’s consort developed a tumor on her head.
The medical practitioners were utterly at a loss for a cure. The king, his princes, and his ministers offered prayers at mountains, rivers, and divine shrines, leaving no sacred site unvisited.
A shaman declared, "If one dispatches someone to another country to seek medicine, this illness will finally be healed. Thereupon, the king dispatched an envoy.

He sailed across the sea to enter Tang China, seeking to recruit those skilled in medical arts. Amidst the vast expanse of the ocean, he suddenly beheld an old man who leaped forth from the waves and boarded his vessel.
The man invited him to enter the sea, where they beheld a magnificent and resplendent palace. There they saw the Dragon King; his name was Qianhai.
He said to the messenger: "The Queen of your country is the third daughter of the Azure Emperor.
In my palace, there is previously a *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*, which reveals the practice of the Bodhisattva through the perfect penetration of the two types of awakening.

Now, relying upon the illness of the Queen as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), I wish to entrust this sūtra to her so that it may be transmitted to and circulated in your country. Thereupon, he took three...
About ten sheets of paper, containing layered and scattered sūtras, were entrusted to a messenger. He further said, "These sūtras have crossed the ocean;
I fear they may encounter demonic obstacles. Your Majesty has ordered that you take a knife and slit open the messenger's calf muscles, place the sūtras therein, and wrap them with waxed paper."
He applied medicine to it, and his calf was restored to its former state. The Dragon King said, "Have the Dharma Master Wonhyo compose a commentary to explain it;
then the Lady’s illness will undoubtedly be cured. The Dragon King sent him out across the sea, whereupon he boarded a ship and returned to his country.
