When the King heard of this, he was filled with joy and summoned Wonhyo. Wonhyo composed the commentary in five fascicles. The King requested that a date be set for the lecture at the Yellow...

At Longsi Temple, he expounded [the text], which was titled the *Lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary). Xuǎnxiào’s exposition was performed with ritual propriety; his resolutions of difficulties served as a model.
As he raised his fingers in praise, the sound resonated through the air. There were two versions of this commentary, an extensive and an abridged one, both circulating in their native land.
The abridged version flowed into China, where it was later revised into a *lùn* (treatise) by a Tripiṭaka Master who translated the scriptures.
In the second year of the Dali era, Shi Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Monastery in Hengzhou, where he practiced diligently without slackening.
Within the alms bowl during the morning gruel in the Sangha hall, he suddenly beheld auspicious clouds of five colors; within these clouds appeared a mountain monastery.
Fifty li northeast of the monastery was a mountain, at the foot of which was a stream. To the north of the stream was a stone gate. Five li further inside was a monastery with golden plaques.
The inscription reads: "At the Great Sage’s Zhulin Monastery, although I witnessed this clearly with my own eyes, my heart remained filled with distress and despondency.
On another day at the time of the midday meal, within five-colored clouds above his alms bowl, Mount Wutai appeared;

all the monasteries were made of golden ground, devoid of mountains, forests, or impurities, consisting entirely of ponds, terraces, and pavilions adorned with various jewels. Therein resided Mañjuśrī and ten thousand sages."
He stood amidst the assembly, whereupon he further manifested the pure lands of various Buddhas; these vanished only after he had finished his meal.
With lingering doubt yet unresolved, he returned to the monastery and asked the monks: "Is there anyone here who has ever traveled to Mount Wutai?

At that time, the two masters Jiayan and Tanhui stated that they had been there, and what they described matched exactly with what he had seen within the bowl. In the summer of the fourth year, at Hude (Lake East) in Hengzhou...
Within the temple, there was a high tower ninety *zhang* tall, where a five-assembly *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) practice hall had been established.

On the second day of the sixth month, from afar he saw auspicious clouds completely covering the tower and temple; within the clouds were various multi-storied pavilions, and inside the pavilions were several Indian monks, each about one *zhang* in height, holding *khakkhara* staffs and walking in meditation.
Guo Xian of Hengzhou clearly beheld Amitābha Buddha together with Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

The worthy one was accompanied by ten thousand bodhisattvas, all present in this assembly. His body was tall and massive; those who saw him all wept blood and performed prostrations, which only ceased at the hour of You (the seventh watch).

At evening, as he was illuminating the area outside the *dharmodāna*, he encountered an old man who said to Zhào, "Master, you previously made a vow to go to the Golden World to pay homage to the Great Sage. Why do you not go now? Zhào replied with astonishment.

He said, "The times are difficult and the roads are perilous; how can one go there? The old man replied, "Simply go with haste. There will certainly be no obstacles on the way. Having spoken, he vanished.
Zhaojing was startled and entered the meditation hall, where he made a renewed vow of sincerity. He agreed to depart once the summer retreat was over.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, several fellow practitioners from Nanyue came forward of their own accord; indeed, there were no hindrances. Five.
On the fifth day of the fourth month, he arrived at Wutai County. From afar, he saw several streaks of white light to the south of Foguang Temple.

On the sixth day, he reached Foguang Temple; indeed, it was just as he had seen in his bowl. That night, during the fourth watch, he saw a beam of light descend from the northern mountain, shining and illuminating the area.
He hurriedly entered the hall and asked the assembly, "What auspicious sign is this? There was a monk who...
He replied, "This Great Sage’s inconceivable light constantly responds to those with whom it has a karmic connection.

Having heard this, he immediately adjusted his dignified demeanor and followed the light for fifty *li* to the northeast of the temple. Indeed, there was a mountain; at its foot was a stream, and to the north of the stream stood a stone gate.
There he saw two youths dressed in green, aged eight or nine, with handsome features, standing at the entrance of the gate. One—
He was named Sudhana; the second was named Nanda. They greeted each other with joy, exchanged inquiries after one another’s welfare, and performed the rites of salutation.
He led the way into the gate, and after traveling five *li* toward the north, they saw a golden gate-tower. Gradually approaching the gateway, he found it to be a monastery.
Before the monastery stood a great golden plaque inscribed with the words: "The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery," exactly as he had seen within the bowl. It was square and circular.
It was twenty *li* [in circumference] and contained one hundred and twenty monasteries, all adorned with precious stupas.
The ground was made entirely of pure gold, and flowing channels and flowering trees filled the area. The light entered the temple and reached the lecture hall, where he saw Mañjuśrī on the west side.
Samantabhadra was in the east, each seated upon a lion throne; the sound of his preaching the Dharma could be heard clearly and distinctly.

To the left and right of Mañjuśrī were more than ten thousand bodhisattvas, and Samantabhadra was likewise surrounded by innumerable bodhisattvas. The radiance reached the two sages, who rose to pay their respects and asked:
"In this final age, ordinary people are far removed from the time of the Sages; their spiritual knowledge has grown increasingly inferior, and their defilements and obstructions are even deeper."
The Buddha-nature has no means by which it may manifest. The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound; I do not yet know which dharma-gate among the practices is most essential.
I only pray that the Great Sage will sever the net of my doubts. Mañjuśrī replied: "Now that you are mindful of the Buddha, this is precisely the right time.
Among all gates of practice, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. To make offerings to the Triple Gem is to cultivate both merit and wisdom simultaneously. This—
These two gates are the most direct and essential. Why is this so?

Because in past kalpas, it was by virtue of contemplating the Buddha, by virtue of recollecting the Buddha, and by virtue of making offerings to him that I have now attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, regarding all dharmas:
The Prajñāpāramitā, profound meditative concentration, and even all the Buddhas—all arise from the recollection of the Buddha.
Therefore, know that the recollection of the Buddha is the King who requests the Dharma. You should constantly recollect the Unsurpassed Dharma King without ceasing.
Zhao asked again, "How should one recollect him? Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha. That Buddha..."
"The power of your vows is inconceivable; you should maintain this mindfulness so that it remains uninterrupted, and you shall then swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Having spoken thus, the two great sages recited verses to one another. Upon hearing them, Āloka was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; the net of his doubts was entirely removed.
He prostrated once more, and having finished his salutation, he joined his palms. Mañjuśrī said, "You may now go to visit the various bodhisattvas..."
He visited the various monasteries in succession. After receiving instruction, he paid his respects in order until he reached the Garden of Seven-Jeweled Fruits.
The fruits had just ripened, each as large as a bowl; he took one and ate it. Having eaten, his body and mind became serene. He proceeded before the Great Sage, prostrated, and took his leave.
Upon returning, he saw two youths in green robes who escorted him outside the gate. After bowing, he raised his head and suddenly lost sight of them.
Wherever he was, his sense of sorrow and gratitude redoubled, and he thus erected a stone monument to record these events.
Shi Canghai’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Huating in Suzhou. During her pregnancy and at the time of his birth, his mother constantly smelled a wondrous fragrance.
When he was a child, he once fell into a well, but a divine being received and pulled him out. At the age of seven, he left the household life and paid homage to Chan Master Daokuang.

He subsequently traveled to Mount Song to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). His mother wept every time she thought of him, eventually losing sight in one eye; when he returned home to visit her, her vision was restored that very day.
Upon her death, he mourned so deeply that he emaciated himself and lived in a hut by her grave. He then traveled abroad to seek the Way, returning to Mount Wuxie where he met Master Lingmo.

After a single conversation, their understanding was analyzed and reconciled, and their fundamental purposes accorded perfectly. Later, when the Zhou dynasty re-established its capital at Luoyang, he went there once more.
He resided at Changshou Temple by imperial decree. At that time, the internal scriptures had been incinerated and the Sanskrit manuscripts reduced to ashes;

he personally compiled those scattered fragments to form what truly became a Great Canon. In the twelfth year of the Dazhong era, the lay patron Ren Jingqiu of Yinchui donated his residence to establish a monastery.

Huan was invited to reside there. When the bandits of Shan sought out Dao-fu, he led two thousand followers and entered with weapons brandished during the day. Huan sat in meditative repose with his eyes closed; his countenance showed no sign of agitation.

The bandits were all struck with terror and crouched down, bowing their heads to apologize for their transgressions. Once the rebellion was quelled, the provincial governor submitted a petition requesting that the temple’s name be changed to Qixin Monastery.
Huan’s learning and insight gushed forth like a spring, and his discernment was as precise as a forked path. In the autumn of the seventh year of the Xiantong era...

On the third day of the eighth month, he manifested illness and announced his passing; his disciples wailed in mourning. He was temporarily interred at Tiantong Rock, and three years have already passed.

One day, a rare fragrance filled the air, its intense scent pervading both near and far. The disciples said to one another, "In the past, our Master entrusted us with the instruction that after three years, we should cremate his body.
Now that the extraordinary fragrance is so pervasive, let us open the stupa to see him. When they opened it, he appeared as if alive.
On the third day of the eighth month of his passing, he was cremated according to the methods of the Western Regions (India).

Several thousand grains of śarīra were obtained, which were a brilliant reddish-green color. His disciple Jie Xiu took the śarīra and presented them to the Emperor, who issued an imperial eulogy and changed his posthumous name to Xinjian.
The stupa is called Shouxiang (Life-Phase).
It was built by the Great Master Liangzhun, a divine monk who took joy in the Dharma.

When he went into the mountains to procure timber for the construction of Faxi (Dharma-Joy), he returned alone, carrying both large and small logs, which all emerged from the river. To this day, there are wooden beams at the bottom of the river that no one can move. One.
He manifested physical traces that appeared and disappeared unpredictably; he was suspected of being a sage or a holy one appearing through transformation.

According to the inscriptions on the *jingdang* (stele for the Dharma) and stone carvings, both the fourteenth year of the Dazhong era and the fifth year of the Xiantong era bear the name of Liangzhun. Furthermore, examining the temple stele rebuilt during the Jingyou era, it states:
"A transcendent person appeared among men such as Liangzhun, who specialized in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and whose wisdom and practice were profoundly refined. His stupa is located here.
On the eastern corridor of the temple, fifty paces from the main hall, no birds alighted and not a speck of dust settled.

From time to time, auspicious light converged and manifested as omens. In the first month of the spring of the fourth year of the Xuanhua era, when they wished to erect a pagoda pavilion and move [the image] toward the western eaves, the sacred statue and its monastic robe leaped away into the distance.
Radiant and wondrous, brilliant and shimmering, the light pierced through the doors and windows. The assembly was terrified and offered prayers.
He recited them, and they returned to their original state exactly as before.
Shi Zhihuan, whose courtesy name was Houjue, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Hongya in Meizhou. His mother, Lady Wei, dreamed that the moon entered her womb when he was born.
At the age of seven, he encountered Dharma Master Fatai at Ningyi Temple, who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; the temple was located near his residence.
His neighbor, Xuán, attended a lecture assembly one day and listened to the Dharma discourse; it was as if he were witnessing a past cause.

That evening, he dreamed that the Buddha’s hand stroked his head atop the temple hall. Upon waking, he informed his grandfather and requested to become a *śrāmaṇera*. His relatives consented, and at the age of eleven, he shaved his hair.
He then followed his teacher to Sīhān Temple in Tángxìng County, where he was granted the transmission of forty-two fascicles of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
The commentaries of Master Huiyuan and the profound principles of Master Kong together comprise one million two hundred and fifty thousand words;
all of them encompass the most profound mysteries. At the age of thirteen, he pointed out errors to the monastic community, manifesting the air of a mature master.

At that time, Prime Minister Du Yuan-ying, who was stationed as Governor of Western Shu, heard of Xuan’s reputation and ordered him to ascend the hall at Daci Temple’s Puxian Pavilion to deliver lectures and discussions.
The assembly below, both ordained and lay, numbered ten thousand people daily; they listened with focused devotion, their exclamations of wonder never ceasing.
From this time on, the people of Shu revered his reputation, calling him "Chan Pusa" (Bodhisattva Chen). At Jingzhong Temple, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Bianzhen.

Hardly had he begun studying the *Vinaya* when he subsequently mastered the *Abhidharmakośa*. He then followed his preceptor down the Three Gorges, traveling through Jingzhou and Xiangyang before arriving at Shen.
When Emperor Wenzong of the Tang heard of Jingzi Temple, he summoned him for an audience and consultation; the Emperor was deeply pleased with his responses.

Later, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Wei shi lun) under Master Xian of Anguo Temple and further researched the classics and scriptures of external traditions. There was no discourse among the hundred schools that he did not master.
Because Huan always regretted that his native accent was unfit for lecturing, he went to Mount Xiang’er to recite the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*.

Incantation. A dream deity-monk cut out his tongue and replaced it with another. The following day, he suddenly began speaking in the Qin dialect. When Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, he initially revered the followers of Śākyamuni;
later, however, he succumbed to delusions and plotted to offer sacrifices at Mount Penglai, constructing a high terrace to pray for immortality.

Although memorial officials submitted remonstrances and ministers repeatedly spoke out against it, the Emperor’s resolve never wavered. Consequently, he issued an edict pitting Xuanxue against the Daoist school.

He asked, "Can the Way of the Immortals be learned, or can it not? The Emperor again placed his hand within the teachings of Laozi, citing the principle of governing a great state as if cooking small fish.
Together with the Daoist priests, they engaged in a dialogue, profoundly expounding the ruler’s way of governance and the fundamental principles of transformation and education.
He spoke of the arts of the divine immortals, which are the lofty pursuits monopolized by solitary recluses in the mountains and forests;

furthermore, these necessarily rely upon past causes and conditions and are not suitable for a sovereign. His eloquence flowed like a river cascading downward and his arguments surged like a vast ocean, totaling several thousand words.
Those who heard him were struck with trembling. The Left Guardian General Qiu Shiliang and the Inner Secretariat Official Yang Qinji lamented [his departure].

Fearing that his talent and eloquence might provoke an order for his dismissal, he secretly exhorted Gong to compose poems in praise of Yao. Xuan composed five pieces on the spot; the final chapter read:
"Birth in heaven arises naturally from the karma of heaven; one does not necessarily attain immortality merely by seeking it.

The crane’s back is precarious and the dragon’s back is slippery; O Sovereign, please remain for another thousand years. Upon reading the poem, the Emperor was slightly appeased and permitted him to depart in a small boat.
When [Wuzhuo] entered the region of Lake Xiang, the Imperial Censor Yang Han was conducting an inspection tour of Guilin. He invited [Wuzhuo] to Kaiyuan Temple.

It happened that Emperor Xuanzong had ascended the throne; Yang, having been promoted from the Inner Chancellery to command the Left Imperial Guard and having achieved great merit through his role in the imperial succession, requested the restoration of the Tiantai (Indian) teachings.
He commissioned [Wuzhuo] to seek out the traces of Master Xuan. Xuan returned to Baoying Temple in the capital, where he encountered the Emperor.
On the auspicious anniversary of his birth, he gave a lecture and eulogy, for which he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* and appointed as the Head Seat (*śuōzuò*) of the Three Teachings.
The Emperor took his former princely residence and built Fagǎn Temple, issuing an edict for Xuán to reside there.

At the Yùxū Pavilion, on the third year of the Dàzhōng era, during the Emperor’s birthday celebration, he issued an edict for Li Yísūn, Palace Counselor, and Yang Hànɡōng, Palace Attendant, along with a great assembly of monastics and lay scholars, to engage in debate. This greatly pleased the Emperor’s heart, and consequently, [Xuán] submitted a memorial.

The imperial edict was issued to rebuild the foundations of all abandoned temples throughout the realm, greatly restoring Buddhist monasteries. He commanded painters to depict his likeness within the imperial palace;
such was the degree of esteem and honor accorded to him. He shared a close friendship with the Chancellor, Duke Pei Xiu, and together they vigorously promoted the revival of the Buddhist teachings.

In the eighth year [of the reign], he submitted a memorial and returned to his native mountains, where he extensively practiced acts of beneficence, and many were those who received his aid. — Emperor Xizong.

He ordered the scholars to compose a posthumous title for the Master Xuán. Emperor Wǔdá was granted the title of National Teacher (Guōshī). Xuán repeatedly declined the honor, but his requests were not granted.

He then petitioned to return to his old residence at Jiǔlǒng. On the twenty-first day of the first month, while lying in bed, he saw all the sacred realms and famous sites he had previously visited appear before him.
On the seventh day of the second month, he heard a voice from the sky say: "You shall certainly be reborn in the Pure Land."
The interrogator asked, "Whose words were those? Kong replied, "They were the Buddha's. During the seventh month, he heard a sound outside his door;

after hesitating for a moment, a Bodhisattva descended before the courtyard and gradually approached his physical body. He offered earnest praise and exhortation, saying, "Do not let this suffering be a burden to you.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. Furthermore, one night, a pearl emerged from beneath the Master’s left foot.
It flowed away. He endured ten thousand kinds of suffering. Looking closely at the pearl, he saw clearly the two characters "Chao Cuo.
Only then did he realize that Xuan was actually Yuan Ang. It was because of the rebellion of the seven kingdoms that Ang had petitioned for Cuo’s execution to appease the kings of Wu and Chu.
"Therefore, I have merely been feigning illness. He summoned his disciple Cideng and dictated a final testament for him to submit.
He instructed that his corpse be abandoned, half to feed the bellies of fish and half to be devoured by birds and beasts. "I have long had an appointment with the Western Pure Land," he said.
Having finished speaking, he passed away lying on his right side, facing west.

Shi Huiji’s secular surname was Ye; he was a native of Xuchang in Shaoyou Prefecture. At the age of fifteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not grant their permission.
When he requested it again at seventeen, his paternal relatives remained hesitant and undecided.
That night, two streaks of white light emanated from Caoxi and pierced straight through his house. Only then did his parents realize that this was the result of their son’s utmost sincerity.
Ji cut off his left ring finger and little finger. Placing them upon a tray, he knelt at the hall steps and said, "I thank you for your labors.
His parents, knowing they could not keep him, let him go. He followed Master Tong of Nanhua Temple to shave his head and dye his robes.

At the age of eighteen, he prepared his ritual implements and first met Master Tan Yuan, from whom he gained some realization. Later, he attended upon Master Chan of Mount Dagu. He raised [the question]:
He took pity on him. He lived there for fourteen or fifteen years until his feet became lame; he was then known as "The Lame One Who Drives Away Crows.
Whenever he engaged in philosophical deliberation, he would frequently manifest signs of realization. At that time, Wei Zhou approached Jue and requested a *gāthā*.
Jue then took paper and drew a circular diagram, with a circle enclosing another, and beneath it he wrote: "To know by means of thought falls into the second head; to know without thought..."
He composed four verses and presented them as an offering. From that time on, he possessed a certain degree of spiritual power, which he displayed to his disciples;
this was known as the "Gate Style of Mount Yang. The assembly gathered like the sea, and those who attained the Way were beyond counting; many among them manifested divine and extraordinary powers.

He appeared and vanished in an instant; no one could fathom his movements. Later, by imperial decree, he was posthumously honored with the title Zhìtōng (Wisdom-Penetration), and his stupa was named Miàoguāng (Wondrous Light).
Shí Sēngmiào originally resided in Jīzhōu and later lived in Púbǎn, HéDōng. He was austere and diligent in his ascetic practices.

Naturally intelligent and precocious, he had perused a wide range of scriptures and was particularly adept at lecturing and debate. By nature, however, he was humble and retiring; joy and anger never disturbed his inner composure.
Therefore, at the conclusion of every lecture, he would invariably join his palms and repent, saying: "The intent of the Buddha is difficult to fathom; how could it be measured by an ordinary person?

What has been expounded here is that which was transmitted from former masters; I have not dared to act on my own authority. I beg the great assembly to bestow their joy upon this Dharma teaching, whether it be correct or incorrect.
At that time, Hui Guan was preeminent among the eminent scholars; his conduct was lofty and his understanding profound. Observing his humility...

All submitted to his virtue and righteousness, and the multitude followed him even more closely. Later, he resided at Renshou Temple in his native village, where he gathered disciples and cultivated his studies;
his reputation for excellence was immense. Emperor Taizu of the Zhou dynasty accorded him special respect.

During the Datong era, when relics of the Buddha were presented from the Western Regions, Taizu—recognizing that Miaohong had greatly propagated and praised the Buddha-dharma—sent them to him for veneration. Consequently, [Miaohong] received them upon the crown of his head. Xiaohong...

Night after night it turned upward, and after a year had passed, suddenly in the middle of the night it emitted light that filled the room. The light spiraled out through the window and gradually extended outside;
in a brief moment, its radiance illuminated the far reaches, and as its flames surged and fanned out, they shone throughout heaven and earth.
Those who saw it thought the temple was on fire and rushed to extinguish it, but upon observing the divine light, they realized it was emerging from the golden vase.
All sighed that it was unprecedented. Miaoyang gazed up at the sacred manifestation with tears streaming down his face. He then burned incense, knelt, and addressed it, saying:
"The sentient beings of the Dharma-realm have already beheld the holy traces. I humbly pray that you will conceal this miraculous radiance and return to quiescence within emptiness.
Thereupon, the light returned in a spiral, winding back into the vase. That night, the men and women of the provincial seat burned incense and offered praises.
The sound was heard for more than several tens of *li*. In the monastery, there was a monk who was sleeping in his room;

when the assembly called out to him together, he remained drowsy and unconscious, and ultimately did not see the manifestation of light. Before long, he contracted a pestilential disease. Everyone said it was caused by his past karma.
Thus, there arose sighs of lamentation over his visionary appearances; since the passing of Miaozhi, his light no longer manifested.
Shi Jingzhen received the tonsure under Dharma Master Ruoping of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang and studied the Xianshou school.

In the third year of the Jiaxi era, he traveled among various monasteries along the Yangtze River. At that time, the dykes of the Qiantang River were destroyed, causing the river tides to overflow and bringing disaster upon the people.
The Master presented a verse to Zhao Duanming, the Pacification Commissioner, saying: "The seas boil and the rivers flow in continuous succession;
The residents are tossed about, their anxieties ever more intense. I cast myself directly into the Dragon Palace, Seeking to stop the surging waves that strike against the heavens.
He then threw himself into the sea and returned after three days. He said to the residents: "I preached the Dharma within the Dragon Palace. The dragon deities..."

"Listen and receive this; this embankment shall no longer be destroyed. Having finished speaking, he threw himself back into the sea. Zhao Duanming was moved by his virtue and reported the matter in detail to the court.
By imperial decree, he was bestowed the title of State-Protecting Pure-Truth Dharma Master (Huguo Jingzhen Fashi), and a shrine was established for him at Huicisi in Hangzhou.
Shi Jiao-heng, whose courtesy name was Xuming, was the son of Wang of Rencheng in Jizhou.

Previously, there had been a monk named Fuan from Ciji Temple in Bianjing who resided in Rencheng for many years; he cultivated pure deeds with such diligence that both monastics and laypeople looked up to him with reverence.
One day, while attending a vegetarian feast at Mangshan Village, he leaned against a tree and passed away. That evening, he appeared in a dream to his younger sister, Feng Zibeng.
In the village, they saw a multitude of white horses descend. [The horse] said, "I was born in the family of Wang Guangdao of Xichen Village.
Feng Jue spoke this to his mother and their son; the dreams of all three were identical. At dawn the following day, they went to Guangdao’s house to inquire about it.
His mother, Lady Liu, had also dreamed the previous evening that Master An requested lodging for the night. On that very day, a son was indeed born to him. He was then... (punched).
His right thumb appeared unable to extend; he merely blinked his eyes but did not smile. The following day, two fellow monks, Fuguang and Fuqian, heard of this and came to visit.
Upon seeing him, they called out, "Brother An, are you well? Heng gazed at them intently and raised his hand.
He extended his fingers and smiled. His mother once lay him in the room;

when there was the sound of someone reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, as soon as he awoke, he would either take up a Buddhist scripture or a cup of wine to test him. Ultimately, he took the sutra scroll.
He never consumed meat or blood, and seeing monks, he would joyfully follow them. Travelers all called him "Master An of the Mountain," and thus the village of Mangshan was named after him.
A stele was erected at his teacher’s site to record these marvels. At the age of seven, he left the household life and received the tonsure under Master Won of Chonggak Temple in the prefecture.
At thirteen, he received the full precepts. When he met Master Mugwa, the latter prophesied of him:
"This boy shall one day sit upon the seat of enlightenment and surely lead ten thousand monks. At fifteen, he traveled abroad and opened the Pujo Temple in Zhengzhou.
The assembly was so magnificent that [Dahui] carried his staff from Bianjing to join them. That night, Master Bao dreamed of auspicious clouds like golden lotuses falling in profusion.
He said to the assembly, "I have had no dreams for ten years; now that I have this, what omen is it? The following day, Dahui arrived.
Bao alone treated him with extraordinary distinction. Dahui visited and questioned him morning and evening, and Bao also prodded and challenged him with great intensity.

One day he went to Suiyang. Suddenly, while on horseback, he recalled the circumstances of striking the bamboo; his state of doubt did not dissipate, and he entered as it were into a meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Upon reaching the river crossing, he was entirely without awareness. His companion Deman called out, "This is the river crossing!
Heng was startled, immediately dismounted, and was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. When he returned, he told Master Baoyun of this with tears. Baoyun said, "This is a 'stiff person'."
"Hear me! You must revive once more; only when you move will you succeed. Have you ever looked at the public case (gong'an) of Fudo Nyorai? He replied, "I have been able to recite it since childhood.
Master Bao laughed and said, "I only teach you to investigate the Chan that has been dropped by those of all quarters.

Just continue your investigation; there will naturally be a place where you gain strength. One day, while Heng was sitting quietly in the Cloud Hall, he suddenly heard the sound of the wooden board being struck.

Suddenly he attained realization and presented this verse: "The face of the sun, the face of the moon, A shooting star, a flash of lightning— If you hesitate even longer, An arrow will strike you right before your eyes.
*Du!* (Hark! Master Baogong said, "I cannot deceive you. Later, the Master appeared in the world and presided over five monastic seats:
the Precept Platform at Mount Song, Yunmen at Mount Shao, Puzhao at Zhengzhou, and Linji... [text ends].
The Great Awakened One of the Creek, the Dharma King of Mount Song, was subsequently invited by the Chancellor of the Jin Dynasty, Jiayug Qingchen,
to preside over Tanzhe in the Central Capital and later moved to Puzhao in Jizhou. Not long after, amidst the thickets behind the abbot’s quarters,
there suddenly appeared a solitary tree standing some ten feet high, upon which flocks of crows came in succession to nest, their formation resembling a stupa from top to bottom.

At the twelfth level, the multitude congratulated him, saying, "The Master’s Buddha-dharma is flourishing more than ever! Less than ten days later, an imperial edict appointed him as the abbot of Qingshou Monastery;
his followers regularly numbered ten thousand. After three years, he succeeded to the leadership of Shaolin, where the Dharma assembly flourished greatly.

Before long, the Master withdrew and wandered among the peaks of Songshan and Shaozhou. Sometimes he would sing aloud, sometimes he would let out long, resonant whistles. He remained thus for several years. One day—
One day, he suddenly felt that the four great elements were slackening. He closed his door and sat steadfastly, declining all visitors.
On the tenth day of the seventh month of the Jinxingding Jimao year (1219), he instructed his assembly, saying, "Each of you must diligently cultivate yourselves.

He then requested a bath, recited a verse, and passed away while sitting upright at the age of seventy. He had spent fifty-eight summer retreats in meditation. After his cremation, the śarīra relics were beyond counting. The Master himself—
In his childhood, a round pearl appeared, protruding from the skin on his forehead; at this point, it suddenly burst forth and flew away.
His disciples divided the relics and enshrined them in stupas.
Shi Fazhong, whose style name was Muan, was the son of the Yao family of Siming. At nineteen, he underwent the scriptural examination and received ordination.

He studied the Tiantai teachings and attained realization of the principle of the three contemplations within one mind. Later, he went to Longmen, where he gained further insight by observing the rotation of a water mill.
Zhong composed a verse and presented it to Foyan, saying: "The Great Dharma Wheel is turned; it envelops all before one's eyes.

If one asks further how it is, it is like water pushing a stone across a grindstone. Foyan asked, "What is the matter within it? Zhong replied, "The water flows ever longer through the mountain stream.
Foyan said, "I have a final phrase to entrust to you. Zhong immediately covered his ears and departed. Later, he went to Mount Lu.
At Tong’an, he sat in pure meditation for a long time within a withered tree, abstaining from food. During the Xuānhuá era, there was a great drought in Xiāngtán;

when prayers were offered without response, Zhōng leaped into the Dragon Abyss and cried out, "You wretched beast! It shall rain one chi! and the rain arrived immediately. He once resided at Mount Nányuè.
Whenever he rode a tiger out for excursions, both Confucians and Buddhists would bow upon seeing the dust raised by his chariot. Entering the hall, he said:

"I have a single phrase that does not borrow the mouths of the various sages, nor does it move my own tongue. It is neither sound, breath, nor respiration; it is neither emotional consciousness nor conceptual discrimination.
Even if Vimalakīrti had remained silent in Vaiśālī and Śākyamuni had confined himself in his room at Magadha, it would still be much like covering one's ears while stealing a bell. Unfinished.

This is to prevent the leakage of the celestial mechanism. Even if you were to employ Deshan’s staff or Linji’s shout, if you approach the gate of Master Muguan, you will receive nothing but a single wedge.
Though there are a thousand kinds of words and ten thousand ways of speaking, they all simply aim to cause you to rest within yourself.
Let the great earth and empty space be as they are—seven hollows and eight protrusions; it matters not.
Shi Daowu, styled Fuguang, was the son of the Guan family from Lanzhou in Shaanxi. From birth, his teeth and hair grew fully formed, and he possessed the marks of a great man.
At the age of sixteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life; however, his parents would not permit it, so he fasted until he was nearly dead.
He then left home to enter a temple in the village and shaved his head. After two years had passed, he happened to stay overnight at a shop in Wanzi, Lintao.
He dreamed of a monk who called out to him with a resonant voice; upon waking, he suddenly heard the sound of horses neighing. He attained a sudden, great enlightenment and was overcome with joy.
Returning home, he told his mother, "I picked up something on the road. His mother asked what it was, and the Master replied, "That which has not been seen since beginningless time."
He then took his leave, intending to travel to various regions to seek instruction. His mother asked, "Where will you go? He replied, "Water must flow to the sea;
a crane emerges from atop the white clouds. Previously, at Mount Xiong’er, there was the Chan Master Baoyun Hai; although he resided at an ancient monastery, [he was highly regarded].
He did not keep a single disciple. When someone entered and asked why he did not select a Dharma heir to carry on his lineage, Hai replied, "The *zhilan* (orchids) have blossomed in splendor;
they emerge uniquely from Western Qin. The visitor asked, "When will you arrive? Hai replied, "My journey is finished; the Master is approaching with his bundle over his shoulder.
Hai then ordered his attendant to strike the bell to assemble the congregation, saying, "A disciple from Guansi is coming. Now, this temple was originally...
It was founded by Guo Ziyi. Now, Qu Lai serves as the abbot; you should go to welcome him.

Just as the Master was entering the gate, Hai saw him from afar and said, "Why have you come so late, Minister? The Master stepped forward and replied, "Yes. Hai laughed heartily and eventually bestowed upon him the dharma-garment and the transmission of the Dharma, commanding him to succeed to the seat.
Hai himself then withdrew into seclusion beside the temple. Previously, a band of robbers had been plundering and looting there, oppressing the local people.
They suffered harm from him, and some requested that he be captured by sea. Hai said, "This is not within the old monk's power.

Before long, Lord Guo will arrive; he will surely capture him himself. The people did not understand his meaning. Later, three days after the Master had taken up residence at the temple, he led the assembly to go and seize him.
They bound him completely and broke into his den. Just as they were about to execute him all, the bandits piteously begged for their lives. The Master spoke to them with composure:
The Master said, "You have plundered wealth and taken human life; by right, you deserve death. Now that you beg for your life, do you not consider the lives of those others?
The bandit bowed his head until blood flowed, vowing to follow the Triple Gem and pledging never again to commit evil. The Master recited a verse for him, shaved his hair, and released him.
From then on, for several decades, people did not pick up lost items along the road; only then did they believe that the Master was truly Guo.

He was the reincarnation of Master Linggong. In the twenty-fourth year of the Dading era of the Song dynasty, after Master Hai had passed away, the Master first emerged to take charge of Puzhao Monastery in Zhengzhou, and later moved to Zhuge Hermitage in Sanxiang.
Clad in white robes and riding a yellow calf while blowing a short flute, he roamed through Luoyang.
He once said: "If you call me an ordinary person, I have come from the rank of the sages; if you call me a sage..."

"Indeed. Furthermore, when one was still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), did you not say that you were neither ordinary nor holy? Yet now, atop the crown of Vairocana, there is yet another place of practice.
In the fifth year of the Taihe era, he entered the summer retreat at Dashi Temple in Lintao and expounded the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

He addressed the assembly, saying, "This session is nearly over; I shall now depart. On the evening of the twelfth day of the fifth month, he gave a small-scale sermon (xiaochan) for the assembly, discoursing upon the primary truth (paramārtha).
Rising at dawn, he called to his attendant monk, saying, "I am ill and shall go to seek medicine.

Just as the attendant was about to step out the door, the Master had already passed away. Above him were auspicious clouds of five colors, swirling and coiling like a canopy, with a crimson radiance like the sun that filled the sky.
It filled the four quarters and did not dissipate for three days. His worldly lifespan was fifty-five years, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was thirty-nine.
His disciples enshrined his entire body and erected a stupa over it.
Shi Zhenjing, whose style name was Ruan, was the son of the Yao family of Huating in Yunjian. His mother, Lady Zhu, dreamed that a moon rose from the sea and fell into her lap;
upon waking, she became pregnant. At the time of his birth, auspicious light filled the room, and a strange monk passed by.
The Master pointed and said to his mother, "This child is the reincarnation of the Dharma Master Haiyue.
At the age of nine, he relied upon the Dharma Master Mingjingzhi of Huacheng Temple; having heard the *Lotus Sūtra* but once, he could recite it from memory. At sixteen, he received full ordination.

He extensively investigated all the vehicles (*yāna*), and as his innate wisdom suddenly blossomed, he considered himself a master of the study of nature (*xingxue*). He first visited Yungongze of Guangfu Temple in Hangzhou.
When Gong heard that Dharma Master Wujidu’s reputation for transformation was greatly resounding, he went to his quarters and mastered all of his teachings.

Later, when Yuan Dade resided at Dezang Temple in Haiyan, the temple was on the verge of collapse; Jing exerted all his strength to support and rebuild it, and the scattered congregation was reunited once more.
The temple lands had been seized by powerful families; [the Master] returned them, and within a few years, they were restored to their former state.

In the Zhìzhì era, he moved to Chāoguó Temple in Sōngjiāng. In the Yǎndìng year of Yǐchǒu, the late Prime Minister Wǎnhuān appointed him to reside at Xiàzhú. He lived there for seven years, never tiring of his lectures.
He cleared the path in front of the temple and enlarged its gate, inscribing "Buddha-land Mountain" (Fógùoshān) upon it to mark it. Upon his arrival...
In the year of Xunxinwei, Master Cheng of Zhantang at Upper Zhu Mountain announced his retirement due to old age and nominated Jing to succeed him.

Previously, while Jing was sleeping during the day due to illness, he dreamed of the Great Being dressed in white, who held a golden pitcher of water and poured it into his mouth, saying: "Do not worry."
"It will heal naturally before long. When asked about future fortunes and misfortunes, he indicated, "In two years' time, you should seek seclusion beneath a great tree.
His illness subsequently recovered. [Daosheng] deeply suspected that seeking seclusion under a tree was an omen for his entry into *parinirvāṇa*.
Later, when Fotudeng proposed residing at Upper Zhucheng, Daosheng went to see him and saw a large tree to the west of the main hall; the hall was inscribed with the name "Qing" (Tranquility).
While residing there, he finally realized what his dream had indicated. Thereupon, he devoted his heart to propagating the Dharma, and his students constantly numbered in the thousands.
The Emperor Yuan admired his Way and bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-Mind Great Eloquence" (Fuxin Hongbian), as well as a purple *kāṣāya* robe with golden embroidery.
Not long after, he manifested illness; he wrote a verse and passed away. He had lived for seventy-two years and spent fifty-six summer retreats in meditation. His body was cremated.
He obtained a tongue-root and a cranial bone that remained undecayed, as well as relics of five colors.
Shi Hongji, whose courtesy name was Tongzhou and alternative style name Tian'an, was a native of Yuyao in Yue. His surname was Yao.

Having lost his father at an early age, he left home to become a monk under the Venerable Shuntian Man of Baoji Temple in his hometown. Even in his childhood, his brilliant talents were peerless; Man bestowed [the precepts upon him].
He committed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to memory. At the age of sixteen, he upheld the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, never daring to transgress its rules even by the width of a single step.

Later, he sighed, saying, "While the precepts must certainly not be neglected, can the thorough study of the doctrinal vehicles (*śāsana-yāna*), which provide support for practice and understanding, be postponed?
Thereupon, he went to Ningbo to rely upon Master Quan of Bāngshān and studied the Tiantai teachings for a long time.
He thoroughly mastered their essential meanings. He once practiced the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the Pure Land sutras.
One day, while in meditative concentration, he had a vision of the Venerable Siming, who bestowed upon him a rhinoceros-horn ruyi scepter. From that time on, his eloquence overflowed daily.

If a river flows from a spring or gushes forth from a height, it passes through without the slightest obstruction. In the first year of the Yuantai Ding era, he appeared in the world and resided at Wanshou Yuanjue Temple.
The following year, the coastal embankments of Yanguan were destroyed; the local residents were filled with trepidation day and night, fearing they would become the abode of fish and turtles.

The former Chancellor Tuo-huan was deeply concerned about this. He then prayed to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara at Upper Zhushan and commanded Jieji to go to the seashore to establish a great *shuilu* (water and land) vegetarian feast.
Entering the *samādhi* of compassionate heart, he took sand from the sea and recited the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī, leading the assembly to scatter it everywhere across that area.
Wherever his footsteps reached, the shoreline was restored to its firm state; people marveled at this as a divine miracle.

The imperial calendar shifted, and at the two temples Qingxian and Cixiang, which were situated in a period of famine, he withdrew to a separate chamber. The people of Suzhou invited the Great Virtue (Dade) to restore Wanshou Temple;
after six years of winter and summer, the temple was completed. In the fifth year of the Zhizheng era, the Xuanzheng Yuan requested him to preside over Yuantong Temple in Kuaiji.
After residing there for four years, he returned to Baoji. In the seventh year, the Yuan Emperor issued an edict commanding him to preside over [the temple].
At Pufu Monastery in Hangzhou, Jijian lay prostrate and did not rise; he wrote a verse and passed away. He had lived for eighty-six years and had observed seventy-one summer retreats.
Seven days later, his countenance remained as if alive. The assembly interred him in a ceramic vessel at Songhua Wu on Mount Emei within the village.
Shi Mengrun, style name Yugang, was a native of Haiyan in Jiahe. His surname was Gu; his father, Min, was a recluse and scholar.
His mother was Lady Sun, the niece of the Dharma Master Guyuanqing. During both her pregnancy and his birth, they were each moved by extraordinary dreams.

When Mengrun was fourteen years old, he followed Guyuan to Bailian Monastery in the prefecture. Just as he was about to pay homage to the deity of the monastery, the earthen statues all toppled over. One...
The assembly was struck with wonder and amazement. Guoyuan commanded that he follow Master Xiang to tonsure his head and receive full ordination.
Guoyuan bestowed upon him the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the *Jingangbi*, the *Shierbufamen*, and other texts; [Zhixu] was immediately able to comprehend their general meaning.
When Guoyuan passed away, he served Master Chuan of Zhutang. Due to his arduous studies, he contracted a strange illness; he then practiced the *Qing Guanyin Chan* for seven seven-day periods.

Having obtained this spiritual response, his illness was cured and his mind became doubly clear and sharp. When Master Cheng of Zhantang came to preside over Nan Zhu, Zhirun served as the first seat attendant (*upasthāyaka*).
Before long, he entered the world to serve as abbot at Dezang Monastery in Danghu, Haiyan, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* during the summer retreat.

The assembly constantly numbered in the thousands; even butchers and wine-sellers changed their vocations [to join him]. He moved to Yanfu Temple, where his spiritual influence flourished even further.
In the sixth year, he retired from monastic affairs and lived in seclusion at the White Lotus Hermitage on Fenghuang Ridge by Longjing Lake, as the Lower Zhihuasi was then suffering from a disaster.
Only the Fuxian Hall remained towering amidst thorns and rubble. He sighed with emotion and said to the assembly, "This temple was established through the grace of Ciyun;
that this hall still stands is due to the power of the Patriarch’s vows. Thereupon, he renovated it step by step and restored it to newness.
Morning and evening, he expounded the teachings without weariness and led the assembly in the practice of the Lotus Samādhi, thereby invoking the manifestation of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

The Venerable Fangguang manifested various auspicious signs while residing at Sanji. One day, he summoned his disciples Shiming, Cei, and others, and instructed them on the principles of calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) for settling the mind.
Having done so, he declared, "My karmic conditions for this life are nearly exhausted;
now is the time. He then recited the name of the Buddha several hundred times and passed away in serene stillness.

Shi Weizhe, whose courtesy name was Tianzhen, was surnamed Fei and was a native of Wuxing. His father was Junze and his mother was Lady Shen. She dreamed of a strange monk begging for alms; upon waking, she conceived.
When he was born, a wondrous fragrance permeated the air. After his father passed away, he followed his mother to Qinchuan and Gushang.
From his childhood, he resolved to leave the household life and took Master Gaolin Shou of Youfu Monastery in his home prefecture as his preceptor. At ten [years of age]...

At the age of six, he received full ordination. At twenty-three, he first visited Master Chushi Qi, followed by visits to Masters Qianyan Chang, Wujian Du, and Wuyong Kuan—eighteen masters in total—with whom his karmic conditions were not yet harmonious.
Later, he went to Mount Kuanglu, where he heard of Master Wuji Yuan, the son of Chan Master Xueyan Qin; the master was already one hundred years old and sat in solitary meditation.
At the Reed Hermitage, [Fayan] remained silent all day long. The Master went directly to him and happened upon Yuan on the latrine.

He hurried forward and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Yuan seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! At these words, the Master was suddenly and completely enlightened.
He merely shook his hand. Yuan said, "Have you attained anything? The Master replied quickly, "What is there to attain?

Yuan asked again, "Are you engaging in intellectual reasoning? The Master brushed out his sleeves and departed. From that time on, his spiritual eloquence surged like a vast tide, possessing a sharp edge that could not be encountered.
He served Yuan diligently for over a month, and his realization grew increasingly profound and mysterious; those from all quarters who heard of this were filled with awe.
He served [the master]. Master Lin Shan of Lingyin invited him to take charge of the treasury keys.

Later, the assembly requested that he open the Dharma at Haomen Youfu Chan Monastery, where he was surrounded by a thousand followers. As he addressed the assembly, he said: "The fish blows the waves; the kite raises the wind."
The crowing of the cock and the barking of the dog differ; merely attaining realization at this point is not yet sufficient. Looking up and down, one is shrouded by a thousand layers of black clouds.
If you wish to penetrate through, apply yourself with urgency. Be careful not to rely on intellectual understanding; you must polish and refine yourself.

It was not without having long established an unchanging resolve that a single shout could deafen one for three days. The manifestation of dynamic function is inexhaustible; when the iron wall and silver mountain are struck with a single blow—
Penetrating. Capturing alive and seizing the living without leaving a trace; swallowing and spitting out, shifting and interchanging—this is called the Great Hero.

If one passes by the river on an autumn wind, the reeds will surely be white and the smartweeds surely red. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, eminent monks from all under heaven were summoned to the capital; the Master’s name was listed at the head of the list.
Suddenly, due to an ailment of his feet, he returned to the sea. He transformed wood to build a Chan monastery; spirits transported it and ghosts carried it—the wood [arrived].
He emerged from the well. At that time, a great drought had occurred, and the salt shipments bound for Jiaxing were blocked because the river had run dry.

The Prefectural Governor of the region, having heard the Master’s reputation, went specifically to Sichuan to pray for rain. The Master told the Governor to prepare his seat on a boat and return home.

He immediately wrote a small wooden spoon, gave it to a young boy, and instructed him to go out through the eastern gate of the city of Sichuan and cast it into the sea. He then charged the boy with the task.
The son finally returned home, not once turning his head to look back. This youth had not yet reached the city when a great rain poured down like a torrent, opening up all the river paths.
The Great Honored One, riding upon a swan-shaped boat, returned.
Shizuzu was styled Huanyi. A native of Dantu, his surname was Yang and his mother was Lady Zhu.
She dreamed that a *brahmacārin* entered her chamber, and upon waking, she gave birth to the Master. From his youth, he was profound and reserved, taking delight in performing Buddhist rites.

At the age of thirteen, his parents sent him to Longpan Mountain to rely upon the Venerable Chaoyang, where he received the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other major Mahāyāna scriptures. At seventeen, he underwent the tonsure and received the precepts. At twenty...

At nine, he received full ordination. He thoroughly mastered the great meaning of the various sutras and considered that what his consciousness relied upon was not related to the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Consequently, he traveled with a staff to Mount Shaoshi, where he relied upon Master Dazhang for five years. Later, he went to Mount Funiu and relied upon Master Ga'ang for twelve summer retreats.
What he subsequently attained was certified by both masters. Thereafter, he traveled to the capital to pay his respects to the two Dharma Masters Song and Xiu.

He fully attained the essential purport of the *Qingliang* (Pure Cool) school. Hu Geshi of Huai'an invited him to reside at Bocishan, where he oversaw the production of the Tripitaka and the holding of a *shuilu wuzhe* assembly.
He then traveled to Nanjing to visit Master Wuji, serving as his second seat attendant (*duwei*).

During intervals between the striking of the *gan-dai*, he would immediately join the assembly in manual labor. Upon completion of these tasks, he went to Wanshousi Temple in Jingkou to expound the *Huayan dacao*.
Upon reaching the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*), the earth shook and the heavens rained down ambrosial jeweled flowers.

At that time, Wujie led his followers to join him, as did Miaofeng Chengyin and two other Chan monks from the second dhyāna. From then on, the reputation of his Way flourished and the monastic communities venerated him.
He tirelessly exhorted and guided others, and wherever he went, they established precious monasteries. The Master expounded the forty-eight...
Vow. At that time, there was a strange man with a white crown upon his head and four snake-like legs who came to listen to the preaching of the Dharma; suddenly he vanished.
In the Jia-shen year of the Wanli era, [the Master] rested his staff at the foot of Lotus Peak in Suzhou and built a hermitage to dwell there.
In the ninth month of the Ding-hai year, he suddenly manifested illness. On the twenty-second day, rising in the morning, he bathed, sat in the full lotus posture, and spoke this verse: "The void..."
"Faceless and formless; where there is no position, one forcibly arranges it. The 'head-word' is not a head-word; everywhere is the Tathāgata. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
A strange fragrance lingered for a long time without dispersing. His body was cremated, his remains were collected, and they were enshrined in a stupa on the northern slope of Lotus Peak.
He was sixty-six years old [in secular age] and fifty-four years of ordination seniority. King Shi Zhen composed an inscription for him.
The monk Mingde was styled Yueting; because he succeeded the Chan Master Wansong Lin as his dharma heir, he was also known as Qiansong.
He was the son of the Zhou family of Wucheng in Huzhou. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted and clearly distinguished from the ordinary.

While still a child with hair tied in a topknot, he accompanied his father to the Xizi Monastery. Thereupon, pointing to a painting of Arhats on the wall, he asked his father, "Are these monks or laypeople?"
His father said, "He is a monk. He sighed with resolve and said, "I wish to become one such as this.
At the age of thirteen, he entered the Ssangrim Gyeongseon Hermitage in his district and studied the Yoga teachings under the monk Jinhyang. After four years, he received the tonsure;

hearing that there were matters of the "Ultimate Direction," he first went to consult Master Baechan Haegong, but they did not reach accord. Consequently, clad only in a single robe and straw sandals, he traveled extensively among the monastic assemblies.
Having undergone many hardships, he reflected that his karmic affinity for Prajñā was thin and intended to travel to India.

He prayed with deep sincerity to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara to encounter an enlightened teacher. On his way through Central India, he heard of Wansong preaching the Dharma and went first to pay his respects.
Wansong asked, "Virtuous One, where have you come from? What do you seek? He replied, "I wish to knock at the Universal Gate (Pumen) and seek a worthy guide. Wansong—
[Song] held up one finger and said, "Go now and pay respects to the Great Being (Mahāsattva); then come back and see me. The Master was moved to tears;

he prostrated twice and sought a resolution regarding the great matter of birth and death. Song said, "If you wish to escape birth and death, you must know that birth and death are without attachment before you can succeed.

Upon hearing this, the Master was bewildered. He then received the full precepts (*upasampadā*). From then on, he attended him morning and evening, knocking at his door for instruction, yet after a long time he made no progress. Song did not...
Having received [the transmission], he was granted the essential principles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent effort to his studies until he reached the passage:

"How is it that from this state of pure essence, suddenly mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise? At that moment, it was as if clouds had dispersed across the vast sky and the cold moon shone alone in its brilliance.
He then composed a verse and presented it, saying: "Within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* there is no sūtra; Facing one another, why need one ask for names? The sixth month..."
"The blazing heavens are as hot as fire; the cold of midwinter is like ice.

Panshan nodded his head and instructed him, saying, "Since you have already awakened to the teachings of the scriptures, there shall be none in the lecture halls of Jiangnan who surpasses you in days to come. By means of this, you may clarify the great matter that lies beyond."
While residing at Mount Jing, the Master served the community by carrying rice and gathering firewood, never shrinking from toil or hardship.
Once, while walking among the forest foothills, he encountered a tiger crouching in the path; the Master planted his staff firmly before it, and the tiger fled.

He frequently studied the *Zaopo He Lun* (The Combined Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), and upon reaching the "Ten Stages" chapter, he sat leaning on his armrest in the middle of the night and dreamed that he traveled to the world of Tūla-cotton silk, where he ascended a throne to expound the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Regarding the profound purport [of the teachings], when it came to the conclusion of the assembly and the recitation of the verses, Wubai said to Song, "This is the subtle influence of the power of the Sage.
Not only will my Way be propagated, but the Qingliang school shall also flourish greatly. Before long, Song passed away.
The Master stayed at the stupa for three years. Hearing of the flourishing reputation of Dharma Master Fohui of Qiyuan Monastery, he donned a bamboo hat and went to join him.
Qiyuan also silently recognized his worth and held him in high esteem. His disciple Shaquan, however, was quite conceited and did not rely on the Master’s name.
The Master then hung up his staff to inform Baixian of his arrival at the temple. Baixian and Fohui were but a few feet apart;

thus, in the morning the Master would carry his bowl for alms, at noon he would attend the lectures, and in the evening he would discuss the essential meanings with more than ten fellow practitioners.

Consequently, the assembly grew larger day by day until the offerings from the *Gandhakuṭī* could no longer sustain them. The Master secretly prayed to the deity of the monastery, saying: "If I and the holy teachings..."
There was a karmic connection. Shenqiu was generous and protected him. After some time, a non-Buddhist practitioner came from the clouds and offered one hundred *shi* of rice.

From then on, the rewards for his former deeds surpassed even those of the Buddha’s wisdom. On the day he opened the hall, Zhiyuan ordered an attendant monk to present him with a robe and a fly-whisk;
the Master declined and returned them. He offered a fragrant incense stick for Wan-song to present. Subsequently, he returned once more as a solitary figure.
At Mount Jing’s Lingxiao Peak, because the obstruction in his breast remained unbroken, he again applied himself to intensive study for three years.

One night, during the first watch, as he sat in meditation, his mind and the object of contemplation suddenly merged in a state of vast clarity; his doubts and stagnations were dissolved like melting ice. He then leaped up and uttered this verse:

"A thousand years of emerald bamboo, ten thousand years of pine— Leaf by leaf, branch by branch, it is the ancestral wind. Amidst clouds and peaks, on high crags, is the place of seclusion and concealment; It is wordless."
The bright sun shines equally upon all. He hurried to pay homage at the Wansong Pagoda and said, "This old man has not deceived me.
From then on, his reputation for the Way flourished even more; students flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel, and invitations arrived from all quarters without a single idle day passing.

When he opened the hall at Lingyin Monastery, his demeanor was so stern and majestic that unruly monks such as Chekong and Tianran could only glare at him from afar, not daring to approach, ultimately remaining unable to fathom him.

The matter was falsely accused against the Master; before the day was over, the truth was made clear. The Master sat in meditation as the false accusation was laid upon him and then fled. Twenty members of his faction were flogged to death.
The Master traveled south to Mount Chicheng (Chìchéng), where those who converted from among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) were beyond counting.

That the teachings of the Dharma-vehicle reached the Tai prefecture was indeed due to the Master’s initiative. He expounded the profound discourses at Dazhong Hermitage (*Dàzhōng Ān*); after three days, a fire broke out at the hermitage, and only the Master’s staff remained unharmed.

The chamber remained majestic and undamaged. While he was lecturing on the *Commentary and Sub-commentary to the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* at Fahai Temple, white lotus flowers grew from the ground and purple *zhī* fungi sprouted from the latrine.
Layman Wutai consequently inscribed the name of his hall as "Tonglian" (Pervasive Lotus). While the Master resided at Dongchan Temple, he dreamed one night that Mañjuśrī emerged riding a lion;
the Master then left the lion behind, who ascended into the air and departed. The lion suddenly transformed into a youth, whom the Master [consequently...].
The Master asked, "Just now you were a lion; are you now a child? Try opening your mouth. The child opened his cheeks, and his mouth was as red as vermilion.
The Master patted his back and said, "You are still a lion. The child asked, "How about your mouth, Master? The Master opened his mouth to show it to him. The child leaped in and was swallowed.
Startled awake, the Master broke into a sweat and said with joy, "Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom is within my belly!"
Before several months had passed, Lord Lu of Wutai led a multitude to command him to lecture on the *Huayan dacao*. His assembly regularly numbered in the thousands.
Master Jue of Miaofeng was a入室 (入室) disciple [of Zhiyuan]; he followed the lineage of Siming from afar and propagated the Way of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations.

Because the Master [Zhiyi] had expounded the teachings of Xianshou (Fazang) but was not yet familiar with those of Tiantai and Jingxi (Zhiyi), he questioned [Yanshou] regarding the meaning of the "six stages of realization" (*liujì*). The Master said:

"The six stages of realization in the Tiantai school concern the distinction between the delusion and enlightenment of the practitioner. For example, when I am at the stage of 'name' (*míngzì*), all ten realms are merely names;
when I realize the ultimate (*jiùjìng*), all ten realms are the ultimate. If I were a dung beetle (*quēqiāng*), then all ten realms would be dung beetles."
It is the *qiāng* (dung beetle); it is not that there is something else above the *qǐqiāng*. There are six "stages" (*jí*). Jué said: "This is not so.

Tiantai’s 'six stages' do not distinguish between the mundane and the supramundane, nor between sentient and insentient beings; every single thing possesses them. Take any single phenomenon, and the six stages are present therein."

"Why must you judge their superiority or inferiority based on my own states of delusion and enlightenment? The Master said: "The Sage established the teachings truly as a means to draw those lost on the path toward awakening.

If you say that 'whenever one dharma is mentioned, the six are already present therein,' this is merely speaking of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and results in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Of what use is this to the student? Let us set aside the previous five 'inclusions' for now. As for what you call 'ultimate,' it is a single ultimate..."
When it is complete, all things are ultimately perfected. It is like gold extracted from ore, or like a jade disc separated from its raw matrix.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he observed that all sentient beings within the nine realms simultaneously become Buddhas.

Not only are the primary retributions (the bodies) of the nine realms entirely Vairocana, but the secondary environments (the lands) of the nine realms are none other than the Land of Tranquil Light. Thus, he exclaimed: "How marvelous!"
Sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts that they do not realize this for themselves.

Is this not to say that because I have attained Buddhahood, I perceive them all as having attained Buddhahood? If it were truly as your words suggest, then even the most lowly dung beetle would never have a day of attaining Buddhahood.
If not a single sentient being among them were to give rise to the Bodhicitta—what is called the "Ten... [is left incomplete].
The Dharma-realm is, in its entirety, a single piece of solid, unperforated iron.

If one says that even a dung beetle can ultimately attain Buddhahood, on what day could the Tathāgata ever again fall into delusion and become a sentient being? To mistake gold for ore—what loss could be greater? Jue said:

"Ultimately, the dung beetle is not what is being discussed. Because its mind-body is fundamentally complete, it is said that when the principle is identical to the phenomenal form, one is then called 'ultimate.
If this is so for one realm, it is likewise for all realms. When considered within a single realm, the six stages of identity are naturally present.
Why must you trouble yourself with the question of whether it has become a Buddha or not? The Master laughed and said, "You go and become one."
He was truly a thoroughbred *gongqiáng* (dung beetle). Those who heard him did not fail to hold his discourse in high esteem.

In the autumn of the Dinghai year of the Wanli era, he informed the assembly that he was ill and repeatedly instructed them on matters concerning the teachings of the Buddha. On the second day after the full moon of the first month the following year, he passed away in auspicious circumstances.
He was fifty-eight years of age and had been a monk for forty-six years. His body was cremated and his stupa enshrined at Mount Jing.
Shi Wuyi was originally a son of the Sha family from Shucheng. From birth, he wore lay clothing with double folds; meat and wine never entered his mouth.
At sixteen, he traveled to Jinling to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*, whereupon he sighed, saying, "The pursuit lies within myself;

how can I merely follow the words and chase the phrases? He then paid homage at Mount Wutai, where he received the tonsure from Tong of Jing’an. Subsequently, he visited Shouchang, though their exchange of words did not reach a point of resonance.
Qi entered Min Province. One day, while reading the kōan concerning Zhaozhou’s “If there is a Buddha, do not dwell upon it,” he had an awakening. He visited Chang again.
Chang asked him, “Ants know how to scurry toward places of rot; flies tend to fly toward what is foul. Is this your own business?”
The Master said, "The matter of the borderlands. Chang scolded him, saying, "There are many who will laugh at you.
One day, while using the toilet, the Master saw a man climbing a tree and attained great enlightenment. He hurried to see Chang. Chang asked, "How have you been doing lately?
The Master said, "I have found a way to live, but I simply do not permit others to know it. Chang asked, "Why do you not permit others to know it? The Master said, "Because..."
When Chang asked, "I know that you do not know," the old woman burned the hermitage and drove the monk away. The Master said, "The gold has been made even more brilliant.
He then cited the public case where a monk asked Xuanze, "The dragon roars and the mist rises; the tiger roars and the wind is born," and commanded [the assembly] to compose a verse on it.
The Master’s verse says: "Killing and bringing to life, each vies for mastery with its own marvels; How could the dim-sighted eyes of the common flesh perceive them?"
"Understood. He emitted light, yet his intent did not follow the flow of time; the spring breeze of old still pursued the horse's hooves.
Chang laughed and said, "Only today do you finally believe that I have not deceived you. In the thirtieth year of the Wanli era, while residing at Boshan, he said:
"This matter is not attained through meritorious deeds, nor through cultivation and realization, nor through conceptual thought, nor through learning and inquiry."
It is attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). There is a class of people who shut their doors to practice;

they bring the mind to rest in the darkness, refining their own body and mind until it is like withered wood or cold ashes. They remain unaware even as insects gnaw at their clothes, nor do they notice the spiders weaving webs.

Even if one remains in meditative concentration for a hundred years, in the end it is like being a single dead person; regarding the matter of one’s own fundamental nature, there is no engagement at all.

Thus Xuan Sha said: "Even if it were like the moon's reflection in a clear pool or the sound of a bell in a still night—remaining unimpaired by whatever strikes it and not dispersing when touching the waves—this is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. A practitioner of the Way..."
It is like fire melting ice; once the arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return. One must take the measure within clarity:
at the street of flowers and willows, one seizes the spring colors of the nine avenues; on the banks of the lotuses, one brings back the autumn winds from all eight directions.
Application is without deficiency, and one acts with freedom according to conditions. But tell me, how is it that this is the place where Boshan walks?
After a long silence, he said: "I have only this pair of hands of a pauper; I have never lightly bowed to those who are merely ordinary people.

Furthermore, although Bozan and you all travel the same path, you do not reach the same destination. You all come from within the position of correctness (*samyaktva*), whereas Bozan does not abide in the position of correctness.
You all are within Bozan’s whisk-broom. You all come from within the position of partiality, whereas Bozan does not."
In this state of partiality, the whisk (fly-whisk) is permitted among the robes of all people. Therefore it is said: "Face to face, they do not recognize one another;
yet from a thousand miles away, their winds are the same. If you penetrate this point thoroughly, you will know your home immediately, leaving no trace behind.
Thus, our Great Master Śākyamuni, for the sake of courageous sentient beings, attained Buddhahood in a single thought-moment; for the sake of indolent beings...
"Birth. Attaining the fruit after a full *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. 'Broad Mountain'—even such a saying is still a tangle. All you people must cut it off before you can proceed.
But tell me, after it has been cut off, how do you conduct yourself? He struck the ground with his staff and said:
"If it were not for the woodcutter’s path, how could one reach Ge Hong’s house? In the autumn of the third year of the Chongzhen era, he fell ill. The Head Seat asked him, "Master..."
"How is your honored body? The Master replied, "I have quite a bit of enjoyment. The Seat-holder asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill?
The Master said, "Are you making such a fuss about the heat? The Seat-holder said, "Coming and going is free and easy; please speak one word.
The Master wrote the four characters "Li-li-fen-ming" (Clear and Distinct) and, setting down his brush, sat in passing away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the mountain monastery.
Shi Longqi, style name Yinyuan, was the son of the Lin family of Donglin in Fujian. While his father was working in the fields, his mother was of the Gong clan.

When Longqi was six years old, his father went away to Xiang, and the family’s assets began to dwindle daily. Unable to pursue formal studies, he gradually took up farming and wood-gathering as his livelihood.
Every quiet night, he would sit or lie beneath the pines with two or three friends, gazing upward at the Milky Way’s rotation and the stars.
The moon flows with its radiance; who binds it, and who is its master? Its winding course does not err, yet my heart was greatly startled by this.
Consequently, the thought of longing for the Buddha arose within me. At the age of twenty, my mother and elder brother wished to arrange a betrothal for me.

I reflected to myself: "As a man, I do not know my father's whereabouts. To be in haste over marriage is not filial piety. Thereupon, I informed my mother and brother, intending to use the betrothal funds as travel expenses. I set out directly.
He traveled to Yuzhang and reached Nanjing, eventually arriving at Zhoushan in Ningbo where he visited his paternal cousin.
He then proceeded to Shaoxing, and after a year had passed, his provisions were exhausted. Following a fragrant incense boat to the South Sea, he went to pay homage to Avalokiteśvara.

Beholding the majestic splendor of the Buddha-land, all his mundane thoughts were instantly dissolved like ice melting away. He then resolved to observe the fast and sought ordination under the master of Chaoyin Cave. The following year, in the second month...
In the month of [the lunar calendar], he set sail for Fujian to visit his mother. His mother, believing him to have descended from heaven, was overcome with joy beyond measure.
She exhorted him to observe the fasts and take refuge in the Buddha. The following year, his mother passed away. He met Jianyuan at Yinline Temple, who skillfully guided him;
he subsequently underwent tonsure and immediately made a vow to practice diligently. In the year of Xinyou, he went to Xiansheng Temple in Shaoxing to hear the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At that time, having heard the name of his original teacher, Master Fei, he traveled everywhere in search of him. In the year *Renxu*, he listened to the *Lotus Sūtra* at Yingwo Peak;
during the winter, he was at Biyun on Jia Shi listening to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Suddenly hearing that Master Mi had come to serve as abbot at Jinsu, he went immediately to visit him.
Following this, he asked: "A student who has newly entered the gates of Chan does not yet know how to apply himself to the practice."
He requested instruction. Yunmen said, "I have no work to do here. When I wish to walk, I walk; when I wish to sit, I sit;
when I wish to lie down, I lie down. The Master said, "When there are so many mosquitoes that one cannot lie down, what then?
Yunmen said, "A slap! At this, the Master attained realization. He prostrated and said, "I understand the meaning behind the Master’s palm. Yunmen said:
"Speak further," the Master said. The Teacher then gave a shout. "Speak further," the Master said again. The Teacher gave another shout. "What about after three or four shouts? the Master asked.
The Teacher replied, "This year salt is as precious as rice; from now on, I shall live with constant vitality."
One day, suddenly, as the wind blew in through the window, his hair stood on end and his entire body broke into a cold sweat. He attained great enlightenment to the very source and bottom;

he immediately knew that the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all the old monks of the world—both sentient and insentient beings—are entirely contained within a single hair-tip.
It was perfectly clear and distinct, without duality or distinction, yet it could not be expressed to others. (Gengwu year)
In the spring, the Abbot of Huangbo’s original monastery invited the Old Monk to enter the mountain; the Master returned with him to the temple.
In the year Xinwei, the assembly requested that he reside at Shiziyan. In the winter of Guiyou, Ma Feng invited Master Fei to preside over the seat and appointed the Master as West Hall Head.
One day, various Zen practitioners offered verses on Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu, regarding the occasion when Mazu’s single shout deafened his ears for three days. Huangbo heard of this.
Regarding the circumstances of [Zhaozhou] involuntarily sticking out his tongue, the Master also composed a verse: "A single sound of poisoned lacquer causes all who hear it to perish;
Skulls lie scattered across the wilds, with nowhere to hide. The three-inch tongue extends the state-stabilizing sword; For a thousand autumns, it remains chillingly white as frost.
He presented this to Elder Fei, who immediately circled it and showed it to the assembly. Ascending the seat, he said: "I have a fly-whisk; it is from..."
"It is something that cannot be exhausted by use. The Master said, "How will you uphold it? The monk gave a shout and then departed.
Upon reaching the Abbot’s quarters, he prostrated. The Old Man raised his whisk and said, "Take this and practice with it.

The monk seized it and struck him once with the whisk. The Old Man said, "I thought this was for Baoen [the temple name]. He struck him once more and returned to his quarters. (Recorded in the year Jiashu.)
While dwelling in seclusion at Lion Rock during the summer of the Bingzi year, the Master was invited by his home mountain to succeed to the Dharma seat of Huangbo.
Unable to decline, he sighed that everything—even the flat stones beneath the rock that resembled boats—was uneven.

One night, the Master sat upon a stone and recited the Great Compassion Mantra three times, silently praying to the dragons and devas: "When I depart for Huangbo, may my Way flourish greatly and bring prosperity to this mountain."

"Shi-se (Color/Form). This stone may be leveled. [The Master] sat in silence while incense was offered. Upon returning to his quarters, the attendant Zhaoliao reported, "The stone has already leveled itself by itself.
The Master thereupon named it the "Self-Leveled Stone. At that moment, Fatao arrived as a special envoy, delivering the great robe and the lineage of transmission.
In the second month of winter in the year Dingchou, I arrived at the mountain and ascended the Dharma hall. As on the eighth day of the twelfth month, I said:
"In the past, the World-Honored One ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother. What Dharma did he preach? [Suddenly raising his whisk] It was simply this.
Today, I, this mountain monk, without moving from my fundamental limit, shall speak of Chan for all you elders. What Chan do I speak of? It is also simply this."
This one—what is this one? It is just like an eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall; truly, it is no child’s play.
If you can grasp the message within this very point exactly as it is, I will permit you to enter the gate of Huangbo and see the people of Huangbo.
You will then share the same root and destiny as Huangbo, sharing his vital energy and being joined with him as one branch. Otherwise, you are all merely outside the gate.
To circle the Han River and yet wish to see the fine hairs on Huangbo’s body—this is truly difficult.
*Huagao Seng Yaoyao*, Volume Four (End).
